who.versions_affected: 2018 Update 15 and earlier, 2021 Update 5 and earlier; also affects ColdFusion 2016 and ColdFusion 11, both past end of life with no fix available

what.summary: An improper access control flaw allowing arbitrary code execution was exploited by unidentified actors at a federal agency, and the same flaw affects two older versions of the product that reached end of life and will never receive a fix.

how.logic: The advisory notes the flaw also affects two versions that reached end of life, which means those installations are permanently vulnerable. That is a different remediation conversation from a patch: the options are upgrade, isolate, or replace, and none of them is a maintenance window. Inventory application server versions and separate those with an available fix from those without, because reporting both as unpatched hides which ones can actually be fixed.
how.caveat: Application servers running end-of-life versions usually host an application nobody wants to touch, which is why the version is old. The blocker is the application owner rather than the patching team.

how.logic: Code execution through the application server surfaces as that server process creating a shell or interpreter child. On an application server the legitimate child set is small enough to allow-list.
how.caveat: Some applications shell out for scheduled tasks or reporting. Baseline before enabling.

how.logic: The exploitation was confirmed through analysis of network logs after the fact rather than by an alert at the time. That is the second record in this corpus where retained network data answered the question, and it reinforces retention as the enabling control rather than an archival nicety.
how.caveat: Only works if retention reaches back to before the intrusion began.

what.summary: 18 advisories published by a coordinated disclosure programme against ALGO 8180 IP Audio Alerter, none of them present in the catalogue of vulnerabilities known to have been exploited. The programme states where in the product each flaw sits, which the vulnerability database does not: web-based user interface (10); API interface (1); SCI module (1). 10 of the 18 advisories sit in one component, web-based user interface, which is a fault recurring in one place rather than 18 separate problems. 8 of the 18 require no authentication and 18 are reachable by a remote or network-adjacent attacker. The vendor took a median of 70 days from report to public disclosure, so the flaw existed, known and unfixed, for that long before anyone outside could act on it. No detection logic is attached: an advisory states that a flaw exists, not that anyone exploited it.

what.summary: A message broker flaw permitting remote code execution was among the known vulnerabilities a ransomware operation used for initial access, alongside flaws in collaboration, load balancing, remote access and directory products.

how.logic: The broker runs as a Java service, so exploitation surfaces as that process creating a shell or download utility. A message broker exists to move messages and has no reason to spawn a shell, which makes this close to unambiguous on that host.
how.caveat: Confirm no broker plugin or integration legitimately shells out before enabling.

how.logic: Message brokers and integration middleware sit between systems and are therefore frequently forgotten in exposure reviews, which look at applications and appliances. Enumerate broker and queue services and establish which are reachable from outside, since almost none should be.

fields.note: broker and management ports; confirm against the products deployed

how.caveat: Brokers are usually owned by an application or integration team rather than by infrastructure, which is how they escape exposure reviews. Ownership is the first question.

notes: The health department co-authored this advisory, which is the signal about who was being hit. The vulnerability set spans collaboration, load balancing, remote access, directory and middleware products, all published, which is the same breadth-of-known-vulnerabilities shape recorded elsewhere in this corpus for state-sponsored actors. Ransomware operators and state-sponsored actors are converging on the same entry routes.

who.versions_affected: Builds vulnerable to CVE-2021-44228

what.summary: A state-sponsored group exploited a logging library flaw in widely used software as part of a pattern of taking newly published vulnerabilities into operations, with the authoring agencies expecting proof of concept code to be exploited within hours of becoming public.

how.logic: A logging library is embedded inside other products rather than installed as one, so the asset inventory names the application and not the component. Finding where it runs means working through vendor advisories and dependency inventories, not scanning for a product name. This is the same structural problem as an embedded network stack or an application server bundled inside control equipment.

fields.note: populated from vendor advisories and dependency manifests rather than active discovery

how.caveat: Passive fingerprinting rarely identifies an embedded library. Where an equipment vendor has not published a statement, the honest answer is that you do not know.

how.logic: Exploitation of a library inside a web or application server surfaces as that server process creating a shell or interpreter child. It does not depend on recognising the exploit string, which matters because the request encoding has many variants.
how.caveat: Some applications shell out by design. Baseline and allow-list by command line, since the legitimate set on a given server is small.

how.logic: The exploitation path has the vulnerable server reach outward to fetch and load a remote class, so an application server making an outbound directory-protocol or remote-invocation connection is the observable. Servers have no routine reason to do this, which makes it a narrow question.

fields.note: directory and remote invocation ports; confirm against what the platform legitimately uses
restrict to server-role assets and exclude their known directory back ends

how.caveat: Servers legitimately query internal directory services. The signal is an external destination, so the internal directory servers must be excluded first.

who.versions_affected: All BlackBerry programs with a dependency on the affected C runtime library

what.summary: An integer overflow in a memory allocation function in the C runtime library of a real-time operating system, allowing a remote attacker to cause a denial of service or execute arbitrary code on affected devices. It is part of a wider collection of integer overflow flaws affecting a range of real-time operating systems and supporting libraries used across connected and industrial equipment. The operating system is used in a wide range of products whose compromise could give control of highly sensitive systems. Exploitation requires the attacker to control the parameters to the allocation call and what memory is accessed afterwards, and could be performed remotely where the vulnerable product is running and the device is exposed. No active exploitation was known at publication.

how.logic: All programs with a dependency on the affected runtime library are affected, and that operating system is embedded in a wide range of products. The operator generally cannot determine which of their equipment includes it, because it is a component of a component. The answerable form is to ask each supplier directly per product family and record the answer, since this class of flaw recurs.
how.caveat: No active exploitation was known at publication and exploitation has real preconditions, so the urgency here is inventory rather than incident. The durable problem is that the affected product list is unknowable without asking every supplier, and embedded devices frequently have no update path at all.

how.logic: Because the flaw is in a shared runtime rather than in any product, remediation depends entirely on each device manufacturer rebuilding and shipping an update. The practical question for an operator is which suppliers have an update mechanism at all for the equipment concerned, and what the route is where they do not.
how.caveat: This is the recurring shape for shared-component flaws in embedded equipment: the vulnerability is disclosed centrally, the fix arrives per manufacturer on their own timescale, and some never arrive. Recording which suppliers can update is more durable than tracking any single identifier.

where.title: BadAlloc Vulnerability Affecting BlackBerry QNX RTOS

notes: The corpus's clearest example of a vulnerability an operator cannot answer for themselves. The flaw is in a C runtime library, the runtime is in a real-time operating system, and that operating system is embedded in an unknown set of products across medical, automotive, industrial and other equipment. Every affected program depends on the same library, so the exposure question can only be answered by asking each supplier, and the fix can only arrive from each manufacturer separately. Recording which suppliers have a working update mechanism is more durable than tracking the identifier, because this class of shared-component flaw recurs.

who.versions_affected: Builds vulnerable to CVE-2024-37085

what.summary: A ransomware operation deployed encryptors against virtual machines at the hypervisor layer and exploited an authentication bypass in the hypervisor's directory integration, which encrypts every guest at once rather than each operating system individually.

how.logic: Encrypting at the hypervisor removes every guest simultaneously, so guest-level endpoint detection never runs. The observables are all on the host: shell access to the hypervisor management interface, unexpected commands run there, mass power-off of virtual machines, and datastore file modification at a rate no administrator produces. Because guest agents cannot see any of it, hypervisor logging has to be collected centrally or there is no detection at all.

fields.note: shell or secure shell access enabled on the host is itself worth alerting on
count guests powered off per host in a short window against the normal rate

how.caveat: Maintenance and patching legitimately power guests off in batches. Reconcile against the change window. The harder problem is that many estates do not forward hypervisor logs anywhere, which makes this undetectable rather than merely noisy.

how.logic: The authentication bypass works through the hypervisor's trust in a directory group, so creating or renaming a group to the name the hypervisor grants administrative rights to yields full host control. Watch directory group creation and rename events for the specific names hypervisors trust, and audit which groups actually hold that mapping.

fields.note: the default trusted group name; confirm what the deployment maps

how.caveat: The cleanest fix is removing the implicit group trust rather than detecting its abuse. Where the mapping must stay, the group name is a short and stable watch list.

markers.note: raw field group_name

where.publisher: CISA, FBI, Europol EC3 and NCSC-NL
where.title: #StopRansomware: Akira Ransomware

notes: Also recorded in the same advisory: payloads targeting a different vendor's hypervisor platform in a June 2025 incident, so this is not confined to one product. A hypervisor belongs in the same protection tier as a domain controller and a backup server, since compromising any of the three converts directly into estate-wide impact.

who.versions_affected: Unpatched, out-of-service and out-of-date ESXi versions, particularly those past end of life

what.summary: A ransomware campaign compromised more than 3,800 hypervisor servers globally by exploiting known vulnerabilities in servers likely running unpatched, out-of-service or out-of-date software. The ransomware encrypted configuration files on those servers rather than the virtual machine data itself, potentially rendering virtual machines unusable. Because the encryption was incomplete, an agency published a recovery script allowing victims to attempt to restore access to their files. Recommended actions are updating to the current version, hardening the hypervisor by disabling the service location protocol, and ensuring the hypervisor is not exposed to the internet.

how.logic: The ransomware encrypted configuration files rather than the virtual machine data, so the underlying disks remained intact and reconstruction was possible without a key. An agency published a recovery script on that basis. During response, establish exactly what was encrypted before deciding anything, and check whether published recovery tooling already exists for the identified family.
how.caveat: One of very few records here where the answer is recovery rather than negotiation, and it depends entirely on establishing the scope first. Preserve the encrypted state untouched while that is determined, because a well-intentioned rebuild destroys the material the recovery depends on.

how.logic: The actors were assessed as likely targeting end-of-life servers or those without available patches applied. Over 3,800 servers globally indicates opportunistic scanning against a population defined by version rather than by sector, which makes the inventory question, which hypervisors are past support and which are internet reachable, the whole of the exposure.
how.caveat: A hypervisor reachable from the internet is the highest-consequence exposure in most estates, because compromise reaches every guest at once and guest-level controls never see it. Two other records here reach the same layer by different routes.

how.logic: One of three prioritised actions is to disable the service location protocol on the hypervisor. That service is enabled by default, is rarely needed, and is a known discovery and exploitation surface, so disabling it removes exposure without requiring an upgrade, which matters where the version is out of support.
how.caveat: The cheapest of the three actions and available even on unsupported versions, which makes it the right first move where upgrading is blocked. Enabled-by-default services nobody uses recur across this corpus as the practical exposure.

where.title: ESXiArgs Ransomware Virtual Machine Recovery Guidance

notes: The only record in the corpus where recovery without payment was demonstrably possible, because the ransomware encrypted configuration files rather than the virtual machine data and an agency published a working recovery script. The transferable lesson is procedural: determine exactly what was encrypted before making any decision, and check for published recovery tooling, because both are cheap and the alternative assumption forecloses the option. It is also a reminder that disabling an unnecessary default service can remove exposure on a version that cannot be upgraded.

what.summary: A group targeting health sector organisations obtained remote access credentials through unpatched appliances and through phishing, moved laterally by secure shell and remote desktop, obtained privileged accounts through credential dumping and hash reuse, then used those accounts to reach the virtualisation management server and reset the passwords of the hypervisor hosts. It connected to those hosts over secure shell and encrypted the virtual machine files directly on host storage. The ransomware is reported to be based on leaked source code from another family.

how.logic: The chain has three observable stages before any damage. Privileged accounts reach the management server and reset the hypervisor host account passwords, which is an administrative action with a clear audit record. A secure shell session is then opened to each host, and on most builds that service is disabled by default so enabling it is itself anomalous. Finally files under the virtual machine storage path are modified by extension.
how.caveat: Encryption at the host means no guest agent observes any of it and every guest is lost simultaneously. Where backups are held as virtual machine files on the same storage they are lost with the guests, which is the specific failure this chain is designed to produce.

how.logic: Privileged access was obtained by credential dumping and by reusing password hashes rather than passwords. Hash reuse produces a successful authentication with no password ever submitted, so it is detectable on the authentication side by logon type and on the endpoint side by access to the authentication process memory.
how.caveat: Hash reuse is unaffected by password complexity and unaffected by rotation until every affected credential is changed, which is why the remediation scope has to be the whole privileged tier rather than the accounts seen in use.

how.logic: Entry was through remote access, with credentials obtained from unpatched appliances and from phishing with a malicious attachment. Both routes are defeated by a second factor on the remote access path, which makes the inventory question, which remote access paths actually enforce a second factor, the primary control rather than a detection.
how.caveat: Recurs in nearly every ransomware record in this corpus as the single control that would have broken the chain at the first step.

where.publisher: CISA, FBI and Department of Health and Human Services
where.title: #StopRansomware: Daixin Team

notes: The most concrete hypervisor attack chain in the corpus, and the most useful because every stage is observable and every stage precedes the damage: a host password reset from the management console, a secure shell session to a host where that service should be off, then file modification under the virtual machine storage path. It also states the mechanism by which backups are lost alongside the guests, since backup virtual machines on the same storage are encrypted in the same pass. Pairs with the hypervisor-layer encryption record, which reaches the same place through an authentication bypass instead of a credential reset.

who.versions_affected: Builds bundling a vulnerable logging library, per CVE-2021-44228

what.summary: State-sponsored actors exploited the logging library flaw in a virtual desktop gateway at a federal civilian agency, detected retrospectively through network monitoring that showed the server calling back to an attacker-controlled directory server.

how.logic: The confirmed-compromise signal was a directory protocol callback from the victim server to an attacker address, and critically that callback arrived on the web port rather than a directory port. So a rule watching directory ports alone would have missed it. The durable version is: an application server originating an outbound session to an external address, on any port, where the protocol carried is directory rather than web. That is the protocol-mismatch check applied to a specific case.

fields.note: the callback used the web port; do not assume the directory port
protocol identified independently of port
restrict to server-role assets, which should not originate directory traffic externally

how.caveat: Requires a sensor that identifies protocol independently of port. Where the sensor is port-based, this specific compromise is invisible, which is precisely what happened until retrospective analysis was run.

markers.note: raw field detected_protocol

how.logic: This compromise was found by going back over retained network data with a newly obtained indicator, not by an alert firing at the time. That is the operational lesson: retention long enough to re-examine, and a process for sweeping historical data whenever a new indicator arrives. Without either, a compromise like this stays unknown regardless of detection quality.

fields.note: swept retrospectively against newly published indicators rather than matched live

how.caveat: Depends entirely on retention. Ninety days of flow data cannot answer a question about an intrusion that began earlier, which is the practical constraint most estates run into.

how.logic: A name lookup was observed resolving to the same attacker address the callback went to, which links the two observations. Recording name-to-address resolution rather than names alone is what makes that correlation possible, and it also survives the actor changing domain while keeping infrastructure.

fields.note: retain the resolved address, not only the queried name

how.caveat: Many name resolution logs discard the answer. Retaining it costs little and enables correlation that is otherwise impossible.

where.title: Iranian Government-Sponsored APT Actors Compromise Federal Network, Deploy Crypto Miner, Credential Harvester

notes: Worth noting what the actors did with the access: deployed a crypto miner and harvested credentials. A miner is often dismissed as low-impact nuisance, but here it sat alongside credential theft on a federal network, so treating mining as merely a resource problem would have understated the intrusion considerably.

who.versions_affected: Horizon and Unified Access Gateway versions vulnerable to CVE-2021-44228, where the December 2021 fix or workaround was not applied

what.summary: Actors including state-sponsored groups continued exploiting the Log4j flaw against internet-facing virtual desktop gateways for at least six months after fixes were available, implanting loader malware that impersonated three trusted system administration utilities. At one victim they moved by remote desktop from the gateway into a security management server, a certificate server, a law enforcement database and the organisation's disaster recovery network.

how.logic: The loaders were modified versions of three separate well known system utilities, each carrying an embedded packed executable that provided remote control, keystroke logging, payload delivery and proxying. One ran as the highest privilege account on the system. Because the names are recognised by analysts and by allow-lists alike, the discriminator has to be signature state, hash and path rather than the name.
how.caveat: Matching on the utility name alone will fire on legitimate use of these tools, which administrators do run. The pairing with signature or hash state is what makes it usable.

how.logic: From the compromised gateway the actors reached a security management server, a certificate server, a sensitive database and a mail relay, and then the disaster recovery network, all by remote desktop with credentials for several accounts including administrators. The recovery network is the environment the organisation would rebuild from, and it was reachable from production by the same protocol as everything else.
how.caveat: Recovery networks are commonly excluded from monitoring on the grounds of being out of band, which is the same reasoning that leaves them reachable.

markers.note: raw field target_zone

how.logic: On first execution the loader created a scheduled task with an administrative sounding name that ran the malware every hour, and wrote two randomly named temporary files to the user profile temporary directory. The hourly cadence and the plausible task name are both ordinary in isolation; the task pointing at a binary in a user temporary path is not.
how.caveat: Task names chosen to resemble platform maintenance defeat review by name. Anchor on the target path instead.

markers.note: raw field scheduled_task_name

how.logic: The embedded executable connected to a hard-coded address on a non-standard high port with communications encrypted under a fixed key, and one server presented a self-signed certificate with a distinctive machine-name common name. A self-signed certificate whose common name is a Windows default hostname, presented by an external service, is a workable pivot across an estate and across time.
how.caveat: Addresses and ports date quickly. The certificate shape, a default Windows machine name as the common name on an internet-facing service, outlives the specific indicators.

markers.note: raw field tls_certificate_subject_cn

how.logic: Both engagements began from observed traffic to a known address rather than from an alert, and one victim had been compromised since January but was investigated in late April. The advisory instructs organisations that did not patch immediately to assume compromise and hunt. Retention has to reach back past December 2021 for that instruction to be actionable at all.
how.caveat: The gap between initial access and discovery was around three months at one victim and longer at the other. Retention shorter than that turns an assume-compromise instruction into an unanswerable question.

where.publisher: CISA and United States Coast Guard Cyber Command
where.title: Malicious Cyber Actors Continue to Exploit Log4Shell in VMware Horizon Systems

notes: Distinct from the other Log4Shell record in this corpus, which covers the same library flaw exploited at a federal agency for cryptomining. Same vulnerability, entirely different objective and tooling, which is the argument for indexing this corpus by observed behaviour rather than by vulnerability. Exploitation continued for six months after fixes existed.

who.versions_affected: Workspace ONE Access 20.10.0.0 to 21.08.0.1, vIDM 3.3.3 to 3.3.6, vRA 7.6, Cloud Foundation 3.x and 4.x, vRealize Suite Lifecycle Manager 8.x

what.summary: Actors, assessed as likely state-sponsored, chained a server-side template injection flaw in the web interface with a local privilege escalation flaw in support scripts to reach root on identity management appliances. A working exploit was built by reverse engineering the vendor update within 48 hours of its release. At one victim two separate actors were present; one exfiltrated credentials and firewall rules in an archive staged inside a web-served directory, then restored the logs.

how.logic: The exploit was a template engine expression placed in a parameter of an otherwise ordinary request to the verification endpoint, arriving URL-encoded. Because the expression has to reach the server in clear to be evaluated, the request line holds the whole exploit, which makes this answerable retrospectively from web logs as well as prospectively.
how.caveat: Cover the encoded form as well as the literal one; the observed request used percent encoding for the delimiters.

how.logic: The vendor released fixes on 6 April and a third party assessed that actors reverse engineered the update to produce a working exploit inside 48 hours, with exploitation beginning immediately. The government catalogue added the two flaws on 14 and 15 April and set remediation dates of 5 and 6 May, by which point exploitation was three weeks old. Treat the vendor release date, not the catalogue date and not the compliance deadline, as the start of the exposure window.
how.caveat: The gap between what a compliance deadline permits and what an actor needs was three weeks here. Meeting the deadline was not the same as being safe.

how.logic: A script run with elevated privilege collected user names, passwords, master keys and firewall rules into an archive, which was written into an image directory beneath the application web root and later collected by a request. Nothing left the host outbound, so the file write plus the subsequent successful request for it are the only evidence of exfiltration.
how.caveat: Egress monitoring does not see this, because retrieval is an inbound request to a service that is meant to serve files.

markers.note: raw field file_path

how.logic: The actor modified logs back to their original state and deleted a certificate file, the web access logs and the application logs for the single day of activity. A check that the log file exists and is being written to would pass. Only a copy held off the host reveals the bounded gap.
how.caveat: Restoration rather than deletion is the harder variant, since the usual health checks on a log source still pass.

markers.note: raw field file_path

how.logic: At the first victim two actors were distinguished by their tradecraft against the same flaw: one automated, downloading and running a shell script for collection and exfiltration; the other working the server by hand and installing several web shells and a reverse proxy. Scoping the incident around whichever was found first would have missed the other.
how.caveat: The behavioural difference between scripted and interactive activity against one flaw is what separated them. Neither actor's indicators would have led to the other.

how.logic: Both actors placed web shells in application directories, including a page written to the Horizon script library path and a publicly available shell offering command execution, a file manager, a database manager and a port scanner. Application directories on an appliance change only at upgrade, so any file appearing between upgrades is worth an alert.
how.caveat: Requires file integrity monitoring on the appliance, which is not enabled by default and on some appliances is not supported at all.

what.summary: Iran-based actors used a security gateway information disclosure flaw among a set of remote access appliance vulnerabilities to obtain and develop network access, which they then handed to ransomware affiliates while separately conducting state-directed collection.

how.logic: This advisory is more explicit than the earlier one on the same theme: the assessment is that a significant proportion of the operations against organisations in one country were intended to obtain access and then collaborate with ransomware affiliates to deploy it, while the same actors separately conducted state collection. So one intrusion can have two unrelated downstream outcomes, arriving at different times from different hands. Do not close a credential or appliance compromise as unexploited because no state-typical activity followed; the ransomware may be the follow-on.

fields.note: and whether unrelated activity followed weeks later on the same access

how.caveat: Changes closure criteria rather than detection. The specific error to avoid is reasoning from a state actor's expected objectives when the actor's business model is resale.

how.logic: An information disclosure flaw on a gateway yields the credentials and material held by that gateway, so patching closes the flaw and leaves the attacker holding what it disclosed. Confirm rotation of every credential and key that the appliance held, dated after the patch.
how.caveat: Disclosure flaws are the clearest case for mandatory rotation, because the vulnerability's whole effect is handing over secrets. Patching alone is not remediation here.

how.logic: Six appliance vulnerabilities across five vendors in one advisory. The actor is loyal to the asset class, not the brand, so the standing query against newly published appliance proof of concept paths is the general control rather than any vendor-specific rule.
how.caveat: Noisy after every disclosure. What succeeded matters, not what was attempted.

what.summary: An actor chained a denial of service flaw with a persistent code execution flaw in the WebVPN service to load memory-resident and disk-resident implants on perimeter appliances.

how.logic: A perimeter appliance reboots or produces a crash dump with no matching change record, then a configuration write or client profile change lands within a short window. Either event alone is routine; the pairing is not.

how.caveat: Planned maintenance produces the same pair. Correlate against the change window before treating it as an issue.

how.logic: The vendor integrity check reports a mismatch, or a file appears in the appliance filesystem that is not part of a shipped image.

what.summary: Russian state-sponsored actors reached a non-governmental organisation's network by taking advantage of a misconfigured account left on default second-factor settings, which allowed them to enrol a device of their own for that account. They then exploited a critical print service vulnerability to run arbitrary code with system privileges, and moved into the organisation's cloud and mail environments to exfiltrate documents. The agencies recommend reviewing authentication configuration for fail-open and re-enrolment scenarios, and disabling inactive accounts uniformly across both the directory and the authentication system, noting that users who enable a second factor are far less likely to have an account compromised.

how.logic: The account was left on default settings which permitted enrolling a new device, and it was an account that should not have been usable at all. The agencies name two configuration scenarios to review, fail open and re-enrolment, and one reconciliation, that inactive accounts are disabled uniformly across the directory and the authentication system. The reconciliation is the one that fails silently, because an account disabled in one and enrollable in the other is reported as closed by both.
how.caveat: Strong authentication reported as implemented was bypassed by its own defaults, which is the point: presence of the control is not the same as effectiveness of the control. Note this is the same combination as the later cloud advisory in this corpus, dormant account plus attacker device enrolment, three years earlier and against a different product.

how.logic: Enrolling a device of their own converted a password into durable, policy-compliant access, after which every subsequent authentication looked entirely correct. The observable moment is the enrolment itself, evaluated against whether the account had ever enrolled a device before and whether the account should have been active at all.
how.caveat: Enrolment events are usually retained in the authentication product rather than the directory, so this detection often requires a log source that is not being collected. Worth checking before assuming coverage.

how.logic: With network access established the actors exploited the print service flaw to run arbitrary code with system privileges. The durable detection is the print service loading a library from a user-writable path or creating a child process, which it does not do in normal operation, and the cheaper answer is disabling the service where it is not needed.
how.caveat: The same flaw appears in a criminal ransomware campaign elsewhere in this corpus. A print service enabled on servers that do not print is a recurring free win.

how.logic: The account exploited was inactive, and the recommended remediation is to disable inactive accounts uniformly across both systems. The uniformity requirement is what distinguishes this from an ordinary dormant account problem: the reconciliation must span the directory and the authentication product, which are usually owned by different teams.

markers.expr: authentication_success by account with last_activity older_than 90d

how.caveat: Now the third record in this corpus where a dormant account is the entry point, and the second where it is combined with device enrolment. The pairing is common enough to treat as a single expected sequence rather than two separate weaknesses.

where.title: Russian State-Sponsored Cyber Actors Gain Network Access by Exploiting Default Multifactor Authentication Protocols and PrintNightmare Vulnerability

notes: The clearest case in the corpus of a control being defeated by its own defaults rather than by any weakness in the technology. Strong authentication was present and reported as implemented; a dormant account left on default settings let the actor enrol their own device, after which every authentication was correct. The pairing of dormant account plus attacker device enrolment recurs three years later in a different advisory against a different product, which makes it an expected sequence rather than a one-off. The reconciliation the agencies ask for, that disabled accounts match across the directory and the authentication product, spans two systems usually owned by different teams, which is why it fails silently.

what.summary: A Russian military intelligence unit exploited a known network management protocol flaw against Cisco routers to conduct reconnaissance and deploy malware onto the devices, using a vulnerability that had been patched years before the activity.

how.logic: The management protocol should only be reachable from the monitoring systems that use it, and the community strings should not be the defaults. Two checks follow: which sources send management protocol queries to network devices, and whether any device still answers to a default or weak community string. Both are inventory questions with definite answers, and the second is frequently yes on older devices because changing it means touching the monitoring configuration too.

fields.note: compare against the monitoring systems authorised to poll

how.caveat: Network monitoring platforms poll constantly and will dominate the results, so enumerate them first. Version 2 of the protocol has no meaningful authentication, so where it is still in use the community string is the whole control.

how.logic: Malware deployed onto a router persists where no endpoint agent runs and where the device's own reporting may be unreliable. The available signals remain indirect: unexplained memory or storage use, image or configuration integrity mismatch, and sessions originating from the device's own address.
how.caveat: A compromised device cannot be trusted to report on itself. Suspicion warrants out-of-band examination or replacement rather than interrogation.

where.title: APT28 Exploits Known Vulnerability to Carry Out Reconnaissance and Deploy Malware on Cisco Routers

notes: The same unit appears elsewhere in this corpus targeting logistics companies, IP cameras and a mail client flaw, which is worth noting: one unit working across network infrastructure, physical surveillance and endpoint software. Assessments that treat those as separate threat pictures will underestimate a single actor's reach. The vulnerability used had been patched for four years at the time of the activity.

what.summary: Chinese state-sponsored actors compromised routing and switching infrastructure at scale to feed a global espionage system, modifying router configurations to pivot between separate networks and running virtualised containers on the network devices themselves to evade detection.

how.logic: Running a container on a router puts attacker code inside the device where no endpoint agent exists and where the device's own configuration listing may not show it. This is the hardest evasion in the corpus to detect from the outside. The available signals are all indirect: application hosting or container features enabled on a device where nobody deliberately enabled them, unexplained memory or storage consumption, and outbound sessions sourced from the device's own address rather than passing through it. That last one is the important distinction, because a router originating traffic is categorically different from a router forwarding it.

fields.note: application hosting or container features enabled on the device
sessions whose source is the device's own management address, meaning the device originated them

how.caveat: Some organisations legitimately use device application hosting for monitoring agents. Enumerate that once. The deeper problem is that a compromised device cannot be trusted to report its own state, so a suspected device needs out-of-band examination rather than interrogation.

how.logic: Configuration changes were the mechanism for pivoting between otherwise separate networks, which means the change record is the primary evidence. Any route, tunnel, access list or interface change on infrastructure, reconciled against an approved change. Where device configuration is under version control this is a diff; where it is not, this cannot be answered at all.

fields.note: changes with no corresponding approved change record

how.caveat: Busy networks generate constant legitimate change. Without configuration version control or a change feed this is unanswerable, which is the more common state.

how.logic: One of the exploited flaws is an authentication bypass on the device web management interface, so the management interface should not be reachable from anywhere except the management network. Any administrative access from outside it is either the intrusion or the gap that permits it.
how.caveat: Out-of-band and emergency access paths are the legitimate exceptions and need enumerating before this is enabled.

where.publisher: CISA, NSA, FBI and international partners
where.title: Countering Chinese State-Sponsored Actors Compromise of Networks to Feed Global Espionage System

notes: The advisory is explicit that the actors continue to use these techniques but expects them to evolve, and that older techniques may still be used opportunistically, so the descriptions are useful for retrospective hunting as well as current detection. It also lists five separate industry names for the same activity and warns they are not a one-to-one mapping, which is worth remembering when correlating with vendor reporting.

what.summary: A group linked to the People's Republic of China, active since 2010, modified router firmware without detection and abused domain trust relationships to pivot from international subsidiaries to headquarters networks in Japan and the United States. On compromised routers it installed modified unsigned firmware carrying a secure shell backdoor allowing unlogged interaction, sometimes with a modified bootloader for persistence across reboots, and installed automation policies that strip chosen strings from the output of legitimate commands and block the file operations a responder would need. It used stolen code-signing certificates, custom malware for three operating systems, and public-facing branch routers as proxy infrastructure.

how.logic: The actors hid automation policies that wait for specific commands and then either remove lines containing chosen strings from the output, or refuse to run the command at all, specifically blocking copy, rename and move so the policy itself cannot be extracted for analysis. So the device answers questions about itself dishonestly and obstructs the responder. The only reliable evidence is a configuration copy held where the device cannot reach it, plus what adjacent devices observe.
how.caveat: This targets the responder rather than the detection, which makes it the most complete evasion recorded here. A filtered command output is indistinguishable from a clean device, and blocking file operations prevents evidence collection. It is the network-device analogue of the kernel module that hides its own components elsewhere in this corpus, and it leads to the same conclusion: continuously export configuration somewhere the device cannot reach.

how.logic: Running firmware was modified in memory to permit installation of unsigned modified firmware with a built-in secure shell backdoor giving unlogged interaction, and in some cases a modified bootloader so it survives reboot. Images were delivered to the device over file transfer or secure shell. Because the backdoor is unlogged, the detectable evidence is the image transfer, the reboot outside a change window, and sessions to the device that adjacent equipment sees but the device's own log does not.
how.caveat: That unsigned firmware installed at all means image verification was already bypassed, so a later verification success proves nothing. This is the same conclusion the appliance integrity-tool record reaches from a different direction.

how.logic: The actors targeted international subsidiaries, then pivoted from trusted internal routers to other subsidiaries and to headquarters, abusing the trusted relationship of small branch office routers, and used the public-facing branch routers as proxy infrastructure so their traffic blended with corporate traffic. The advisory recommends multinationals review every subsidiary connection and verify access.
how.caveat: The vulnerability is governance rather than technology. Branch and subsidiary routers are frequently administered locally, left outside central patching and monitoring, and trusted by the core regardless. Acquisitions are the usual origin.

how.logic: The actors signed malicious payloads with stolen code-signing certificates so they appear legitimate and are harder for security software to detect. Signature validity therefore carries no information, and detection has to rest on behaviour and on whether the signing certificate is one you expect for that software.

markers.expr: code_signature_valid and signer not in expected_signers_for_product

how.caveat: The third distinct route to a valid signature over attacker-chosen content in this corpus, alongside a compromised build process and a certificate validation flaw. The consistent lesson is that signature validity is not evidence of provenance.

how.logic: On hosts the actors persisted by installing network utility shells and by editing the registry to enable remote desktop and secure shell, used a scanner for enumeration and a local file transfer server to move data internally. Enabling a remote access service by configuration change is an ordinary administrative action, so it is the absence of an authorising change record that makes it detectable.
how.caveat: Living off the land here means the actions are indistinguishable from administration except by authorisation. Reconciling against change records is the only discriminator, which makes the quality of those records a detection dependency.

where.publisher: NSA, FBI, CISA, Japan National Police Agency and Japan NISC
where.title: People's Republic of China-Linked Cyber Actors Hide in Router Firmware

notes: Holds the single most complete evasion in the corpus: automation policies that edit the output of the administrator's own commands and block the file operations needed to collect evidence. Alongside the kernel module that hides its components and the appliance integrity checker that can be deceived, this is now the third independent case of a device lying about its own state, and all three lead to the same architectural conclusion, which is that integrity evidence must be held somewhere the device cannot reach. The subsidiary pivot is the other durable lesson and it is a governance finding rather than a technical one: a branch router administered locally, outside central patching, and trusted by the core is the documented route from an acquisition nobody governs into headquarters.

what.summary: Eighteen national agencies reported that a Russian state security service centre continues to exploit poorly configured and vulnerable networking devices worldwide, opportunistically compromising multiple critical infrastructure networks, in activity spanning more than a decade. The named identifiers include a router vulnerability first published in 2008 and a widely exploited device management protocol flaw. Sectors assessed most at risk are communications, the defence industrial base, energy, financial services, government services and facilities especially at state and local level, and healthcare. The advisory lists six separate industry names used to track the same activity.

how.logic: An advisory published in 2026 names a vulnerability first identified in 2008 as still being exploited. That is only possible because network devices are rarely replaced, rarely inventoried by software version, and carry management services enabled by default that nobody turns off. The useful measure is the oldest unremediated identifier on any internet-reachable network device.
how.caveat: Disabling an unused management protocol is almost always cheaper and faster than upgrading the device, and on the named management flaw it removes the exposure entirely. Poorly configured is listed alongside vulnerable in the advisory for that reason.

how.logic: Activity against routing devices by this actor set follows the pattern established by the other router records here: configuration retrieval and modification are the objective, and the device cannot be trusted to report on itself. The reliable evidence is a configuration copy held where the device cannot reach it, compared regularly.
how.caveat: Now the fourth router-focused record in this corpus reaching the same architectural conclusion: export configuration continuously to somewhere the device cannot reach, because that copy is the only trustworthy one.

how.logic: The advisory describes opportunistic compromise of poorly configured and vulnerable devices worldwide, which implies management interfaces reachable from beyond the management network. Restricting administrative access to management space removes both the named identifiers and every future flaw in the same interfaces.
how.caveat: The management protocol port associated with the named flaw is one many operators do not know is listening, because the feature is enabled by default and has no obvious symptom when unused.

how.logic: Opportunistic compromise of critical infrastructure networks sustained over more than a decade, by a state security service, on devices that carry traffic rather than data, is consistent with holding access rather than exploiting it. The sectors named are communications, defence industrial base, energy, financial services, government and healthcare.
how.caveat: Eighteen agencies co-sealing a single advisory is itself a signal of assessed significance. The six different industry names listed for the same activity is also a practical reminder that tracking by group name across vendors produces double counting and gaps.

where.publisher: NSA, CISA, FBI, DC3 and fourteen international partner agencies
where.title: Improve Router Hygiene to Protect Against Russian State-Sponsored Targeting

notes: The most recent advisory in the corpus and it names a vulnerability from 2008. That single fact is the argument: network devices are the one asset class where an eighteen-year-old flaw remains a current threat item, because they are rarely replaced, rarely inventoried by software version, and ship with management services enabled that nobody disables. The same service centre appears elsewhere in this corpus operating a decade-old espionage implant, which places routine router hygiene and the most sophisticated tooling here under one organisation. Six industry tracking names for one activity set is also a useful caution against organising defensive work around group names.

what.summary: A ransomware operation obtained initial access mostly through remote access services with no multi-factor authentication configured, exploiting three known appliance vulnerabilities including an information disclosure flaw and an authentication bypass, and had claimed roughly 244 million dollars in proceeds by late 2025.

how.logic: The stated common factor was remote access without multi-factor authentication, not a novel technique. So the highest-value check is an inventory one: for every remote access path, is a second factor actually enforced, for every account, including service and legacy accounts. An information disclosure flaw yielding credentials plus a portal with no second factor is a complete intrusion chain with nothing else required.
how.caveat: Partial enforcement is the usual finding: a second factor on interactive users but not on service accounts or a legacy authentication path. Check per account, not per gateway.

how.logic: Where the flaw discloses credentials rather than granting execution, the follow-on is a legitimate-looking authentication. Source network history per account is what separates it, and it keeps working after the appliance is patched because disclosed credentials outlive the patch.
how.caveat: Rotate credentials after any appliance compromise. The information disclosure flaw here means assuming credentials were taken, not asking whether they were.

who.versions_affected: Unpatched and end-of-life releases carrying the Smart Install flaw, which has been fixed since 2018 but remains present on devices past support

what.summary: A Russian state group has spent a decade collecting network devices that nobody can patch, using a flaw fixed in 2018 against equipment that reached end of support before or since. The implant lives in the firmware image and survives reboot, and the surrounding work is all quiet configuration change: a read-write management community string added, the authentication and accounting server configuration altered so the device stops reporting centrally, access lists widened, and a tunnel built to carry traffic back out.

how.logic: Turning on the device's own file transfer service and pointing it at the stored startup configuration converts config theft into a supported feature that needs no tooling and no shell. The command is unusual enough to alert on directly, and unlike an interactive harvest it leaves the device serving the configuration to anyone who asks until somebody turns it off again.
how.caveat: Some estates genuinely use this for backup, which makes it the same problem as every other configuration-egress detection: enumerate the legitimate users first and alert on the rest. Where backup runs over a different mechanism entirely, this is close to a zero-false-positive rule.

how.logic: Rather than deleting entries, the accounting configuration itself was altered so that the device stopped sending them. The visible effect at the collector is a device whose logging volume drops and stays down, which is a different shape from the bounded gap seen on the router campaign and easier to spot because it persists. Volume per device against its own history is the measure; an absolute threshold cannot work across a mixed estate.
how.caveat: Reachable but quiet is the condition worth alerting on, because unreachable and quiet is an outage and will dominate any rule that does not separate them. Requires per-device baselines, which is more work than a single threshold and the only thing that survives a mixed estate.

how.logic: A read-write management community string added to a device, or a default one left in place, turns configuration retrieval into a single unauthenticated request. Two separate checks: the configuration change that adds it, and traffic on the management protocol arriving from anything that is not the monitoring platform.
how.caveat: Source addresses on this protocol are trivially spoofed, which the report notes was used to get past address-based restrictions, so the traffic half of this is weaker than it looks and the configuration half is the one to rely on.

what.summary: The central management platform for a firewall estate shipped with a hard-coded low-privileged account, letting a remote unauthenticated attacker log in to its web interface and read sensitive data. The vendor confirmed exploitation in the wild, scored it 8.9, and stated that it may be chained with other flaws in the same product to escalate and further compromise the management platform. The vendor's own indicator of compromise is a file appearing on the appliance, and its recovery guidance is to rotate every credential, key and certificate the appliance holds -- which is the part that matters, because those secrets are for the managed firewalls rather than for the manager. Discovered by an offensive research team and added to the known-exploited catalogue.

how.logic: A successful authentication to the management appliance's web interface by a built-in account that no administrator provisioned, particularly from a source outside the management network. The account is low-privileged and legitimate-looking, so the discriminator is not the privilege but the provenance: it is in no joiner record and belongs to no person.
how.caveat: Vendor support sessions and initial commissioning legitimately authenticate with accounts nobody in the organisation provisioned. Reconcile against the support case record before treating a hit as intrusion.

how.logic: The vendor's published check is to search the appliance's system log for licence-related entries and look for a specific temporary file appearing. Treat the file path as an on-box indicator and the log search as the collection method, because the appliance will not forward this to a SIEM by default -- it is a console check, and that limitation is the reason to schedule it rather than wait for it.

markers.note: vendor-published indicator; presence means suspected compromise. The licence-related entries are read from /var/log/messages on the appliance console -- that path is the collection target, not a second indicator

how.caveat: A negative result is weak evidence. A temporary file is exactly the kind of artefact that gets cleaned up, by the attacker or by the appliance, so its absence does not clear the box. Where the appliance was exposed and unpatched, investigate on that basis rather than on this check.

how.logic: The recovery instruction is the finding. Every credential, key and certificate held by the management platform must be treated as disclosed, and those authenticate to the managed firewalls, so the blast radius of a low-privileged read on the manager is the estate it manages. Enumerate what the platform holds before an incident, so that rotation is a list to work rather than a discovery exercise during one.
how.caveat: Rotation on a firewall estate is itself an outage risk, which is why it gets deferred and why this belongs in a plan written before the day it is needed. Rehearse it on one device.

notes: Added to the known-exploited catalogue on 2026-07-29, so this corpus already held the product as an exposure record with no detection logic; this record is where the logic lives. The indicator and the rotation guidance originate with the vendor and are reproduced from the research write-up that cites them, whose authors discovered the flaw. Common weakness type CWE-259.

who.versions_affected: 14.1 before 14.1-8.50, 13.1 before 13.1-49.15, 13.0 before 13.0-92.19, 13.1-FIPS before 13.1-37.163, 12.1-FIPS and 12.1-NDcPP before 12.1-55.300, and 12.1 which is end of life with no fix

what.summary: Ransomware affiliates exploited a memory disclosure flaw in a load balancer and remote access appliance, sending a crafted host header that caused the appliance to return system memory containing a valid session cookie. With the cookie they established authenticated sessions with no username, no password and no second factor, then harvested credentials, moved laterally and reached data. Exploitation was identified as early as two months before public disclosure. One affected organisation shared its findings voluntarily, in a business unit it maintained as a separate environment.

how.logic: The exploit is a request with a crafted host header against the appliance's own web endpoint, which returns system memory information containing a valid session cookie. Two independent detection surfaces follow: the anomalous header on the request side, and on the appliance side a session established with no preceding credential submission. The second is the same absence-of-authentication shape as a forged identity token elsewhere in this corpus.
how.caveat: Bypasses the password and the second factor simultaneously, so strong authentication provides no protection whatsoever. Patching alone is insufficient because sessions established beforehand remain valid; terminating all active sessions is a required second step and is the one most often skipped.

how.logic: The stolen cookie yields a session that the appliance considers legitimate, so downstream systems see an authorised user. Detection has to key on properties of the session rather than of the authentication: a session whose source address changes mid-life, a session active with no corresponding sign-in event, and a session with permissions being used in ways that account has not used before.
how.caveat: The appliance is behaving correctly throughout, which is why no authentication control catches it. Session-level anomalies are the only remaining surface.

how.logic: The affected list includes a version line that is end of life, for which no fix is issued. Those installations are permanently vulnerable to a flaw that bypasses multi-factor authentication, which makes them a replacement or isolation decision rather than a patching one.
how.caveat: An end-of-life remote access appliance carrying an authentication bypass is the worst combination in this corpus: internet-facing by purpose, credential-holding by design, and unfixable by definition. Isolation or replacement are the only options.

how.logic: The advisory notes that observed techniques for this ransomware vary significantly between affiliates while the entry route here was a single appliance flaw. That argues for detecting at the entry and the intermediate stages, which are shared, rather than at the ransomware itself, which varies by affiliate.
how.caveat: Affiliate variability is the reason a family-named detection performs poorly here. The appliance flaw is the invariant, and the sectors affected span education, energy, financial services, food and agriculture, government, healthcare, manufacturing and transport, so no sector should read itself out.

how.logic: Session takeover gave elevated permissions used to harvest credentials, so remediation extends past the appliance to every credential reachable through the sessions that were hijacked. Because the sessions were legitimate, there is no failed authentication anywhere to bound the scope by.
how.caveat: Scope is defined by what the hijacked accounts could reach rather than by observed activity, because the observed activity is indistinguishable from legitimate use.

Strategically it is the cleanest example of multi-factor authentication being irrelevant rather than defeated: the actor never authenticates at all, it inherits a session that was already authenticated. That places it alongside the forged identity token and the browser extension records as the third distinct mechanism in this corpus for arriving inside an account without ever passing an authentication control. who.versions_affected: Builds vulnerable to CVE-2023-3519, with CVE-2023-3466 and CVE-2023-3467 disclosed alongside

what.summary: An unauthenticated remote code execution flaw was exploited as a zero-day against a critical infrastructure organisation, and the appliance used to get in was in a non-production environment, where patching and monitoring discipline is habitually weaker than for the production estate.

how.logic: The most transferable detail in this advisory is which appliance was used: a non-production one. Test, staging and development instances of the same appliance are routinely internet-reachable for convenience, excluded from the patch cycle because they are not production, and absent from the monitoring scope for the same reason. Enumerate every instance of a given appliance family, not just the production ones, and check patch level and exposure for each. The same reasoning applies to any appliance class in this corpus.
how.caveat: Non-production instances are frequently owned by a project rather than by operations, which is why they escape both the patch cycle and the monitoring scope. Finding them usually means asking teams rather than querying an inventory.

how.logic: A web shell was dropped on the appliance, so the durable check is for files the appliance's own release did not install. On an appliance this means the vendor's integrity facility or filesystem examination rather than an endpoint agent, since no agent runs there.
how.caveat: Appliance filesystems are not designed to be examined, so this often needs vendor support or an out-of-band image. Where compromise is suspected, replacement is faster than proving cleanliness.

how.logic: Exploited as a zero-day first and then widely once published, which is the normal sequence for this appliance class. The standing query against published proof of concept paths catches the second wave, which is the larger one by volume.
how.caveat: By definition useless against the zero-day phase. The record exists partly to make that limitation explicit: for the first wave, exposure reduction and rapid patching are the only controls.

who.versions_affected: Multiple releases across five separate identifiers; each fix addressed one parsing path and the class persisted

what.summary: Five separate vulnerability identifiers published across roughly two years, all in the same product line, all the same underlying fault: an authentication endpoint that returns uninitialised memory when a request omits something the parser assumed would be present. The triggers differ each time because each is a different parsing path, so a detection written against any one of them stops working at the next. In the case examined most closely, the request is a POST carrying a parameter name with no equals sign and no value, and the response is an XML field that should be empty carrying stack contents instead.

how.logic: Detect on the response rather than the request. An authentication endpoint answers with a bounded, predictable shape when it is working: the same fields, similar length, printable content. Leaking memory changes that shape and cannot avoid changing it, because the leak is the payload. Alert where one endpoint returns responses whose length varies materially between requests from one source, where a field expected to be empty or textual carries bytes outside the printable range, and where the same source repeats the request quickly, since a single request returns whatever happened to be on the stack and the technique needs many.

fields.note: the field that should be empty carrying non-printable bytes; the tag name is vendor-specific and the shape is not

markers.expr: stddev(response_length) by url_path, source_ip exceeds measured_baseline_for_that_endpoint
count(request) by source_ip, url_path within measured_short_window

how.caveat: The request half is the part that expires. Every one of the five identifiers has a different trigger because each is a different parsing path, so a marker written against a specific parameter or path catches one and misses the rest; the response-side markers are the ones worth carrying forward. The response length baseline has to be measured per endpoint, since a patched appliance and a vulnerable one differ by a few hundred bytes rather than by an order of magnitude. Note also that exploitation is indistinguishable from failed authentication at a glance, and that the leaked content itself does not appear in a standard access log, so this needs response inspection rather than access logging alone.

how.logic: Count identifiers per product grouped by fault class rather than counting identifiers. Where one product yields the same class repeatedly under different identifiers, each fix has addressed an instance rather than the cause, and the next instance should be assumed. The practical consequence is that the detection must key on the class and the exposure decision must stop depending on being patched.
how.caveat: A procurement and exposure argument rather than a query, and it is deliberately narrower than the repeat-offender pattern: that one is about a class recurring across vendors, this one is about a single product yielding the same fault repeatedly, which is a stronger and more uncomfortable claim. Where it holds, being current on patches is not evidence of much, because the next identifier in the sequence is not yet published.

what.summary: Three organisations warned about malicious use of legitimate remote monitoring and management software after identifying a widespread campaign in which criminal actors sent phishing emails leading victims to download genuine remote management products, then used them in a refund scam to steal money from victim bank accounts. Suspected activity was identified on two federal civilian networks through retrospective analysis of a government-wide intrusion detection system. The agencies note the actors could sell victim account access to other criminal or state actors, and that actors ranging from criminals to state-sponsored groups use legitimate remote management software as a backdoor for persistence and command traffic. Critically, using portable executables of that software establishes local user access without administrative privilege and without full installation, bypassing common software controls and the risk management assumptions built on them.

how.logic: Portable executables need no administrative privilege and perform no installation, so software inventory, installation monitoring and any control that assumes unapproved software requires elevation all see nothing. What remains is process execution from a user-writable path with no matching installation record, and outbound sessions to the vendor's relay infrastructure from hosts where the product is not licensed.
how.caveat: The precise finding worth keeping is that portable execution defeats software allow-listing and installation monitoring simultaneously while requiring no elevation, which invalidates a common risk assumption. Reputation blocking also fails because the software is genuine and widely licensed.

how.logic: The agencies note that actors from criminals to state-sponsored groups use legitimate remote management software as a backdoor for persistence and command traffic. Since the products are genuine, the only decidable test is whether your organisation licensed this one, which makes an accurate inventory of approved remote access products a detection control.
how.caveat: This appears in more records in this corpus than any other single post-access technique, spanning criminal ransomware, state espionage and this fraud campaign. The control is identical in every case and is an inventory question.

how.logic: Although the campaign appears financially motivated, the agencies assess it could lead to other malicious activity, specifically that the actors could sell victim account access to other criminal or state actors. So an apparently self-contained fraud incident may be the first stage of an unrelated intrusion by a different party, and remediation scope should reflect that.
how.caveat: A refund scam reads as a consumer fraud problem and gets closed accordingly. Here it landed on two federal networks, and the same access is saleable, which is a different risk from the money taken.

how.logic: The campaign was found by retrospective analysis of a government-wide intrusion detection system using trusted third-party reporting, months after the phishing emails were sent. That is the same shape as several other records here: the detection existed only because the data had been retained and could be re-examined against information that arrived later.
how.caveat: Worth noting the gap: phishing in mid-June, identification in October. Retention shorter than that interval would have made the campaign undiscoverable on those networks.

where.title: Protecting Against Malicious Use of Remote Monitoring and Management Software

notes: Contains the most precise statement in the corpus of why legitimate remote management software is hard to control: a portable executable establishes local user access with no administrative privilege and no installation, which defeats software allow-listing, installation monitoring and the assumption that unapproved software requires elevation, all at once. The campaign itself reads as consumer fraud and would normally be closed as such, but it landed on two federal networks and the agencies note the same access is saleable to other actors, which is a materially different risk from the money stolen.

who.versions_affected: Builds vulnerable to CVE-2024-1709

what.summary: A ransomware operation used an authentication bypass in a remote support platform, alongside a flaw in an endpoint management server, as its initial access routes. Compromising a remote support platform grants the access it was built to provide, across every endpoint it manages.

how.logic: A remote support platform exists to run commands and open sessions on endpoints, so an attacker holding it needs no further tooling and every action looks like intended product behaviour. Endpoint agents will not flag it, because the platform is trusted by design. The observables come from the platform's own audit trail: sessions or deployments created by accounts outside the authorised set, targeting an unusually broad endpoint population, or occurring outside working hours.

fields.note: compare against the technicians authorised to open sessions
an unusually broad target set for one operator in one window

how.caveat: Legitimate mass support activity looks identical in shape, so only authorisation and timing separate them. Requires the platform's audit log to be collected off the platform, since an attacker holding it can edit what stays on it.

how.logic: Both named products are management or security tooling with broad estate reach, which is the recurring shape in this corpus: the tools bought to provide control already hold the access an attacker wants. Check their exposure and patch currency at the same priority as a domain controller.
how.caveat: These platforms are often internet-facing by design so technicians can reach them remotely, which makes exposure reduction a support-model conversation rather than a firewall change.

notes: The third record in this corpus where compromising a management or security product was the entry route, after an endpoint management platform and an audit product. Worth treating that as an established pattern rather than three coincidences: these platforms are internet-facing, hold privileged access to everything they manage, and are frequently outside the patch cadence applied to servers.

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound; the exposure is the daemon socket being reachable by an application process

what.summary: When a download of the encryptor into the container failed, the operator did not abandon the objective; it built a way to carry the binary across the namespace boundary instead. Six scripts were written and corrected through the same code-execution channel over five and a half minutes, converging on a pipeline that discovers the host process identifier through the container runtime's own API, creates a privileged container binding the host root filesystem read-write and sharing the host process namespace, copies the binary out of the original container's process filesystem, runs it in scan mode, launches the live pass and then counts the resulting files to confirm it worked. The first script was delivered one line per request, keeping any single request inert to signature inspection; from the second onward the whole script arrived base64-encoded in a single call and decoded inside the execution sink, with the write confirmation leaked back through the application's error channel.

how.logic: An application process talking to the container daemon socket at all is the first signal, because an application framework has no reason to create containers. The second is the shape of the container it asks for: privileged, sharing the host process namespace, with the host root bound read-write. The third is a namespace-entering utility run with the init process as its target from inside a container, which crosses to the host and is never legitimate in an application container.
how.caveat: Orchestrators, build agents and monitoring sidecars legitimately create privileged containers, so this needs an allow-list of the identities permitted to call the daemon before it is usable; without one it will fire on the platform team. The escape container here borrowed an existing internal image name, so image reputation is not a discriminator.

what.summary: A load balancer and application delivery platform was exploited through its management interface by both Chinese state-sponsored actors and, in a later flaw, by ransomware operators, giving unauthenticated code execution on a device that terminates traffic for the applications behind it.

how.logic: Both flaws are reachable through the device's configuration interface, which should never be exposed beyond the management network. Any access to that interface from outside management space is either the intrusion or the exposure that allows it, and the check is the same for either flaw or for the next one.

fields.note: compare against management network ranges

how.caveat: The management interface being reachable is the finding; detecting its abuse is second best. Restricting it is a configuration change with no operational cost in most deployments.

how.logic: Because the device terminates traffic for the applications behind it, compromise yields both the traffic and the credentials in it. Check for files and configuration the release did not install, and treat any finding as compromise of everything that passed through the device.
how.caveat: The blast radius is the point: a compromised load balancer means assuming exposure of all session data and credentials it handled, not just the device itself.

where.title: Chinese State-Sponsored Cyber Operations: Observed TTPs

notes: Drawn from two advisories: a Chinese state-sponsored TTP overview naming the 2020 flaw, and a ransomware advisory naming the 2023 one. Both actor classes reached the same device through the same interface three years apart, which is the argument for restricting the management interface rather than tracking individual vulnerabilities.

who.versions_affected: Builds vulnerable to CVE-2022-42475

what.summary: State-sponsored actors exploited a firewall appliance flaw to establish presence on the perimeter device of an aeronautical sector organisation, in the same incident where a different actor had already entered through an unrelated application vulnerability.

how.logic: Establishing presence on a firewall means code or configuration on the appliance that no release put there. The vendor integrity check and the appliance's own filesystem listing are the available evidence, and both need running deliberately because nothing on the device reports it spontaneously.
how.caveat: An appliance an attacker controls may not report honestly on its own integrity. Where compromise is suspected the answer is out-of-band examination or replacement, not trusting the device's self-report.

how.logic: Two distinct nation-state actors were present at this organisation through two different vulnerabilities. The practical lesson for incident response is not to stop at the first entry point found: a victim exposed enough to be compromised once is exposed enough to be compromised twice, and evidence attributable to one actor does not account for the other. Scope by exposure surface rather than by the actor identified.

fields.note: enumerate every exposed service, not only the one that was exploited

how.caveat: An investigative discipline rather than a query. It is recorded because the natural instinct is to scope an incident around the actor identified first, which in this case would have missed a second intrusion entirely.

where.publisher: CISA, FBI and Cyber National Mission Force
where.title: Threat Actors Exploit Multiple Vulnerabilities in Zoho ManageEngine and Fortinet Devices
