who.versions_affected: Builds vulnerable to CVE-2020-12812

what.summary: A ransomware operation gained access through a remote access flaw where a change to the letter case of a username caused the second authentication factor to be skipped, meaning organisations that had correctly enabled two-factor authentication were still bypassed.

how.logic: This is the case that defeats an inventory check for whether a second factor is enabled, because it was enabled and it was skipped. The detection is to record, per successful authentication, whether a second factor was actually presented rather than whether the policy requires one. Any success without a presented factor is either a misconfiguration or a bypass, and both need finding. Comparing the username case against the enrolled form is the specific tell for this flaw.

fields.note: on a gateway where policy requires one
compare the case of the submitted username against the enrolled form

how.caveat: Many gateways do not log whether a second factor was presented, only that authentication succeeded. Where that field is unavailable this cannot be written, and the inventory check alone will report the control as working.

how.logic: Where the second factor is bypassed the session is otherwise indistinguishable from a legitimate one, so source network history per account is the remaining signal.
how.caveat: Travel and mobile networks move accounts legitimately. Rank on distance from that account's own history.

notes: The most instructive entry in the corpus for anyone auditing controls by configuration rather than by outcome. Every inventory check would have reported second-factor authentication as correctly enabled on this gateway. Recorded alongside the other second-factor records deliberately: one covers the factor not being enabled, one covers it being socially engineered away, and this covers it being enabled and silently skipped.

who.versions_affected: Per the vendor advisory accompanying the report; exploitation predates the fix by roughly four months

what.summary: A flaw in the management platform let an attacker-controlled appliance register itself to a victim's management server and pull the stored configuration of every firewall that server managed, including the managed device serials, addresses, policy packages and hashed local passwords. Better than fifty management appliances were assessed as potentially affected. Notably no follow-on activity was observed: the configurations were taken and, so far as the investigation could establish, not used.

how.logic: The attack begins with a device the operator did not add appearing in the management platform's own inventory. That is an administrative event with a very low legitimate rate in a steady estate, it is recorded by the platform in its own log, and it precedes the theft rather than following it. Alert on any device registration and reconcile against the change record, rather than trying to characterise which registrations are suspicious.
how.caveat: The legitimate rate is low but not zero, and it spikes during estate expansion or a migration, which is exactly when nobody wants extra alerts. Reconcile against the change record rather than suppressing during change windows, because a change window is the obvious time to hide a registration.

how.logic: Compromising the management server collapses the whole harvesting problem into one request: rather than logging into every firewall in turn, the actor took a single archive from the server that manages them. The detectable shape is an archive assembled in a temporary path on an appliance that has no reason to build archives, followed by an outbound transfer of comparable size. Appliance file systems are small and predictable, which makes a new multi-megabyte archive in a temporary directory unusual in a way it would not be on a general-purpose host.

markers.note: a dot-prefixed file in a temporary path on an appliance

how.caveat: Appliances rarely expose file creation telemetry, so in most estates only the outbound half is observable and the staging half has to be taken on trust or recovered forensically afterwards. Where the appliance does support it, size correlation between the staged file and the transfer is the strongest single discriminator available.

where.title: Mandiant investigation into FortiManager zero-day exploitation

who.versions_affected: Per the vendor advisory for the directory traversal flaw; the persistence technique is a property of the platform's boot design rather than of a particular release

what.summary: An espionage group took an internet-exposed management appliance, used it to push scripts to the firewalls it managed, and wrote implants into the compressed image those firewalls rebuild their filesystem from at every boot. The implants were then deleted from the running filesystem, so an operator inspecting a live device finds nothing. The binary that verifies boot signatures was patched by a single byte to skip verification, and the patch was reapplied on each boot so that hashing it later shows no change. The compromise was ultimately found because a compliance mode the operator had enabled compared checksums, failed to boot, and forced a forensic image.

how.logic: The running filesystem and the image it is built from are two different things on an appliance, and only one of them was modified. Every check that reads the live device returns clean, which is the property being bought. The only reliable answer is to compare the boot image against the vendor's, which on most platforms means a forensic acquisition rather than a query, so the practical detection is the boot-time evidence instead: a start-up script gaining an entry, and processes that exist briefly at boot and then remove themselves.

markers.note: start-up scripts are inside the persisted image, so an added line survives where a dropped file does not

how.caveat: Hunt rather than alert because most estates cannot read the boot image of a running appliance at all, which is the asymmetry the technique relies on. Where the vendor offers an integrity or malware removal tool, running it is worth more than any query available here, and it should be run after an upgrade rather than before, since the upgrade is what rewrites the image.

how.logic: The signature verification binary was altered by one byte so a conditional jump became unconditional, and the alteration was reapplied at each boot. Hashing the binary at any point after boot therefore shows the same value it has always shown. Two things still betray it: the reapplication itself is a write to a system binary at start-up, and a symbolic link stood where the platform ships a standalone binary, which is a structural fact no re-patching hides.

markers.note: byte-level write into a system binary at a fixed offset

how.caveat: File type and size are the checks that survive here, because content hashing is exactly what the technique defeats. Both need a per-version vendor baseline, and the baseline has to come from the vendor rather than from a device in the estate.

how.logic: Rather than dropping a file into a served directory, the platform's own interpreted source was edited to register a new route and the handler that serves it, with the authentication decorator omitted and the cross-site request check explicitly waived. The result is an endpoint that is part of the application, will survive a file-integrity check scoped to the web root, and answers without credentials.
how.caveat: Appliance vendors do not generally publish per-version hashes of their interpreted source, so the baseline usually has to be taken from a freshly imaged unit of the same version. The request-side marker is the one that works without any baseline at all, and is worth implementing first for that reason.

where.title: Fortinet Zero-Day and Custom Malware Used by Suspected Chinese Actor in Espionage Operation

who.versions_affected: Per the vendor advisory for the SSL VPN heap overflow; exploitation preceded public disclosure by roughly two months

what.summary: A backdoor built specifically for this platform, by somebody who had reverse engineered it thoroughly enough to disable the logging daemons by patching their memory at known offsets, and to parse and surgically rewrite the vendor's proprietary binary log format rather than deleting log files. Its most consequential feature is a watchdog: it monitors a platform library and, when that library changes size because the appliance has been patched, restores its own trojanised copy from a hidden backup. Patching the appliance therefore does not remove it.

how.logic: The implant expects to be patched and plans for it. It watches a library it has trojanised, and when an update replaces that library it writes its own copy back from a staging file kept elsewhere on the appliance. The detectable consequence is that a file which should have changed at update time reverts shortly afterwards, and that a copy of the legitimate library exists under a name the vendor does not ship. Verify integrity after an upgrade, not before, and verify again a short while later.
how.caveat: This is the pattern that invalidates patching as a remediation, and the response to it is replacement or rebuild rather than another update. It also means a single integrity check immediately after an upgrade is the one check guaranteed to return clean, so the timing of the check is the whole of its value.

how.logic: Two distinct methods on one appliance. The logging daemons were disabled by writing to their memory at fixed offsets, which leaves the processes running and reporting nothing, and separately the stored log records were parsed and individual entries rewritten in place. Neither produces a missing file or a stopped service, so a check on either finds nothing. What remains is volume: an appliance whose logging processes are alive while its forwarded log volume has fallen against its own history.

markers.expr: forwarded_copy_record_count exceeds on_device_record_count for same window

how.caveat: The record-level rewrite is only visible by comparing the forwarded copy against what remains on the appliance, which requires the logs to have been shipped somewhere the implant could not reach. Where they were not, this is undetectable after the fact, and forwarding becomes the control rather than the detection.

where.title: Suspected Chinese Threat Actors Exploiting FortiOS Vulnerability (CVE-2022-42475)

who.versions_affected: Multiple releases across five products; the subject is the spread across the family rather than any single release

what.summary: Eight pieces of research across four products in one vendor family, covering at least five distinct fault classes: two authentication bypasses, a pre-authentication command injection in the security monitoring product, a pre-authentication SQL injection reaching code execution in the web application firewall, a heap overflow in the remote access service and a format string flaw in the device-to-manager protocol. Unlike the recurring single fault seen elsewhere, this is breadth. The consequence that matters is that these products manage and monitor one another, so a flaw in the management or monitoring component reaches the enforcement devices rather than merely sitting beside them.

how.logic: The authentication bypass worked because a management channel became usable before the check governing it had finished. The web tier opened a session-upgraded channel on the presence of a token parameter rather than on its value, and the command interpreter behind it accepted input during its greeting, before the process enforcing the login context was ready. The durable detection is not the parameter but the consequence: a privileged command session existing on the appliance with no corresponding administrative login recorded on the web tier, and administrative actions attributed to a profile that never authenticated.

fields.note: the upgraded channel for this vendor; the shape is a management channel reached by protocol upgrade, and the path is vendor-specific

how.caveat: The first marker is the one to build and it needs the two logs joined, because each on its own looks normal: the appliance records a legitimate command session, and the web tier records nothing at all, which is the point. Where the appliance does not log command sessions separately from web logins this cannot be written, and that should be established before relying on it.

how.logic: Map which products in the family administer or monitor which others, and treat each management relationship as an access path rather than as an operational convenience. The practical checks are that the management components are not reachable from the internet, that the protocol they use between each other is restricted to known peers, and that a script or configuration push from a manager to a managed device is a recorded and reconcilable event.
how.caveat: This is a scoping finding before it is a detection, and the scoping is what people skip. Monitoring and management products are frequently excluded from exposure reviews on the grounds that they are security tooling, which inverts the actual risk: the one that can reconfigure everything else is the one worth reaching.

The vendor took a median of 127 days from report to public disclosure, so the flaw existed, known and unfixed, for that long before anyone outside could act on it. No detection logic is attached: an advisory states that a flaw exists, not that anyone exploited it.

what.summary: A five-nation advisory warning critical infrastructure operators that a conflict could expose organisations both inside and beyond the region to increased activity, as a response to economic measures and to materiel support given to one side. It names five Russian government and military organisations with demonstrated capability against both information and operational technology networks, including one belonging to a defence ministry research institute, and separately documents criminal groups publicly pledging allegiance and threatening retaliation against countries and organisations supporting the other side.

how.logic: The advisory's stated basis for warning organisations outside the region is the economic measures imposed and the materiel support provided by allied states. That makes the selection criterion the organisation's country and its commercial relationships rather than anything about its technology. Establish whether your organisation, its parent, its customers or its suppliers fall inside a category a threat actor has publicly named.
how.caveat: A risk assessment built on asset criticality and vulnerability counts cannot see this, because nothing in the estate changed. It also means a supplier's alignment can make you a target through a trusted connection nobody counted as attack surface.

how.logic: The advisory records criminal groups publicly pledging support for a government and threatening operations against countries and organisations providing materiel support, while others conducted disruptive attacks apparently in support of a military offensive. The tradecraft stays criminal while the objective may become disruption, which leaves a ransomware playbook without a counterparty to negotiate with.
how.caveat: Merges two response plans that are normally written separately and owned by different people. A group that extorts one week and destroys the next defeats each plan read on its own.

how.logic: The advisory cites two named destructive campaigns against government and critical infrastructure and warns that further options are being explored. Destructive activity removes the option of paying for recovery, which most ransomware planning silently assumes exists. The testable question is whether a known-good state can be reached with no cooperation from the attacker, within the stated tolerance, with the directory service and the virtualisation platform also assumed lost.
how.caveat: One of the named campaigns spread far beyond its intended targets and caused losses at organisations with no connection to the conflict, which is the argument for treating this as a preparedness question even where alignment-based targeting seems remote.

how.logic: The advisory states these actors have demonstrated the ability to exfiltrate from both information and operational technology networks and to disrupt control system functions by deploying destructive malware. One of the named organisations is a defence ministry research institute, which in this corpus is associated with the safety instrumented system intrusion, so the operational technology claim is not theoretical.

markers.expr: enumerate every reachable path from enterprise_zone to control_zone including vendor and licensing paths

how.caveat: The paths that get missed are rarely the remote access ones, which get listed anyway. They are business intelligence connections, licensing servers and vendor telemetry that reach out because a product requires them.

how.logic: The four actions the advisory puts above everything else are patching with priority on the published exploited catalogue, enforcing a second authentication factor, securing and monitoring remote desktop and similar services, and user training. Notably none of them is actor-specific, which is the point: against a named state threat the recommended response is the baseline done properly.
how.caveat: Worth quoting directly when a board asks what to do about a named state actor, because the honest answer is unglamorous and the advisory says so first.

where.publisher: CISA, NSA, FBI, ACSC, CCCS, NZ NCSC and NCSC-UK
where.title: Russian State-Sponsored and Criminal Cyber Threats to Critical Infrastructure

notes: The corpus's clearest example of a targeting model no technical control can influence: the reason to attack is the organisation's country and its commercial relationships. Two consequences worth carrying into a strategy conversation. First, a risk register built on vulnerabilities and asset criticality will not register the change, because nothing in the estate changed. Second, where criminal groups declare political allegiance the objective may shift from extortion to disruption, which invalidates the assumption underneath most ransomware planning that there is someone to pay. The advisory's own prioritised actions are all baseline controls, which is the most useful thing to quote when the question is what to do about a named state threat.

products: Internet-facing applications and appliances across many vendors
who.versions_affected: The vulnerabilities named in the annual list for the year in question

what.summary: An annual joint publication names the vulnerabilities most routinely exploited during the preceding year, drawn across many vendors, and is the closest thing available to an evidence-based prioritisation list for a mixed estate.

how.logic: Use it as an annual review input rather than a detection. Two things it gives that a scanner does not: evidence of which vulnerabilities attackers actually used at volume, and a spread across vendors that reveals which product classes carry the most exploited exposure. Working the list against your own exposed inventory produces a defensible remediation order, and the recurrence of the same flaws year on year is itself the finding worth escalating.

fields.note: joined against the annual list for each year, not only the current one

how.caveat: Publication lags the year it describes, so it is a review instrument rather than an early warning. Pair it with the continuously updated known-exploited catalogue for current work.

how.logic: Reading several annual lists together shows which product classes appear repeatedly: remote access appliances, file transfer products, collaboration platforms, directory services. That is a procurement and architecture signal as much as a patching one. Where a class recurs every year, the question is whether it needs to be internet-facing at all, not merely whether it is patched.

fields.note: count how many separate annual lists each product class appears on

how.caveat: An analytic exercise rather than a query, and it produces conclusions that belong to whoever owns architecture decisions rather than to a security operations team.

where.publisher: CISA, NSA, FBI and international partners
where.title: 2023 Top Routinely Exploited Vulnerabilities

notes: Recorded as a document class rather than a one-off, because the publication is annual and each edition is worth the same treatment. The vulnerability list here is a sample of the 2023 edition, not the whole of it. Worth pairing with the top-ten misconfigurations record: between them they cover what attackers exploited and what assessors keep finding, which is a more defensible basis for a work programme than either alone.

what.summary: Agencies described actors using an anonymising overlay network for reconnaissance, penetrating systems, exfiltrating and manipulating data, taking services offline and delivering ransomware, and relaying command traffic so that the location and ownership of their servers is concealed. Because activity appears to originate from an exit node rather than the user's own address, identity and point of origin cannot be determined, which makes recovery and response harder. The recommendation is that each organisation assess its own likelihood of being targeted and then block or closely monitor traffic to and from known nodes accordingly.

how.logic: The two directions carry very different weight. Inbound from exit nodes is constant background on anything internet-facing, so handling it is a filtering and risk decision rather than a detection. Outbound from an internal host to an entry or guard node is the valuable signal, because in a managed estate almost nothing has a legitimate reason to reach that network, and it indicates either relayed command traffic or a user deliberately evading controls.
how.caveat: Node lists are published and change constantly, so an automatically updated feed is required rather than a static list. Outbound from a server or a control-network host has essentially no legitimate case and deserves a much lower threshold than outbound from a user workstation.

how.logic: Because activity appears to originate from an exit node, identity and point of origin cannot be determined, which the agencies note makes system recovery and response harder. That is the same constraint the compromised-device networks impose by a different mechanism, and it leads to the same place: detection has to rest on session and account behaviour rather than on source.
how.caveat: Worth pairing with the covert network record. Two entirely different anonymisation methods, one volunteer-operated and one built from compromised devices, produce the same defensive conclusion about source-based reasoning.

how.logic: The agencies frame this as an individual risk assessment: judge the likelihood that an actor will target your systems and the probability of success given current controls, then choose to block, monitor closely, or accept. That is unusual and correct, because the answer differs sharply between an organisation whose service is meant to be publicly reachable and one whose is not.
how.caveat: The same network carries legitimate use including by people relying on it for safety, so a blanket inbound block is a policy decision with consequences beyond security. The advisory is careful about this and defenders should be too.

where.title: Defending Against Malicious Cyber Activity Originating from Tor

notes: Useful mainly for the asymmetry between the two directions, which is easy to get backwards. Inbound from exit nodes is noise and a filtering decision; outbound from an internal host to the network is close to a pure signal because nothing in a managed estate legitimately needs it. It also pairs with the covert network record: two completely different anonymisation mechanisms, one volunteer-run and one built from compromised consumer devices, arrive at the same conclusion that source address carries no information and detection must rest on behaviour.

what.summary: A financial trojan, itself an evolution of two earlier families whose code it shares, that infiltrates browsers, detects access to online banking applications and websites, and injects code and keylogging through interface hooking to steal customer login information. Modules package, encrypt and transmit captured data and screenshots over peer-to-peer networks, which improves concealment and redundancy. After stealing login data the actors can issue fraudulent payment instructions. Actors distributing it have also deployed ransomware. The advisory was produced with financial sector and financial crime authorities to inform that sector directly.

how.logic: The trojan hooks browser interfaces to detect a banking session and then injects code and keylogging into it. Detection is a process injecting into or loading a module inside a browser where it is not a known extension or security product. Because the loss event is a payment rather than an outage, reconciliation of payment instructions is a second and independent detection surface.
how.caveat: The harm appears in finance, often days later, not in security telemetry. Out-of-band verification of payment instructions limits the loss whether or not the endpoint compromise was ever found, which makes it the more reliable control of the two.

how.logic: Captured data and screenshots are packaged, encrypted and transmitted over peer-to-peer networks, which the advisory notes improves concealment and redundancy over earlier variants. Peer-to-peer command traffic means there is no fixed server to block and the destinations are other victims, so the detectable shape is a workstation holding many peer sessions rather than client-to-server traffic.

markers.expr: count_distinct(peer_ip) by host, bin(_time, 1h) on non_standard_ports

how.caveat: The same peer-relay shape as the espionage implant record here, arrived at for the same reason: resilience against takedown. Blocklists are ineffective by design because the destinations are ordinary victim machines.

how.logic: The objective is customer login information, taken both by keylogging and by reading stored credentials. Access to the browser credential stores by anything other than the browser itself is the tractable detection and it covers the theft even where the hooking is missed.
how.caveat: Also the supply side of the stolen-credential access route recorded elsewhere in this corpus: credentials taken here are used later, elsewhere, by someone else.

where.publisher: CISA and Department of the Treasury Financial Crimes Enforcement Network
where.title: Dridex Malware

notes: The only record in the corpus where the loss event is a payment rather than an outage or a data breach, which changes who detects it and when: finance notices a reconciliation discrepancy days later, not security noticing an alert. That makes out-of-band verification of payment instructions the control that bounds the damage regardless of whether the endpoint compromise is ever found. It is also a reminder that code lineage persists across family names, since this family shares code with two predecessors and its operators also deploy ransomware, so the malware identified says little about what will follow.

what.summary: A group that entered networks using valid remote desktop credentials, used open-source tooling and command-line scripting for discovery and credential harvesting, and exfiltrated by file transfer protocol and consumer cloud storage. It began with a double-extortion model, encrypting after exfiltrating, then shifted primarily to exfiltration-based extortion with victim systems left intact, and later to that model exclusively. The reporting agencies also state they are aware of multiple groups choosing foreign-language names to complicate attribution, and assess this group as likely based in a country different from the one its name suggests.

how.logic: The shift is documented across three stages: encryption plus exfiltration, then primarily exfiltration with systems left intact, then exclusively exfiltration. So every detection placed at the encryption stage fires never, and the remaining surface is bulk read, archiving and outbound transfer. Egress volume per host against its own baseline is the backstop when the tooling is not recognised.

markers.expr: sum(bytes_out) by host, bin(_time, 24h) against host_baseline

how.caveat: The consequence for programme measurement is stark: a ransomware capability assessed on encryption prevention scores perfectly here while the organisation still loses its data and is still extorted. It also removes the natural discovery moment, since with systems intact the first sign may be the extortion contact or a leak site listing.

how.logic: The agencies state directly that multiple groups choose foreign-language names almost certainly to complicate attribution, and assess this one as likely based in a country unrelated to its name, with affiliates in the same country. The name, the language of the notes and the apparent nationality of the branding are all attacker-chosen.

markers.expr: attribution_basis includes infrastructure_or_tooling rather than group_name_or_note_language

how.caveat: Matters wherever geography drives a decision, notably sanctions screening before payment and regulatory notification that turns on nationality. This is the third distinct mechanism in this corpus for deliberately corrupting attribution, alongside a state actor posing as a criminal group and a wiper posing as ransomware.

how.logic: Initial access was through valid remote desktop credentials, so there is no exploitation and no failed authentication to find. The detectable shape is a successful remote access session for an account from a source, device or autonomous system it has not used before, with no preceding failures.
how.caveat: Valid credentials for remote desktop is the single most repeated initial access route across the ransomware records in this corpus. A second factor on remote access is the control that breaks it, and its absence is the finding rather than the alert.

how.logic: With encryption abandoned there may be no technical event at all inside the estate to notice, which makes external signals materially more important. Monitoring extortion leak sites for your own name and your suppliers' names becomes a primary detection channel rather than a supplementary one.
how.caveat: An uncomfortable position to be in, since it means learning of a breach from the attacker's publication schedule. It is nonetheless the honest conclusion where the adversary leaves systems intact.

where.publisher: FBI, CISA and Australian Cyber Security Centre
where.title: #StopRansomware: BianLian Ransomware Group

notes: Strategically the most disruptive record in the corpus for how ransomware programmes are measured, because it removes the encryption stage entirely. A capability assessed on encryption prevention or recovery time scores perfectly against an adversary that never encrypts, while the organisation still loses its data and is still extorted. It also completes a set: this corpus now holds three independent mechanisms for corrupting attribution, a state actor branding itself as a criminal group, a wiper branding itself as ransomware, and a group choosing a name pointing at the wrong country. In each case the attacker-supplied identity was the least reliable input available.

what.summary: A ransomware operation that rebranded from an earlier name reached victims mainly by phishing, then by remote desktop and by buying access harvested from information stealer logs. It encrypted only a chosen percentage of each file to run faster and evade detection, disabled antivirus centrally by editing Group Policy from a domain controller, and exfiltrated before encrypting. Demands ranged from around one to ten million United States dollars, with over five hundred million demanded in total and a largest single demand of sixty million.

how.logic: The operator could choose what percentage of each file to encrypt and lowered it for larger files, which both accelerates the run and reduces what a detector keyed on whole-file rewriting sees. Any rule tuned against families that encrypt files completely, whether by entropy averaged over the file or by bytes written per file, will under-trigger here. Rate of files modified per process per minute survives the evasion; per-file measures do not.
how.caveat: The reason to record this is that it invalidates a specific and common tuning decision. It also affects recovery, since a partially encrypted file is unusable but may not register as corrupt to an integrity check.

how.logic: Using a legitimate administrator account, the actors logged on to a domain controller over file sharing and deactivated antivirus by modifying Group Policy Objects. Every affected endpoint then reports only that it applied policy correctly, so the detection has to live on the directory. Pair the policy modification event with an alert on protection coverage falling across many hosts at once, since the second is the consequence and is usually visible in a management console that nobody alerts from.
how.caveat: Antivirus being disabled fleet-wide is often reported as a coverage or health statistic rather than as a security event, which is how this succeeds. The account used was legitimate, so no authentication anomaly accompanies it.

how.logic: The actors sourced access from brokers who harvest remote access credentials from information stealer logs. The credential was valid and taken from somewhere else entirely, possibly a personal device and possibly long before, so the first sign inside the estate is a successful remote access authentication with no failure preceding it and a source or device that account has not used. Where a stealer campaign is reported, treat it as a reason to force rotation rather than as someone else's incident.
how.caveat: Directly connected to the information stealer record in this corpus, which counted tens of thousands of marketplace listings from one family. That is the supply side of this initial access vector, and multi-factor authentication on remote access is the control that breaks the link.

how.logic: Publicly available tools intended for driver-level process termination were used to kill security processes, alongside credential dumping and password recovery utilities. The tools are recognisable by name and, more durably, by the behaviour of one process terminating many others in quick succession, which nothing legitimate does.
how.caveat: Name matching dates quickly; the termination-count behaviour does not.

how.logic: Legitimate remote monitoring and management software was used for persistence, alongside several secure shell and terminal clients for command and control tunnelling and two loader families for maintaining access. Remote management tooling that is not the tooling your organisation licensed is the tractable form of this: the approved set is short, known, and everything else is an alert.
how.caveat: Remote management software is signed, legitimate and often already present for a business reason, so blocking by reputation fails. Maintain the approved list as an allow-list instead.

how.logic: Network share enumeration and network scanning tools were used to map victim networks, with credential dumping and password harvesting tools found on victim systems. Share enumeration across many hosts from one source in a short window is the shape, and it precedes encryption by long enough to matter.
how.caveat: Discovery is the last stage before staging and encryption, which makes it the last cheap opportunity to intervene.

notes: The rebrand from an earlier name is worth recording as a corpus fact in its own right: detections and blocklists indexed by family name silently stop matching, while the coding similarities and the tradecraft persist. Indexing by behaviour rather than by family is what survives a rename. Also notable is out-of-band pressure, with victims receiving telephone and email contact from the actors directly, which belongs in incident communications planning rather than in a detection.

what.summary: Following a coordinated international operation that took over a long-running loader botnet and severed the connection between victim computers and its command servers, two agencies published the infrastructure indicators identified through investigation. They state directly that the disruption does not mitigate other malware or ransomware already installed on victim computers, and they publish the hash of the uninstaller used in the operation for situational awareness. The stated purpose of releasing the indicators is to promote identification of infections and of the ransomware the loader facilitated.

how.logic: The agencies state plainly that disrupting the botnet does not mitigate other already-installed malware or ransomware on victim computers. So a takedown is a hunting trigger, not a resolution: search retained telemetry for historical contact with the named infrastructure, then examine those hosts for whatever the loader delivered before the disruption.
how.caveat: Takedowns are reported as good news and read as the end of the matter. This one removed the command channel, not the access that had been sold, the credentials taken, or the ransomware staged. The corpus elsewhere records that access to hosts compromised by this same loader family was bought repeatedly by unrelated actors, which is exactly the residue a takedown leaves behind.

how.logic: The published indicators are infrastructure identified as of the operation date, which makes them most valuable against data from before it rather than for forward matching, since the infrastructure is now under law enforcement control. Retention reaching back past the operation is what makes the release useful at all.
how.caveat: A recurring shape in this corpus: an indicator set published after the fact is only actionable where retention predates the activity. Several records here depend on the same condition without stating it.

how.logic: This loader appears on the annual top malware list elsewhere in this corpus as one of two families in use for more than a decade, and it facilitated ransomware for other operators. Coverage for the loader stage is therefore reusable across every payload it delivered, which is the argument for detecting at that stage rather than per family.
how.caveat: Family name matching is weak here because the code base evolved over more than a decade. The delivery surface, a mail attachment, is the durable part and is shared with most of the other families on that list.

where.title: Identification and Disruption of QakBot Infrastructure

notes: The only takedown record in the corpus and worth keeping for the caution the agencies state directly: disrupting the botnet does not mitigate malware or ransomware already installed on victim machines. A takedown removes the command channel and nothing else, so the correct response is a retrospective hunt against retained data from before the operation, followed by examination of any host that contacted the infrastructure. It pairs with the ecosystem record here noting that access to hosts compromised by this same family was repeatedly sold to unrelated actors, which is precisely the residue left behind.

who.versions_affected: A large set of separately disclosed vulnerabilities spanning 2017 to 2022

what.summary: A state-sponsored espionage campaign against defence and aerospace targets exploited a very large catalogue of separately disclosed vulnerabilities across many vendors, rather than relying on a small number of favoured flaws or on unpublished ones.

how.logic: Where an actor's approach is breadth across dozens of published vulnerabilities rather than depth in a few, no per-vulnerability detection strategy scales. The workable response is a join: take the published catalogue of vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild, intersect it with your own externally reachable asset inventory, and treat the result as the queue. That covers this actor and every other one working the same way, and it updates itself as the catalogue does.

fields.note: joined against the published known-exploited catalogue rather than a per-advisory list

how.caveat: This is a vulnerability management process, not a detection, and the corpus records it as such. The catalogue is a maintained structured file, so the join can be automated and re-run rather than assembled from advisories by hand.

where.publisher: FBI, CISA, NSA and international partners
where.title: North Korea Cyber Group Conducts Global Espionage Campaign to Advance Regime's Military and Nuclear Programs

notes: The advisory lists considerably more vulnerabilities than the twelve recorded here; the field is a representative sample rather than the full set, because the full list belongs in a vulnerability management tool joined to the published catalogue rather than in a detection record. This is the clearest case in the corpus for the exposure record type: the value is coverage of which products are named, not detection logic, and each one carries none of the latter.

who.versions_affected: Any version storing credentials in a local database

what.summary: Saved browser credentials were taken by copying the browsers' own credential database files using a signed Windows database maintenance utility, which avoids reading the live files and avoids bringing in any tooling.

how.logic: The utility is a legitimate database repair tool that ships with Windows, invoked here with a recovery switch to produce a copy of a locked credential database. The command line is the detection and it is close to unambiguous: this utility has no reason to be referencing a browser profile directory at all. Both major browsers' credential stores were targeted, so match on the utility plus a browser profile path rather than on either alone.
how.caveat: Effectively no false positives for this combination, which makes it one of the cheapest high-value endpoint rules available. It does require command line capture; without it there is nothing to match.

how.logic: Independent of how the copy is made, the credential database files themselves are a small fixed set of names in predictable locations. Any process that is not the browser opening them is worth an alert, which covers tooling this advisory did not name.

fields.note: anything other than the owning browser or an approved backup product

how.caveat: Backup and endpoint management software reads these paths. Allow-list by signer. Browser processes themselves must be excluded or this is constant noise.

where.publisher: CISA, FBI, Europol EC3 and NCSC-NL
where.title: #StopRansomware: Akira Ransomware

notes: The same utility appears in this corpus from an unrelated industrial-sector advisory, used for a different purpose. Worth treating the utility as a general-purpose signal rather than tying it to one campaign: it exists to manipulate database files and attackers use it for whichever database they want.

what.summary: A joint advisory on Chinese state-sponsored activity assessed that the actors chiefly exploited publicly known vulnerabilities across more than thirty identifiers and relied on commonly available offensive frameworks and utilities rather than bespoke capability. It also documents the preparation stage in unusual detail: acquiring third-party services that cannot be traced back, compromising other parties' infrastructure to deliver from, hijacking domain registrations to use legitimate domains as launch points, and scanning with public internet-wide search tools to select targets.

how.logic: The advisory names the frameworks and utilities used: a commercial command and control framework with its agent, a credential dumping tool, an older remote access trojan, a public post-exploitation framework and a widely reused web shell. That converts a state-actor advisory into a coverage checklist with a definite answer, because for each named item you either detect it or you do not.
how.caveat: Cuts both ways, and that is the strategic value. Baseline detections earn their keep against a state actor, and equally a rule built around this actor's tooling will fire on unrelated criminal activity, so attribution must not be inferred from the tool.

how.logic: The exploited set spans remote access appliances, load balancers, mail servers, directory services, small business routers, application servers and an office suite flaw first published in 2012 that was still being used. Joining the published catalogue to the inventory covers all of it without tracking individual advisories, and the presence of an eight-year-old identifier in an active state campaign is the argument against prioritising by disclosure date.
how.caveat: Several of these identifiers appear on multiple annual routinely-exploited lists, which means the exposure is not a backlog to clear but a standing condition to manage.

how.logic: Three preparation techniques in the advisory all point the same way: staging from software-as-a-service platforms that cannot easily be tied back to the actor, compromising infrastructure owned by other parties to deliver from rather than buying it, and hijacking domain registrations so a legitimate domain becomes the launch point. Every one of these makes the origin look trustworthy, so origin reputation is not a usable control against this actor.
how.caveat: A recent registrar or nameserver change on an established domain is the closest thing to a marker for registration hijacking, and it is noisy because legitimate transfers happen. Useful as enrichment on an already-suspicious destination rather than as a standalone signal.

how.logic: Target selection used public internet-wide search services to find exposed devices, followed by analysis of the scan results to identify architectural flaws and misconfigurations. The defensive counterpart is to query those same public services for your own ranges, which tells you what the actor's selection stage would return.

markers.expr: asset appears in public_internet_scan_index(shodan, censys) for owned_ranges

how.caveat: One of the few detections in this corpus that can be run from the attacker's side of the problem, at no cost, with an unambiguous result. Anything it returns that is not on your inventory is the finding.

where.title: Potential for China Cyber Response to Heightened US-China Tensions

notes: Worth holding onto for the strategic argument rather than the indicators. A state actor achieving its objectives with public vulnerabilities and public tooling means the gap being exploited is patching and baseline detection, not a shortfall in advanced capability. The advisory's own framing supports this: using known vulnerabilities complicates attribution, reduces cost and avoids risking a zero day that would be lost once known. The preparation-stage detail is the other reason to keep it, because it explains directly why domain reputation and geography fail as controls.

what.summary: A two-nation review of the eleven most observed malware families in a year, finding that most had been in use for more than five years and two for more than a decade. The families are remote access trojans, banking trojans, information stealers and ransomware, operated predominantly by criminals to deliver ransomware or steal credentials. Two of the most prolific are marketed by their developers as legitimate remote management and penetration testing products and can be purchased online cheaply. Access to systems compromised by one loader was bought repeatedly by different actors, and one loader family enabled a ransomware operation used in around 450 attacks in six months.

how.logic: The advisory names eleven families and states plainly that actors using known strains gives defenders the opportunity to prepare, identify and mitigate. That converts the report into a coverage audit against a short, published, stable list, where each entry has a definite answer: does anything in the estate detect its delivery, its execution or its command traffic. The shared delivery surface across the list is a mail attachment, which is where a single control covers many of them.
how.caveat: Family-name matching dates quickly and the code bases have evolved into many variants, which the advisory notes. The durable use is as a checklist to audit coverage against, not as a signature set. That two families over a decade old still top the table is evidence the binding constraint is coverage rather than adversary novelty.

how.logic: The advisory records that the developers of two named families market them as legitimate tools for remote management and penetration testing, that they can be bought online for low cost, and that actors have been observed using both for malicious purposes. So the binary is commercial software with a vendor and a licence. A decision procedure based on whether software is malicious cannot resolve this; one based on whether the organisation licensed it can.
how.caveat: The same reasoning already applies to the remote monitoring products in the ransomware records in this corpus, and this is the case that generalises it: maintaining an accurate inventory of the remote access software you actually bought is a detection control, not an asset management chore.

how.logic: Developers build, distributors broker and end users operate, and the advisory records that access to systems compromised by one loader was purchased on multiple occasions by different actors for different operations. So the family that got in predicts very little about what happens next, and the same foothold may be used by parties with no connection to each other.

markers.expr: incident_scope covers all_access_reachable_from_foothold rather than observed_family_behaviour

how.caveat: The practical consequence is about eviction rather than detection. A host cleaned of a loader whose harvested credentials were never rotated remains sellable, so remediation that looks complete can be followed by unrelated access using what the first actor took.

how.logic: One named loader is recorded as often enabling the ransomware operation used in around 450 attacks in the first half of a single year. The loader stage is shared across those attacks while the final payload varies, which makes the loader and the stages between it and encryption the economical place to detect rather than the ransomware itself.
how.caveat: Reinforces the loader-stage argument made by the healthcare record in this corpus: the same loaders recur across unrelated ransomware operations, so detections placed at that stage are reused across many end payloads rather than needing one per family.

how.logic: The named information stealers take data from mail clients, browsers and file transfer clients, capture screenshots and clipboard contents, and the advisory notes the resulting credentials and tokens become available for purchase. That is the supply side of the stolen-credential access route recorded elsewhere in this corpus, and it links a commodity infection on one device to a later authenticated intrusion somewhere else.
how.caveat: Mass phishing campaigns using three of these families carried pandemic themes, which is a reminder that lure topicality tracks the news rather than the target, so content-based user training dates faster than the technique does.

where.publisher: CISA and Australian Cyber Security Centre
where.title: 2021 Top Malware Strains

notes: The most useful record in the corpus for arguing where detection effort should go, because it is a bounded published list rather than a single campaign. Three findings compound into one strategic point. The top families are old, most over five years and two over a decade, so novelty is not what defeats defenders. Two of the most prolific are commercial products with a vendor and a licence, so maliciousness is not a decidable property and only an allow-list of licensed software resolves it. And the developer, distributor and operator are separate parties who resell access, so the family that got in tells you almost nothing about what comes next and eviction must cover everything the foothold could reach rather than what the family is known to do.

what.summary: An agency responded to an attack affecting control and communication assets on the operational network of a natural gas compression facility. A spearphishing link gave initial access to the business network, from which the actor pivoted to the operational network because robust segmentation between the two had not been implemented, then deployed commodity ransomware encrypting assets on both. Operator interfaces, historians and polling servers lost availability, so operators could no longer read and aggregate real-time data from lower-level devices, producing a partial loss of view. No controllers were affected and control of operations was never lost. The victim's emergency response plan did not specifically consider cyberattacks, and a deliberate controlled shutdown was chosen, lasting about two days with consequent loss of productivity and revenue before normal operations resumed.

how.logic: The plan did not consider cyberattacks, and the operator chose a controlled shutdown despite retaining control of the process throughout. That makes the two-day outage a decision rather than a technical consequence. Deciding in advance whether operations continue under loss of view with control retained, with engineering and safety input, is what separates that outcome from a monitored degraded run.
how.caveat: The controllers were untouched and control was never lost, so the shutdown was precautionary. That is a defensible decision in the absence of a plan, which is precisely the argument for having one: without it the safe default under pressure is always to stop.

how.logic: The agency states directly that the victim failed to implement robust segmentation between the business and operational networks, which allowed the adversary to traverse the boundary and disable assets on both. Initial access was an ordinary spearphishing link, so what turned a business network compromise into an operational outage was entirely the reachability between them.

markers.expr: enumerate every reachable path from enterprise_zone to control_zone including vendor, licensing and telemetry paths

how.caveat: Nothing about the malware was operational-technology aware. Commodity ransomware caused an operational outage purely because it could reach those assets, which means the boundary, not the payload, determined the impact.

how.logic: The assets that lost availability were operator interfaces, historians and polling servers, so operators could no longer read and aggregate real-time data from lower-level devices. That is a partial loss of view with control intact, and it presents as several data-collection assets going silent together rather than as anything obviously malicious.
how.caveat: Loss of view without loss of control is a distinct state worth naming in the plan, because it is recoverable and does not necessarily require stopping. Several collection assets falling silent simultaneously is the signal for it.

how.logic: Ransomware encrypted assets on both networks, so recovery depended on backups for operational assets as well as business ones. Operational estates frequently have no tested restore path for interfaces and historians, because those systems are treated as appliances rather than as servers.
how.caveat: Two days of downtime for a partial loss of view suggests recovery of those assets was not rehearsed. The restore path for operator interfaces and historians is the one most often missing from an operational continuity plan.

notes: The cleanest demonstration in the corpus that operational impact does not require operational-technology-aware malware. Commodity ransomware, delivered by an ordinary spearphishing link, produced a two-day shutdown purely because the business and operational networks were not properly separated. The most instructive detail is that control was never lost and no controller was touched: the shutdown was a precautionary decision taken because the emergency plan did not cover the scenario. Deciding in advance whether operations continue under loss of view with control retained is what turns that into a monitored degraded run instead of an outage.

what.summary: Two agencies set out the sequence actors follow against control systems and state twice that traditional approaches to securing these assets do not adequately address current threats. The reasons given are structural: the assets are designed for availability and safety, frequently run decades-old software with no recent security updates, their designs and documentation are publicly available, they incorporate known vulnerable information technology components, and newer models add remote connectivity that enlarges the attack surface. The advisory notes that advanced actors have developed tools specifically for scanning, compromising and controlling operational technology devices, and that consequences are physical, including loss of life and property damage.

how.logic: The five stages are: establish the intended effect and select a target, collect intelligence about the target system, develop techniques and tools to navigate and manipulate it, gain initial access, and execute to create the effect. The advisory notes well-resourced actors run these concurrently and repeatedly. The useful exercise is to name, for each stage, what would be observable in your environment and which control addresses it. Stages one to three happen largely outside your network, so a defence built only around initial access engages the sequence late and only once.
how.caveat: The advisory is unusually blunt that the traditional approach is inadequate, and its proposed replacement is prioritising hardening by actor behaviour rather than working a control catalogue. That is a resourcing argument as much as a technical one.

how.logic: Device designs and documentation are publicly available and the systems incorporate known information technology components, so the intelligence collection stage can be completed without touching the target. The defensive counterpart is to perform the same collection against yourself, across public scan indexes, vendor documentation, procurement records and staff profiles, and treat anything found that is absent from your inventory as the finding.
how.caveat: Explains directly why obscurity is not available as a control in this domain: the information an attacker needs is published by the vendor as a matter of course, and increasingly by the operator through procurement and planning records.

how.logic: The advisory identifies the convergence of information and operational technology platforms as the mechanism that increased exploitation risk, alongside external connections and remote access added to newer assets to allow remote control and operations. So the enumeration has to include the connections added for operational convenience, not only the ones added for administration.

markers.expr: enumerate every reachable path from enterprise_zone to control_zone including vendor, licensing, telemetry and remote_operations paths

how.caveat: The paths added to enable remote operations are the ones least likely to appear on a network diagram, because they were justified as a business capability rather than as an administrative access route.

how.logic: The advisory records that advanced actors have developed tools for scanning, compromising and controlling operational technology devices, which means purpose-built tooling now exists for this environment rather than only repurposed information technology tooling. On a control network the set of software that should ever run is small, fixed and enumerable, which makes anything outside it a strong signal.
how.caveat: The strongest detection available on a control network precisely because the legitimate software set barely changes. Its weakness is that the inventory has to exist and be maintained, and on estates with decades-old assets it frequently does not.

where.title: Control System Defense: Know the Opponent

notes: The most useful strategic frame in the corpus for operational technology, because it is organised around the attacker's sequence rather than around a control catalogue, and because it states plainly that the traditional approach is inadequate. The two structural facts worth carrying into any funding conversation are that these assets are designed for availability and safety rather than security and often cannot be patched at all, and that the reconnaissance stage is free because the designs are published. Every OT record in this corpus is an instance of one of the five stages, which makes this the natural index for them.

products: small office and home office routers

what.summary: Fifteen national authorities described a major shift by China-nexus actors away from individually procured infrastructure towards externally provisioned large-scale networks of compromised devices, mainly consumer routers and connected devices. The assessment is that most China-nexus actors now use these networks, that several exist and are constantly updated, and that one network may serve multiple actors. They are used at every phase of an intrusion, from reconnaissance scanning through malware delivery and command traffic to exfiltration, and also for deniable browsing while actors research techniques and victims. Some also carry legitimate customer traffic. There is evidence these networks are built and maintained by Chinese information security companies, with one publicly named example having infected more than two hundred thousand devices worldwide under the control of a named commercial company. Two named state groups used them, one to pre-position on critical national infrastructure and one for espionage.

how.logic: The networks exist to connect in a low-cost, low-risk, deniable way that disguises origin and attribution. So the source address is a consumer connection in a plausible geography, it changes constantly, one network may be shared between unrelated actors, and some networks also carry genuine customer traffic. Every conclusion drawn from where a session appears to originate is unsafe, which forces detection onto session and account behaviour.
how.caveat: Three consequences follow. Geographic and reputation blocking is defeated by design. Attribution from infrastructure is unsafe, because one network serves several actors. And an address attacking you may belong to a household or small business that is itself a victim, which matters before reporting or publishing it.

how.logic: The networks are built mainly from compromised consumer routers and connected devices, and one named example reached over two hundred thousand of them. The inventory question is which devices at your sites and at home-working locations are consumer grade, unmanaged, unpatched and internet reachable, followed by the relay shape of a device both receiving and originating sessions with no local user activity to account for either.

markers.expr: device_class in (soho_router, iot, camera, nvr) and internet_reachable and outside_central_management

how.caveat: Recruitment is not targeting: the organisation may never be the intended victim, yet it carries the traffic, appears in someone else's incident reporting and hosts an unmanaged compromised device. Home-working locations are the hardest part to inventory and the easiest to leave out of scope.

how.logic: Consumer routers and connected devices are the raw material because they are numerous, unpatched, rarely inventoried and frequently past vendor support. That makes the defensive action the same one recorded elsewhere in this corpus for end-of-life edge equipment, approached from the direction of what the device becomes for someone else rather than what it exposes for you.
how.caveat: The corpus now holds three separate advisories naming small-router and camera vulnerabilities in state-sponsored activity. At that point the device class is the finding and replacement is the control, since patching is not available for much of it.

how.logic: Because the relays are consumer connections chosen for plausibility, traffic arriving from them resembles a member of staff working from home. The advisory records use across every phase, including reconnaissance scanning and exfiltration, so the same source category appears at both ends of an intrusion.
how.caveat: Consumer broadband is also where legitimate remote workers are, which is the entire point of the choice. Only the behaviour of the session separates them, never the address.

where.publisher: NCSC-UK with fourteen international partner agencies
where.title: Defending Against China-Nexus Covert Networks of Compromised Devices

notes: The most current strategic record here and the one that most constrains how the rest of the corpus should be used. If most China-nexus actors now route through shared networks of compromised consumer devices, then source address, geography and reputation carry no information, and any record whose detection leans on them is weaker than it appears. It also completes an argument the corpus has been building across several records: unmanaged edge devices matter less for what they expose than for what they become. The commercial dimension is worth noting too, since one such network was operated by a named information security company, which places this alongside the front-company and contractor records as state capability delivered through commercial entities.

who.versions_affected: Not applicable

what.summary: Iranian actors used password spraying and multi-factor push bombing against healthcare, government, information technology, engineering and energy organisations, and the assessed aim was to obtain credentials and network descriptions in order to sell that access on to criminal groups.

how.logic: The same technique recorded elsewhere in this corpus for a criminal extortion group, here used by a state-sponsored actor. That matters for triage: the shape in the logs is identical, so the detection does not distinguish them and should not try to. A burst of denied or expired prompts for one account followed by an approval is the signal regardless of who is behind it.

fields.note: count denials per account in a window, then look for a subsequent approval

how.caveat: Number matching and prompt rate limiting remove the technique outright, which is a better answer than detecting it.

how.logic: Password spraying inverts the brute force shape: few attempts against many accounts rather than many against one. Count distinct accounts attempted per source as well as failures per account, or the spray passes under a per-account threshold entirely.
how.caveat: A per-account lockout threshold does not detect spraying by design. The distinct-account count is what catches it.

how.logic: The stated aim was resale rather than direct exploitation, which changes what to expect after a credential compromise. A broker takes credentials and a description of the network and then leaves, so the follow-on activity may arrive weeks later from an entirely different actor with different objectives, including ransomware. Treat a credential compromise as an event with a delayed and unrelated second stage rather than as an intrusion that either progressed or did not.

fields.note: and whether any subsequent unrelated activity followed weeks later on the same account

how.caveat: Changes incident closure criteria rather than detection. A credential compromise with no observed follow-on is not necessarily contained, and closing it as unexploited is the error this record exists to prevent.

where.publisher: FBI, CISA, NSA, ASD's ACSC and international partners
where.title: Iranian Cyber Actors' Brute Force and Credential Access Activity Compromises Critical Infrastructure Organizations

notes: The most consequential detail is the motive. A state-sponsored actor harvesting access to sell to criminals collapses the usual separation between state and criminal threat models, and it means the actor who eventually causes the damage may have no relationship to the one who got in. Any risk assessment that reasons from a state actor's likely objectives will misjudge this.

what.summary: A data extortion group whose victims reported no encryption of machines or files at all. It claimed to have stolen data and threatened to auction or publish it, with demands from twenty-five thousand to thirteen million United States dollars in cryptocurrency and payment deadlines typically expiring within a week of first contact. Proof was supplied as screenshots or copies of file directory listings. The group contacted the victims' employees, business partners and clients with harassing emails and phone calls to increase pressure. Access came through outdated and unpatched remote access appliances and servers, followed by a commercial intrusion framework, credential dumping, commercial remote access software, and exfiltration of very large volumes, in many cases entire shared drives over a terabyte, by file transfer services. The advisory was co-authored with financial crime authorities.

how.logic: Victims reported no encryption of any machine or file, so every detection placed at the encryption stage fires never and there is no outage to prompt investigation. The remaining surface is bulk read, archiving and outbound transfer, and here the volumes were extreme enough that egress measurement alone would have caught it.
how.caveat: The second exfiltration-only group in this corpus and the earlier of the two, which establishes this as an established model rather than a recent shift. A programme measured on encryption prevention scores perfectly against both.

how.logic: Data was compressed, typically with a common archiver, and exfiltrated in volumes that in many cases exceeded a terabyte and covered entire network-connected shared drives. That is unmissable if egress per host is measured at all, and the staging step leaves a very large archive in a location archives do not belong.
how.caveat: One of the few genuinely obvious signals in this corpus, missed because egress volume per host is often not measured. An entire shared drive leaving one workstation has no benign explanation.

how.logic: The group contacted employees, business partners and clients with harassing emails and phone calls to pressure the victim into paying. That is a communications and preparedness question rather than a technical one: whether the plan anticipates the attacker briefing your customers before you do, and who is authorised to respond.
how.caveat: The hardest element to prepare for, because the recipients are people you cannot brief in advance unless the plan already says how. Deadlines expiring within a week of first contact compress the decision window further.

how.logic: Initial access came through remote access appliances and servers that were outdated, unserviceable or unpatched, including a named remote access client and server platform, plus a logging library flaw. All are inventory-answerable rather than requiring any actor indicator.
how.caveat: The unserviceable case is the harder one, since no patch exists. That makes it a replacement decision rather than a maintenance task, consistent with the other end-of-life records here.

where.publisher: FBI, CISA, Department of the Treasury and Financial Crimes Enforcement Network
where.title: Karakurt Data Extortion Group

notes: Establishes exfiltration-only extortion as an established model rather than a recent development, since it predates the other such group in this corpus by two years. Two things distinguish it. The volumes were extreme, entire shared drives over a terabyte, which means egress measurement alone would have detected it and the absence of that measurement is the failure. And pressure was applied through the victim's own employees, partners and clients, which moves part of the response into communications planning for audiences the organisation cannot brief in advance. The involvement of financial crime authorities also signals the payment decision carries reporting obligations beyond the incident itself.

who.versions_affected: Vulnerabilities disclosed between 2009 and 2021, all long patched

what.summary: A ransomware operation gained initial access using vulnerabilities disclosed as far back as 2009 and 2010, alongside 2017 file-sharing flaws and the 2021 chained mail server flaws, demonstrating that a patch being fifteen years old does not mean it has been applied.

how.logic: Vulnerability programmes rank by score and by recency, and both biases work against this. A 2009 flaw on an internet-facing application server scores badly on recency and is often absent from a scanner's current plugin priority, yet it was exploited successfully. The check is to sort your exposed inventory by the age of the oldest unpatched vulnerability rather than by severity, which surfaces a different and usually more alarming list.

fields.note: sort exposed assets by the age of their oldest unpatched flaw, not by severity

how.caveat: Assets carrying decade-old unpatched flaws are usually unsupported, forgotten, or owned by nobody currently employed. The remediation is rarely patching; it is decommissioning or isolating, which needs an owner to be found first.

how.logic: The advisory recommends phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication specifically for all privileged accounts and email service accounts. The distinction from ordinary second-factor enforcement matters: push and code-based factors are defeated by the social engineering recorded elsewhere in this corpus, and phishing-resistant methods are not.

fields.note: on privileged and email service accounts, where phishing-resistant methods are the recommendation

how.caveat: Phishing-resistant enrolment is a rollout project rather than a setting. Prioritising privileged and mail accounts is the achievable subset the advisory itself names.

notes: The most useful counterweight in the corpus to the hours-scale exploitation records. Both are true: newly disclosed flaws are weaponised within hours, and fifteen-year-old flaws still work. A programme built only around the former leaves the latter entirely open, and the latter is where the forgotten assets are.

who.versions_affected: Not applicable

what.summary: Russian state-sponsored actors regularly targeted cleared defence contractors over two years, deliberately including small contractors and subcontractors with varying levels of security resourcing, to reach programmes covering command and control systems, surveillance and targeting, weapons and missile development, and vehicle design.

how.logic: The targeting explicitly spanned large and small contractors because the programme information is shared down the chain while the security resourcing is not. For a prime contractor the question is which subcontractors hold programme data or have network access, and what their actual security posture is rather than what their contract asserts. For a subcontractor the question is whether being small is being treated as a reason for low likelihood, which this advisory contradicts directly.

fields.note: verified rather than contractually asserted

how.caveat: Verification of a subcontractor's posture is a contractual and commercial matter, and small suppliers often genuinely cannot afford what a prime would specify. Recording the disparity is achievable; closing it usually is not.

how.logic: One of the named mitigations was simply enabling the productivity suite's unified audit log, which is off or under-retained by default in many tenants. Without it, mailbox access, forwarding rule creation and administrative changes leave no durable record, so an investigation into email theft has nothing to work from. Confirm it is enabled, confirm retention, and confirm the logs leave the tenant.
how.caveat: Longer retention is frequently a licensing purchase rather than a setting, which is why it goes unaddressed. Worth knowing before an incident rather than during one.

how.logic: The named vulnerabilities were a remote access appliance flaw and two mail server flaws, all published and patched before the campaign. Same shape as elsewhere in this corpus: the exposure was patch lag on internet-facing services rather than anything novel.
how.caveat: Detection here is secondary to patch currency on the two product classes named.

where.title: Russian State-Sponsored Cyber Actors Target Cleared Defense Contractor Networks to Obtain Sensitive U.S. Defense Information and Technology

notes: The programme areas named are worth recording because they indicate what the collection was for rather than only who was hit: command, control, communications and combat systems; intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and targeting; weapons and missile development; and vehicle design. Complements the records on managed service providers and partner domain trusts as a third variety of the same structural weakness.

who.versions_affected: Not applicable

what.summary: An incident response engagement at a federal agency identified three failures rather than a clever adversary: public-facing vulnerabilities were not promptly remediated, the incident response plan had never been tested or exercised, and the endpoint detection tool's alerts were not being continuously reviewed. The tool had generated the alerts that eventually revealed the intrusion.

how.logic: The uncomfortable finding is that detection worked and response did not. Measure the gap directly rather than assuming it away: what proportion of alerts raised in the last quarter were opened by a human, what the median time to first review was, and how many alert classes have never been reviewed at all. An unreviewed alert is indistinguishable from no detection, so a corpus of detections like this one is worth precisely nothing without that review capacity.

fields.note: against alerts triaged, per alert class, over a defined period

how.caveat: This is a resourcing measurement, not a query, and it usually surfaces an uncomfortable number. It belongs in front of whoever decides staffing levels. Every alert-fidelity detection in this corpus assumes somebody is reading the output.

how.logic: An incident response plan that has never been exercised fails at the points nobody anticipated: who has authority to disconnect a system, where the out-of-hours contact list lives when the mail system is down, whether anyone can actually restore from the backups. Exercise it, and specifically exercise it under the assumption that the normal tooling and communications are unavailable.
how.caveat: Not technical work and not something a security team can complete alone, since it needs the people with authority to make decisions in the room. That is why it goes untested.

how.logic: The recommendation is specific and worth taking literally: comprehensive and verbose logging, aggregated centrally and out of band. Out of band matters because an intruder with administrative control of the estate can reach an in-band log platform and alter or delete what it holds, and because a ransomware event that encrypts the log platform destroys the evidence needed to scope it. Verify that the aggregation point is not reachable with estate credentials.
