fields.note: whether the log platform is reachable and administrable with ordinary estate credentials

how.caveat: Most log platforms are joined to the same directory they collect from, which makes them in band by definition. Fixing that is an architecture change, so the interim measure is an independent copy of the highest-value log sources.

where.title: CISA Shares Lessons Learned from an Incident Response Engagement

notes: The most self-critical record in this corpus and arguably the most important. Everything else here describes what to detect; this describes an organisation that had the detection, generated the alerts, and did not read them. Worth reading alongside the top-ten misconfigurations record and the insufficient-logging record: all three say the constraint is capacity and process rather than knowledge.

who.versions_affected: Not applicable

what.summary: In two separate red team assessments the perimeter network was not adequately firewalled from the internal network, giving a path from the demilitarised zone straight into internal segments, which a correctly configured perimeter should block outright.

how.logic: The finding is a rule set question, not an event. Enumerate what a host in the demilitarised zone can actually reach on the internal network, by testing rather than by reading the intended policy, because the two diverge over years of change requests. Any path from an externally exposed segment into internal networks is the finding. Separately, alert on observed sessions originating in that segment toward internal hosts, since even where the path exists it should be a short known list.
how.caveat: Requires zones to be defined in the asset inventory. The reason this keeps being found is that the rule set is correct when built and erodes afterwards, so it needs periodic re-testing rather than a one-off review.

where.title: CISA red team assessment findings, combined from three published assessments

notes: Distilled from three CISA red team advisories that reported the same finding independently. Because these are authorised assessments rather than intrusions, the findings describe what a competent operator would have been able to do, which makes them prioritisation evidence rather than incident history.

what.summary: An agency reported a global campaign hijacking name resolution infrastructure. Using compromised credentials for an account able to change name records, attackers altered address, mail exchanger and name server records, replacing the legitimate address of a service with one they controlled, and so redirected and intercepted web and mail traffic, able to manipulate or inspect it before passing it on. Because they could set the record values, they were also able to obtain valid encryption certificates for the organisation's domain names, which allowed redirected traffic to be decrypted while end users received no error warnings. The agency notes this creates a risk that persists beyond the period of redirection.

how.logic: Three surfaces. Change events on registrar and hosting accounts, which should be rare and are the moment of compromise. Continuous comparison of published records against an authoritative reference you hold yourself. And certificate transparency monitoring for your own domains, because a certificate issued to someone else is both the evidence and the mechanism by which the interception becomes invisible to users.
how.caveat: The persistence point is the one most likely to be missed: the certificate obtained during the hijack stays valid after the records are restored. Remediation must include finding and revoking any certificate issued for your domains during the window, otherwise the attacker retains the ability to impersonate the service.

how.logic: The campaign begins with compromised credentials for an account able to change name records. Those accounts are frequently held outside the identity directory, at a registrar or hosting provider, shared between a small number of people, and excluded from joiner and leaver processes because nobody owns them.
how.caveat: Registrar accounts are among the highest-consequence and least governed credentials most organisations hold. They typically sit outside the directory, outside single sign-on and outside the account review that covers everything else.

how.logic: With records altered and a valid certificate obtained, traffic to the organisation's own domains reaches attacker infrastructure, is decrypted and inspected, and is then passed on to the real service. Users see the correct domain and no certificate warning, so no user-facing cue exists at all and credential capture is silent.
how.caveat: Unlike a lookalike domain, this is the real domain with a valid certificate, so every user-facing check passes. Detection has to be external, comparing what the world sees for your domains against what you published.

where.publisher: CISA National Cybersecurity and Communications Integration Center
where.title: DNS Infrastructure Hijacking Campaign

notes: The only record here where the attacker obtains a genuinely valid certificate for the victim's own domain, which removes every user-facing cue: correct domain, valid certificate, no warning. The detail worth carrying is the agency's own note that the risk persists beyond the redirection, because restoring the records does not revoke the certificate. Remediation therefore has to include certificate discovery and revocation for the affected window. It also highlights registrar and name hosting accounts as among the highest-consequence and least governed credentials an organisation holds, typically sitting outside the directory and outside every account review.

who.versions_affected: Publicly available tools used for their intended purpose

what.summary: A Russian military intelligence unit conducted reconnaissance against government and critical infrastructure address ranges using ordinary publicly available scanning and enumeration tools, and the advisory notes they were not observed using those tools for anything beyond their intended purpose.

how.logic: Reconnaissance against your own published address ranges is observable at the perimeter as broad port and path sweeps, and specific tools leave recognisable request patterns and identification strings. The realistic value is low for alerting and moderate for context: knowing your ranges were swept shortly before an intrusion attempt helps scope an investigation. Treat sustained targeted scanning of a narrow range as more meaningful than the constant background of internet-wide scanning.

fields.note: count distinct destinations and ports per source; a targeted sweep is narrow and deep, background scanning is wide and shallow
scanner identification strings, where not suppressed

how.caveat: The advisory is explicit and worth repeating: use of these tools should not be treated as malicious without analytical evidence of actor use or control. They are standard tools that your own testers and asset discovery services use, so a detection built on tool identity alone will accuse your own colleagues. This record exists as much to caution against that as to enable detection.

where.publisher: FBI, CISA, NSA and international partners
where.title: Russian Military Cyber Actors Target US and Global Critical Infrastructure

notes: Recorded primarily for the attribution caution, which is unusual for a government advisory to state so plainly and is a discipline worth carrying across this whole corpus: a tool appearing in an advisory does not make that tool an indicator. Several patterns here name commodity tools, and every one of them has legitimate users inside a normal estate.

who.versions_affected: Public-facing network appliances with known or unpatched vulnerabilities

what.summary: A state-sponsored group obtained initial access to critical infrastructure networks by exploiting public-facing network appliances from several vendors, then connected in over the victim's own VPN. Seven agencies assessed with high confidence that the purpose was pre-positioning to enable later movement into operational technology and disrupt it, not espionage.

how.logic: Publicly available exploit code for known vulnerabilities was the usual route, though the group is also capable of finding and using unpublished ones. That means patch currency on internet-facing appliances is the dominant control, and the appliance's own logs are where the attempt appears. Treat any successful authentication following exploitation attempts as compromise rather than as a failed probe.

fields.note: compare against sources with prior successful authentication

how.caveat: Known-vulnerability exploitation means the window was patch lag rather than anything clever. Being also capable of zero-day use means patch currency alone is not sufficient, only necessary.

how.logic: After compromising the appliance the group connected to the network over the victim's own VPN using obtained administrator credentials, so the sessions are legitimate in every respect except who is using them. Source network history per account is the discriminator, and it keeps working after the appliance itself is patched because the credentials outlive the patch.

fields.note: compare the source network against that account's own history

how.caveat: Rotate credentials and keys after any appliance compromise or this detection is the only thing standing between a patched appliance and continued access.

how.logic: The assessed objective was reaching operational technology from the business network. That makes the reachability question the risk: which business-network hosts can reach control assets, and by what path. Segmentation and storing operational documentation and network diagrams where only authenticated users can read them were both named as mitigations, the second because the group was looking for exactly that material.
how.caveat: An inventory and architecture question rather than a query. Worth noting that operational documentation and network diagrams were themselves targets, so access control on that material is part of the same problem.

where.publisher: CISA, NSA and FBI with international partners
where.title: PRC State-Sponsored Actors Compromise and Maintain Persistent Access to U.S. Critical Infrastructure

corroborations.publisher: NSA, CISA, FBI and international partners

notes: The targeting pattern was explicitly assessed as inconsistent with espionage or intelligence gathering, which is what makes this different from most edge-appliance advisories: the access was held for future disruption rather than for collection. Affected sectors were communications, energy, transportation and water. This record complements the existing IT to OT boundary records in this corpus and provides a public citation for the same argument they make from restricted sources. An earlier seven-agency advisory on the same actor, published nine months before this one, is linked in where.corroborating_url. It named two further initial access vulnerabilities in a network appliance and an identity self-service product, and established the living-off-the-land framing that the later advisory develops.

what.summary: A criminal group disproportionately targeting education, including schools, where agencies noted that institutions with limited security capability and constrained resources are the most vulnerable and anticipated attacks rising as the academic year began. Impacts recorded include restricted access to networks and data, delayed examinations, cancelled school days and theft of personal information about students and staff. The group used living off the land techniques against the management instrumentation service, tainted shared content so that other users spread the malware, exploited a print service flaw to escalate privileges, and persisted through scheduled tasks, undocumented autostart registry keys and by pointing legitimate services at their own libraries.

how.logic: The group tainted shared content so the malware spread through users opening files they were supposed to open. No lateral movement technique is involved and no exploit is used, so the only detectable moment is the write: executable or shortcut content modified on a share by an account that does not author there, and many files changed by one account in a short window.
how.caveat: Restricting who may write executable content to shares turns this into a control rather than a detection, which is the better answer and is usually achievable even on constrained estates. Education file shares are frequently broadly writable by design.

how.logic: Privilege escalation used a print service flaw. The detectable form is the print service process loading a library from a user-writable path or creating a child process, neither of which it does in normal operation, which holds independently of the specific identifiers.
how.caveat: Disabling the print service where it is not needed removes the exposure entirely, and on servers it very often is not needed. That is a cheaper answer than the detection.

how.logic: Persistence combined scheduled tasks, undocumented autostart registry keys, and pointing legitimate services at attacker-supplied libraries. The last is the durable one to detect: a signed service process loading a library from a path outside the system and program directories.
how.caveat: Three persistence mechanisms in one intrusion means eviction has to check all three; removing one leaves the access intact. The library redirection is the hardest to spot because the running process name is legitimate.

how.logic: The agencies noted that institutions with limited security capability and constrained resources are often the most vulnerable, and anticipated attacks increasing as the academic year began. Both parts are actionable: a constrained organisation should pick the smallest control set that breaks the most common chains, and a predictable calendar peak can be planned for.

markers.expr: minimum_viable_control_set defined and covers(second_factor_on_remote_access, offline_backup_tested, known_exploited_vulnerability_patching)

how.caveat: Most guidance assumes a resourced security function. Where that assumption fails a long control catalogue delivers nothing, and the agencies' own observation is that the constrained organisations are the ones being hit. The impacts listed, cancelled school days and delayed examinations, are also a reminder that availability harm here is measured in disrupted lives rather than revenue.

where.publisher: FBI, CISA and Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center
where.title: #StopRansomware: Vice Society

notes: The only record in the corpus written explicitly about organisations that cannot afford a security function, which makes it the natural place for the prioritisation argument. Two things are distinctive. Tainting shared content spreads the malware through users doing their jobs, so no lateral movement detection engages and the write to the share is the only moment to catch, which also means restricting write access to executable content is a control most constrained estates can actually implement. And the timing is predictable, tied to the academic calendar, which is unusual enough to plan against.

what.summary: A long-running loader distributed by stealing an existing email chain from an infected host and replying into that chain with a spoofed identity and a malicious document attached. It also lured users on mobile devices into enabling macros to view documents, scraped mail addresses and mail content from the local mail client, brute forced accounts from a hard-coded password list, dumped credentials from process memory and moved laterally over administrative shares.

how.logic: The technique steals a real email chain from an infected host and replies to it with a spoofed identity and a malicious attachment. The body is genuine, so content inspection and user judgement both fail. What remains inconsistent is the envelope: a reply into a thread whose original participants did not include the sender's actual domain, or a display name matching a known contact over a domain that does not match.

markers.expr: reply_references_existing_thread_id and sender_domain not in original_thread_participants

how.caveat: The most effective phishing shape recorded here, because every cue users are taught to check is genuine: known sender, familiar subject, real thread history, expected reply. One compromised mailbox therefore becomes a trusted delivery channel to every correspondent, including other organisations, which is how this crosses organisational boundaries.

how.logic: Dedicated modules scraped mail addresses and mail content from the local mail client. That is what supplies the stolen threads and the recipient list for the next wave, so detecting bulk local mail access is detecting the propagation engine rather than only a data loss.
how.caveat: Reading the local mail store is the step that turns one infection into the next campaign, which makes it worth alerting on even though the immediate impact looks like ordinary data access.

how.logic: Delivery relied on users enabling macros in an attached document, with lures tailored to appear as a requirement for viewing the file on a mobile device. The document application creating a shell or scripting engine child remains the highest-fidelity endpoint detection for this whole class, and it is independent of the lure.
how.caveat: Note the mobile-device framing of the lure, which anticipates that the recipient is reading mail on a phone and will open the attachment on a computer later. Awareness content built around desktop cues misses that.

how.logic: The loader brute forced accounts from a hard-coded password list, dumped credentials from process memory using a well-known module, and moved laterally over administrative shares. The hard-coded list is the useful detail: it makes the brute force detectable as repeated failures against many accounts from one host, with a fixed and finite candidate set.

markers.expr: count_distinct(target_account) by source_host, bin(_time, 5m) with auth_failure

how.caveat: Requires authentication failure collection on member servers and workstations, not only on domain controllers, which is a common gap.

where.publisher: CISA and Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center
where.title: Emotet Malware

notes: Holds the single most effective phishing technique in the corpus. Thread hijacking defeats every user-facing cue simultaneously, because the sender is known, the thread is real and a reply was expected, and it turns each compromised mailbox into a trusted delivery channel to that person's entire correspondence list. That is also why it crosses organisational boundaries so easily: the next victim is a supplier or customer who has a genuine conversation history with the last one. Detection has to move from message content to envelope consistency, since the content is authentic.

who.versions_affected: Consumer and small office routers past vendor support, specifically Cisco and NETGEAR models

what.summary: Command and control was relayed through small office and home office routers that had passed end of life, implanted with botnet malware, so traffic arriving at a victim came from ordinary residential and small business addresses in the same region rather than from anything suspicious.

how.logic: The relay addresses belong to residential and small business connections, so geographic and reputational checks pass: the traffic looks like a member of staff working from home. The usable signals are behavioural rather than reputational. An administrative or remote access session from a residential address that the account has never used before, and particularly several accounts arriving from the same unfamiliar residential range, are the shapes worth pursuing.

fields.note: resolve to network owner type; residential or small business ranges with no prior history for this account
count distinct accounts arriving from the same unfamiliar range

how.caveat: Remote working makes residential source addresses entirely normal, which is precisely why the technique works. Country-level blocking is useless here because the relays are deliberately chosen in the victim's own region. This is an argument for per-account source baselining, not for a blocklist.

how.logic: The devices used as relays were past vendor support, meaning no patch existed and none was coming. For an organisation this cuts two ways: your own end-of-life edge devices are candidates to become someone else's relay infrastructure, and they cannot be remediated by patching. Inventory them and plan replacement, because there is no other control.
how.caveat: Not a detection. It is the one case in this corpus where the honest answer is replacement rather than mitigation, since an unsupported device with a reachable management interface has no fix available.

where.publisher: CISA, NSA and FBI with international partners
where.title: PRC State-Sponsored Actors Compromise and Maintain Persistent Access to U.S. Critical Infrastructure

corroborations.publisher: NSA, CISA, FBI and international partners

notes: The botnet supporting this was subject to a law enforcement disruption operation, which is worth knowing when reading older indicator lists: the specific relay addresses were taken down and are stale, while the technique is not. Compare with the existing record on relaying through compromised legitimate third-party servers; the reasoning is the same and the conclusion is that destination and source reputation are both weak signals against a competent operator. An earlier seven-agency advisory on the same actor, published nine months before this one, is linked in where.corroborating_url. It named two further initial access vulnerabilities in a network appliance and an identity self-service product, and established the living-off-the-land framing that the later advisory develops.

what.summary: Actors deployed malware that builds a botnet to find and compromise further networks, primarily to read environment configuration files holding credentials for high-profile cloud, mail and messaging services. It reached those files through internet-exposed dependency directories, a unit testing framework flaw, a web framework flaw and a web server path traversal, then abused the harvested credentials, including for mail sending, and deployed web shells.

how.logic: The target is the environment configuration file, which holds credentials for cloud infrastructure, a productivity suite, a transactional mail service and a messaging platform. Access routes include internet-accessible dependency directories under the unit testing framework and a framework debug flaw. Every one of these paths is one no external client should ever request, so any successful response is actionable on its own.
how.caveat: A successful response means the disclosure already happened, so the action is rotation rather than investigation. The advisory's own first recommendation is to review the platforms whose credentials appear in these files for unauthorised use, which is the right order: assume the credentials are in use elsewhere.

how.logic: The malware includes functions for abusing mail transfer, scanning for and exploiting exposed credentials and interfaces. Stolen transactional mail credentials let an actor send through reputable infrastructure carrying the victim's own sender reputation and authenticated domain, so the sending platform's audit trail is where the anomaly appears rather than on the victim network.

markers.expr: send_volume by api_key, bin(_time, 1h) against baseline_multiple

how.caveat: The harm falls mainly on third parties and on domain reputation rather than on your own systems, so it is frequently reported by a blocklist operator before anyone internal notices. The detection lives in a provider console that needs an owner.

how.logic: The botnet scans for sites with specific vulnerabilities and for exposed dependency directories, so the reconnaissance is automated and continuous. The defensive counterpart is to request the same paths against your own estate and see which return content, which answers the exposure question directly rather than inferring it.
how.caveat: One of the cheapest checks available and it produces an unambiguous answer. Exposed dependency directories are usually a deployment mistake rather than a configuration choice, which means nobody owns them and nobody looks.

where.title: Known Indicators of Compromise Associated with Androxgh0st Malware

notes: The clearest example in the corpus of a cloud compromise that begins with a file left in a web directory. No cloud control is bypassed and no cloud vulnerability is exploited: the access keys are read out of a configuration file served by a misconfigured web server, and used from anywhere. It also makes the point that a credential's blast radius is not the host that leaked it, since one file yields cloud infrastructure, a productivity suite, a mail service and a messaging platform at once.

who.versions_affected: Not applicable

what.summary: An information stealer was delivered by showing the user a fake human verification challenge whose instructions told them to open the Windows Run dialog and paste the clipboard contents, which the page had already filled with an encoded scripting command, so the user executed the payload themselves with no exploit involved.

how.logic: The execution chain is unusually specific and therefore unusually detectable. A command originating from the Run dialog, carrying an encoded scripting payload, is close to unambiguous: an ordinary user has no reason to paste an encoded command there, and the dialog records what was typed in a per-user registry key. Two complementary detections: the encoded invocation itself, and the run history key containing anything that looks like a script rather than a program name or path.

fields.note: long base64 payload on a scripting engine invocation
the Run dialog history key; entries resembling script commands rather than program names
the shell as parent, which is what a Run dialog launch produces

how.caveat: Administrators occasionally paste commands into the Run dialog, so a small exception list by account may be needed. The technique defeats awareness training framed around not opening attachments and not clicking links, because the user is neither: they are following instructions that look like a routine verification step.

markers.note: raw field registry_key_path

how.logic: The same malware was also distributed inside spoofed copies of popular media player and utility software, so the second delivery route is a user installing something that looks like a legitimate free tool. An approved software inventory catches this where signature and reputation checks do not, since the installer is attacker-built rather than a tampered legitimate one.

fields.note: compared against the approved software inventory rather than a reputation service

how.caveat: No purchase at all on unmanaged or personal devices, which is where free utility software is most often installed.

how.logic: The stealer takes browser-stored credentials, session material, cryptocurrency wallets, browser extension data and multi-factor details. The last of those matters most: stolen multi-factor material and session tokens mean the second factor is bypassed downstream, which links this record to the session replay record. Watch for non-browser processes opening browser credential and session stores.

fields.note: anything other than the owning browser or an approved backup product

how.caveat: Once this has run, treat the affected user's saved credentials, active sessions and multi-factor enrolment as compromised. Password reset alone is insufficient because the session material was taken too.

where.title: Threat Actors Deploy LummaC2 Malware to Exfiltrate Sensitive Data from Organizations

notes: The most genuinely novel delivery technique in this corpus. It bypasses the two things most user education covers, attachments and links, by having the victim type the command themselves in response to a plausible verification prompt. Private sector figures cited in the advisory put more than 21,000 listings of stolen data from this one stealer on criminal marketplaces, which is the scale that makes an infostealer a supply chain problem rather than an individual one: the credentials reaching an organisation may have been taken from a personal device years earlier.

what.summary: Six national authorities warned that most networks have a gap in detecting and blocking rapidly changing name resolution used to obscure the location of malicious servers and to build resilient, highly available command and control. They describe the technique as a significant threat to national security, used by both criminal and nation-state actors, and note that the speed at which the infrastructure changes is what defeats tracking and blocking.

how.logic: Detect on properties of the resolution rather than on the name, because the name is disposable and the addresses change faster than any list can be maintained. A very short record lifetime, an unusually large set of distinct addresses for one name in a short window, and those addresses spread across many unrelated networks. The double-flux variant also rotates the authoritative name servers, which is a separate and equally cheap check.
how.caveat: Content delivery networks and large cloud services produce a very similar shape legitimately and must be excluded before this is usable, which is the main reason the detection gets skipped. The exclusion list is finite and worth building once.

how.logic: The technique defeats address blocking specifically because the addresses rotate, so retaining the answer alongside the query is what makes any retrospective analysis possible at all. Where only queried names are kept, an investigation cannot establish which infrastructure a host actually contacted, and the rotation guarantees the name alone will not match later.
how.caveat: This is a collection decision that many organisations have made the wrong way without noticing, and it is only discovered during an investigation when it is too late to change. Worth auditing as a standing question rather than an incident finding.

where.publisher: NSA, CISA, FBI, Australian Cyber Security Centre, Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and NCSC-NZ
where.title: Fast Flux: A National Security Threat

notes: Unusual among these advisories in naming a defensive gap rather than an actor or a product: six agencies state that most networks cannot detect or block this. Its real value here is as a collection argument. The technique specifically defeats address blocklists by rotating faster than they update, which means the resolved answer has to be retained alongside the query or no retrospective analysis is possible. Several other records in this corpus depend on the same decision without saying so, and it is usually discovered to be wrong during an investigation rather than before one.

what.summary: Five national authorities jointly examined the publicly available tooling seen in incidents worldwide, grouping it into five functional categories with a named example of each: a remote access trojan, a web shell, a credential stealer, a lateral movement framework, and a command and control obfuscation and exfiltration tool. They record these tools compromising health, finance, government and defence organisations, state plainly that even the most sophisticated actor groups use common publicly available tooling, and note that the widespread availability of these tools makes attribution harder. Initial compromise in these incidents was typically through unpatched software or poor configuration, with the tools coming into play afterwards.

how.logic: The five categories are the durable output, and the advisory says directly that its named examples are not exhaustive and should not be treated as a checklist. So the useful exercise is five questions: for a remote access trojan, a web shell, a credential stealer, a lateral movement framework and a tunnelling tool, name the detection you would rely on and the telemetry it needs, then test it. A gap in a category is a gap for every present and future tool in it.
how.caveat: This is the oldest advisory in the corpus and its specific tool names have aged, which is exactly why the categories are what to keep. Four of the five named tools still appear in advisories published years later, including in the state-sponsored records here.

how.logic: The named credential stealer reads authentication material out of process memory, which remains the single most reused post-access capability across this corpus. Detection is access to the authentication process's memory by anything that is not a known security or diagnostic product, which is robust against the tool being renamed or reimplemented.
how.caveat: Name matching catches only unmodified builds, and this tool is very commonly modified. The memory access behaviour is the durable form and it is where the detection effort belongs.

how.logic: The named web shell is a very small file placed in a served directory, giving command execution through ordinary web requests. Because it arrives as a file in a directory that changes only at deployment, the file appearing is the detection, and it does not require recognising the shell itself.
how.caveat: This web shell is among the most reused single artefacts in the corpus, appearing in Iranian, Chinese and criminal activity across more than a decade. Its presence therefore carries no attribution information at all.

how.logic: The named relay tool provides command and control obfuscation and exfiltration by forwarding traffic through a compromised host, so connections appear to originate inside the network. The behavioural signal is a host holding a concurrent inbound and outbound session of similar volume while not being a routing device.
how.caveat: Relaying rather than serving is the distinction, and it survives the tool being renamed or rewritten. Worth pairing with the peer-relay record in this corpus, which describes the same shape at the scale of a global covert network.

how.logic: The advisory states that tools for exploiting networks are not the preserve of states or criminals, that they are freely available to everyone from penetration testers to amateurs, and that even the most sophisticated groups use common publicly available tooling. It also notes this widespread availability complicates attribution, which means the tool found says nothing reliable about who used it.
how.caveat: The attribution warning is the part worth carrying. Several records in this corpus show state actors using exactly these tools, so inferring an actor from a tool is unsafe in both directions.

where.publisher: Cyber security authorities of Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and the United States
where.title: Publicly Available Tools Seen in Cyber Incidents Worldwide

notes: The oldest advisory in the corpus and one of the most useful, because it is organised by function rather than by campaign. Four of its five named tools still appear in advisories published years later, including in the state-sponsored records here, which validates its central claim that even sophisticated groups use common public tooling. Two things to carry: coverage is more honestly measured per category than per tool, since a category gap covers every future tool in it; and the ubiquity of these tools means their presence carries no attribution information, which cuts against the instinct to read an actor from an artefact.

what.summary: Affiliates of a ransomware operation used open source research on the target company, then posed as its information technology or help desk staff and used phone calls and text messages to obtain credentials from employees. Having gained access they deployed commercial remote access software in preparation for exfiltration, created a plausibly named administrative account, and generated Kerberos tickets for domain access. Demands and file restoration were handled through a live chat link.

how.logic: The approach is a phone call or text message impersonating the company's own support function, informed by open source research on the organisation. Nothing on that channel is observable to any security control, so detection has to sit on the use of the credential: a success from a source or device new to the account, and any second-factor approval or enrolment from an unrecognised device shortly afterwards.

markers.expr: mfa_factor_enrolled or mfa_approved from unrecognised_device within 1h of authentication

how.caveat: The direction of the approach is what defeats conventional training: the attacker impersonates the team staff are told to cooperate with. Independent callback verification is the control and has to be a documented process rather than guidance, because under pressure people default to being helpful.

how.logic: The affiliates created an administrative account with a name closely resembling a legitimate administrative convention. A name one character away from a plausible standard defeats review by eye, so this has to be a comparison against the authorised account set rather than a visual check.
how.caveat: The specific name will change; the shape, a new privileged account resembling an existing naming convention and created without a request record, does not.

how.logic: The affiliates generated Kerberos tickets for domain access, which produces authenticated access to services with no corresponding authentication event at the domain controller. Look for service access with no preceding ticket request for that account, and tickets whose lifetime or encryption type is inconsistent with domain policy.
how.caveat: The third mechanism in this corpus for holding valid credentials that were never issued, alongside forged federated tokens and a stolen session cookie. All three defeat authentication controls by not using them.

how.logic: Three named commercial products were deployed after access was gained, in preparation for exfiltration. All are legitimate, signed and have real customers, so the tractable form is an allow-list of the remote access software the organisation actually licensed, with everything else alerting regardless of reputation.
how.caveat: Consistent with the dual-use tooling record here: maintaining an accurate list of the remote access software you bought is a detection control, not an asset management chore.

notes: The most important initial access route in this corpus that no technical control observes: a phone call or text message impersonating the organisation's own support team, informed by open source research. It inverts the assumption behind most awareness training, which is that the suspicious contact arrives by email from outside. Together with the service desk and account recovery material here, it makes identity verification of people the weakest link rather than authentication of accounts, and the only control that engages is a documented independent callback.

what.summary: A ransomware-as-a-service operation that reached over 1,300 victims and around one hundred million dollars in payments in eighteen months, with developers maintaining the malware and affiliates conducting the attacks, so the intrusion route varies by affiliate. Entry was by single-factor remote access, by a remote access appliance flaw allowing the second factor to be skipped through username capitalisation, by phishing, and by a mail server exploit chain. Before encrypting it terminated backup, antivirus and file-copy processes, destroyed shadow copies, deleted the system, security and application event logs, and removed virus definitions through the registry. It has variants for four operating systems and left a key file that exists only on the machine that made it.

how.logic: The appliance flaw lets an actor log in without being prompted for the second factor when the case of the username is changed. Two markers follow from the appliance's own authentication log: a successful session with no second factor recorded, and a submitted username whose capitalisation differs from the canonical directory form. The second costs nothing to check because normalised comparison is already standard in authentication pipelines.
how.caveat: The wider lesson is that a second factor is only as strong as the code path enforcing it, and that single-factor remote access was the other main entry route here. Both point at the same inventory question: which remote access paths actually enforce a second factor, as opposed to offering one.

how.logic: The actors deleted the system, security and application event logs specifically. Clearing a log is itself a logged event, so the record of the act survives provided forwarding already happened. Near-zero legitimate frequency makes this one of the cleanest markers available.
how.caveat: Fires late, at the covering-tracks stage, usually minutes before encryption. Its real value is that it is as much a test of whether central forwarding works as a detection of the adversary.

how.logic: Shadow copy services were stopped and all existing copies removed, by command line and by script interpreter. This is the standard pre-encryption step across most families in this corpus and remains one of the highest-value pre-damage detections because legitimate use is confined to deliberate maintenance.
how.caveat: Fires before the damage, which makes it worth actioning in minutes rather than triaging. If it fires alongside the log-clearing marker on the same host, encryption is imminent.

how.logic: Prior to encryption the actors removed virus definitions and disabled all portions of the platform's built-in protection and other common products through the system registry, in addition to terminating backup, antivirus and file-copy processes. A health check asking only whether the service runs will report healthy while the product has nothing to detect with.
how.caveat: Pair with an alert on definition age or protection coverage degrading across several hosts at once, which is the consequence and usually surfaces only in a console nobody alerts from.

how.logic: Exfiltration used a combination of a bulk transfer utility and a named consumer cloud storage service. The utility plus a consumer file-hosting destination is a two-marker combination that is rare in a server estate and appears in several unrelated records in this corpus, which makes it worth covering once rather than per family.
how.caveat: Legitimate use of consumer file hosting exists in some organisations and has to be enumerated first. On servers the legitimate rate is close to zero.

how.logic: A key file is created in the root of the drive during encryption, required for decryption, existing only on the machine that created it and not reproducible. A ransom note is dropped into each affected directory. The key file's uniqueness is operationally important during response: destroying or moving it removes any possibility of recovery even if payment were made.
how.caveat: Worth putting in the responder runbook rather than only in a rule: the note warns the key file must not be modified, renamed or deleted, and a well-intentioned responder collecting evidence can destroy the only recovery route.

how.logic: The advisory states the method of initial intrusion depends on which affiliate targets the network, so entry varies while the pre-encryption sequence does not. Detection effort belongs on that shared sequence, process termination, shadow copy destruction, log clearing and protection disabling, rather than on the entry route or the family name.
how.caveat: The highest-value form of this record. Four independent pre-encryption markers exist here, and two or more firing on one host inside a short window is close to a confirmed imminent encryption event.

where.publisher: FBI, CISA and Department of Health and Human Services
where.title: #StopRansomware: Hive Ransomware

notes: The best worked example in the corpus of why detection belongs on the pre-encryption sequence rather than the family. Four independent markers fire before any file is encrypted, and the advisory is explicit that entry varies by affiliate while that sequence does not. Two operational points worth carrying separately. The appliance flaw that skips the second factor by changing username capitalisation is a reminder that a factor is only as strong as the code path enforcing it. And the per-machine key file cannot be reproduced, so a responder collecting evidence can permanently remove the recovery option, which belongs in a runbook rather than a rule.

who.versions_affected: Anything externally reachable and behind on patches

what.summary: A state-sponsored group conducted regular reconnaissance to find unpatched, end-of-life and unmaintained devices, and the authoring agencies stated the expectation that it would exploit proof of concept code for new high-profile vulnerabilities within hours of publication.

how.logic: This sharpens a figure recorded elsewhere in this corpus from days to hours, stated by the authoring agencies as an expectation rather than an observation. Two practical consequences. First, a monthly patch cycle offers no protection at all for internet-facing assets, so those need a separate and faster process. Second, the group's own reconnaissance was continuous, meaning your externally reachable inventory should be re-enumerated on the same cadence rather than annually.

fields.note: the tolerance for this asset class is hours, not the monthly cycle
unmaintained devices were an explicit reconnaissance target

how.caveat: Prioritisation guidance, not a query. The operational difficulty is real: patching an internet-facing service usually means an outage, which is exactly why the window stays open.

how.logic: Reconnaissance specifically sought end-of-life and no longer maintained devices, because those have no fix coming. Your own inventory of unsupported externally reachable equipment is therefore a list of what an adversary is already looking for.
how.caveat: No patch exists for these by definition, so the answer is replacement or removal from exposure, not mitigation.

where.publisher: ASD's ACSC, CISA, NSA, FBI and international partners
where.title: People's Republic of China (PRC) Ministry of State Security APT40 Tradecraft in Action

notes: The group was still succeeding with vulnerabilities disclosed as early as 2017, which is the uncomfortable half of this: the hours-scale figure describes the new disclosures, while the long tail of unpatched old ones stays exploitable indefinitely.

who.versions_affected: Not applicable

what.summary: An incident response at a defence industrial base organisation found that likely multiple separate state-sponsored groups had compromised the network, some holding long-term access, using an open-source protocol toolkit to establish and extend their foothold alongside a custom data exfiltration tool.

how.logic: The toolkit implements Windows protocols directly rather than using the operating system's own client software, which is what makes it detectable: the protocol traffic is present but the usual local process activity that accompanies it is not. Look for remote service creation, remote command execution and directory replication where no corresponding administrative tool ran locally, and for file-sharing and management protocol sessions whose client behaviour does not match the built-in utilities. Because the toolkit is Python, watching for a Python runtime on hosts that should not have one is a cheap complementary check.

fields.note: remote service creation with no local administrative tool as parent
an interpreter present on a host with no development or automation role

how.caveat: The toolkit is widely used by legitimate testers and by administrators for automation, so this needs excluding by host and account. The protocol-without-local-process shape is the durable half; the interpreter check fails against compiled builds.

markers.note: raw field process_name

how.logic: The third instance of this in the corpus, and the strongest: multiple groups present, some with long-term access, at one organisation. Two consequences for response. Scope by exposure surface rather than by the actor identified, and do not assume a single intrusion timeline, because evidence from one actor will not account for another's activity and reconstructing one narrative from mixed activity produces a wrong answer that looks coherent.

fields.note: enumerate every exposed service, not only the one exploited

how.caveat: An investigative discipline. The failure mode is subtle: mixed activity from several actors assembles into a plausible single story, and that story will be wrong about capability, objective and dwell time simultaneously.

how.logic: The named vulnerabilities are the 2021 mail server chain, so the entry point was the mail platform. Bulk mailbox access and outward forwarding rules are the follow-on to watch, alongside web shells in the mail server's servable directories.
how.caveat: Requires mail platform audit logging, which is the recurring dependency across the mail records in this corpus.

where.title: Impacket and Exfiltration Tool Used to Steal Sensitive Information from Defense Industrial Base Organization

notes: Sits alongside the defence subcontractor record as the second view of this sector: one describes who gets targeted and why, this describes what was actually found inside one of them. The combination of an open-source toolkit and a custom exfiltration tool is worth noting, since it means tool-based detection catches the commodity half and misses the bespoke half.

what.summary: Five national authorities published a playbook for incident investigation setting out both the analytical approaches an investigation needs and the order in which response steps must be taken. The approaches are searching known indicators, frequency analysis against calculated normal patterns across many variables, pattern analysis to separate automated and routine human activity from noise, and analyst-led anomaly review drawing on system administration experience. The sequence is to collect and remove artefacts, logs and data for analysis first, then apply mitigations chosen so as not to tip off the adversary that their presence has been discovered, then consider third-party support to confirm eradication and avoid follow-up compromise after the incident is closed.

how.logic: Indicator search is listed first but is only one of four approaches, and the other three are what find activity nobody has published an indicator for. Frequency analysis requires a calculated baseline across timing, source and destination location, port, protocol adherence, file location, hash, size and naming convention. Pattern analysis requires enough history to distinguish automation from routine human activity. Anomaly review requires analysts who know what a correctly administered system looks like.
how.caveat: Most programmes can do indicator search and struggle with the rest, which is why they are structurally dependent on someone else publishing first. The variable list for frequency analysis is worth using as a checklist against what your telemetry actually retains.

how.logic: The order is explicit and the middle step is the one usually missed: mitigations must be chosen so as not to tip off the adversary. Remediating first destroys the evidence needed to scope the incident and warns the adversary to change tradecraft, accelerate, or trigger destruction. Who authorises containment, what is preserved first, and how the response is coordinated out of band all have to be settled beforehand.
how.caveat: The third step matters too: the advisory recommends third-party support specifically to avoid residual issues causing follow-up compromise once the incident is closed, which is an admission that incomplete eradication is common. Pairs with the record where the adversary read the responders' mail.

how.logic: Every approach in this playbook is a function of the data held. Frequency and pattern analysis in particular need history rather than feeds, so the honest test is whether the retention and coverage would support each of the four approaches for an intrusion that began a year ago.
how.caveat: Several records in this corpus report dwell times of three months to years. Retention shorter than the dwell time makes the assume-compromise instruction that appears in many of those advisories unanswerable.

where.publisher: Cyber security authorities of Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and the United States
where.title: Technical Approaches to Uncovering and Remediating Malicious Activity

notes: The methodological index for this corpus. Nearly every record here assumes one of the four approaches is available, and most assume the first. The two lasting points are that indicator search is the least capable of the four and the only one most programmes can do, and that the response sequence puts evidence collection before mitigation with mitigation chosen not to alert the adversary. That second point is the one violated most often, usually by disconnecting something immediately, which destroys scope and warns the intruder at the same time.

what.summary: Three national authorities warned vendors, developers and operators about access control flaws in which an application uses an identifier to reach an object without adequately checking that the requester is authenticated and authorised for it. Requests naming other valid users' identifiers therefore succeed. The agencies record these as frequently exploited in breach incidents because they are common, hard to prevent outside the development process and abusable at scale, and as having exposed personal, financial and health information belonging to millions of people.

how.logic: No individual request is malformed and every response is a legitimate success, so nothing signature-based or error-rate-based will fire. The abuse shows as breadth within one authenticated session: many distinct object identifiers requested in a short window, frequently in sequence. That has to be counted per session rather than matched per request.
how.caveat: Thresholds must come from the application's own usage, since a caseworker or clinician legitimately opens many records. Sequentiality is the stronger discriminator than volume, because humans do not work through identifiers in order.

how.logic: Because the flaw is abusable at scale, the consequence is bulk retrieval through an interface built to serve single records. Response volume per session against that session's own history is the backstop when the identifier pattern is not recognisable, and it catches the same abuse through an interface whose parameters look nothing like the pattern above.
how.caveat: Deliberately generic because the parameter naming varies by application. Worth having as the second layer, since the first depends on recognising how this particular application names its identifiers.

how.logic: The agencies address vendors and developers first: perform authentication and authorisation checks on every request that reads, changes or deletes sensitive data, and replace direct identifiers in addresses with unguessable random values. For an operator the actionable form is a procurement and assurance question, since the fix is not available to whoever runs the application.
how.caveat: The honest position for a defender is that this class cannot be fixed from the outside. Detection buys time; the remedy is a development practice, which makes it a question to ask before buying rather than after deploying.

where.publisher: Australian Cyber Security Centre, CISA and NSA
where.title: Preventing Web Application Access Control Abuse

notes: The only record in the corpus about a vulnerability class rather than a campaign or a product, and worth keeping for that reason. It is also the clearest case where every request is authenticated, every response is a correct success, and the breach is nonetheless total: no error rate moves, no signature fires, and only per-session breadth reveals it. The agencies address developers before defenders, which is the honest ordering, so for an operator this belongs in procurement and assurance as much as in monitoring.

who.versions_affected: Not applicable

what.summary: Across investigations the most common problem slowing incident response was not a missing detection but missing logs: insufficient coverage and insufficient retention, so the questions an investigator needed to answer had no data behind them.

how.logic: Not a detection. Audit two things per asset class: whether the log sources the detections in this corpus depend on are actually being collected, and whether retention exceeds the dwell time you should assume. Several records here rest on logs that are off by default, including script block logging, remote desktop session manager operational logs and the directory database application log. A detection library that assumes uncollected logs is a list of intentions.

fields.note: per asset class, whether collected and for how long
compare against the dwell time the threat model assumes, not against a compliance minimum

how.caveat: Retention is a cost decision as much as a security one, so this belongs in front of whoever owns that budget rather than in a detection backlog. The specific figure to argue with is the assumed dwell time; where an actor is described as holding access for years, a ninety-day retention window cannot answer anything.

where.publisher: ASD's ACSC, CISA, NSA, FBI and international partners
where.title: People's Republic of China (PRC) Ministry of State Security APT40 Tradecraft in Action

notes: Recorded deliberately as a record rather than left as a caveat scattered across others. It is the single most common reason a detection in this corpus cannot be deployed, and stating it once makes the dependency visible instead of implicit.

what.summary: Two agencies urged immediate action on internet-accessible operational technology assets, noting actors' continued willingness to attack critical infrastructure by exploiting them, and that civilian infrastructure is an attractive target for foreign powers seeking to cause harm or retaliate. They identify why exposure is increasing: organisations expanding remote operations and monitoring, accommodating a decentralised workforce, and increasing the outsourcing of key skill areas including instrumentation and control, asset management and maintenance, and in some cases process operations and maintenance themselves. Legacy assets not designed to withstand malicious activity, combined with readily available information identifying those assets, compound the problem.

how.logic: The named drivers are commercial rather than technical: remote operations, a decentralised workforce, and outsourcing of instrumentation and control, asset management, maintenance and in some cases process operations. So each remote path should be traced back to the contracted function that created it, with a named owner, a defined scope and a time bound.
how.caveat: These are the paths least likely to appear on a network diagram, because each was justified as a commercial arrangement rather than a network change. Where process operations themselves are outsourced, a provider compromise is indistinguishable from an operator error.

how.logic: The immediate action is to establish which operational assets are reachable from the internet at all. That is answerable by scanning your own ranges for the industrial protocol ports and by checking public scan indexes, and the agencies note the information identifying these assets is already readily available to anyone looking.
how.caveat: The industrial controller record in this corpus is the worked consequence: seventy-five devices compromised because they were reachable with default or absent credentials on the vendor default port.

how.logic: Legacy assets not designed to defend themselves, combined with readily available information identifying those assets, is the stated combination. Because the identifying information is public, the reconnaissance stage costs nothing and obscurity is unavailable as a control, so the only response is knowing what is discoverable about your own estate.
how.caveat: Consistent with the control system defence record here, which reaches the same conclusion from the attacker's five-stage sequence rather than from the exposure trend.

where.title: NSA and CISA Recommend Immediate Actions to Reduce Exposure Across Operational Technologies and Control Systems

notes: Names the commercial causes of operational technology exposure rather than the technical ones, which is unusual and useful. Remote operations, a decentralised workforce and the outsourcing of instrumentation, control, maintenance and sometimes process operations are all business decisions that create network paths, and those paths are the least likely to be documented because each was approved as a contract rather than as an architectural change. Where process operations themselves are outsourced, a provider compromise and an operator error look identical from inside.

who.versions_affected: Potentially all internet-exposed programmable logic controllers regardless of manufacturer

what.summary: Seven agencies urgently warned of ongoing Iranian-affiliated targeting of internet-connected operational technology devices including programmable logic controllers. The activity disrupted controllers across several critical infrastructure sectors through malicious project file interactions and through manipulation of the data shown on operator interface and supervisory control displays, causing operational disruption and financial loss. A later update added guidance on detecting malicious changes in reusable code modules within one manufacturer's controller programs and expanded the observed scope to two further manufacturers and potentially others, emphasising restriction of direct internet access. Key actions are to install controllers according to manufacturer guidance, remove them from direct internet exposure behind a secure gateway and firewall, query logs for traffic on the industrial protocol ports especially from foreign hosting providers, and place the physical mode switch on affected controllers into the run position.

how.logic: Disruption was caused partly by manipulating the data shown on operator interface and supervisory displays, so the operator's view and the physical reality diverge and no single source can be trusted alone. Detection is disagreement between independent measurements of the same quantity: the displayed value against the controller's own register, against the historian record for the same timestamp, and against any instrument reporting on a separate path.

markers.expr: historian_recorded_value != hmi_displayed_value for same tag and timestamp

how.caveat: This undermines the operator-observation defence that worked at the water treatment facility recorded elsewhere in this corpus, where the operator could see the true dosing value and correct it. Where the display itself is manipulated the human is being deceived rather than assisting, and only an independent measurement path resolves the disagreement.

how.logic: The later update adds guidance specifically on detecting malicious changes in reusable code modules within controller programs. A reusable module is included across many programs, so one alteration propagates wherever it is used and inspecting the top-level program will not reveal it. The comparison has to be of the running program including its subroutines against an authoritative project file held offline.
how.caveat: The propagation property is what distinguishes this from an ordinary program change, and it means the authoritative offline project file must exist and be trusted. On older estates that file is frequently missing, out of date, or stored on the engineering workstation the attacker also reached.

how.logic: The affected population is described as potentially all internet-exposed controllers regardless of manufacturer, and the primary key action is removing them from direct internet exposure behind a secure gateway and firewall. The agencies also direct defenders to query logs for traffic on the named industrial protocol ports, particularly traffic originating from foreign hosting providers.
how.caveat: Three manufacturers named and the scope stated as potentially all internet-exposed controllers makes this a device-class problem rather than a vendor one. The hosting-provider observation is a useful narrowing filter, though the covert network record here cautions against relying on source characteristics alone.

how.logic: One of the key actions is to place the physical mode switch on affected controllers into the run position, which prevents remote program changes regardless of network access. That is a physical control unaffected by any network compromise, and it is checkable as an inventory state across the estate.
how.caveat: One of very few controls in this corpus that an attacker with full network access cannot defeat. Its cost is that legitimate programming then requires a site visit, which is why controllers are commonly left in a remotely programmable position.

where.publisher: FBI, CISA, NSA, EPA, Department of Energy, CNMF and Department of the Treasury
where.title: Iranian-Affiliated Cyber Actors Exploit Programmable Logic Controllers

corroborations.publisher: FBI, CISA, NSA, EPA and international partners

notes: The most recent operational technology record here and it adds two things the earlier controller record did not. Manipulating the data on operator and supervisory displays means the operator's view is itself the attack surface, which directly undermines the operator-observation defence that succeeded at a water treatment facility elsewhere in this corpus: there the operator could see the true value, here they cannot. And malicious changes inside reusable code modules propagate to every program that includes them while remaining invisible in the top-level logic, which makes an offline authoritative project file a prerequisite for detecting it at all. The scope covering three named manufacturers and potentially all internet-exposed controllers confirms this as a device-class exposure rather than a vendor problem.

who.versions_affected: Internet-reachable cameras, frequently with default or unchanged credentials

what.summary: The same Russian military intelligence campaign that targeted logistics companies also conducted wide scale targeting of internet-connected cameras in Ukraine and neighbouring NATO states, using them to observe the physical movement of goods rather than to reach any network.

how.logic: The objective was watching physical activity, which means the cameras themselves were the intelligence source and no network compromise was needed. That reframes the risk: a camera overlooking a loading bay, a rail siding or a substation yard is a sensor an adversary may be reading. Enumerate which cameras and recorders are reachable from outside, what each one overlooks, and who is authenticating to them. Default credentials remain the dominant route in.

fields.note: what the camera actually overlooks, which decides whether exposure matters
who authenticates to the camera or recorder, compared against expected sources

how.caveat: Cameras are frequently owned by facilities or physical security rather than IT, so they are often absent from the asset inventory entirely and outside any patch process. Establishing who owns them is usually the first obstacle.

where.publisher: NSA, FBI, NCSC-UK and international partners
where.title: Russian GRU Targeting Western Logistics Entities and Technology Companies

notes: Worth carrying beyond the immediate geography. The general lesson is that a camera is an intelligence collection asset from the adversary's point of view, and the question to ask of any exposed camera is not what it gives access to but what it can see. That is a different question from the one asset security normally asks.

what.summary: A North Korean group operating since around 2012 with a global intelligence collection mission against named subject-matter experts, think tanks and government bodies, focused on Korean peninsula foreign policy, nuclear matters and sanctions. It builds rapport with benign correspondence before sending a payload, hosts tooling on legitimate domains whose hosting credentials it stole from unrelated victims, runs scripts through the HTML application host rather than the script interpreter, and persists through browser extensions and file association changes.

how.logic: Posing as reporters, the actor exchanged several benign interview-themed emails to agree a date, then sent the malicious document as an attachment or as a file-sharing link once the target had agreed, then cancelled the interview as the date approached. Every first-contact heuristic passes, because the first contact is genuinely clean. The detectable moment is an established external thread that begins carrying attachments or file-sharing links.

markers.expr: count(prior_clean_messages) in thread with same external sender

how.caveat: Awareness training framed around unexpected mail from strangers does not touch this: by the time the payload arrives the sender is expected, known, and has a reason to be sending a file. Lures were tailored to the target's own subject area, including current affairs topics.

how.logic: The chain runs the native HTML application host to fetch and execute a remote application file, which then decodes and runs the script payload. The advisory states directly that script commands can be executed without invoking the interpreter's own executable through this route, and that executables were fetched into memory without touching disk. Any detection keyed on the interpreter's process name is blind to all of it.
how.caveat: This is the single most transferable finding in the record, because it invalidates a control most organisations believe they have. Script block logging captures the content whichever process hosts the engine, and it is off by default.

how.logic: The script persists by creating a startup registry key, then collects system information and sends it to the operator before awaiting commands. Startup keys pointing at user-writable locations are the durable marker, since legitimate startup entries point into program directories.
how.caveat: High volume on estates where users install their own software. Scoping to script and proxy-binary targets rather than any executable keeps it usable.

how.logic: The actor used an extension that was available in the official browser store to obtain login and password information, and separately directed victims to install malicious extensions. The extension sits inside the browser's trust boundary and reads pages after decryption and after authentication, so no network control sees what it takes.
how.caveat: Publication in the official store is not a trust boundary, and this is the corpus example proving it. Session tokens taken by an extension defeat multi-factor authentication, because the factor was already satisfied when the token was issued.

how.logic: Changing the default application for a file type both persists and, as the advisory notes, launches malware outside some application allow-listing solutions. Association keys are written at installation and almost never otherwise, so the write is worth alerting on rather than waiting for the resulting execution.
how.caveat: A control bypass as much as a persistence mechanism, which is why it belongs in the same conversation as allow-listing coverage rather than only in a persistence checklist.

how.logic: The actor used web hosting credentials stolen by phishing from victims outside its usual target set, then created subdomains on those legitimate domains imitating well-known mail providers. Domain age and reputation return reassuring answers because the parent domain is genuinely old and genuinely legitimate; the imitating subdomain on a domain with no relationship to that service is the discriminator.
how.caveat: The parent domain's owner is an unwitting victim, so blocking the parent domain is usually the wrong action and harms a third party. Act on the subdomain.

how.logic: Targeting is of named individuals identified as experts in their fields, think tanks and government bodies, on a defined topic set. The advisory recommends organisations and individuals within that profile raise their posture, which is an admission that the organisational perimeter is not where this arrives.
how.caveat: The approach arrives at a personal mail account, a professional network message or a home device, where the employer has no control. The two things that help are strong authentication on personal accounts and a reporting route that does not make the approach an incident about the person who received it.

where.publisher: CISA, FBI and US Cyber Command Cyber National Mission Force
where.title: North Korean Advanced Persistent Threat Focus: Kimsuky

notes: Strategically the most useful record in the corpus for organisations whose risk is carried by a handful of named people rather than by their infrastructure: policy bodies, research institutes, newsrooms, executive teams. Two findings transfer well beyond this actor. Running the script engine through a proxy binary defeats a control most organisations believe they have. And an extension published in the official store, stealing session tokens after authentication, is the clearest case in the corpus of multi-factor authentication being satisfied and then bypassed rather than defeated.

who.versions_affected: Platforms too old for a current endpoint agent

what.summary: A red team persisted for several months undetected on hosts running a legacy operating system that could not carry an endpoint detection agent, and separately the assessed organisation was found to have relied too heavily on host-based detection while lacking network layer protections.

how.logic: Reconcile the endpoint agent inventory against the asset inventory and treat the difference as a named population rather than a gap to be closed later. For each such host, the only available visibility is network observation and whatever the platform itself can forward, so those hosts should be the priority for network sensor placement rather than an afterthought. Several months of undetected persistence is the demonstrated consequence.

fields.note: distinguish cannot-install from not-yet-installed; the two need different responses

how.caveat: In industrial environments this population is large and permanent, since vendor support conditions frequently forbid agents outright. Treating it as a temporary gap rather than a standing design constraint is the mistake this record exists to prevent.

how.logic: The assessment's own conclusion was over-reliance on host-based tooling with insufficient network layer protection, and that the endpoint product failed to catch all payloads even where it was installed. Network layer visibility is therefore not a supplement to endpoint detection but the compensating control for both the hosts that cannot run an agent and the payloads the agent misses.
how.caveat: Stated plainly by the assessors: the endpoint product did not catch everything. Any coverage claim resting entirely on endpoint detection is contradicted by the assessment evidence.

where.title: CISA red team assessment findings, combined from three published assessments

notes: Directly relevant to the industrial records in this corpus, many of which carry a caveat that agents cannot be installed on operator stations and engineering workstations. This advisory supplies the empirical consequence of that caveat from an assessment of a general enterprise: several months of undetected persistence.

what.summary: A joint health-sector warning of an imminent criminal threat, describing a loader-led chain in which phishing delivers a loader, the loader retrieves modules for credential harvesting, mail exfiltration and lateral movement, and ransomware follows. Command traffic is carried over DNS with a single-byte cipher, persistence is a task running every fifteen minutes, and the loader deletes its own file after execution. The advisory notes the difficulty of balancing this against pandemic pressures when deciding security investment.

how.logic: The backdoor communicates with its controllers over DNS specifically to evade network defence products and blend into legitimate name resolution. The advisory gives two things that make this detectable rather than theoretical: the traffic is obscured with a single-byte cipher using a stated key, and once decrypted the tool's own name appears in the request. The request naming convention is also fixed, carrying the host name and build number in a structured path.
how.caveat: A published key and a plaintext string inside the decrypted payload is an unusually generous gift from an advisory, and it will not survive the operator changing either. The volumetric half, one host making an abnormal number of queries under a single parent domain, outlives the specific indicators and is what to keep.

how.logic: Persistence is a scheduled task running every fifteen minutes, named to resemble an update job with a fixed prefix and five random digits, placed in a randomly named folder under the roaming profile. Two things are anomalous independently: the interval, since almost nothing legitimate runs quarter-hourly, and a task action pointing into a user profile directory.
how.caveat: The interval marker generalises well beyond this family and needs no indicator list: enumerate scheduled tasks repeating more often than every fifteen minutes and the legitimate set is small enough to allow-list once.

how.logic: The loader copies itself under a twelve-character random name into the Windows directory, the 32-bit compatibility directory or the roaming profile, then writes architecture-suffixed modules and named configuration files into a modules subdirectory. The module and configuration names are fixed and unusual enough to match directly, and the random-name-in-a-system-directory shape holds even when they change.
how.caveat: The module names cover mail exfiltration, network spread and share enumeration, which is a useful read on intent: their presence indicates which capabilities were actually deployed rather than which the family is capable of.

how.logic: The malware tested internet connectivity against four named public address-reporting services. They are legitimate and reputable, which is why they were chosen, and which is also why the marker is durable: any replacement will also be a reputable public address service, and the set of those is small and enumerable.
how.caveat: Scope by host role. On developer workstations this happens legitimately; on a server, a clinical system or an operator station the legitimate rate is zero.

how.logic: The loader removes its own file with a short timeout followed by a delete through the command shell, and with a sleep followed by a removal through the script interpreter. Both exact command shapes are given in the advisory. The delay is present so the parent has exited first, which is what makes the command line distinctive.
