how.caveat: The second reason for being targeted is the one organisations overlook: an individual of no intelligence value in themselves is worth approaching as a route to someone who is. That includes suppliers, advisers and former colleagues.

how.logic: The actor registered malicious domains resembling legitimate organisations to appear authentic. Because the approach arrives from consumer webmail and leads to a lookalike domain, the credential capture happens away from corporate infrastructure, so web proxy and name resolution telemetry are where it is visible if the device is managed at all.
how.caveat: Only observable where the device is managed and the traffic is inspected. Where the approach lands on a personal device, as this campaign intends, none of this telemetry exists.

where.publisher: NCSC-UK, CISA, FBI, NSA, CNMF, Australian Cyber Security Centre, Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and NCSC-NZ
where.title: Russian FSB Cyber Actor Star Blizzard Continues Worldwide Spearphishing Campaigns

notes: The most refined social engineering in the corpus, because the impersonated party is a real person the target actually knows, identified through research on platforms the employer does not control. It completes a set with the help desk impersonation and thread hijacking records: three separate ways of arriving as someone trusted, none of which any content-based control resolves. The stated logic for target selection is also worth carrying, since an actor approaches someone who has the information, is a route to someone who does, or both, which means being a stepping stone is sufficient reason to be targeted and explains the inclusion of academics and advisers alongside defence staff.

what.summary: Two agencies addressed a spearphishing campaign against government, intergovernmental and non-governmental organisations in which a sophisticated actor used a compromised end-user account at a legitimate email marketing company to impersonate a government organisation and distribute links to malicious destinations. The agencies acknowledged open-source reporting attributing the activity to a named state group but stated they were investigating and had not attributed it to any actor at that time, and that they had not determined that any individual accounts were specifically targeted.

how.logic: The mail genuinely originates from a legitimate marketing platform using an account that platform holds, so sender authentication passes and the platform's reputation is good. The discriminators are the mismatch between the organisation the message claims to represent and the platform account sending on its behalf, and the destination of the links rather than the origin of the message.

markers.expr: spf_dkim_dmarc_pass and claimed_sending_organisation not in known_senders_via_that_platform

how.caveat: Defeats every sender-authentication control at once because the authentication is genuinely correct. Blocking the platform by reputation would take out a widely used commercial service, so the workable surface is the link destination and the sender-organisation mismatch.

how.logic: The agencies explicitly acknowledged open-source attribution to a named state group and then declined to adopt it, stating they were still investigating. That separation between what their own evidence supported and what others had reported is worth mirroring, because downstream decisions on disclosure, insurance and regulatory notification may turn on the actor's identity.
how.caveat: Worth holding as a standard given how many records here involve deliberate attribution corruption. Repeating an attribution confidently is easy, frequently wrong, and can carry consequences the repeater did not intend.

how.logic: The delivery infrastructure is a genuine commercial service with genuine customers, and the sending account belongs to it rather than to the attacker. That places the origin beyond the target's ability to block and beyond any reputation system's ability to flag, leaving the link destination as the only attacker-controlled element.
how.caveat: The same structural problem as compromised third-party infrastructure elsewhere in this corpus: the origin is a real organisation, so origin reputation carries no information and the analysis has to move downstream.

where.title: Sophisticated Spearphishing Campaign Targets Government Organizations, IGOs, and NGOs

notes: The fourth distinct way in this corpus of arriving as a trusted sender, after thread hijacking, help desk impersonation and contact impersonation, and technically the cleanest: the mail is genuinely sent by a reputable marketing platform on behalf of an account it legitimately holds, so every sender-authentication control returns a correct pass. Only the link destination is attacker-controlled. The advisory is also a good model of attribution restraint, acknowledging open-source attribution to a named state group while declining to adopt it, which is worth mirroring given how much deliberate attribution corruption this corpus records.

what.summary: Eight national authorities assessed a group affiliated with an Iranian military force as continuing to exploit known vulnerabilities for initial access across fourteen identifiers spanning a network appliance vendor, a mail server product family and a logging library, including through a virtual desktop product. The access was used for follow-on activity including disk encryption and data extortion to support ransom operations. Targets spanned multiple critical infrastructure sectors in the United States, Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom. The advisory was co-authored with financial authorities and updates earlier reporting that had described the same activity before the affiliation was judged.

how.logic: The authoring agencies judge these actors to be affiliated with a state military force and record them using their access for disk encryption and data extortion in support of ransom operations. That makes the encryption ambiguous in a way a criminal event is not: it may be revenue, cover for collection, or an effect in itself. The scoping consequence is that restoring from backup and closing the incident would leave any collection objective unexamined.
how.caveat: The involvement of financial authorities among the co-authors signals the payment dimension directly. Together with the state-sponsored ransomware and false-branding records here, this is the third case where treating a ransomware event as a commercial negotiation would be the wrong frame.

how.logic: Fourteen published identifiers, all with fixes available, concentrated in three product families: a network appliance vendor, a mail server family and a logging library reached through a virtual desktop product. The logging library appears as three separate identifiers, which is the incomplete-fix pattern: an organisation tracking only the first would have reported the exposure closed while it remained open.
how.caveat: Three identifiers for one library flaw is the reusable warning. The same shape appears with the web server path traversal elsewhere in this corpus, where the first fix was incomplete and a second identifier was required.

how.logic: One of the named appliance identifiers is the flaw that lets an actor skip the second factor by changing the capitalisation of the username. Its appearance here, in a state-affiliated campaign, alongside its appearance in a criminal ransomware campaign elsewhere in this corpus, shows the same appliance weakness serving both.
how.caveat: Worth noting that the advisory's own prioritised actions are patching known exploited vulnerabilities, enforcing a second factor, and offline backups. The second of those is undermined by this specific flaw, which is why enforcement has to be verified on every code path rather than assumed from configuration.

how.logic: Exploitation of the logging library flaw causes the vulnerable application to make an outbound directory or remote-invocation connection to fetch and execute code. A server initiating that kind of outbound lookup is anomalous regardless of which application is vulnerable, which makes this detection independent of the specific product and of the version inventory.
how.caveat: The most durable Log4j detection in this corpus because it does not depend on knowing which of your applications embeds the library, which was the hardest question of that event.

where.publisher: FBI, CISA, NSA, CNMF, Department of the Treasury, ACSC, CCCS and NCSC-UK
where.title: Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Affiliated Cyber Actors Exploiting Vulnerabilities for Data Extortion and Disk Encryption for Ransom Operations

notes: The clearest case in the corpus of a state-affiliated group running ransom operations, which makes the encryption ambiguous in a way a criminal event is not: revenue, cover for collection, or an effect in its own right. The practical consequence is scoping, since restoring from backup and closing the incident would leave any collection objective unexamined. Two reusable details sit alongside that. The logging library appears as three identifiers, so a programme tracking only the first would have reported itself closed while remaining open. And the appliance flaw that skips the second factor by changing username capitalisation appears here and in a criminal campaign elsewhere in this corpus, which is why enforcing strong authentication has to be verified per code path rather than assumed from configuration.

what.summary: A group active since at least 2009, located in one province of the People's Republic of China, targeted government organisations, companies and universities across biomedical, robotics and maritime research, and industries associated with a national infrastructure initiative, across North America, Europe, the Middle East and the South China Sea region. A prosecution established that state security intelligence officers directed employees of a named commercial front company to conduct the exploitation, resulting in theft of trade secrets, intellectual property and other high-value information from organisations and multiple foreign governments. Affected industries included academia, aerospace and aviation, biomedical, the defence industrial base, education, government, healthcare, manufacturing, maritime, research institutes and transport. The advisory notes that some file hashes in its own published indicator set identify legitimate tools rather than malicious files.

how.logic: The advisory states plainly that some hashes in its machine-readable indicator set identify legitimate tools, naming a common remote access client and core operating system binaries, because the actor used those tools rather than because the files are malicious. So the set must be separated before ingestion: attacker-built artefacts can go to blocking, hashes of legitimate tools can only go to hunting with context.
how.caveat: Unusually candid, and worth carrying as a standing caution because the same problem exists in many feeds without the warning. Blocking a core operating system binary by hash is an outage; alerting on one generates enough noise that the whole feed loses credibility with analysts.

how.logic: The prosecution established that intelligence officers directed employees of a commercial front company to carry out the exploitation. Where operations run through contractors, tradecraft quality varies between operators on the same programme, tooling is shared with unrelated commercial work, and objectives may serve both the state requirement and the contractor's own interest. None of that is inferable from artefacts.
how.caveat: The second contractor-run state programme in this corpus. In both cases a commercial motive coexisted with the state one, so inferring a single coherent objective from the intrusion was unsafe.

how.logic: The objective was trade secrets, intellectual property and high-value research information across biomedical, robotics, maritime, aerospace and defence industrial targets. That means the detection surface is bulk read of research and design repositories rather than anything destructive, and the loss is silent, with no outage and no extortion contact to reveal it.
how.caveat: Requires knowing which repositories each population legitimately reads, which research organisations rarely document because broad internal access is a cultural norm. The absence of any disruptive effect is also why intrusions of this kind run for years before discovery.

how.logic: Universities and research institutes are named alongside companies and governments. Academic environments combine valuable research with open collaboration, transient user populations and devolved administration, which makes the individual researcher and their collaborations part of the attack surface in a way corporate controls do not cover.
how.caveat: Consistent with the two spearphishing records here that name academia and think tanks. Research collaboration is designed to be permeable, which means the control has to be about what is reachable once inside rather than about keeping people out.

where.title: Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures of Indicted APT40 Actors Associated with China's MSS Hainan State Security Department

notes: Two things make this worth keeping beyond the actor detail. It is the corpus's only explicit warning that a published indicator set contains hashes of legitimate tools, including core operating system binaries, which is a standing caution for anyone ingesting feeds and applies to many feeds that carry no such warning. And the front company structure, established by prosecution rather than inference, is the second contractor-run state programme here, which means tradecraft quality varies within one programme and a commercial motive can coexist with the state one. The objective being silent theft of research also explains the twelve-year activity span: nothing breaks, so nothing prompts an investigation.

what.summary: An agency reported consistently observing actors affiliated with a Chinese state security ministry using publicly available information sources and common, well-known techniques to target government networks, and using readily available exploits and exploit toolkits to engage targets quickly. Its stated key finding is that a rigorous patching cycle remains the best defence against the most frequently used attacks, because where critical vulnerabilities remain unpatched an actor can operate without developing custom malware or exploits and without using previously unknown flaws. A related prosecution described a campaign lasting over ten years across high technology manufacturing, medical devices, engineering, software, solar energy, pharmaceuticals and defence, with the individuals acting both for personal gain and for the benefit of the state service.

how.logic: The agency's key takeaways are that these actors use open-source information to plan operations, use readily available exploits and toolkits to engage networks quickly, and that unpatched critical vulnerabilities remove any need for custom malware or unknown flaws. The measurable form is the interval between a fix being published for an internet-facing product and its deployment, because that interval is the entire opportunity this tradecraft depends on.
how.caveat: The reframing worth carrying is that patching is not hygiene competing with real security work; it is what forces a state actor to spend capability it would rather conserve. All four named identifiers also appear elsewhere in this corpus in unrelated criminal and state campaigns.

how.logic: The actors use commercially available information sources and open-source tooling to plan and execute operations, which means the reconnaissance stage costs them nothing and happens entirely outside the target's visibility. The defensive counterpart is to run the same collection against yourself and treat anything discoverable that is absent from your inventory as the finding.
how.caveat: The same conclusion the control system advisory reaches from a different direction: where the information an attacker needs is published, obscurity is not available as a control and the only response is to know what is discoverable.

how.logic: The prosecution describes individuals acting both for their own personal gain and for the benefit of the state service, across a campaign spanning more than a decade and many unrelated industries. Where the operator has a private motive alongside the state one, the target set widens beyond anything a purely intelligence-led assessment would predict, and the objective of any single intrusion is ambiguous.
how.caveat: The third instance of a state programme with a commercial motive attached in this corpus. The practical consequence is that industries with no obvious intelligence value are still in scope, because the operator has their own reasons.

where.title: Chinese Ministry of State Security-Affiliated Cyber Threat Actor Activity

notes: The most quotable advisory in the corpus for a funding conversation, because a national agency states plainly that a state intelligence service reaches government networks using public information and publicly available exploits, and that unpatched critical vulnerabilities remove any need for custom capability. That converts patching from hygiene into the control that forces an adversary to spend capability. The decade-long campaign described in the associated prosecution, with operators acting for both personal gain and state benefit, also explains why the target industries look commercially rather than strategically selected.

what.summary: A six-agency advisory on North Korean state-sponsored ransomware against health and other critical infrastructure, where the proceeds are assessed to fund state cyber operations against the same governments and defence industrial base organisations being targeted. The actors deliberately obscure their involvement, operating under third-party foreign affiliate identities, using foreign intermediaries to receive payment, and in some cases presenting themselves as an unrelated criminal ransomware group. They used both privately developed and publicly available ransomware, including the operating system's own encryption, and trojanised a messenger used specifically by staff at small and medium hospitals in one country.

how.logic: The advisory states the actors have portrayed themselves as a named criminal ransomware group, operate under third-party foreign affiliate identities, and use third-party foreign intermediaries to receive ransom payments. Treat the claimed family and the note's branding as an assertion by the attacker rather than as evidence. Where the branding says commodity criminal but the targeting is a defence industrial base network, the branding is the least reliable input available.
how.caveat: The consequence is financial and legal rather than analytical. A payment decision taken on the note's claimed criminal identity may in fact be a payment to a sanctioned state actor, which the authoring agencies cite as a reason to discourage payment alongside the fact that it does not guarantee recovery.

how.logic: Alongside privately developed families the actors were observed using or holding a long list of public encryption tools, including the operating system's own full-disk encryption. That case defeats signature and reputation controls completely, because the binary is a signed platform component doing what it exists to do. The discriminator is encryption being turned on, or a recovery protector changed, where the organisation's own encryption management holds no record and no escrowed key.
how.caveat: Escrow coverage is the control that decides whether this is an outage or an unrecoverable loss, and it is worth auditing independently of any detection. The named public families also include several aimed at network attached storage, which is frequently where backups sit.

how.logic: The actors trojanised an open-source messenger used specifically by employees of small and medium hospitals in one country, distributing it from two lookalike domains with six named file hashes. Software with a narrow sector or regional user base sits outside the coverage of global reputation products, is often installed by staff rather than by the organisation, and is frequently absent from the asset inventory.
how.caveat: The indicators are narrow and dated; the strategic question they raise is not. Ask which software in your estate is specific to your sector or country, who installed it, where it updates from, and whether any commercial product would recognise a tampered build of it.

how.logic: Initial access used a logging library flaw and remote code execution in unpatched remote access and storage appliances. All three are published identifiers with available fixes, so the exposure is answerable from the inventory rather than requiring any of the actor-specific indicators in this record.
how.caveat: A state actor funding its own operations through ransomware, using three published vulnerabilities with available patches, is the strongest form of the argument that patching internet-facing appliances is a strategic control rather than a hygiene task.

how.logic: The actors purchase remote access services, virtual private servers and third-country addresses so their traffic appears to come from innocuous locations, and procure that infrastructure with cryptocurrency obtained from earlier crime. Country-based blocking and reputation checks therefore return clean answers by design.
how.caveat: Hosting-provider address space is where a large share of legitimate remote work and vendor access also originates, so this cannot stand alone. Its value is as enrichment on an authentication that is already interesting for another reason.

how.logic: The authoring agencies assess that revenue from these operations supports state-level priorities including operations against the United States and South Korean governments, with named interest in defence networks and defence industrial base members. That places the payment decision in a different frame from a commercial extortion event.
how.caveat: This has to be decided before an incident, because during one the only identity information available is the note, and the note is deliberately misleading. Organisations in the named sectors should assume the branding may be false and take the decision on that basis.

where.publisher: NSA, FBI, CISA, HHS, Republic of Korea National Intelligence Service and Defense Security Agency
where.title: #StopRansomware: Ransomware Attacks on Critical Infrastructure Fund DPRK Malicious Cyber Activities

notes: The most important record in the corpus for anyone who owns a ransom payment decision, because it breaks the assumption that a ransomware event is a commercial negotiation. Three things compound: the branding may name an unrelated criminal group, payment may run through foreign intermediaries to a sanctioned state actor, and the proceeds are assessed to fund operations against the payer's own sector. It also contains the corpus's clearest instance of the platform's own tooling being the weapon, where there is nothing malicious to detect and the only meaningful control is whether recovery keys were escrowed somewhere the attacker could not reach.

who.versions_affected: Not applicable

what.summary: A two-week assessment at a healthcare organisation found no significant or exploitable conditions in externally available systems and could not gain access by phishing either, then compromised the entire domain from inside through misconfigurations, weak passwords and multiple separate attack paths.

how.logic: This is the clearest evidence in the corpus that perimeter strength and interior strength are unrelated. The external week found nothing and phishing failed, which is better than most organisations achieve, and the domain still fell through multiple paths once inside. So an assessment programme that tests only the perimeter measures the wrong thing. The action is internal path testing: from an ordinary workstation with an ordinary user account, what can be reached and what privilege can be obtained. Multiple paths existing means fixing one changes nothing.

fields.note: whether internal path testing from an ordinary account has ever been performed, separately from external testing

how.caveat: Not a detection. It is an argument about where assessment budget goes, and it cuts against the common preference for external testing because external findings are easier to explain and cheaper to fix.

how.logic: The named causes were misconfigurations and weak passwords, not vulnerabilities. That matters because neither appears in a vulnerability scan. Audit password strength against a breach corpus rather than against a complexity policy, and audit the specific misconfigurations from the top-ten list recorded elsewhere in this corpus. Both are findable before an assessor finds them.
how.caveat: Complexity policies do not prevent weak passwords, they shape them predictably. Checking against known-breached credentials is the test that reflects what an attacker actually tries.

where.title: Enhancing Cyber Resilience: Insights from the CISA Healthcare and Public Health Sector Risk and Vulnerability Assessment

notes: Worth reading directly against the record on insufficient internal network monitoring, which says the same thing from the monitoring side: the perimeter is well instrumented and well defended, and the interior is neither. The advisory also addresses software manufacturers directly, on the grounds that some of what the assessors exploited was default product behaviour rather than customer error.

who.versions_affected: Not applicable

what.summary: Two agencies aggregated their red team, blue team, hunt and incident response engagements and published the ten network misconfigurations they most commonly found in large organisations, explicitly including organisations with mature security postures.

how.logic: This is a prioritisation input rather than a detection, and its value is empirical: these ten are what assessments actually keep finding, so they outrank a threat-led list when deciding what to fix first. In order as published: default configurations of software and applications; improper separation of user and administrator privilege; insufficient internal network monitoring; lack of network segmentation; poor patch management; bypass of system access controls; weak or misconfigured multi-factor authentication; insufficient access control lists on network shares and services; poor credential hygiene; unrestricted code execution. Work through them as an audit and record which apply, because the finding that they persist in mature organisations means assuming your own maturity exempts you is the mistake.

fields.note: the ten as published; record present or absent per environment rather than treating as a query

how.caveat: Nothing here is a query and none of it is new. The contribution is prevalence: knowing which weaknesses assessments find most often is what makes a remediation queue defensible, and every one of the ten already has detections elsewhere in this corpus. The advisory is equally explicit that several of these are the software industry's problem rather than the operator's, naming eliminated default passwords, audit logs provided at no extra cost, and multi-factor authentication mandated by default rather than offered as an option.

how.logic: Insufficient internal network monitoring appears third on the list and is the one that silently disables the largest number of detections in this corpus. Many records here depend on seeing host-to-host traffic inside the network: workstation-to-workstation sessions, file sharing between peers, industrial protocol traffic, lateral movement of any kind. Perimeter sensors see none of it. Establish where internal visibility exists and where it does not, then read the detection library against that map.

fields.note: per segment, whether east-west traffic is observed at all
perimeter only, or internal chokepoints too

how.caveat: The usual answer is that the perimeter is well instrumented and the interior is not, which means the detections that matter after initial access are the ones that cannot run. Worth knowing before promising coverage.

where.title: NSA and CISA Red and Blue Teams Share Top Ten Cybersecurity Misconfigurations

notes: Unusual and worth its place: most advisories describe what one actor did, while this describes what assessors keep finding regardless of actor. That makes it the right thing to consult when the question is where to spend effort rather than what to hunt for. The observation that these persist in organisations with mature postures is the part to quote when a remediation programme gets deprioritised on the grounds that the basics are already covered.

who.versions_affected: Not applicable

what.summary: A joint threat hunt at a critical infrastructure organisation, searching host, network, industrial control system and cloud telemetry for specific adversary techniques, found no evidence of any threat actor present and still identified several cybersecurity risks worth remediating.

how.logic: The method is the transferable part. The hunt searched for specific named techniques and their associated artefacts across host, network, industrial control system and cloud telemetry, rather than looking for anything unusual. That is what makes a hunt finishable and its result meaningful: a negative finding against a defined technique list means something, where a negative finding against no list means nothing. This corpus is usable as the technique list, since every pattern here names its evidence type.

fields.note: the defined set of techniques searched for, so a negative result has scope
gaps in coverage bound what the negative finding can mean

how.caveat: A negative hunt result is only as strong as the telemetry it ran against, which is why recording coverage gaps alongside the finding matters. A clean hunt over partial telemetry is not a clean environment.

how.logic: The valuable outcome was the risk findings rather than the absence of an actor. That reframes what a hunt is for: an exercise that finds nothing has still audited the environment against a real technique list and produced remediation work. Organisations that judge hunt value by whether an adversary was found will conclude the exercise failed, which is the wrong conclusion.

fields.note: risks identified, independent of whether any actor was present

how.caveat: This is an argument about how to evaluate hunting programmes rather than a detection. Recorded because the incentive to find something is what pushes hunts toward chasing noise.

where.publisher: CISA and United States Coast Guard
where.title: CISA and USCG Identify Areas for Cyber Hygiene Improvement Following Threat Hunt Engagement

notes: Unusual and worth its place for the method rather than the findings. Most advisories describe what was found; this describes a structured search that found no adversary, which is the more common outcome of hunting and the one least often written up. The involvement of a maritime authority alongside the cyber agency also reflects how sector regulators and cyber agencies increasingly hunt jointly in critical infrastructure.

what.summary: A North Korean state-sponsored group targeted organisations and individuals across blockchain and cryptocurrency, including exchanges, decentralised finance protocols, play-to-earn games, trading companies, venture funds and individual holders of large amounts of cryptocurrency or valuable tokens. It used social engineering over a variety of communication platforms to encourage individuals to download trojanised cryptocurrency applications built for both Windows and macOS, then used those applications to reach the victim's computer, spread across the network and steal private keys or exploit other gaps, enabling fraudulent blockchain transactions. The advisory was issued with financial authorities.

how.logic: The applications are functional cryptocurrency tools, which is what earns the install, and they were built for both major desktop platforms rather than only Windows. So the discriminators are provenance and behaviour: software installed from somewhere other than the vendor's own distribution, an unexpected or absent signature, and access to key material or wallet files beyond what the application's stated function requires.

markers.expr: application_installed and download_source not in vendor_official_distribution

how.caveat: macOS coverage is the part most estates lack, and this campaign built for it deliberately. Where the target is an individual holding assets rather than an organisation, no corporate control sits in the path at all: the approach arrives on a personal messaging platform and the install happens on a personal device.

how.logic: The named target set explicitly includes individual holders of large amounts of cryptocurrency or valuable tokens, alongside organisations. Social engineering came over a variety of communication platforms rather than corporate mail, which means the approach channel is one no organisational control inspects.

markers.expr: person in (asset_custodians, treasury_staff, executives) and personal_device_or_account_used_for_work

how.caveat: Where an individual is the target and the asset is bearer-like, the loss is irreversible once the transaction settles. That removes recovery as an option entirely, which is rare in this corpus and puts all the weight on prevention.

how.logic: Once installed, the application was used to reach the computer and propagate across the victim's network environment, so the compromise does not stay with the individual who installed it. On a corporate estate the propagation stage is the detectable one, since a cryptocurrency application has no reason to contact other internal hosts.
how.caveat: A desktop application of this class talking to internal hosts at all is anomalous, which makes a low threshold defensible. The financial authority involvement also signals that the theft carries reporting obligations beyond the intrusion.

where.publisher: FBI, CISA and Department of the Treasury
where.title: TraderTraitor: North Korean State-Sponsored APT Targets Blockchain Companies

notes: Distinctive in this corpus for three reasons. The malicious software is a working application in the victim's own professional domain, so the install is a considered decision rather than a mistake. It was built for macOS as well as Windows, which is the coverage most estates lack. And the loss is irreversible once a blockchain transaction settles, so unlike ransomware or data theft there is no recovery, negotiation or remediation path, which puts the entire weight on prevention and on out-of-band verification of transfers.

who.versions_affected: Modified builds distributed as legitimate products

what.summary: State-sponsored actors built and distributed cryptocurrency trading applications that looked and functioned like legitimate products but carried malware, targeting exchanges and financial services firms in more than thirty countries, assessed as a means of circumventing international sanctions.

how.logic: The application is not a compromised legitimate product but an entirely attacker-built one presented as legitimate, sometimes with a signing certificate and a plausible corporate website. Provenance checks against a vendor therefore fail, because the vendor is fictitious. What works is the inverse: an inventory of approved software and an alert on anything installed outside it, particularly on hosts with access to financial systems. Signature validity is not evidence of legitimacy here.

fields.note: compared against the approved software inventory rather than against a reputation service
recorded to make the point that a valid signature does not help; the certificate was obtained legitimately by a fictitious entity

how.caveat: Only works where an approved software inventory exists, which is the harder half. On personal or unmanaged devices used for work this has no purchase at all, which is how several of these intrusions began.

how.logic: The installed application fetches and runs further components then establishes a command channel, so the sequence of install, download from a destination with no history, and outbound connection to a second unfamiliar destination captures it without needing to recognise the application.
how.caveat: Needs file, process and network telemetry correlated on host identity.

where.publisher: FBI, CISA and US Department of the Treasury
where.title: AppleJeus: Analysis of North Korea's Cryptocurrency Malware

notes: The distinction from ordinary supply chain compromise is worth keeping: nothing legitimate was tampered with. The vendor, the product and the website were all constructed for the purpose, which defeats every control that rests on verifying a real vendor. Recorded with a financial sector focus, but the technique applies to any sector where staff install specialist tooling that IT does not supply.

what.summary: An agency set out how actors use network tunnelling and spoofing to obscure their location, stating that attribution requires analysis of multiple variables and that it is not possible to identify the true physical location of malicious activity based solely on the geolocation of an address. It notes that geolocation is derived from public registration or proprietary data whose precision and accuracy vary widely by source, and that even where the geolocation is accurate the actor may be elsewhere. Spoofing an arbitrary source address is described as most common with connectionless activity such as denial of service and amplification, while encapsulating tunnels serve interactive activity. The stated purpose of the advisory is to explain how these techniques mislead incident responders.

how.logic: Record source geography as an observation and never as a conclusion, and keep it out of scoping, disclosure and escalation decisions. The two techniques limit different investigations: spoofing applies mainly to connectionless activity such as denial of service and amplification, where no session is established, while tunnels apply to interactive activity where a session is.
how.caveat: The agency states the purpose of these techniques is to mislead responders, which makes source geography an adversary-controlled input rather than merely an unreliable one. Note also that geolocation accuracy varies widely between providers before any deception is considered.

how.logic: Combined with the other records here on shared networks of compromised consumer devices and on anonymising overlay networks, four independent mechanisms now defeat source-based reasoning. Detection has to rest on the behaviour of the session and the account, and blocking by geography or reputation is defeated by design in all four.
how.caveat: Worth stating as a corpus-level conclusion rather than a per-record caveat: no record here should be built on source address, and several would be weaker than they appear if they were.

how.logic: The advisory's stated purpose is to explain how these techniques mislead responders, which is an argument for separating what telemetry supports from what is inferred. Where the inference rests on location, it rests on something the adversary chose.
how.caveat: Attribution requires multiple variables, and location is the one most easily manipulated and most often quoted. It is also the one non-specialists find most persuasive, which is why an incident report should state its basis explicitly.

where.title: Malicious Cyber Actor Use of Network Tunneling and Spoofing to Obfuscate Geolocation

notes: The corpus's foundational statement on why source address carries so little information. Together with the records on shared networks of compromised consumer devices, anonymising overlay networks, and relays chosen in the victim's own region, there are now four independent mechanisms defeating source-based reasoning, which makes this a corpus-level conclusion rather than a per-record caveat: no detection here should rest on where traffic appears to come from. The agency's framing is stronger than unreliability, since it states the purpose of these techniques is to mislead responders, making location an adversary-controlled input.

who.versions_affected: Not applicable

what.summary: Most hosts in an assessed organisation, including domain controllers, could reach broad cloud provider address ranges directly, letting a red team make outbound web requests without any detection response, and revealing that no application layer firewall was checking whether traffic on a port matched the protocol it should carry.

how.logic: Attacker infrastructure sits in the same cloud provider ranges as legitimate services, so a broad allow rule to a provider is effectively a broad allow rule to anywhere. Two questions follow. Which hosts can reach provider ranges directly, and why does that list include servers and domain controllers, which have no business browsing. A domain controller with general outbound internet access is a finding on its own regardless of whether anything used it.

fields.note: restrict to server and domain controller roles, where the answer should be no general egress
cloud provider published ranges

how.caveat: Genuine cloud service dependencies make a blanket block impractical, so the workable version is per-host-role rather than per-destination: servers and controllers reach a named list of endpoints, not a provider.

how.logic: The absence of an application layer firewall able to detect protocol mismatches on common ports was called out explicitly. The detection is traffic on a well-known port whose actual protocol is not the expected one: something other than web traffic on the web ports, non-resolution traffic on the resolution port. This catches tunnelling that a port-based rule set permits by definition.

fields.note: flag where the identified application protocol does not match the port's expected protocol

how.caveat: Requires a sensor that identifies protocol independently of port, which is exactly the capability the assessment found missing. Where the firewall is port-based only, this cannot be written at all and that is the finding.

how.logic: Proxy server use from hosts intended to be restricted from internet access appeared in the missed-opportunity list. Where a host is supposed to have no internet path, any successful outbound session, including one through a proxy, contradicts the intended state and is worth alerting on rather than ranking.

fields.note: the population declared as having no internet access

how.caveat: Depends on someone maintaining the list of hosts that are supposed to be isolated. That list existing at all is the prerequisite, and its absence is a more common finding than its violation.

where.title: CISA red team assessment findings, combined from three published assessments

notes: Also recorded in the same assessment: network address translation between parts of the network obscured data streams and hindered incident response. Worth carrying as a design consideration, since translation is usually introduced for addressing reasons with no thought given to what it does to an investigation.

products: VNC remote access on HMI devices
who.versions_affected: Any operator interface reachable over remote framebuffer protocol, particularly with weak or absent authentication

what.summary: Pro-Russia hacktivist groups targeted operator interfaces reachable over VNC, using simple and easily copied techniques. The authoring organisations assess their capability as limited and note they frequently misunderstand the processes they are trying to disrupt, yet have still caused real harm to vulnerable critical infrastructure.

how.logic: The whole technique depends on an operator interface being reachable over remote framebuffer protocol from outside. Enumerate which control-network assets answer on those ports and from where, because that inventory question closes the entire attack path rather than detecting it. For anything that must remain reachable, alert on every session: the legitimate user population for an operator interface is tiny, named, and does not change.

fields.note: remote framebuffer and its web variants; confirm the ports actually in use
these interfaces are frequently deployed with no password at all

how.caveat: Deployed for legitimate remote operations, often by an integrator years earlier and forgotten. Removing exposure needs the operations team's agreement about how the site is supported out of hours, so this is an operational conversation and not only a firewall change.

how.logic: Because these actors do not reliably understand the process, their changes are erratic rather than targeted, which makes envelope monitoring the right defence: alert on any setpoint moved outside its safe operating range regardless of who moved it or why. A detection built around plausible attacker intent would miss changes made in ignorance, and those have still caused harm.

fields.note: compare against the documented safe operating range rather than against a plausible attack pattern

how.caveat: Needs process engineers to supply the safe ranges. The advantage against this actor class is that random changes trip envelope limits readily, where a knowledgeable operator would stay inside them.

how.logic: An interactive session on an operator interface from a source outside the known set, especially outside shift hours. Pair it with the operator's own view: a control action nobody in the control room initiated is the strongest available confirmation, and it comes from the process side rather than from security telemetry.

fields.note: operator interface assets
compare against the operator workstation set and the shift pattern

how.caveat: Out-of-hours callouts are legitimate and unscheduled. The reconciliation is with the control room rather than with a change ticket, which means the detection needs a human in the loop who can be reached quickly.

where.title: Pro-Russia Hacktivist Activity Targeting Operational Technology Devices

notes: This record matters precisely because the actors are unsophisticated. Most of the corpus describes state-sponsored operators whose activity is hard to detect; this describes low-capability actors using replicable techniques against targets that should never have been reachable. The authoring organisations note they primarily seek notoriety and regularly make false or exaggerated claims about their attacks, so public claims should not be taken as evidence of impact. The countermeasure is exposure removal, not detection sophistication, which makes it one of the highest value-to-effort items in the corpus for any operator with internet-reachable operator interfaces.

what.summary: Agencies set out the threat profile for water and wastewater facilities, naming spearphishing for initial access to business networks that are integrated with control networks, exploitation of internet-connected remote access services including remote desktop used for process control equipment, unsupported or outdated operating systems and software, and control devices running vulnerable firmware exposing publicly known remotely executable flaws. They note these are inconsistently resourced municipal systems that tend to allocate funds to physical infrastructure needing repair rather than to technology modernisation, and that actors likely seek to exploit that. Insider threat from current or former employees with improperly active credentials is named alongside ransomware. Two recorded incidents illustrate the pattern: one variant present for about a month and discovered only when three control servers displayed a ransom message, and another introduced by remote access onto a wastewater control computer, after which the treatment system was run manually until the computer was restored.

how.logic: At one facility the treatment system was run manually until the compromised control computer was restored, which converted a control system compromise into an operational inconvenience rather than a service failure. The question is answerable per process: can it be run manually, for how long, by how many trained people, and when was that last rehearsed.
how.caveat: One of very few genuinely mitigating factors available in this domain, and it degrades quietly as experienced staff leave and as processes are re-engineered to assume automation. Worth rehearsing rather than documenting.

how.logic: The agencies state that these facilities are inconsistently resourced municipal systems which tend to allocate resources to physical infrastructure in need of replacement rather than to technology, and that actors likely seek to take advantage of that. The honest response where capability is constrained is a very small control set that breaks the most common chains rather than a broad programme that will not be completed.

markers.expr: minimum_viable_control_set defined and covers(second_factor_on_remote_access, offline_backup_tested, known_exploited_vulnerability_patching)

how.caveat: The competing priority named here is not negligence but pipes that need replacing, which is a real and defensible allocation. That makes the argument for a minimum set rather than a maturity programme, and it is the same conclusion the education sector record reaches.

how.logic: Insider threat from current or former employees who maintain improperly active credentials is named as one of two headline threats alongside ransomware. On small municipal operations the same few people often hold control system access for years, and offboarding is frequently informal, which makes reconciliation of enabled accounts against the current roster both more important and less likely to exist.
how.caveat: The third record in this corpus where a former employee's credential is the route in, and the only one where the agencies name it as a headline sector threat rather than an incidental finding.

how.logic: Named exposures are internet-connected services enabling remote access to the facility network, remote desktop insecurely connected to the internet and in some cases used for process control equipment, unsupported operating systems, and control devices with vulnerable firmware exposing publicly known remotely executable flaws. The agencies also note remote operations increased during the pandemic, which raised the prevalence of these weaknesses.

markers.expr: internet_reachable and (device_class = control_system or service = remote_desktop)

how.caveat: Remote desktop exposed to the internet and used for process control equipment is the specific combination named, and it recurs across the ransomware records in this corpus as the single most productive entry route.

how.logic: In one recorded incident the ransomware had been present for about a month and was discovered only when three control servers displayed a ransom message. A month of dwell time on control infrastructure with no detection means the discovery mechanism was the damage itself, so any signal that several control assets have changed state together is worth more than its false positive rate suggests.
how.caveat: A month of undetected presence on control systems is the finding rather than the ransomware. It indicates no monitoring existed at all on those assets, which is consistent with the resourcing picture the same advisory describes.

where.title: Ongoing Cyber Threats to US Water and Wastewater Systems

notes: The sector profile that best explains why the same weaknesses persist: these are inconsistently resourced municipal operations that reasonably prioritise replacing failing physical infrastructure over modernising technology, and actors are assessed as targeting exactly that. Two details are worth carrying. One incident ran for a month and was discovered only when the ransom note appeared on three control servers, which means the discovery mechanism was the damage. And at another facility the treatment process was run manually until the control computer was restored, which is one of the few genuinely mitigating factors available in operational technology and the one most likely to decay unnoticed as experienced staff leave.

what.summary: Unidentified actors obtained unauthorised access to the control system at a drinking water treatment facility and used the system's own software to increase the dosing of a caustic chemical used in treatment. Plant personnel noticed the change in dosing amounts immediately and corrected it before the control software itself detected the manipulation and raised an alarm, so the treatment process was unaffected and continued normally. The actors likely gained access by exploiting weaknesses including poor password security and an outdated operating system, with early information suggesting desktop sharing software may have been used, though this could not be confirmed. Investigators were not able to confirm the incident was initiated by a targeted intrusion. The agencies note they have observed actors targeting desktop sharing software and systems running operating systems past end of life.

how.logic: The operator noticed the dosing change immediately and corrected it before the control software detected the manipulation and alarmed. Two things follow. Operator observation is a genuine detection capability and should be supported with a reporting route that does not depend on the control system agreeing. And setpoint writes outside engineering-safe ranges should alarm on the value at the moment of the write, rather than on the downstream process consequence, because the two thresholds are set for different purposes.
how.caveat: The human was faster than the system's own alarm, which had not yet fired. That is worth designing for rather than treating as luck: the alarm was configured for process safety, not for detecting deliberate manipulation, and those are different requirements with different thresholds.

how.logic: Early information suggested desktop sharing software may have been used for access. The agencies note such software has multiple legitimate uses including remote work, technical support and file transfer, and is exploited through social engineering and other means. On a control network the approved set is very small and everything outside it is alertable.
how.caveat: The advisory is careful that this could not be confirmed, and investigators could not establish that the incident was even a targeted intrusion. That uncertainty is itself instructive: on a small operation with shared credentials and remote access, distinguishing an intrusion from an accident may not be possible after the fact.

how.logic: Access was likely enabled by poor password security and an outdated operating system, with the agencies noting that continuing to use any operating system past end of life may provide access into systems, and that the named version would become progressively more exploitable as new flaws were found without fixes.
how.caveat: Neither weakness required any sophistication to exploit, and both are common on small municipal operations for the resourcing reasons the water sector advisory in this corpus sets out.

where.publisher: FBI, CISA, EPA and Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center
where.title: Compromise of US Water Treatment Facility

notes: The only record in the corpus where the detection was a person. An operator noticed a chemical dosing setpoint change and corrected it before the control system's own alarm fired, which means the human was faster than the automation and the automation was configured for process safety rather than for manipulation. Both are worth designing for deliberately. It is also the clearest example of an incident where investigators could not confirm whether it was a targeted intrusion at all, which on a small operation with shared credentials and remote access may be unanswerable after the fact.

what.summary: Six national authorities set out the weak security controls, poor configurations and poor practices that actors routinely exploit to gain initial access, alongside the five techniques those weaknesses enable: exploiting public-facing applications, external remote services, phishing, trusted relationships and valid accounts. Named weaknesses include a second authentication factor not being enforced, with the agencies singling out remote desktop as one of the most common ransomware infection vectors and instructing that no user, particularly administrators, be excluded; incorrectly applied privileges and errors in access control lists; software not being up to date, described as one of the most commonly found poor practices; and continued use of vendor-supplied default configurations and default credentials.

how.logic: Every item on the list is a configuration state with a definite answer rather than something to detect. Work it as an audit: is a second factor enforced everywhere including administrators, are privileges and access control lists correct, is software current, are vendor defaults gone, are internet-facing services securely configured, is logging centralised, and are detection tools deployed. Its value is that it is short, ordered by observed frequency and finishable.
how.caveat: The administrator exemption from a second factor is the specific failure worth checking first, because it is usually granted deliberately for convenience and the agencies name it explicitly. Remote desktop being called out as one of the most common ransomware vectors matches every ransomware record in this corpus.

how.logic: A second factor not being enforced heads the list, with remote desktop named as one of the most common ransomware infection vectors. The tractable form is an inventory of every remote access path with an explicit answer on whether the factor is enforced rather than merely available, including for administrative accounts.
how.caveat: Enforced is not the same as available, and the corpus contains two separate cases where a factor was configured but bypassable through the product's own defaults or a code path flaw. Verify enforcement per path rather than reading it from policy.

how.logic: Vendor-supplied default configurations and default credentials appear on the list alongside privilege and access control list errors. These are the weaknesses that require no exploit at all, and several records in this corpus describe complete compromises that used nothing else.
how.caveat: The industrial controller record in this corpus is the extreme case: seventy-five devices compromised with default or absent passwords and no vulnerability involved. Defaults are not a hygiene footnote, they are a complete attack path.

where.publisher: CISA, NSA, FBI, Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, NCSC-NZ, Netherlands NCSC and NCSC-UK
where.title: Weak Security Controls and Practices Routinely Exploited for Initial Access

notes: The natural index for the initial access half of this corpus. Five techniques and a short list of the weaknesses that enable them, every one a configuration state with a definite answer rather than something to detect. Two items are worth prioritising from the corpus's own evidence: administrators exempted from a second factor, which is granted deliberately and appears in several records here, and vendor defaults, which the industrial controller record shows can constitute a complete attack path with no vulnerability involved at all.

what.summary: Destructive malware deployed against organisations in one country ahead of a military invasion, in at least five named families across January and February. One corrupted the boot record, displayed a ransomware note and encrypted files by extension, while the targeted data was in fact destroyed and unrecoverable even if a ransom were paid. Another manipulated the boot record causing boot failure and was installed on hundreds of machines. A separate component existed purely to spread the wiper. The advisory warns that further disruptive attacks are likely and may unintentionally spill over to organisations in other countries.

how.logic: The first family runs in two stages, corrupts the boot record, displays a ransomware note and encrypts files by extension, and the disclosing vendor states the targeted data is destroyed and not recoverable even if a ransom is paid. A second family was described as having similarities to it, with the wiper disguised as ransomware. So the ransom note is a deliberate misdirection about the nature of the event, not a demand.
how.caveat: The costliest misreading available during a live incident. Treating this as ransomware produces a payment decision over data no key can restore, and a recovery plan resting on negotiation instead of rebuilding. Decide the destruction-versus-encryption question before the payment question.

how.logic: Three of the named families manipulate the boot record, with the result that the host fails to boot. Raw writes to the physical drive device or to the partition table by anything that is not a known imaging or partitioning tool is close to a pure signal, because the legitimate rate on a running estate is effectively zero.

markers.expr: raw_write_offset within boot_record_or_partition_table and writing_process not in imaging_tool_allowlist

how.caveat: Fires at the moment of damage rather than before it, so it buys containment speed rather than prevention. Firing on more than one host at once should be treated as a coordinated destructive stage and actioned across the estate immediately, not triaged host by host.

how.logic: The advisory's guidance is architectural rather than detective: network architecture, security baseline, continuous monitoring and incident response practices. The testable question is whether a known-good state is reachable with no cooperation from the attacker, given that there is no key to buy, and with the directory service assumed lost since these campaigns propagated through it.
how.caveat: This is the case where preparedness is the only control that matters, because by the time the wiper runs every detective option has been spent and there is nothing to negotiate for.

how.logic: The advisory states that further disruptive attacks are likely and may unintentionally spill over to organisations in other countries. So exposure is not limited to organisations in the targeted country or to those any actor intends to hit, which is borne out by an earlier destructive campaign in this corpus that spread far beyond its targets and caused losses at unconnected organisations.
how.caveat: Unintentional spill-over is the part that makes this everyone's problem rather than a regional concern, and it is the hardest element to get funded because the organisation is not the intended target.

how.logic: One of the named families exists specifically to spread the wiper across the network rather than to destroy anything itself, which separates the propagation stage from the damage stage. That separation is the detection opportunity: the spreader runs first, and it looks like lateral movement rather than like destruction.

markers.expr: count_distinct(target_host) by source_host, bin(_time, 10m) with file_write to admin_share

how.caveat: The threshold needs local calibration against legitimate deployment tooling, which produces the same shape. The reason to invest in it is that this is the last stage before irreversible damage.

where.title: Destructive Malware Targeting Organizations in Ukraine

notes: The most important record in the corpus for anyone who owns a ransom decision, alongside the state-sponsored ransomware record. Both attack the same assumption from different directions: here the note is real but the data is gone, there the note is real but the actor is not who it claims. Together they mean the ransom note is evidence of nothing except that someone wants you to read it. Five families in two months against one country, with an explicit warning of unintentional spill-over, is also the corpus's clearest argument that destructive-attack preparedness is not a regional concern.

who.versions_affected: Several products across virtualisation, edge and authentication tiers; the pivot rather than any single flaw is the subject

what.summary: A campaign held four layers at once and treated each as insurance for the others: the edge firewall, the hypervisor, the guest machines and finally the authentication server that the network devices themselves trust. The last of these is the objective. Having taken the accounting server, the actor intercepted the protocol that authenticates administrators to routers and switches, and replaced the daemon that serves it, so that further movement across the network estate required no exploit and produced no failed login anywhere.

how.logic: Two ways at the same credentials, run together. A packet capture process on the authentication server reading the administration protocol off the wire and decrypting it with the shared key, and the authentication daemon itself replaced with a build that writes each credential aside after verifying it. Both produce a successful authentication and no failure anywhere, so the authentication log is the wrong place to look. The server's own process and file state is the right place: a capture process where none should run, and a daemon binary that does not match its package.

markers.note: administration and accounting protocols carrying device credentials

how.caveat: The authentication server is usually treated as infrastructure and monitored for availability rather than for what runs on it, which is what makes this survive. It also inverts the value of centralised authentication: the thing that gives you one place to manage device credentials gives an actor one place to collect them. Verifying the daemon against its package is cheap and is the single highest-value check here.

how.logic: Rather than backdooring the secure shell daemon and being caught by a package check, a second server was run behind it, reached over a local socket, with a small injected library redirecting selected sessions to it based on the client identification string. Sessions handled that way never reach the real daemon, so they appear in no authentication log at all. Separately, the genuine client and daemon binaries were replaced to record credentials, and the package manager was told to hold those packages at their current version so that an update could not overwrite them.
how.caveat: A version lock on a security package is close to a zero-false-positive signal on a server that is otherwise kept patched, and it is trivially cheap to check estate-wide, which makes it the best value marker here by a distance. Some estates do legitimately pin packages for application compatibility, so enumerate those first, and note that the list of legitimately pinned packages is itself worth reviewing.

how.logic: Kernel modules loaded from paths outside the platform's own module tree, loaded by custom start-up units rather than the normal module mechanisms, and named to resemble ordinary drivers. Because the module hides files, processes and connections from the operating system, anything asking the operating system a question is answered by the rootkit, and the module inventory itself is the last reliable thing to read.
how.caveat: The last marker is the only trustworthy one once the module is loaded, and it requires a second vantage point: comparing what the network sees of the host against what the host reports of itself. Everything read from the host alone is subject to the thing being looked for.

where.title: Cloaked and Covert: Uncovering UNC3886 Espionage Operations

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound; the selection criterion is whether the platform can run an endpoint agent, not which release it runs

what.summary: An implant built in two languages and ported across operating systems, placed only on appliances that cannot run an endpoint agent, and held for more than eighteen months before anyone noticed. Its most useful function to the actor was not the shell but the proxy: traffic to the victim's cloud tenancy sent through the compromised appliance arrives from the victim's own address space, which satisfies the conditional access policy that would otherwise have refused it. It reached victims through their service providers, and returned quickly after the first attempts to remove it.

how.logic: The actor chose targets by monitoring coverage rather than by value or by version, which makes the estate's own coverage map a prediction of where to look. Reconcile the endpoint agent inventory against the asset inventory, separate what cannot take an agent from what merely has not had one installed, and treat the first group as the place to spend network-derived detection instead. Where an appliance cannot be watched from inside, everything left is what crosses its interfaces.
how.caveat: Not a detection and should not be written as one. It is the measurement that tells you which detections you cannot have, and its output is a list of assets where the only available evidence is network traffic. The eighteen months of dwell here is a direct consequence of that gap rather than of any sophistication in the implant.

how.logic: Proxying cloud access through a compromised appliance defeats location-based conditional access, because the session genuinely originates from the trusted address space. Location therefore proves nothing, and what is left is the combination: a cloud sign-in from a corporate address that no user session on the network can account for, and an edge appliance originating outbound sessions to the tenancy when its role is to terminate inbound ones.
how.caveat: The uncomfortable part is that the control was not bypassed, it was satisfied. Any policy resting on network location inherits the trustworthiness of every device inside that location, including the ones that cannot be monitored. This is the argument for device-based rather than location-based conditions, and the detection is a stopgap until that change is made.

how.logic: Name resolution carried inside encrypted web traffic to a public resolver never reaches the organisation's own resolvers, so every detection built on query logs sees nothing. Two things remain: sessions from internal hosts to the well-known public resolver addresses on the encrypted web port, and the more durable form, which is any host resolving names by a path that is not the organisation's resolver set.
how.caveat: Browsers and operating systems now enable encrypted resolution by default, so the volume of legitimate matches is large and rising, and this is only alertable where the policy is that internal resolvers are mandatory. On an appliance it is different: an appliance has no user and no browser, so encrypted resolution from one is anomalous in a way it is not on a workstation.

where.title: VerdantBamboo: Just Another BRICKSTORM in the Firewall

who.versions_affected: Not applicable; the subject is the recurrence of exploitable classes across vendors rather than any single release

what.summary: An independent research team published 97 pieces of vulnerability research over roughly three years. 38 of them name a specific enterprise vendor, and those 38 concentrate on a small number of remote access and edge products: eight on one firewall vendor, seven on one remote access vendor, six on one application delivery vendor. 58 of the 97 carry a vulnerability identifier. The value of this to a defender is not any individual finding but the distribution, which says that the same small set of internet-facing product classes keeps yielding pre-authentication flaws to anyone who looks, and that a working exploit path is usually public within days of a fix.

how.logic: Count how often each product class in your estate appears across independent vulnerability research and annual exploited lists, not how many identifiers each product has. A class that recurs every year regardless of vendor is telling you the class is the problem, and the question stops being whether it is patched and becomes whether it needs to be reachable from the internet at all.
how.caveat: A posture argument rather than a query, and it is aimed at whoever decides what is exposed rather than at whoever runs the detections. The uncomfortable version of the finding is that vendor choice within a recurring class changes very little, because the concentration follows the class rather than the vendor.

how.logic: Public research routinely reconstructs a working exploit path from a released fix, and publishes it. That makes the interval between a vendor release and your deployment the number that matters, measured for your own internet-facing estate rather than assumed. Where that interval exceeds the interval at which exploit analysis appears publicly, patching is not the control it is being relied upon to be, and compensating restriction has to carry the gap.
how.caveat: Not a detection but a scheduling constraint, and the honest output is usually a number nobody wants to see. It is worth measuring separately for appliances, because they are the class where patching most often requires an outage window and therefore where the interval is longest, which is exactly where the research concentrates.

where.title: watchTowr Labs vulnerability research corpus, 97 posts spanning early 2023 to mid 2026

who.versions_affected: Six separate vendors across independent identifiers; the class is the subject rather than any product or release

what.summary: Regrouping an independent research archive by product class rather than by vendor puts six unrelated vendors into one cluster, every one of them with pre-authentication code execution or an authentication bypass in a managed file transfer product. In the case examined closely the vulnerable component is a licensing servlet that is unauthenticated by design, because it has to work before the product is licensed, and it deserialises an attacker-supplied object. The class is internet-exposed by design too, since the counterparties who send and collect files are outside the organisation, and it retains the files rather than merely passing them along.

how.logic: Inventory which of these products you run, whether each is in a patch cycle that can move faster than a quarter, and above all what is retained on them rather than passing through. Retention is the variable that decides impact, because a flaw in this class gives access to whatever the platform still holds, and retention is normally configured once for convenience and never revisited.
how.caveat: The number that matters is retention, not transfer volume, and the two are usually confused. A platform moving terabytes a day but holding nothing loses nothing; one moving very little but retaining a year of completed transfers loses a year. Reducing retention is the control that survives the next identifier in this class, and on the evidence there will be one.

how.logic: Every appliance and platform ships endpoints that must answer before anything is configured: licensing, activation, initial setup, unlicensed-state handling and health. They cannot require authentication and are therefore the pre-authentication surface, whatever else the product does about access control. Enumerate them per product, then alert on any of them being reached from outside the network, because a licensing endpoint has no business answering an internet client after the product has been licensed.

fields.note: generic form; the exact paths are per product and should be enumerated locally

how.caveat: These endpoints are frequently absent from an application's own access control review precisely because they predate authentication, and they are rarely in a threat model that starts at the login page. Enumerating them per product is the work; once enumerated, a request to one from the internet on a configured system is close to false-positive free. Some products genuinely re-check licensing periodically, so confirm the direction and the client before alerting.

how.logic: An object deserialisation attack that fails throws an exception the application records itself, naming the deserialisation call in the stack. That exception is a detection nobody has to write a signature for, and it works retrospectively against logs already held. A successful attempt may throw nothing, so this catches attempts and near misses, which on an internet-facing platform is enough to act on.
how.caveat: Requires the application's own error log to be collected, which is a different source from the access log and frequently is not forwarded at all. Confirm that first, because this costs nothing to run and is impossible without it. Malformed but benign input can produce the same exception, so correlate with whether the request was authenticated.

where.title: watchTowr Labs research across managed file transfer products from six vendors

products: security information and event management platforms
who.versions_affected: Several products across independent identifiers; in the case examined the flaw was in a bundled web server component rather than in the product's own code

what.summary: Security monitoring products recur as targets across this research, and what an attacker gains from one is unlike what they gain from any other server. The platform holds raw logs, which routinely contain credentials submitted in clear by service accounts, along with the integration secrets that let it reach everything it monitors. It also holds the defender's view: an actor inside it can watch the investigation and, more damaging, leave the operator with an assurance of quiet that is now worthless. In the case examined the flaw was not in the vendor's code at all but in a bundled web server component years out of date, reached because the console is proxied through it.

how.logic: Treat the monitoring platform as the highest-value asset it monitors rather than as infrastructure. Three checks that are cheap and rarely done: whether its own console is reachable from outside the management network, whether administrative sessions to it are authenticated the same way as to the estate it watches, and whether the account it uses to reach each integration is scoped to reading rather than to administering. The last is where the real reach comes from, because a platform that can change what it monitors is a distribution mechanism.
how.caveat: The consequence that is hardest to plan for is not the theft but the assurance: after this, an absence of alerts means nothing, and every conclusion drawn from the platform during the compromise window has to be re-established from somewhere else. That argues for a copy of the most important logs held outside the platform, which is the same argument the log-tampering patterns reach by a different road.

how.logic: Log aggregation turns the platform into an unintended credential store, because service accounts and scripts submit secrets in fields that get forwarded verbatim: connection strings in application errors, tokens in query strings recorded by web servers, passwords in command lines captured by process telemetry. Search the platform's own index for credential-shaped content rather than assuming it is absent, and treat every hit as a credential that must be rotated and a source that must be fixed.
