how.caveat: Running this the first time is uncomfortable and usually productive, and the finding is rarely a single leak but a source that has been emitting one for years. Rotation alone does not fix it, because the source will emit the new credential too, so the field has to be masked at ingestion or the emitting component changed. Retention decides how far back the exposure runs.

how.logic: The flaw reached here was in a bundled web server component well behind its upstream, not in the vendor's own code, and it was reachable because the product proxies its console through it. Enumerate the components each appliance and platform bundles, track their upstream versions separately from the product version, and treat a product that is current against its own release notes as saying nothing about what it carries inside.
how.caveat: Vendors patch bundled components on their own schedule and frequently much later than upstream, so being current on the product is not being current on what it contains. Where the vendor publishes a component manifest this is straightforward and where they do not it needs banner fingerprinting, which on appliances has to be done carefully.

where.title: IBM QRadar - When The Attacker Controls Your Security Stack (CVE-2022-26377)

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound; the fault is organisational and architectural rather than in any product

what.summary: A researcher bought a lapsed domain for about twenty dollars and found it had once been the authoritative directory server for an entire top-level domain, migrated away years earlier and left to expire. Within days it received millions of queries from more than a hundred thousand distinct systems, including government departments, security companies and domain registrars, none of which had noticed the change. The serious part is what depended on it: several certificate authorities established who owned a domain by reading that directory, so whoever answered it could have obtained valid certificates for names they did not own. Nothing was hijacked and nothing was exploited; the infrastructure was simply abandoned while everything that trusted it carried on.

how.logic: Two directions, and both are inventory work rather than detection. Outward: enumerate the external endpoints your estate still contacts that nobody owns any more, which shows up as resolution and outbound sessions to domains absent from your own asset register, particularly from appliances and long-lived hosts carrying endpoints hardcoded at build time. Inward: enumerate the domains your organisation has ever registered and let lapse, because anything still pointing at them is now pointing at whoever bought them next.
how.caveat: The cost of the attack was twenty dollars and an afternoon, which is the part worth carrying: this needs no capability, only somebody noticing before you do. Most of the systems affected were not negligent in any way an audit would find, because nothing in their configuration was wrong when it was written. The durable control is a register of every domain the organisation has ever held and a rule that they are renewed rather than released, which is cheaper than any detection here.

how.logic: Certificate transparency monitoring for your own names is the check that catches this from the defending side, because a certificate issued for a name you own by an authority you do not use is visible publicly whether or not you were involved. Pair it with a record of which authorities you actually use, so that the comparison has something to be against.
how.caveat: A certificate obtained this way stays valid until it is revoked or expires, so noticing after the fact still matters and the response is revocation rather than only investigation. Certificate authority authorisation records reduce which authorities can issue for your names at all and are the preventative half of this.

where.title: We Spent $20 To Achieve RCE And Accidentally Became The Admins Of .MOBI

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound; the fault is an inconsistency in how access paths are protected

what.summary: An actor operating from another continent compromised two organisations near the target so that it could reach the target's wireless network from a machine in a building across the street. Credentials were confirmed by spraying the target's internet-facing service, which required a second factor and therefore refused them, and were then used on the wireless network, which did not. The machine used to make the jump had both a wired and a wireless adapter connected at once, so it bridged one organisation's internal network to another's air.

how.logic: Enumerate every way an account can reach the estate and record, per path, what authentication each actually enforces rather than what policy says it should. The weakest path defines the perimeter regardless of how strong the others are, and wireless is the one most often left at a password because it is treated as physical security rather than as remote access. A failed authentication against the strong path followed by a success on the same account through a weaker one is the event worth joining.
how.caveat: The spray against the protected service is the part that looks like nothing happening: it fails, the second factor holds, and the event is filed as a blocked attempt. It was reconnaissance, and the accounts it proved valid are the ones that then appear on the weaker path. Joining the two requires the wireless authentication log, which is frequently held by a network team rather than forwarded, and that is worth establishing before anything else here.

how.logic: A machine with a wired and a wireless adapter active at the same time joins two networks that were designed to be separate, and it does so without anyone deciding that. Inventory hosts reporting more than one active adapter on different networks, and separately watch for the utilities used to enumerate and join wireless networks running on machines that have no business roaming. On the receiving side, a device authenticating to your wireless whose name or directory affiliation belongs to another organisation is close to conclusive.
how.caveat: Bridging collapses a segmentation model that everything else assumes, and it is usually accidental rather than deliberate, which is why it survives audits that check the design rather than the running state. The directory-affiliation marker requires broadcast or authentication telemetry that identifies the client beyond its address, and where a wireless controller records only addresses this cannot be answered.

where.title: The Nearest Neighbor Attack: How A Russian APT Weaponized Nearby Wi-Fi Networks for Covert Access

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound; any application retrieving update instructions over plain HTTP without verifying a signature

what.summary: An actor compromised an internet service provider and altered name resolution there, so that applications on victim machines checking for updates were answered by attacker infrastructure. The applications targeted retrieved a configuration file over unencrypted HTTP naming where to fetch the installer, and did not verify a signature on what came back, so supplying a different configuration was sufficient. Nothing in the victims' own estates was misconfigured and nothing they controlled was compromised first; the trusted component was the network path itself.

how.logic: The detectable shape does not depend on knowing the attacker's infrastructure. An application fetches something over plain HTTP and shortly afterwards an executable appears on disk and runs, with the fetching process as its parent. That sequence is worth alerting on wherever it occurs, because a modern update channel has no reason to be unencrypted and no reason to execute what it retrieved without checking who signed it. Separately, inventory which installed applications update over HTTP at all, which is a finite list and answers the question before an incident rather than after.

markers.note: the update fetch is unencrypted, which is the precondition

how.caveat: The inventory half is worth more than the detection half here, because the list of applications that update over plain HTTP is short, knowable in advance, and mostly consists of software nobody approved. The resolution-comparison marker is the only one that can catch poisoning upstream of the organisation, and it requires resolving the same name independently to compare against, which is a deliberate control rather than a log query.

how.logic: When resolution is poisoned above the organisation, the organisation's own resolvers return the poisoned answer faithfully and nothing internal looks wrong. What remains is comparison: resolve names that matter from a second, independent path and alert on divergence. This is the case that inverts the usual advice, because forcing all resolution through internal resolvers does not help if the internal resolvers are being answered by the same poisoned upstream.
how.caveat: Signed responses would remove this entire class and are the real answer; the comparison is what is available until then. Note that a content distribution network legitimately returns different addresses to different resolvers, so the comparison has to allow for that or it produces constant noise on exactly the large services it is most tempting to watch.

where.title: StormBamboo Compromises ISP to Abuse Insecure Software Update Mechanisms

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound; the fault is that a model is addressed by a mutable name rather than by an immutable digest

what.summary: Models on a public hub are addressed as author and name. When an author account is deleted the name becomes available to register again, and anything that referenced it by name now fetches whatever the new owner uploads. Because loading a model can execute code, that is remote code execution at the point of deployment, and it was demonstrated reaching shells inside two major cloud providers whose model catalogues ingest from the same hub. Thousands of public repositories carry such references hard-coded in defaults, docstrings and documentation.

how.logic: The durable question is not which hub is affected but whether anything in the pipeline resolves a name at fetch time instead of pinning a digest. Inventory every external artefact reference in build and deployment configuration and record whether each is pinned. On the wire, the observable sequence is a redirect or a not-found followed by a successful fetch of the same name, and fetches whose publisher account is newly created relative to the reference that points at it.

markers.note: a transfer redirect or a miss immediately before a successful pull of the same name

how.caveat: The pinning inventory is worth more than any of the network markers and can be answered from source control without touching a log. Note that pinning alone stops the substitution but not a compromise of the pinned artefact itself, so mirroring to an internal registry after scanning is the stronger form. The publisher-age marker needs registry metadata that not every hub exposes.

how.logic: The same fault the corpus recorded for a lapsed directory server, in a different technology: a name is released while everything referencing it carries on. Enumerate the external names your builds and deployments depend on, then check which of them are currently owned by whom, treating a change of owner as the event rather than a change of content.
how.caveat: The propagation is the part that makes this worse than it looks: cloud catalogues ingest from the public hub, so an organisation that never touched the hub directly can still be exposed through a platform it does trust. Asking the platform whether it revalidates ownership on ingest is a procurement question with a real answer.

where.title: Model Namespace Reuse: An AI Supply-Chain Attack Exploiting Model Name Trust

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound; the exposure follows from the protocol permitting servers to request completions

what.summary: The tool protocol connecting assistants to external capability lets a connected server ask the model for completions rather than only answering it. That reverses the direction the surrounding architecture assumes, because requests no longer originate with a person. Three consequences were demonstrated: instructions hidden in a server's request consuming model capacity invisibly, instructions that persist and alter every later turn in the conversation, and tool calls issued without the user ever seeing or approving them. The host frequently condenses tool output before display, so what the user reads is not what the model received.

how.logic: Because the direction is reversed, volume is the first discriminator that works without reading content: requests attributable to a connected server rather than to a user turn, and a ratio of server-originated to user-originated requests that departs from its own baseline. Content-side, requests carrying instruction structure are the signal, and structure is checkable without semantic analysis, which is the same reasoning the corpus applies to account fields carrying foreign grammar. Finally, reconcile executed tool calls against the ones a user actually saw, because the gap between those two is where the covert invocations sit.
how.caveat: Requires the host to log server-originated requests separately from user turns, which is the whole question and is not universal; establish it before designing anything. Confidence is medium rather than high because baselines here are young and a legitimate server may reasonably become chattier after an update. The reconciliation between executed and displayed tool calls is the strongest of these and the least dependent on thresholds.

how.logic: Content arriving from a tool, a document, a page or a message and heading into a model's context is data, and data does not carry the grammar of instructions. Match on structure rather than meaning: role and system markers, turn delimiters, zero-width and bidirectional control characters, encoded blocks in fields that should be prose, and phrases directed at future behaviour rather than describing the content. This is the same instrument the corpus uses for account fields carrying template or shell grammar, applied to a different field.
how.caveat: Hunt rather than alert because legitimate technical content discusses these markers constantly, and documentation about prompts contains prompts. The discriminating question is where the content is heading rather than what it contains, so scope this to content entering a model context and not to content generally. The last marker matters most: an injection that reaches stored memory outlives the session it arrived in, which is the difference between an incident and a recurring one.

where.title: New Prompt Injection Attack Vectors Through MCP Sampling

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound; these are protocol and architecture properties of mobile networks rather than product defects

what.summary: A public knowledge base of adversary behaviour against mobile networks, structured like the enterprise framework this corpus already uses. Of its 183 techniques, 111 are labelled theoretical and 53 observed, and only the observed ones inform this record. Those cover signalling abuse across operator interconnect to locate subscribers and bypass home routing, transport tunnelling used as a covert channel, false base stations standing up in coverage, network functions deployed outside the orchestrator, and collection of messages at the network rather than the handset.

how.logic: Signalling requests arriving over operator interconnect asking where a subscriber is, or bypassing the home routing that should answer on the subscriber's behalf. The framework's own guidance is a plausibility check rather than a signature: compare the request against whether that subscriber has actually roamed into the network it claims to come from.
how.caveat: The same abuse has now carried across three generations of signalling protocol, which is the argument for checking against subscriber state rather than against message syntax. Joining the roaming register to the signalling log is the practical obstacle and it is organisational rather than technical.

how.logic: Transport tunnelling between network functions used to carry command and control, including keepalive messages that carry payload they have no reason to carry. On the host side the same activity shows as an unexpected process or a raw socket on a user plane function.
how.caveat: This is the one technique two independent sources reaching this corpus describe, the framework and a vendor threat report naming the same implant, which is worth weighting above the single-sourced material around it.

how.logic: A transmitter impersonating operator infrastructure to attract subscriber equipment. Detected through measurement reports the genuine base stations already collect, rather than by locating the transmitter.
how.caveat: Wholly dependent on the accuracy of the cell inventory, and a stale inventory converts every legitimate new cell into an alert. Confidence is medium for that reason rather than because the technique is doubtful.

where.title: MITRE FiGHT, a knowledge base of adversary behaviour against 5G systems

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound; these are properties of how AI services are deployed and trusted

what.summary: A public knowledge base of adversary behaviour against AI systems, structured like the enterprise framework this corpus already uses. It carries 178 techniques and 68 case studies, of which only 18 are incidents and 50 are labelled exercises, so only the incidents inform this record. Those incidents divide into two groups. Some corroborate behaviour this corpus already recorded from other sources: malicious models published under a reused namespace on a public hub, a tool-protocol server taken over by a package rug-pull and used to exfiltrate mail, and a compute framework whose job interface offers remote execution without authentication by design. The rest describe a legitimate AI service being turned into infrastructure for something else: an assistant API used as a command and control channel, and stolen cloud credentials spent on inference and resold.

how.logic: An implant using a major provider's assistant API to fetch commands and return encrypted results, held on the victim for months. The destination has a valid certificate and an excellent reputation, so every control that scores destinations passes it. What does not pass is fit: a web server process holding periodic sessions to an inference endpoint has no legitimate reading.
how.caveat: Blocking the destination is not available, because the organisation almost certainly uses the same service legitimately. The inventory of which hosts may reach it is the control, and it is far cheaper to build before an incident than during one.

how.logic: Stolen credentials used to enumerate which models an account has enabled, then to consume inference the account holder pays for, in one case resold to others through a proxy and in another used to defeat the safety controls the provider applies. The enumeration step is the earliest marker and the one most likely to be in an audit log already collected.
how.caveat: The billing owner frequently notices before security does, which is worth pre-empting so it is treated as an intrusion rather than a budgeting anomaly.

how.logic: Two of these incidents are the same fault this corpus recorded from separate research: a name is trusted rather than a digest. In one, models published to a public hub under names users already referenced. In the other, a package name registered, made popular over months, then replaced with a malicious version once adoption was established. Pinning a digest defeats both.
how.caveat: The rug-pull variant is the harder one, because the artefact was genuinely legitimate for months and any reputation or age check performed during adoption returned a good answer. Only the digest changing gives it away.

where.title: MITRE ATLAS, a knowledge base of adversary behaviour against AI systems

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound; these are behaviours of operating systems and their telemetry rather than product defects

what.summary: A restricted detection library maintained for operational use, examined here for what it covers rather than for what it contains. Against everything this corpus already cites, it adds a further 116 techniques, and they are concentrated rather than scattered: the great majority fall in defence evasion and privilege escalation on endpoints. That is the shape of a library built around endpoint telemetry meeting a corpus built from network advisories and appliance research, and it identifies where this corpus is thinnest. The strongest of the additions concern an attacker controlling what the telemetry says: process ancestry and token identity presented falsely, artefact timestamps and tooling strings edited rather than deleted, and egress shaped to resemble a service the organisation permits.

how.logic: The single most consequential cluster, because parent-child process pairs are what a large share of any endpoint rule library keys on and the actor chooses the parent. The durable checks compare the process's claim against a record it does not control: the creating process as the kernel saw it, and the token owner against the account that actually authenticated.
how.caveat: Whether this can be written at all depends on the sensor recording the creating process separately from the reported parent. Establish that before designing anything, because where it is absent this is not a tuning problem but an impossibility.

how.logic: Editing evidence rather than removing it, so that artefacts remain in place and look ordinary. Detected by comparing recorded times against each other and against the first external observation of the same file.
how.caveat: Tooling stripped of its identifying strings still behaves as the tool behaves, which is an argument for writing detections on sequence rather than on names, and applies to how a rule library is built as much as to any single rule.

how.logic: Command and control shaped to pass as permitted traffic, by fronting through a trusted name, impersonating a protocol on its expected port, or sizing transfers to stay under a threshold.
how.caveat: The size-clustering marker detects the actor's own caution and survives every change of destination, which makes it the most durable of the three and the one to build first.

where.title: Restricted detection library commentary on endpoint defence evasion and privilege escalation coverage

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound; these are platform facilities used as intended by somebody who should not have them

what.summary: Match conditions distilled from a restricted detection library and compared against every technique this corpus already cites. Three clusters were absent entirely. Escape from a container to its host through the kernel interfaces that exist for legitimate reasons, which the corpus had nothing on despite carrying a container class with no observations in it. Manipulation of the organisation tier that contains cloud accounts, which sits above the identity tier already covered and where detaching a control policy silently removes a guardrail from every account beneath without any of them recording a change. And interactive access pushed into a running instance through the provider's own key and console facilities, which needs no credential on the instance and produces no failed authentication anywhere.

how.logic: The routes that do not depend on a particular vulnerability: writing to the cgroup release-agent interface so the host executes a chosen path, loading a kernel image from inside a container, changing root and mounting host filesystems, and a general-purpose relay appearing in an image with no reason to carry one.
how.caveat: Whether any of this is reachable is decided by the privileged-container inventory, which is a configuration fact rather than an event and should be established first. Node agents and build tooling use several of these binaries legitimately, so exclude by image and node role.

how.logic: Policy attachment and detachment, account removal and organisation creation at the tier above the accounts. Administrative, rare, performed by few people, so alert on all of them and reconcile rather than trying to characterise which are suspicious.
how.caveat: Detachment matters more than attachment and is the easier to miss, because removing a restriction produces the same event shape as adding one.

how.logic: Access obtained by asking the provider to push a key or open a console into a live instance. The event is in the cloud audit log and not on the instance, and it succeeds first time because the provider authorises it rather than the instance authenticating anyone.
how.caveat: The absence of a failed authentication is the whole point: every detection built on brute force or credential stuffing is watching the wrong layer. Break-glass procedures use this route, which argues for enumerating them rather than excluding the technique.

where.title: Restricted detection library commentary on container escape and cloud control-plane conditions

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound; these are platform facilities used by somebody who should not have them

what.summary: The remainder of the match conditions distilled from a restricted detection library, after removing everything the corpus already covered. Of 107 techniques the corpus did not cite, 67 carried usable conditions and most of those fell inside patterns that already exist, so they enriched rather than multiplied them. Three clusters were genuinely absent: access to a mailbox obtained by granting a delegation or an administrative role rather than by taking a credential, directory attributes altered so that an account holds privilege no group membership explains, and credential files on Unix hosts read with ordinary interactive tools by a person at a shell rather than by recognisable tooling.

how.logic: Nothing fails and no password changes, because the grant is an administrative operation and every access afterwards is legitimate for whoever holds it. The grant is the event; the relationship between the two parties is the discriminator.
how.caveat: Verify whether the identity, the client and the address making the change should be making changes in your environment at all, because the grant is frequently issued from the session that is itself the intrusion. A role assignment conferring access across the tenancy deserves a different severity from a single delegation.

how.logic: History injection confers another principal's privileges without joining any group, so the account passes a membership review unremarked. The directory's own attribute-change and account-modification events are where it shows.
how.caveat: This defeats group-membership monitoring rather than merely evading it, which is the reason to carry it separately. Migration tooling uses the same mechanism legitimately and in volume, so a migration has to be known about in advance rather than discovered through the alerts it generates.

how.logic: Automated theft brings tooling with a recognisable name; a person at a shell uses whatever is installed. Ordinary readers and editors against the shadow file, root keys and the privilege-configuration directory, and the same material staged into shared memory before it leaves.
how.caveat: Configuration management and backup agents read these paths constantly and are the whole of the tuning work. Build the staging marker first: material copied into shared memory is being prepared to leave, and shared memory is chosen because it is not on disk.

where.title: Restricted detection library commentary on identity, mail and Unix credential conditions

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound; the delivery depends on the visitor rather than on a flaw in what they are running

what.summary: A national authority reported a campaign against networks in its own country in which legitimate business websites were compromised and used to serve a fake verification prompt. The page overwrote its own content, placed an obfuscated command on the visitor's clipboard, and instructed them to run it with administrative privileges themselves. Nothing exploited the browser and no malicious process descended from it, because the person performed the execution. The delivered credential stealer then removed its own file and ran from memory, and retrieved its command and control address from a public messaging or gaming profile rather than carrying one.

how.logic: The chain a detection expects never occurs: no exploit, and no interpreter descending from the browser. What is left is an interpreter started from a shell or run dialog shortly after browser activity, carrying an encoded or obfuscated argument, with no browser anywhere in its ancestry.
how.caveat: Clipboard writes are the most direct evidence and the least commonly collected, so establish whether the sensor records them at all before building around it. Administrators paste commands legitimately, which is why this pairs with the encoded-argument marker rather than standing on paste-then-run.

how.logic: The malware carried no address. It fetched one from a public messaging bot or a gaming profile, which are reputable destinations that resolve and score well, and only then contacted the infrastructure that mattered. The observable sequence is a single short retrieval from such a service followed by a connection to a destination not seen before from that host.
how.caveat: Blocking the public service is rarely available and rarely proportionate. The sequence is what carries the signal: one fetch, then a new destination. A host that reads such a profile once and never again is behaving nothing like a person using the service.

where.title: ClickFix distributing Vidar Stealer via WordPress targeting Australian infrastructure

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound. The exposure is a deployment artefact rather than a flaw in any released version.

what.summary: A research team monitoring a cloud honeypot noticed an unfamiliar storage listing call and followed it to a publicly readable bucket, itself belonging to an earlier victim, holding more than a terabyte of stolen material and the operation's own tooling. The tooling scanned very large address ranges for web servers serving repository configuration files and framework environment files, extracted the credentials inside, validated them, and used the working ones to clone private source and mine it for further credentials. Roughly fifteen thousand cloud, email and service credentials were taken, and credentials for over ten thousand private repositories were collected. Nothing was exploited: the files were served because a deployment copied them into the web root.

how.logic: Serving-side requests for repository metadata and framework environment paths, kept only where the server answered successfully, then joined to a clone of private source from an address with no interactive history and to first use of a cloud credential from an unfamiliar network.
how.caveat: A successful response is the finding; a 404 is background noise and alerting on the request alone is unusable. The loot was held in a bucket belonging to an earlier victim, so treat the infrastructure as possibly borrowed rather than attacker-owned before acting against it.

where.title: EMERALDWHALE: 15k Cloud credentials stolen in operation targeting exposed Git config files

who.versions_affected: Affected package versions published during the campaign; the mechanism is a supported install hook rather than a defect.

what.summary: A supply chain attack against a public package registry used self-propagating malware. The worm executed from the package's install hook, ran system discovery on the developer or build machine, and collected registry, source forge and cloud provider credentials. Where forge credentials were found it iterated the owner's repositories, planted a workflow that fired on push to maintain access and steal further secrets, and made private repositories public. Collected material was sent to a free request-capture service. It then used the stolen registry credentials to publish itself into further packages, which is what made it a worm rather than a single compromise. Around two hundred packages were affected in the first wave and a later wave reached tens of thousands of repositories. A second wave reported by another publisher moved execution from the post-install hook to the pre-install hook, which matters operationally because the code then runs before the dependency tree is even resolved and any control that waits for installation to complete is too late. That wave affected roughly seven to eight hundred packages, created on the order of twenty-five thousand repositories to hold stolen material at a reported peak of about a thousand every half hour, and yielded hundreds of forge tokens and hundreds more sets of credentials across three cloud providers. It left several distinctive artefacts: fixed-name JSON files written into the workspace and picked up as build artefacts, a workflow added to hold a backdoor and another to exfiltrate secrets, repository descriptions carrying the campaign name, and registration of a self-hosted runner under a fixed name. Registering a runner is the one worth alerting on outright, because it converts a transient compromise into standing execution inside the estate.

how.logic: A package manager spawning an interpreter during the install phase, that interpreter reading credential paths, and then the host publishing to the registry or writing to the forge -- which a machine that only consumes packages should never do.
how.caveat: Install hooks fire legitimately across a great many packages to build native code, so the hook alone is not the signal. Publish-after-install and a private repository turning public are the two worth waking somebody for, and self-hosted runner registration is a third: it is rare, it is cheap to watch, and it turns a transient compromise into standing execution. Note the later wave moved to the pre-install hook, so any control that acts once installation finishes runs after the payload has.

where.title: Shai-Hulud: The novel self-replicating worm infecting hundreds of NPM packages

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound. Runner registration is deliberately low-friction and the behaviour is the product working as designed.

what.summary: Researchers described, and a worm campaign demonstrated at scale, the use of self-hosted continuous integration runners as persistent backdoors. An intruder registers a runner on a machine they already control against a repository they control, then drives it with deliberately permissive workflows. Because the runner polls the forge and the forge alone, the command and control channel is an outbound connection to a destination the organisation already permits and usually trusts, so network defences see nothing anomalous. Self-hosted runners are attractive independently of this: they commonly reach internal networks, hold cached secrets, and execute arbitrary code by design.

how.logic: Host and forge, not network. A runner agent installed and persisting on a machine with no build role, long-polling outbound; and on the forge side a runner registered by an account that does not administer runners, or a job pinned to a self-hosted label where its siblings are not.
how.caveat: Do not attempt this on the network. Traffic goes to the forge over the forge's own protocol and every reputation, novelty or domain-age check will score it clean and be correct to. Without an asset inventory that knows which hosts build, the host markers cannot be applied at all.

where.title: How threat actors are using self-hosted GitHub Actions runners as backdoors

who.versions_affected: Affected consumers resolving the action by a mutable tag during the compromise window

what.summary: A widely depended-on pipeline action was altered upstream by a malicious commit. The injected code was a script function carrying a base64-encoded payload, which decoded to a fetch of further code from a public code-sharing service. That code located the runner's worker process, opened its memory mappings and searched them for credentials. In the observed case the recovered secrets were printed into the pipeline's build log, readable by anyone who could read the pipeline output; a variant sent them to a code-sharing service instead. Consumers resolving the action by a moving tag rather than a commit digest received the malicious version automatically. Second-source reporting establishes a root-cause chain worth carrying: a separate action's tag was repointed several days earlier, and the credential recovered from that compromise is assessed to be the automation token used to rewrite the tags of the more widely used action. The earlier compromise also shows the cover-up variant -- the actor force-pushed the original commit back afterwards, so the repository's current state looks untouched and only a consumer's own record of which commit it executed still shows the substitution. Both actions had every affected consumer resolving by tag; digest-pinned consumers were unaffected in each case.

how.logic: One process reading another's memory inside a build is the core observable and nothing legitimate in a pipeline does it. Pair with a build host fetching executable content from a paste or gist service mid-run, and with credential-shaped strings appearing in build output.
how.caveat: Pinning actions to a commit digest rather than a tag prevents this outright and is worth more than any detection here. The memory-read marker is the strongest and the least commonly collected, so confirm the build fleet has process telemetry before relying on it.

how.logic: The compromise reached consumers because the pipeline resolved a moving tag at run time. Inventory every external action reference and record whether it pins a digest.
how.caveat: The pinning inventory answers this from source control without touching a log and is worth more than every network marker. Pinning stops substitution but not compromise of the pinned artefact. The added marker covers the cover-up variant: where the actor restores the original commit afterwards, the upstream repository looks clean and the only surviving evidence is the consumer's own record of the commit it ran.

where.title: Detecting and Mitigating the "tj-actions/changed-files" Supply Chain Attack (CVE-2025-30066)

who.versions_affected: Configuration state rather than a version; present wherever the privileged trigger is paired with a checkout of proposed code

what.summary: A research team audited public repositories and found workflows configured so that a review request from somebody with no write access would execute in the repository's own privileged context, with access to its secrets. The pattern is long documented and still widespread. The repositories affected included ones maintained by security-literate organisations, which is the part worth carrying: the exposure is not a marker of a careless project, and an audit that skips well-run repositories will skip real instances.

how.logic: A repository-state audit rather than an event rule: enumerate workflows using the privileged trigger and flag those that also check out or build the proposed branch, which is the pairing that turns a review request into execution with secrets.
how.caveat: The trigger has legitimate uses and its presence alone is not the finding; the pairing with a checkout of proposed code is. Where the repository is public, the same inventory is available to anybody else reading it.

where.title: Dangerous by default: Insecure GitHub Actions found in MITRE, Splunk, and other open source repositories

who.versions_affected: Not applicable. This is a measurement of a response population rather than a flaw in a product.

what.summary: Eighteen consecutive quarters of incident response trend reporting from one responder, covering the first quarter of 2022 to the second quarter of 2026, read as a series rather than as individual reports. Four findings hold across it. Insufficient logging is named as a weakness in every year, in eighteen to forty-two percent of engagements, and in the earliest reports prevented the initial access vector from being determined at all in most cases. Authentication weakness never falls below roughly a quarter of engagements and reaches sixty-five percent in the most recent quarter, with one quarter recording that every engagement involving phishing had multi-factor authentication bypassed or incompletely enabled. The leading initial access vector alternates between phishing and exploitation of public-facing applications from quarter to quarter rather than trending. And commercial remote management tooling recurs throughout, with the products changing and the technique not. Ransomware's share of engagements fell from half to between thirteen and twenty percent over the last six quarters, which is best read alongside the finding that three quarters of such engagements were reached before encryption.

how.logic: Count your own initial access vectors over at least four quarters and compare the shape against a population that alternates rather than trends. Where coverage is concentrated on one vector, the concentration is the finding.
how.caveat: One responder's population reflects who calls them in as well as what attackers do, so this argues against over-fitting to one vector rather than forecasting the next. Where your own distribution has a large undetermined bucket, it is not yet evidence of anything and the logging gap is the finding.

how.logic: Per asset class, whether each log source a deployed detection depends on is actually collected and arriving, and whether retention exceeds assumed dwell time. The series gives a base rate to compare against: eighteen to forty-two percent of engagements hindered by insufficient logging, every year.
how.caveat: Retention is a budget decision and this belongs in front of whoever owns it. The measured base rate is the argument; the counter-argument is always cost, and a proportion drawn from someone else's population will be disputed on those grounds. Measuring your own undetermined-vector count is the version nobody can argue with.

how.logic: An allow-list of licensed remote management products, with everything else alerting. The series supplies a starting list of products actually observed in engagements across four years, and shows the specific products turning over while the technique does not.
how.caveat: The named list is a starting point and not a closed set, because the supply of these products is effectively unlimited and turns over between quarters. Detection built on the names alone will decay; the licensed-software inventory is the control that does not.

where.title: Cisco Talos Incident Response quarterly trend reporting, first quarter 2022 to second quarter 2026

who.versions_affected: Any programmable logic controller reachable from the internet, regardless of manufacturer; Rockwell Automation MicroLogix 1400 is named only because the vendor published a recovery procedure for the locked-out case

what.summary: CISA reported a significant increase in actors targeting programmable logic controllers in the water and wastewater sector, and urged owners to remove publicly exposed controllers and other operational technology from the internet. The observed activity is anti-recovery rather than subtle: actors modified passwords to lock operators out of their own controllers, and changed device IP addresses to disconnect them. Consequences reached the physical process, with boil water notices issued and facilities running on sustained manual operation. Water entities of all sizes were targeted, and the alert makes the point that organisations with mature security should still revalidate external connections, because the exposure includes cellular modems fitted by operators, vendors or system integrators that are not documented and so do not appear in routine attack surface scans. Recommended actions are to disconnect controllers from the internet and front remote access with a VPN or gateway, enable password protection and change defaults, allowlist remote access to known engineering laptops and critical OT assets, and hold a known-clean controller image against being locked out.

how.logic: The precondition for the whole campaign is a controller answering from the internet, so the inventory question is the detection. Enumerate which controllers are externally reachable and what authentication sits in front of each. The alert widens what counts as reachable: the path may not run through the corporate perimeter at all, so an inventory built only from firewall rules will report an exposure the site does not have and miss the one it does.
how.caveat: Scan passively where possible; some control equipment does not survive being scanned. A reachability answer derived from the perimeter configuration alone is the specific error this alert warns about.

how.logic: Actors modified controller passwords to lock operators out. Detect the credential change arriving from something other than the engineering station that owns the controller, and pair it with the operator side: an engineering station that authenticated to a controller yesterday and cannot today. Where the controller keeps no log of its own, the failed authentication from the engineering station is the whole signal.
how.caveat: Routine password rotation produces the credential change without the lockout, so alerting on the change alone will fire on maintenance. Note also that the recovery path is vendor-specific: for the Rockwell Automation MicroLogix 1400 the vendor published a procedure for restoring access when the password is unknown, which is a different activity from restoring a configuration.

how.logic: Actors changed controller IP addresses to disconnect them. The effect is the same as renaming, and so is the detection: the device's identity in the field no longer matches the identity in the inventory. The address case has a second, cheaper signal, because a controller that stops answering at its inventoried address while the process it drives keeps running is visible from polling alone.
how.caveat: A site using dynamic addressing inside the control network will generate this constantly, though that is itself worth knowing about. The recovery point matters more than the alert: if the response procedure reaches controllers by address, and the address is attacker-controlled, the procedure fails at its first step. Keep an out-of-band record of device identity and addressing.

how.logic: The alert names a specific missed route: cellular modems installed by operators, vendors or system integrators, undocumented and therefore absent from routine attack surface scanning. An external scan of the organisation's own address ranges cannot see these, because the path does not run through the organisation's addresses. Enumerate them physically and contractually instead: walk the asset register for cellular-capable equipment, and ask each integrator what connectivity they fitted.
how.caveat: This is inventory work with no query behind it, and it will not fire in a SIEM. It is here because the alert states that organisations with mature processes were still exposed through exactly this gap, which makes it a finding a well-covered site should not skip.

where.title: CISA Urges Water and Wastewater Systems Sector to Protect OT Against Activity Targeting PLCs

notes: The Environmental Protection Agency and the Federal Bureau of Investigation contributed to the alert, which also points at an FBI product on the same activity. CISA material is public domain. No CVE is named and no vulnerability is claimed: the alert describes exposure and default or weak authentication rather than exploitation, which is why this record carries no vulnerability identifiers.

products: DNS filtering and resolver-based security controls
who.versions_affected: Any control whose enforcement point is name resolution rather than the connection itself

what.summary: Across four million dynamic analysis reports, 45.32 per cent of malware samples with any command-and-control activity made at least one connection straight to an IP address, and direct-to-IP traffic accounted for 23.17 per cent of all command-and-control attempts. Hard-coding the address removes the name lookup, and with it every control that enforces at resolution time. The publisher's separating measurement is the useful part: 20.11 per cent of malicious samples connected to untrusted addresses against 1 per cent of benign ones, so the behaviour discriminates rather than merely occurring. Families observed doing it span commodity and IoT tooling -- a ransomware dropper staging payloads over sequential HTTP paths, a credential-stealing remote access trojan proxying browser sessions and harvesting form fields, and two Mirai-derived botnets carrying exploitation payloads inside the request and fingerprinting themselves with a 2012-era download utility string aimed at unpatched hardware.

how.logic: Join outbound connections against the resolutions that host actually received: a session to a public address for which that host saw no preceding DNS answer is the signal. The publisher frames the enforcement version as verifying that every outbound connection was sanctioned by a prior DNS response, holding the approved addresses with a time-based validity so the allowlist expires as records do. That framing is what makes the older hunt practical, because it says how to build the known-good list rather than assuming one.

markers.note: 2012-era utility string; the botnet fingerprints itself by targeting old hardware

how.caveat: Some legitimate protocols connect to addresses by design and must be exempted or this is unusable: DNS itself, Neighbor Discovery, VoIP, peer-to-peer and various IoT services, plus private address space. Monitoring agents and update clients also hold hard-coded addresses. Build the exemption list first; the base rate above is what justifies spending that effort, not the individual hit.

how.logic: Transport shape separates the two populations in the measurement. TCP carried the behaviour in 94.43 per cent of cases at an average of 4.17 distinct command-and-control addresses per sample, while UDP appeared in 17.50 per cent but at 13.79 addresses per sample, which is the signature of peer-to-peer and scanning rather than of a beacon. Counting distinct destination addresses per host per protocol therefore splits botnet-style behaviour from directed command and control, and the two want different responses.
how.caveat: The averages are population statistics from a malware corpus, not thresholds to paste into a rule. Set the bound from your own estate's distribution; a site running peer-to-peer backup or conferencing will sit above these figures legitimately.

where.title: Almost Half of Malware Samples Communicate Direct to IP

notes: Addresses named in the publication are held in the source rather than here: they are commodity infrastructure with a short life, and this corpus is not an indicator feed. The durable contributions are the base rate and the DNS-sanctioned-egress construction, both of which outlive any address. Named sectors targeted by one campaign were government, airlines and universities.

products: AI coding assistants and agent clients
who.versions_affected: Not version-dependent; the artefacts are a property of how these clients store local state

what.summary: A vendor research team analysed prompt logs recovered from endpoints running AI coding and agent clients, across actors on several continents, and set out how the tooling is actually being used. Three uses dominate: building malicious software, multiplying the reach of ordinary criminal operations, and accelerating vulnerability research. The scale reached in individual cases is the notable part, including a pipeline that processed ninety million URLs and tested over nine thousand distinct hosts, a cryptojacking operation running several hundred accessible clients, and a single credential-guessing workflow attempting 1.9 million password candidates across sixty-four assistant sessions. Guardrails were bypassed with unsophisticated methods rather than clever encoding: asserting ownership of the target, labelling the work as a competition or bounty, splitting a task across sessions, storing a pre-authorisation claim in the assistant's persistent memory, and choosing neutral verbs. The publisher's own conclusion is that the operator's skill still decides the outcome -- weak operators produced weak tooling, capable ones produced effective attack platforms.

how.logic: The research exists because these clients leave prompt history, persistent instruction files and memory stores on disk, and those recovered files carried the operators' objectives, their scope claims and language artefacts in their working notes. Collect those paths on any host under investigation that has such a client installed, and search the content for authorisation assertions and for target scopes naming hosts the organisation does not own.
how.caveat: The publisher records that distinguishing genuine red-team work from a claimed authorisation was difficult for them too, and that some recovered logs were incomplete. Treat a scope file as a lead to check against the engagement record, never as a finding on its own. These files also contain employee prose, so collection needs to sit inside whatever policy governs monitoring personal content.

how.logic: Named clients appearing on hosts where no approval record exists. This is the population question that has to be answered before the artefact hunt above can be run at all, because that hunt needs to know which hosts to look at. It is also the cheaper of the two, and it is worth answering for reasons beyond this research.
how.caveat: These are mainstream developer tools and in most estates their presence is expected and sanctioned, so an inventory result here is a baseline rather than an alert. Do not let it become a rule that fires on every engineer.

where.title: "Keep going, bro. You've got this!" A data-driven look at how adversaries are weaponizing AI

notes: Publication date taken as the date the post appeared in the publisher's own research category listing; the research covers a period the post does not bound precisely, so the observation window is recorded conservatively. The publisher states that some agentic capability was demonstrated under deliberately relaxed safeguards in a controlled evaluation rather than in a production deployment, and that persistence attempts succeeded on relatively few targets -- both worth carrying, because this subject attracts claims the evidence does not support. Actor type is recorded as criminal at low confidence: the cases described are predominantly commercial crime, but the population is mixed and the publisher does not adjudicate it.

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound; the target is the artefact type, not a product

what.summary: The same operator returned to the same entry point with a compiled, packed Go encryptor written for machine-learning infrastructure rather than for documents. It carries roughly 180 target extensions covering the current stack end to end -- checkpoints and serialised weights in every common format, quantised local-model formats, vector indices, columnar training sets and array dumps -- and its own help text offers a flag to append more, using fine-tune adapter files as the worked example. Encryption is a hybrid scheme wrapping a per-run symmetric key with an embedded public key, applied to regions of each file rather than whole files, with the encrypted files renamed. It kills processes holding file locks first, resumes safely after interruption, deletes itself afterwards and drops notes under three fixed names. Analysis of the binary found no network capability of any kind, so there is no exfiltration and no leak site: the encryption is the whole of the leverage. The build also carries live Windows recovery-inhibition code and a Windows process kill list despite being a Linux binary, indicating one codebase compiled per target platform. Neither hash was recognised by common tooling at the time of analysis.

how.logic: Mass appearance of a single new extension in directories that hold model checkpoints, vector indices or training sets, alongside a short-lived process that deletes its own executable. The artefact type is what raises severity: the same burst against a document share and against a model store are the same detection and very different incidents, because one restores from backup and the other costs a retraining run.

markers.note: packed and unpacked builds of this sample

how.caveat: The hashes are this build and the packer makes new ones cheap, so they are the weakest marker here despite reading as the strongest. The encryption covers regions rather than whole files, so file size barely moves and size-based integrity checks will not flag it. Ransom note names are generic enough to collide with legitimate documentation files, so pair them with the rename.

how.logic: The encryptor was fetched over plain HTTP from a host on a high port, under a filename beginning with a dot so that a directory listing does not show it and the undotted path returns not-found. A second tree on the same server staged interpreter binaries, one of which replaces the leading character of its name with a visually identical character from another script, which defeats both a name equality check and a process kill by name.
how.caveat: The addresses are campaign infrastructure and will not survive. The durable half is the homoglyph check, which is worth applying generally: any process or file name that is visually a common binary but not byte-equal to it should be treated as an evasion attempt, and name-based allow-lists and kill lists should be compared after normalisation.

where.title: JADEPUFFER evolves: The agentic threat actor deploys ransomware built to destroy AI models

who.versions_affected: Internet-exposed devices of these classes, current firmware included

what.summary: A ninety-day measurement across eleven internet-exposed devices recorded over sixty million flagged interactions. Once mass fingerprinting was set aside, the perimeter devices took two thirds of what remained and the exposed control devices one third, contradicting the usual assumption about where the pressure falls. Remote shell and terminal credential guessing accounted for most of it, and the web traffic that remained was exploit attempts and malware retrieval from a small number of botnets.

how.logic: Ninety-seven per cent of all interactions were management-protocol requests and ninety-five per cent went to one device, almost all of them probes at the root of the object identifier tree. Classifying and excluding that category took sixty million events to three and a half million and changed which device looked most attacked. Rank targets on the residue, not on the raw count.
how.caveat: Set the floor aside in the ranking, not in the record: a change in its composition is an early sign that a botnet has added an exploit. The proportions here are one honeypot estate over one window and are not transplantable thresholds.

markers.expr: management protocol probes at object identifier tree roots classified and excluded before ranking targets

markers.note: management protocol carrying the fingerprinting floor

markers.expr: residual events after removing the automated floor are what target ranking is computed on

how.logic: Remote shell and terminal protocols carried seventy-two per cent of the requests reaching the perimeter devices and were predominantly credential guessing. The credential lists used are short and stable, which makes the outcome preventable by changing them even though the traffic is not preventable.
how.caveat: This traffic is constant and unavoidable on any exposed device, so alerting on the attempts is noise. Alert on a success from an unexpected source, and treat the attempt volume as a fact about being on the internet rather than as an event.

markers.expr: authentication success on a device management protocol from a source with no prior successful history

how.logic: The web traffic that survived filtering was exploit attempts followed by retrieval of botnet payloads, concentrated in three families of which two were newly identified at the time of writing. An exposed device fetching an executable over plain HTTP immediately after a malformed request is the recruitment moment, and it is visible from the network without any agent on the device.
how.caveat: One of these families was noted as rapidly expanding the set of exploits it carries, so the identifiers it targets today are not the ones it will target next quarter. Anchor on the shape -- malformed request then outbound fetch of an executable -- rather than on the family or its current exploit list.

markers.expr: exposed device retrieves an executable over plain HTTP within minutes of receiving a malformed or exploit-shaped request
outbound connection from a device class that has no legitimate reason to initiate one

where.title: OT network security threats: industrial routers under attack

notes: A class-level answer by design, and an honest one for the vendors this corpus cannot reach by name: the estate was eleven devices from several vendors and the finding is about the class rather than any badge. Two actor labels appear -- an unattributed cluster active for two years that began with exploits against one wireless router vendor and then broadened, and a hacktivist group that defaced a water treatment interface in the same period.

who.versions_affected: Any repository whose workflow runs on a trigger that grants a writable token to code supplied by a fork; a configuration choice rather than a defect.

what.summary: A workflow trigger intended for metadata tasks was used to execute code supplied by an outside contributor with the repository's own token. The trigger runs in the context of the base repository rather than the fork, so it receives a writable token and access to repository secrets, while the code it runs comes from the pull request. In the observed campaign the actor searched for repositories using the trigger, forked them, opened a pull request with an innocuous title describing a build configuration change, and placed the payload in files a build would execute anyway rather than in the workflow file, which is where review attention goes. Once running it read the job token from the environment, enumerated repository secrets through the API, queried the cloud metadata service, and polled process environment blocks on a short interval to catch secrets held by other steps. Collected material was compressed, base64-encoded and written into the workflow log itself, framed by fixed marker strings, so no outbound connection to attacker infrastructure was needed. Where a registry token was recovered the actor published package versions under a namespace it now controlled. Six accounts across several waves were assessed as one operator; the observed success rate was under one attempt in ten, against several hundred attempts.

how.logic: The exposure is decided in source control, not at run time: a workflow that both carries the privileged trigger and checks out the pull request head is exploitable by anyone who can open a pull request. Inventory that pairing first. At run time the shape is a build job reading credential material it was not given -- other processes' environment blocks, the metadata endpoint, the secrets API -- during a run whose head commit is not on any branch of the repository.
how.caveat: The metadata-endpoint marker is worth little on its own -- plenty of legitimate build tooling reads instance identity -- and worth a great deal in a job whose code came from a fork. The inventory marker is the one that closes the exposure rather than observing it, and it answers from source control without any telemetry at all. Note that exfiltration here was into the build log, so a rule looking only for outbound connections to attacker infrastructure sees a clean run.

how.logic: Where the build log is the exfiltration channel the material has to survive being printed, so it arrives compressed and base64-encoded, usually framed by fixed strings so the operator can find it again in a long log. Long base64 runs in step output, especially bracketed by a repeated marker, are the observable.
how.caveat: Build logs legitimately carry base64 -- certificates, encoded fixtures, container digests -- so this is a hunt input rather than an alert. On a public repository the log is world-readable, which means anything found here should be treated as already disclosed and rotated rather than investigated first.

where.title: Six Accounts, One Actor: Inside the prt-scan Supply Chain Campaign

who.versions_affected: Any workflow that expands an attacker-controllable event field into a shell command; a coding defect in the workflow rather than a product vulnerability.

what.summary: Workflow authors expanded fields from the triggering event directly into shell commands. Pull request titles, branch names and comment bodies are attacker-controllable on any repository that accepts outside contributions, and the templating expansion happens before the shell sees the line, so a title containing shell metacharacters becomes part of the command rather than an argument to it. The result is command execution on the runner with whatever the job was granted. Reporting describes an automated campaign using this at scale against open source repositories, generating and testing candidate payloads, and achieving execution in a substantial share of the repositories it tried. Survey figures in the same reporting put roughly two in five organisations as carrying at least one injectable expansion, and around seven in ten as never pinning an action to a commit digest, which is the adjacent exposure.

how.logic: Findable statically and cheaply: a shell step whose script contains a templating expansion of an event field an outside party controls. That is a grep over the workflow directory, not a detection. At run time the shape is a build step spawning processes that step never spawns, with command lines carrying shell metacharacters that arrived from event text.
how.caveat: The static marker is the one to act on; the runtime markers exist for estates that cannot change every workflow at once. Passing the value through an environment variable instead of expanding it into the script removes the class entirely, which makes this a remediation problem wearing a detection costume. Beware treating a scanner's silence as absence -- see the record on scanner coverage.

where.title: Datadog Security Labs on injection and trigger abuse in pipeline workflows

who.versions_affected: Workflows that place untrusted event context into an agent prompt or into input an agent consumes; a design flaw in the workflow rather than a product defect.

what.summary: Academic measurement of pipelines that hand work to a language agent found a distinct injection class. Untrusted event context -- an issue body, a pull request description, a comment -- is placed into an agent's prompt or into material the agent reads, and the agent's tools then act on attacker-chosen instructions. The authors separate two flows: untrusted text reaching the prompt boundary directly, and attacker influence carried through the model's output into a later script that executes it, which is the more dangerous of the two because the injection point and the execution point are in different steps. Across 13,392 agentic workflows drawn from 10,792 repositories and 1,033 AI-assisted actions, the authors reported 519 candidate flaws at 95.6 per cent precision, 496 confirmed exploitable, and 343 previously unknown. The work is demonstration and coordinated disclosure rather than observed intrusion, which is the right way to read the numbers: this is exposure measurement, not incident reporting.

how.logic: Trace the flow rather than the payload: does any path exist from an event field an outside party can write to an agent prompt, and from the agent's output to something that executes or writes. Where the second half exists the workflow is exploitable regardless of what guard text sits in the prompt. At run time the observable is an agent-invoked tool call whose effect is out of family for that workflow -- writing a file, opening a network connection, calling the forge API -- during a run triggered by an outside contributor.
how.caveat: Prompt-level instructions telling the agent to ignore injected commands are not a control and should not be recorded as one; the flow from untrusted input to privileged tool is the thing to sever. Confidence is medium deliberately: the underlying measurement is static analysis with coordinated disclosure, so the exposure is well evidenced while the runtime markers are reasoned rather than observed in an intrusion.

where.publisher: Wang, Hou, Liu, Zhao, Cheng, Zou, Zhang and Wang
where.title: Academic measurement of injection from untrusted event context into agentic pipeline workflows

who.versions_affected: Scanner versions as evaluated in the cited measurements; the finding is about coverage differences rather than a defect in any one tool.

what.summary: Two independent academic measurements found that tools which scan pipeline workflows for security weaknesses disagree substantially about what to look for. Nine scanners evaluated against 2,722 curated workflows differed in both the nature and the number of weaknesses reported, following fundamentally different analysis strategies against a classification of ten common weakness categories. Earlier work applying an assessment tool to 50 open source projects reported 24,905 issues, which says as much about how little was being checked as about the projects. The operational consequence is narrow and important: a clean scan is evidence about one tool's coverage, not evidence that a workflow estate is free of the injection and trigger classes recorded elsewhere in this corpus. Anyone relying on a single scanner to close those classes should confirm the scanner looks for them at all.

how.logic: An inventory question rather than a detection. For each weakness class the estate cares about -- untrusted expansion into a shell, a privileged trigger checking out fork code, an action pinned by tag rather than digest, an agent holding an execute tool -- record whether the deployed scanner tests for it, and treat any class no tool covers as unmeasured rather than absent.
how.caveat: This record carries no attack and will never fire an alert. It is here so that a consultation which recommends the workflow-hardening controls also says how to check the checking, because the failure mode in this area is a green dashboard over an unexamined class.

where.title: Academic evaluation of security scanner coverage across pipeline workflows

who.versions_affected: Consumers resolving the affected actions by tag during the compromise window; in the reported case nearly every published tag of two actions was rewritten.

what.summary: An actor rewrote the published tags of widely used security scanning actions to point at malicious code, then used the resulting execution inside consumers' pipelines to collect credentials from several places at once. Reporting describes 75 or 76 of the tags of one scanning action rewritten, a companion setup action across seven tags, and a second vendor's scanning action from a given release onward, with the payload placed in the container entry point or setup script rather than the action definition. On execution it read the memory of the runner's worker process for marked secrets and environment material, queried the cloud instance metadata service for role credentials, and searched the checked-out workspace for chat webhook URLs. Collected material was encrypted, archived under a fixed name and uploaded with a custom header naming the file; where upload failed the malware created a repository in the victim's own account and left the archive there, which is a fallback that leaves an unusually visible artefact. Stolen tokens were then used to poison further actions, so a single compromise cascaded. A recurrence against the same scanning action was reported within weeks, and a vulnerability identifier was assigned to the first.

how.logic: The collection half is what distinguishes this from ordinary build noise: within one job, the runner reads another process's memory, calls the instance metadata service for role credentials, and greps the workspace for webhook URLs. Any one is arguable; together in a single run they are not. The exfiltration half is an encrypted archive posted outbound to a host the estate has never seen, often a near-miss spelling of the legitimate vendor domain.
how.caveat: Do not build this on the exfiltration domain: it was a typosquat of the vendor's own name in the reported case and will be a different string next time, which is exactly why the collection markers carry the rule. The metadata call is common enough in legitimate build tooling to be useless alone and decisive in combination. The fallback behaviour -- a repository appearing in the victim's own account -- is the cheapest of these to check and the least likely to be collected.

how.logic: Tag rewriting leaves a specific and checkable trace: the tag resolves to a commit that is not an ancestor of any branch in the source repository. Resolve every external action reference to a commit and test that membership. It catches the rewrite whether or not the payload is understood, and it catches the force-push-back variant where the actor restores the old commit afterwards to cover the change.
how.caveat: This is the highest-value check in the whole class and it needs no endpoint telemetry, only the ability to resolve references and ask the forge a question. It is also the one that survives the actor covering their tracks, because the consumer recorded which commit it actually ran. Pinning to a digest prevents substitution but not compromise of the pinned artefact, so pair it with the collection markers above.

where.title: 10 Layers Deep: How StepSecurity Stops TeamPCP's Trivy Supply Chain Attack on GitHub Actions

who.versions_affected: Package versions published during the compromise window; the signing machinery worked correctly throughout, which is the point.

what.summary: An actor with a compromised maintainer account pushed commits to branches of an organisation's repositories without passing review, using orphan commits and purpose-named branches rather than pull requests. The workflow those commits added requested a pipeline identity token with signing permission, and the build then published malicious package versions carrying valid build provenance attestations. Around thirty packages in one vendor namespace were affected, with roughly eighty thousand weekly downloads between them. The important property is that no signature was forged and no attestation was invalid: the pipeline genuinely built and genuinely signed what it was told to build, so a consumer verifying provenance saw a correct answer to the wrong question. Payloads were obfuscated and uniquely encrypted per infection, which makes file hashes useless as indicators, and execution came from an install-time hook. Tradecraft overlapped a previously published worm whose code had been released publicly, so attribution was held as overlap rather than identity.

how.logic: Provenance answers which pipeline built an artefact, not whether the pipeline was told the truth. The observable is divergence: a published package whose contents do not correspond to the source at the commit its attestation names, or an attestation naming a commit that reached the branch without review. Watch also for a workflow newly requesting identity-token write permission, which is a small diff with large consequences and is exactly the change to require review on.
how.caveat: Do not record provenance verification as a control against this and do not let a consultation imply it is one; it is a control against a different attack and it passed cleanly here. Hash-based indicators are worthless when payloads are uniquely encrypted per infection, which is stated in the reporting and is becoming the norm. The manifest-diff marker is the cheapest of these and catches the delivery mechanism rather than the actor.

where.title: Miasma: Supply Chain Attack Targeting RedHat npm Packages

who.versions_affected: Initial access observed against unpatched FortiOS and FortiProxy versions carrying the cited identifiers, and against VPN gateways with default credentials and no lockout policy.

what.summary: A joint government advisory on a ransomware-as-a-service operation derived from leaked Conti source, running a double-extortion model against government and critical infrastructure across ten named sectors. Initial access was primarily exploitation of known vulnerabilities in internet-facing firewall and VPN appliances, and in one case default credentials on an SSL-VPN administrative account where no lockout policy existed. Two pieces of tradecraft are worth more than the rest. First, the actors modified the traffic-handling configuration of an SSL-VPN appliance so it collected credentials and session material from users authenticating to a corporate virtual desktop portal, then replayed the stolen sessions -- the appliance became the collection point rather than a route past it. Second, they edited the authentication processing files on that portal so any login presenting one specific attacker-chosen one-time password value succeeded, which is a durable multi-factor bypass that survives password resets, leaves no failed authentications, and is invisible to any control watching for anomalous login patterns. Beyond that the tradecraft is conventional and well covered elsewhere in this corpus: Impacket tooling over SMB for lateral movement, credential dumping from the directory database, log and command-history deletion, and activity deliberately confined to late-night and early-morning hours. Encryption used ChaCha20 with RSA-4096, renamed files to a fixed extension and wrote a fixed-name ransom note per directory; the binary carries an anti-debugging check and skips system directories and system file extensions. Exfiltration reached tens of terabytes in one case, staged with common archiving and transfer tooling and sent to a consumer file-sharing service.

how.logic: A backdoored authentication handler produces successes and no failures, so every control built on failed-login volume, impossible travel or credential stuffing stays silent. Detect it at the file rather than the event: integrity monitoring on the authentication processing files of the portal and the appliance, because the modification is durable and has to persist on disk. The corroborating behavioural signal is a second factor succeeding for accounts and from locations where the enrolled factor was never used.
