how.caveat: The reason this deserves its own pattern rather than folding into the other multi-factor bypasses in this corpus is that nothing is stolen and nothing is replayed: the check itself was rewritten to accept a constant. Detection has to move to the filesystem, and an estate that monitors appliance and portal binaries but not their configuration and script files will not see it. Verify that the integrity baseline covers authentication handlers specifically before recording this as covered.

how.logic: The appliance is not bypassed, it is enlisted. A change to traffic-handling or inspection configuration that causes authentication traffic for an internal portal to be captured is the observable, and it lives in appliance configuration rather than in any log the portal produces. Pair a configuration diff against a known-good baseline with session identifiers appearing from an address that never performed the authentication.
how.caveat: Confidence is medium because the reporting describes the effect rather than the exact configuration primitive, and the primitive differs by vendor. Treat the pattern as the question to ask of your own appliance -- what setting here could cause authentication traffic to be captured, and would a change to it be logged and reviewed -- rather than as a rule to deploy verbatim.

how.logic: Conventional and already carried by this corpus; cited here so the advisory's lateral movement resolves to detection that exists rather than reading as new.
how.caveat: Nothing here is specific to this operation, which is the point: the distinctive tradecraft is the appliance and authentication work above, and an estate already detecting Impacket has most of the rest of this advisory covered.

where.title: Joint advisory AA26-222A on Gunra ransomware affiliate tradecraft

who.versions_affected: Any tenant holding long-lived model API keys without consumption limits or alerting; the keys work exactly as issued.

what.summary: Credentials for commercial language model APIs were stolen and monetised through intermediary proxy services that authenticate to the real provider using the victim's key and resell access at a discount. Keys were harvested by information stealers, phishing aimed at developers, poorly protected repositories and file shares, and malicious registry packages -- the same collection routes as any other credential, which is the point: nothing about the theft is novel, only what the credential is worth. Because consumption is billed rather than blocked, the loss accrues silently and surfaces on an invoice; reported cases reached tens of millions of API calls a day and charges approaching a million dollars. Reporting also describes attackers removing billing limits and disabling usage alerts after gaining account access, which converts a capped exposure into an uncapped one and is the single most detectable action in the chain. This belongs in a detection corpus because the asset is new and the controls usually are not: an API key with no spending ceiling and no consumption baseline is a financial exposure that most estates do not monitor as one.

how.logic: Two halves, and the second is the one to alert on. Consumption diverging sharply from a tenant's own baseline is the symptom, and it is only useful where a baseline exists. The cause is usually visible earlier and more cheaply in the control plane: a billing limit removed, a usage alert disabled, a new key minted, logging turned off. Those are rare, deliberate administrative actions and they precede the spend.
how.caveat: Do not build this on the published addresses or user-agent strings; intermediary infrastructure is rented and rotates, and the reporting's own indicator list will be stale before it is deployed. The control-plane markers are durable because they describe actions with business meaning rather than infrastructure. The cheapest control is not detection at all: a spending ceiling turns an unbounded loss into a bounded one, and its removal is then itself the alert.

where.title: Token Jacking: Cybercriminals Could Be Stealing Your AI Resources

who.versions_affected: Not version dependent; a commodity loader delivered as a packed executable.

what.summary: A commodity loader retrieved its command and control address by reading a value from a smart contract on a public blockchain rather than carrying one or resolving a domain it controlled. The configuration was obfuscated in the binary, deobfuscated at run time to build a request to a public node endpoint, and the contract's stored value decrypted to the current address; the operator updates that value by transaction, so the whole estate re-points without touching a single implant. This is the second independent instance of the mechanism the corpus already carries a pattern for, and the corroboration matters more than the family: takedown and blocklisting both fail against it, because the resolution channel is a public service that cannot be seized and that a great deal of legitimate software also uses. Beyond the resolution channel the loader is unremarkable -- packed executable, startup shortcut persistence, injection into a signed binary, anti-analysis checks on memory size and sandbox usernames, credential collection against browser wallet extensions and desktop wallets, a coin miner, and a commodity remote access tool, with exfiltration over a consumer messaging platform's bot API and staging from public code and paste hosting.

how.logic: The observable is a workstation making remote-procedure calls to a public blockchain node when nothing on that workstation has any reason to. Developer and finance machines are the false positives and they are enumerable; a general-purpose endpoint reading contract storage is not explainable. Pair with the exfiltration leg, which in this family is a consumer messaging platform's bot API -- also legitimate somewhere in most estates and almost never on the same host.
how.caveat: Do not carry the contract addresses, wallet addresses or node hostnames from the reporting into a rule: the operator rotates the stored value by transaction and the public node endpoints are interchangeable. The durable signal is the shape -- a general-purpose endpoint reading contract storage at all. Enumerate the machines with a legitimate reason first and the rule becomes cheap to run.

where.title: The Permanent Threat: Analyzing Aeternum's Blockchain-Based C2 Operations and Communications

who.versions_affected: Not version dependent; the identity platform behaves correctly throughout and the deception is of people.

what.summary: An extortion group reached enterprise cloud tenants by telephone rather than by exploit. Operators called employees on personal mobile numbers while spoofing the organisation's own help desk number, and used an urgent instruction to enrol a new authentication factor as the pretext -- a pretext that works precisely because it sounds like security improvement. Victims were directed to lookalike domains built on the employer's name, behind which a relaying proxy captured credentials and the resulting session material in real time, so the second factor was satisfied legitimately and then stolen rather than bypassed. With a session established the operators enrolled their own factor, then ran scripted collection against the productivity suite and identity provider, at volumes and with client software no person browsing could produce. Two details are worth more than the rest. They deleted the password-reset confirmations, security notices and factor-change alerts from the victim's own mailbox, which removes the one control that reliably reaches a human being and does not depend on a security team watching anything. And they authenticated through residential and consumer broadband addresses, which defeats geography and hosting-provider reputation as filters. The group had rebranded from an earlier name and operated several brands at once, so tracking by brand understates it. Ransom demands ran to millions with substantial negotiated reductions.

how.logic: The notification a platform sends on a factor change or password reset is often the only control that reaches the account holder directly, and it works whether or not anyone is monitoring. Deleting it is therefore a deliberate, high-value step, and it is visible: a mailbox delete of a platform notification within minutes of the identity change that generated it. Correlate the identity event with the mailbox event rather than watching either alone.
how.caveat: Low volume and high signal: people do delete these notices, but rarely within minutes and rarely for a change they did not make. The pairing is what makes it cheap. Where mailbox audit records deletes but not the item subject, this degrades to a delete-shortly-after-identity-change correlation, which is still worth having. Suppressing the notification is also an argument for sending factor-change alerts somewhere the account holder cannot delete them.

how.logic: Enrolment of a new factor immediately preceded by failed authentication or an abandoned challenge for the same account. A genuine user who is enrolling a device does not usually fail first; an operator who has just relayed a session does.
how.caveat: The geography marker is the weakest of the three here and getting weaker: this operation authenticated through residential and consumer broadband addresses specifically so that hosting reputation and country would not separate them from staff. Lead with the failure-then-enrolment correlation, which describes behaviour rather than infrastructure.

how.logic: Bulk file access from a productivity suite recorded against client software that is a scripting runtime rather than a browser or a sanctioned sync client, at a rate no person reading documents would produce.
how.caveat: Client-software strings are trivially changed and this will decay; the rate marker is the durable half. Inventory the automation that legitimately reads at volume first, or this fires on backup and compliance tooling every night.

where.title: UNC6671 Rebrands: Multi-Brand Vishing Extortion Targets Financial Services and Enterprise Cloud Environments

who.versions_affected: Agent versions before the vendors added prompts or restrictions around project-supplied configuration; the behaviour is documented configuration loading rather than a defect.

what.summary: Opening a repository in a coding agent can execute code from that repository before the developer types anything. The agents load project-scoped configuration during initialisation, and two documented features are enough on their own. A tool-server definition committed to the project causes the agent to spawn the named local process at start-up, so a repository can nominate its own interpreter and script. Separately, project-scoped environment settings can prepend a repository-controlled directory to the executable search path, so the agent's own routine version-control calls resolve to a wrapper the repository supplies rather than the real binary. Both mechanisms run with the developer's privileges on a workstation that usually holds live credentials, and the trigger is the act of trusting and opening the project. That is a materially different exposure from reviewing code before running it, because there is no point at which the developer chose to execute anything. Reporting is demonstration rather than observed intrusion, but cites adjacent real activity: a long-running campaign using fake recruitment to get developers to open hostile repositories, and registry packages shipping session-start hooks.

how.logic: The discriminator is ordering, not the command: a process spawned with the agent as its ancestor before the agent has issued its first model request. Pair with the resolved executable path pointing inside the working tree, which is what separates a repository-supplied wrapper from the real tool. Both are cheap to collect on a workstation that already runs endpoint telemetry.
how.caveat: Legitimate project tooling does spawn processes at start-up, which is why the before-first-request ordering carries the rule rather than the spawn itself. Confidence is medium because the source demonstrates rather than reports an intrusion. The inventory question is worth more than the detection here and is answerable in source control: which repositories carry agent configuration, and does anyone review that file the way they review a build script. Treat cloning an untrusted repository as equivalent to running it.

how.logic: Already carried by this corpus from a run-time case; cited so the initialisation vector resolves to detection that exists. The agent as process ancestor is the shared observable, and an estate collecting it covers both.
how.caveat: The two records this pattern now serves differ in timing, not in shape: one fires at initialisation from committed configuration, the other during a session the developer is driving. Collecting agent process ancestry answers both.

where.title: Datadog Security Labs on project configuration executing when a coding agent opens a repository

who.versions_affected: Organisations whose members hold personal access tokens against private repositories. Classic tokens issued outside SAML single sign-on are the hardest case, because organisation owners can neither enumerate nor revoke them.

what.summary: An incident response team investigated a coordinated campaign in which valid personal access tokens belonging to employees of several unrelated organisations were used to enumerate and then bulk-clone private repositories. The campaign ran in three separable stages across roughly three weeks. First, metadata reconnaissance: the per-repository readme endpoint was queried through the REST API from a single cloud address using an ordinary desktop browser user agent. Two weeks later, a rehearsal: the same tokens cloned a small subset of repositories from a different hosting provider, with the bursts across several victims beginning within seconds of one another, which indicates shared automation. Finally the exfiltration itself, in a single working day, using over a hundred addresses in one cloud region and a git client user agent, cloning up to thousands of repositories per organisation. The reporting is explicit that the source of the tokens was never established: they were not found in code or in cloud resources at any victim, and endpoint compromise is offered as a possibility rather than a finding. Repository theft is treated as more than source code loss, because repositories carry cloud credentials, SaaS tokens, private keys and internal documentation, and the reported response spent most of its effort on rotating what the repositories contained and hunting for its use.

how.logic: The authentication is valid throughout, so the rule is built on the shape of the use. Within one window, one credential clones more distinct private repositories than it ever has, from many addresses belonging to one hosting provider, at a parallelism a single client does not produce. Threshold per credential against its own history: a build service and a developer differ by orders of magnitude and a fleet-wide average conceals both.
how.caveat: The seven-day retention on git events in GitHub Enterprise Cloud is the binding constraint and it decides whether this rule is worth writing at all: an estate that does not stream these events off-platform cannot look back across a campaign that staged itself over three weeks, and will also be unable to establish what was taken once it does alert. Stream first, then write the rule. Do not anchor on the addresses or the client version -- the reported campaign changed both between stages. Legitimate bulk cloning by mirrors, CI and onboarding is common, which is why the comparison is against the credential's own history.

how.logic: Two stages precede the theft and both carry the same credential. Metadata enumeration against the API from one address behind a browser user agent, and a low-volume rehearsal clone from a different network days later. The credential changing character between them -- browser for API calls, git client for clones -- is the strongest single signal, because a developer's own token does not switch presentation that way.
how.caveat: Check the telemetry exists before trusting a negative. The api.request events this depends on are delivered by enterprise-level log streaming and do not appear in the standard audit log, so in most estates the reconnaissance stage is simply not recorded and a clean result means nothing. The rehearsal bursts were simultaneous across unrelated victims, which is a sector-level observable and invisible to any one of them.

how.logic: Treat every credential inside an exfiltrated repository as compromised from the moment of the clone, and drive detection from the inventory rather than from the intrusion. Enumerate the repositories the credential cloned, extract the secrets they contain, establish which are still valid, and then hunt each one forward for use from a network or user agent it has no history of. This is the stage where a repository theft becomes a cloud intrusion, and it is the one the responders reported spending most of their effort on.
how.caveat: Rotation and detection compete for the same hours and rotation should win, but record each rotation time as it happens or the subsequent hunt cannot distinguish the actor's use of a key from the estate's own. Secret scanning that reports presence without validating the secret produces a backlog rather than a finding here, because the question is which of them still works.

where.title: Wiz CIRT on investigating GitHub personal access token compromise across a multi-organisation campaign

who.versions_affected: Travelling users on venue-provided guest networks, where the device is not held in a full tunnel and the tenant permits the device code authentication flow.

what.summary: Reporting attributed by Microsoft Threat Intelligence to a sub-cluster of a Russian state-linked group, analysed here by a second vendor. The actor compromised the shared platforms behind captive portals at hotels and conference venues rather than breaking into each location, then manipulated DNS and HTTP on those networks to place itself in the middle of every device that joined. Traffic was redirected down one of three paths: a counterfeit Microsoft 365 sign-in page, a device code phishing page abusing the Entra ID authentication flow, or a fake browser or operating system update prompt using the paste-and-run technique. The device code path is the one that defeats the usual control, because the victim completes a genuine authentication flow and the attacker's session is the one that gets registered, so conventional multi-factor authentication is satisfied rather than bypassed. Reporting names two payloads on the third path, a Go remote access tool that persists by service, run key, scheduled task and watchdog, and an in-memory PowerShell stealer that disables the scanning interface by reflection and harvests browser cookies, Wi-Fi credentials and cloud tokens from the token broker cache. Compromised gateways were identified across several countries and the campaign extended to Android packages. The reporting also assesses that the actor used AI assistance in developing the tooling, on the evidence of unusually detailed comments in the code.

how.logic: The employer never sees the venue's network, so both observables have to be reachable from the endpoint or the tenant. A managed device resolving a known name to an address its own resolver would not return is the first; tenant authentication starting within minutes of that device joining an unfamiliar network is the second. Neither requires any visibility into the hotel.
how.caveat: Every captive portal intercepts DNS and HTTP, so interception is not the finding and a rule built on it fires in every airport lounge. The destination is what matters: an identity-provider sign-in surface or an update prompt served by the intercepting network. Full tunnel with the local proxy disabled removes the exposure outright and is the real control -- treat this rule as what you write for the devices on which that cannot be enforced.

how.logic: Device code phishing ends in a device registration the user did not intend, and that registration is recorded in the tenant even though every earlier step happened on a network nobody in the organisation can see. Look for a device enrolled during a session that originated on an unfamiliar network, with no joiner or provisioning record behind it, and for the authentication that preceded it completing from a different address than the one that started it.
how.caveat: Do not record this as an MFA bypass. The flow completes correctly and the second factor is genuinely satisfied -- by the victim, on the attacker's behalf -- so a control described as stopping it will not, and reporting it as bypassed sends people to fix the wrong thing. Restricting or disabling the device code flow where it is not needed is the control that acts on this; conditional access on device compliance is the one that acts on what follows.

how.logic: The third redirect path is a fake update prompt that asks the user to paste and run a command, which is the mechanism this corpus already holds from two other publishers. What this account adds is the lure inventory -- Windows Update, Defender scan, DirectX, VC++ redistributable, disk optimisation, network diagnostics, browser update and PDF installer -- and that the same path was used to walk Android users through installing a package.
how.caveat: This block exists to connect the captive portal path to a mechanism already held rather than to restate it. The corpus's fuller treatment is on the two records that own this pattern, and a rule should be written once against those rather than three times.

where.title: Zscaler ThreatLabz on captive portal manipulation at hospitality venues for Microsoft 365 credential theft

who.versions_affected: Estates where reaching a public code hosting service is unremarkable from any host, rather than only from developer machines.

what.summary: A Rust backdoor identified in mid-2026 and assessed as a foothold for a ransomware-related operator establishes itself with plaintext HTTP to a control server, posting a JSON object carrying the username, the hostname, its own process identifier and a bot identifier derived from them. It resolves Windows functions at run time through the loader rather than by import, and decrypts its strings with a single repeated exclusive-or key, both of which frustrate static inspection without changing what the host does on the network. The variant that matters for detection replaces the dedicated control server with a public code hosting service, so the command channel becomes ordinary traffic to a domain almost every estate allows. Delivery is assessed with low to medium confidence as the paste-and-run technique this corpus already holds.

how.logic: Blocking the service is not available to most estates and is not the point. The question is which hosts talk to it: a public code hosting domain reached from a server, a finance workstation or any host with no developer role is the signal, and it survives the operator changing repositories, accounts and payloads. The plaintext variant adds a second, cheaper observable while it lasts -- an HTTP POST carrying a JSON body whose fields are the username, the hostname and a process identifier, which is a shape no ordinary client produces.
how.caveat: Fidelity is hunt rather than alert because developer estates reach code hosting constantly and the role-based split that carries this rule is exactly the inventory most organisations do not have. Build the host inventory first or this produces noise. The plaintext HTTP marker is the weakest of the four and the first the operator will retire -- the reporting already describes the family as under active development -- so do not let it carry the rule.

where.title: C2Looper: A New Backdoor Likely Tied To Ransomware With GitHub C2

who.versions_affected: Consumer streaming and set-top hardware, typically unmanaged, unpatched and outside any enterprise inventory, reached over the internet or from the network it sits on.

what.summary: A seventh version of an Android and internet-of-things botnet family upgrades two things that matter to a defender, and neither is the payload. Its denial-of-service capability gains a flood built on HTTP/2 that constructs complete browser fingerprints, so the attack traffic resembles ordinary browsing rather than the malformed or uniform requests a volumetric filter is tuned for. Its command and control gains resilience through name resolution on a public ledger: the binary carries several hard-coded ledger gateway endpoints and resolves its controller through a blockchain naming service rather than through a domain a registrar can suspend or a blocklist can carry. It primarily affects Android TV boxes and set-top boxes, which is the part that makes it an enterprise problem indirectly -- the infected estate is consumer hardware on staff and guest networks, and the enterprise is the target of the flood rather than the owner of the bot.

how.logic: A controller resolved through a ledger naming service cannot be taken down by a registrar and does not appear in domain reputation, so the observable moves to the lookup itself. Requests from a host outside the approved set to a public ledger gateway provider, followed within minutes by a first-seen outbound destination, is the shape -- and on a network carrying consumer media devices, a set-top box making that request has no legitimate reading at all.

markers.expr: host outside the approved set makes requests to distributed ledger gateway providers
ledger gateway request followed within minutes by a first-seen outbound destination

how.caveat: The gateway list is the weak marker and will age: these are public infrastructure providers, new ones appear, and an operator can run their own node and match nothing on that expression. The durable half is the pairing -- a ledger lookup followed by a first contact -- and the device class making it. Do not extend this to wallet applications and cryptocurrency tooling, which make these requests legitimately all day and are the reason this rule needs the device or role qualifier rather than the domain alone.

how.logic: A flood that constructs complete and plausible browser fingerprints defeats filtering that works by spotting malformed or uniform requests, so the discriminator moves from the request to the population making it. Complete, well-formed, individually unremarkable browser sessions arriving in volume from address space belonging to consumer broadband and media devices, at a concurrency and geographic spread the service has no history of, is the finding. Fingerprint diversity that is too even is itself a signal: real populations cluster on a few browser and version combinations, and a generator that randomises produces a flatter distribution than any genuine audience.
how.caveat: This is a hunt and not an alert because every marker is a comparison against the service's own baseline and there is no threshold that transfers between services. It also fires on legitimate events -- a product launch, a news cycle, a marketing send -- which is why the fingerprint distribution matters more than the volume. A service already behind a scrubbing provider should confirm what that provider passes through before writing this at all.

where.title: Kimwolf v7: An Evolution of the Kimwolf Botnet

who.versions_affected: Any estate where developers run an agent with shell access and no lifecycle-hook logging, which is the default state of every such deployment.

what.summary: A vendor security team deployed an AI coding agent with shell access to hundreds of developers and then found it had no record of what the agent had done. The gap is structural rather than a product defect: the agent runs commands, installs packages, edits configuration and reads files under the developer's own account, inside processes the developer launched, so endpoint tooling attributes every action to the human and cannot separate a command a person typed from one a model generated. That matters in three situations the reporting names -- during an incident, when the question is whether a command was typed or produced by a model that may have been steered by a poisoned repository file or a hostile tool server; when assessing what an agent read; and when establishing scope afterwards. The remedy described is lifecycle hooks: a small script fired by the agent's own hook interface, writing every tool call, shell command, file read and tool-server request as structured events that the existing endpoint agent already ships. The deployment reported over thirteen million tool-call events from more than eleven hundred machines in three months, which is the size of the blind spot rather than a measure of the tooling.

how.logic: This is an inventory question before it is a detection one, and it is answerable today without deploying anything: take the hosts where a coding agent with shell access is installed, and ask which of them emit any record distinguishing agent-originated commands from operator-originated ones. Every host in the first set and not the second is a host where an incident cannot be reconstructed. The follow-on detections -- an agent reading key material, an agent reaching a tool server nobody registered -- are only writable once that record exists, so the coverage check is the finding and the rules come after it.
how.caveat: Do not read the absence of agent telemetry as absence of agent activity -- that is the whole point of the record. The hook interface is the agent vendor's and differs per product, so the collector is per-agent work rather than one deployment, and an estate running several agents will have several blind spots of different shapes. Logging every tool call also captures file paths and command text from developer machines, so the privacy and retention decision has to be made before the rollout rather than after it.

where.title: Elastic Security Labs on auditing AI coding agent tool calls through lifecycle hooks

who.versions_affected: Anything treating a signed commit hash as a unique name for its content: hash denylists, pinned dependencies in package sets, module systems and pipeline action references, and reproducible-build systems keyed on the commit.

what.summary: Academic work shows that a commit hash does not uniquely identify a piece of signed content. Given any signed commit, an actor with no access to the signing key and without breaking SHA-2 can produce a second, distinct commit carrying an identical tree, identical metadata, a signature that still validates, and a verified marking from the forge, differing only in its hash. Because a commit hash covers its parent, the change cascades through every dependent commit, which the paper calls hash chain malleability. Three encoding routes are demonstrated: algebraic inversion of an ECDSA signature component, insertion of an unhashed OpenPGP subpacket, and non-canonical length re-encoding inside an S/MIME envelope. Two of the three pass local verification and all three produce a persistent, independent verified record on a major forge; proof-of-concept tooling automating all three is published with the paper. The consequences named are hash-based commit blocking, dependency pinning in several package and module systems, and reproducible-build systems that use the commit hash as a content-addressable primary key. The precise scope matters and is easy to overstate: the content is identical in every case, so this is not a route to substituting different code under a pinned hash.

how.logic: The control that silently stops working is hash-based blocking, so start there: for any commit hash the estate denies, the question is whether the same tree can present under another hash that also verifies. Compare trees rather than hashes wherever a decision depends on identity. Where the verifier can report how a signature was encoded rather than merely that it verified, an unhashed subpacket, a non-canonical DER length or an inverted ECDSA component are each worth treating as suspect on their own, because none of them is what honest tooling produces.
how.caveat: This is demonstrated capability from a paper with released tooling, not observed intrusion, and it should be weighed as such -- there is no incident behind it. Do not let it argue against pinning: pinning still stops content substitution, which is what it was adopted for, and nothing here touches that. The guarantee it removes is that a hash is a canonical name, which was assumed rather than stated, and hash denylisting is the control that depended on it. Most verification tooling reports only whether a signature validated and not how it was encoded, so two of these three markers are unbuildable in most estates today and the tree comparison is the one to start from.

who.versions_affected: Any authentication or checkout flow whose second factor is a code the user can read and retype, which is what the framework is built to collect.

what.summary: An undocumented phishing framework impersonates checkout and login flows for major payment and shopping platforms, and differs from an ordinary kit in that it is operator-driven rather than a form logger. The client engine keeps an encrypted WebSocket open to the actor, streams the victim's keystrokes as they are typed, renders across dozens of pages, and acts on more than forty distinct instructions issued from a console, so the operator steers each session live and asks for whatever the real site asks for at the moment it is needed. What is collected goes well past card data: identity document and passport images, national identity numbers, driving licence images, site and payment-service credentials, two-factor codes and a full device fingerprint, all committed to the actor's server when the session ends. Delivery in the observed campaign was by message, impersonating toll authorities and postal and courier services across several countries. The framework is assessed with medium confidence as a variant of an existing phishing-as-a-service platform on shared client code.

how.logic: The channel is the discriminator and it is visible without decryption: a page presenting as a payment or login brand while holding a persistent socket open to a host that is not that brand. The second is the ask. No genuine checkout collects a passport image, a national identity number and a one-time code in one flow, so a page that does is enumerating the operator's requirements rather than completing a purchase.
how.caveat: The one-time code is not bypassed here and calling it a bypass sends people to strengthen a factor that already worked. It is requested inside its validity window and the victim answers it correctly on the operator's behalf -- the same shape as device code phishing, and with the same remedy, which is a credential bound to the origin rather than a stronger code. Note also where this is visible: the lures are consumer-directed and arrive by message, so most of this traffic never touches a corporate path, and an estate will typically see the consequence on its own accounts rather than the session that caused it.

products: agent runtimes with a code interpreter
who.versions_affected: Pipelines in which a fast policy-check model screens input for a target model that has higher reasoning effort and a code interpreter the checker does not have. An architecture property rather than a product defect; the researchers state the technique works where the target holds reasoning and interpreter resources the preceding quick check does not.

what.summary: Check Point Research demonstrated a prompt-crafting technique, PuzzleMask, that carries a policy-violating payload past a fast gatekeeper model in a gatekeeper-then-target pipeline using plain English prose alone, with no emoji, Base64 or invisible formatting for a filter to key on. Twenty-three crafted prompts produced by an automated pipeline were put to three gatekeepers running a quick policy check -- gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18, gpt-oss-safeguard:20b and claude-3-haiku-20240307 -- each equipped with an explicit policy the researchers first confirmed flags and blocks the plain form of the same payload. A fourth gatekeeper, llama-guard3:8b, was put the five copyright-lyrics prompts only, and against its own built-in policy rather than a supplied one. Every gatekeeper trial was classified safe, and where a rationale was requested the gatekeeper did not appear aware that anything was embedded or that there was anything to extract. The target model, gpt-5-thinking at high reasoning effort with a code interpreter enabled, recovered the payload, treated it as further input and acted on it in 17 of 18 trials. The researchers state that recovery is gated behind reasoning effort and interpreter access the typical gatekeeper does not have, and that in every successful recovery the target used more than a minute of thinking time and more than two executed Python scripts. This is a laboratory demonstration with coordinated disclosure rather than an observed intrusion, and the researchers are explicit that the technique is not itself a jailbreak: the claim is only that an arbitrary prompt reaches the target unreviewed, not that the target is likelier to disobey its own instructions once it does.

how.logic: Screen text entering a model context for a phrase that makes a quantitative statement about the whole text containing it, rather than about anything outside it. Check Point published a policy clause directing a gatekeeper to classify as unsafe any phrase that is, in their words, "both quantitative in nature and self-referent with respect to the entire text". Added to the policy of a gatekeeper that had previously passed every crafted prompt as safe, it made that gatekeeper flag all twenty-three, citing exactly the relevant phrase in its rationale each time and nothing else. The test is a property of the sentence rather than of its meaning, which is why it survives a wrapper written in any tone or on any subject.
how.caveat: Check Point states the clause carries an expected false positive cost and reports no measurement of it, only a belief that the phrasing has room to improve. Text that legitimately counts or describes itself satisfies the same test, including writing about word counts and documentation about prompts. The encoding is redacted throughout the article, so no literal string, regular expression or structural marker for the wrapper itself can be given and this clause is the only published discriminator. The 'these words ...' clause visible in the redacted samples is stated not to be strictly necessary for the technique to work, so do not anchor on it. The rationale a hardened gatekeeper returns, citing that phrase and nothing else, is the researchers' evidence that the clause works and not an observable in a pipeline that has yet to add it, so it is deliberately not a marker: requiring it would mean the detection only fires where the mitigation has already blocked the prompt. http_proxy supplies this block only where the proxy captures request bodies, which an inline AI gateway does and ordinary web access logging does not.

how.logic: Join the policy check's verdict to what the target model then did with the same input. The observable is a turn in which a prose-only prompt carrying no attachment and asking for no computation is passed as safe by the quick check, and then drives sustained reasoning and repeated code-interpreter runs in the target. Check Point measured that every successful payload recovery took the target more than a minute of thinking time and more than two executed Python scripts, and states that recovery is gated behind exactly the reasoning effort and interpreter access the gatekeeper does not have. Baseline reasoning duration and interpreter invocations per turn on your own pipeline before setting a bound; the published figures are the floor the researchers observed on one configuration, not a threshold to ship.

markers.note: Bound left unresolved on purpose. The published floor is in the caveat and is a floor on one target configuration, not a threshold to compile.
Bound left unresolved on purpose. The published floor is in the caveat and is a floor on one target configuration, not a threshold to compile.

how.caveat: The published floor is more than one minute of thinking time and more than two executed Python scripts, stated for every instance in which the target successfully extracted the payload; the target extracted, considered and acted on the payload in 17 of 18 trials. It was measured on a single configuration: gpt-5-thinking at high reasoning effort, described as the gpt-5 alias in the OpenAI responses API corresponding to gpt-5-2025-08-07. It is a floor on that configuration and not a general threshold, which is why the markers leave the bound unresolved. It is also only a floor: nothing in the source says how often an ordinary turn on that configuration reaches a minute of reasoning, so a consumer who compiles sixty seconds without also enforcing the no-computation qualifier has no published basis for the false positive rate it would carry. The figures for the one failed trial are not reported. Legitimate prose prompts asking for analysis produce the same shape, which is why the discriminator is that the visible request asks for no computation at all. This depends on the pipeline recording reasoning duration and interpreter invocations per turn, which is the first thing to establish; edr_process supplies it only where the interpreter runs on infrastructure the consumer instruments, and a provider-hosted interpreter leaves only the provider's audit trail.

how.logic: Reconcile what the target model did against what the visible prompt asked for. With the payload recovered, the target acted on instructions the displayed text never contained: in Check Point's emulated environments it printed the last word of an uploaded flag file, and it encrypted a documents folder and removed the plaintext copies. The observable is a tool call or file operation whose effect is out of family for the request as a person reading the prompt would understand it, on a turn the policy check passed as safe. Check Point name monitoring the model's output and actions, and not only its input, as one of the published mitigations, and this block is that mitigation written as a detection.

markers.note: One alternation rather than separate conjuncts: a turn carries one payload, so the demonstrated effects are alternatives and would empty the filter if they were ANDed. Fragment as well as contents, because the payload actually run was print flag last word.

how.caveat: Both demonstrated actions ran in emulated environments holding mock content only, so treat them as the shape of the effect and not as reported harm. Confidence is medium because the actions are reported while the runtime reconciliation is reasoned: this is demonstration with coordinated disclosure, not intrusion reporting. Fidelity is hunt rather than alert for the same reason, and because deciding that an action had no antecedent in the prompt is a semantic judgement an analyst makes rather than a field test a rule can run. T1204 is included for the pasted-text route the researchers raise at the individual user level, not for the laboratory submission, in which the prompt was supplied directly. edr_file and edr_process supply this block only where the interpreter or tool runtime sits on infrastructure the consumer instruments; both demonstrations ran in a provider-hosted interpreter, which leaves only the provider's audit trail.

where.title: PuzzleMask: Abusing Plain Prose as a Covert AI Attack Vector

notes: Trial counts as published: gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18, gpt-oss-safeguard:20b and claude-3-haiku-20240307 were each put 23 crafted prompts; llama-guard3:8b was put 5, the copyright-lyrics set only, because the researchers chose to test its implicit built-in policy and that was only possible with those prompts. Gatekeeper bypass was 100 per cent in every arm. Target recovery and execution was 17 of 18, about 94.4 per cent, on gpt-5-thinking at high reasoning effort with a code interpreter; the target arm excluded the 5 copyright-lyrics prompts. The three payloads used were print flag last word, print macarena full lyrics, and encrypt documents with removal of the plaintext copies. Check Point contacted Anthropic, Meta and OpenAI between late November and mid-December 2025. what.attack_surface is deliberately omitted: the source describes the architecture of the pipeline and names the API the tests ran through, but never characterises the deployment's network exposure, and the technique is an architecture property of a gatekeeper-then-target pipeline wherever that pipeline sits. Two further published mitigations are not detections and are not carried in how[]: paraphrasing untrusted input before it reaches the target, which the researchers argue removes the payload as a consequence of how the technique works rather than as a measured result; and, at the extreme, giving the gatekeeper the same power as the target. A third published mitigation, monitoring model output and actions in addition to input, is carried as how[2]. A fourth, caution at the individual user level about pasting web-origin text into a chat box, is advice rather than a control. Separately, the researchers report the attack universally fails against Anthropic's Opus-class target models, which they say were equipped contemporaneously with this research with a built-in classifier that terminates the conversation on detecting the model processing an obfuscated prompt, and that Fable 5 was equipped with it later. That is a target-side control and is stated as contemporaneous rather than as a response to the disclosure; it says nothing about whether a gatekeeper would have caught the same prompt, and claude-3-haiku-20240307 in the gatekeeper role was bypassed in all 23 trials. The prompt-generation pipeline is described as resource-intensive, upwards of 15 minutes for a short payload, with longer payloads impractical, which is what held the sample at 23.

who.versions_affected: Not stated for the operating system or browser. The remote access client deployed was NetSupport Manager 12.44.

what.summary: Two WebDAV infection chains delivered the Amatera stealer by running a 32-bit library straight off a remote share through rundll32 export ordinal one. In the pf.ch chain, recovered in full, ClearFake JavaScript injected by a Cloudflare Worker read its browser stages from BNB Smart Chain contracts and a fake Google verification prompt put a command on the visitor's clipboard for the Run dialog; that build's controller then tasked it with a side-loaded cryptocurrency stealer that terminated security agents through a signed driver, and with a Go reverse proxy. In the verification.google chain the stages before the WebDAV execution were never recovered, and its own controller tasked it with an unauthorised NetSupport Manager installation. Talos assessed with low to medium confidence that the two delivery chains are identical.

how.logic: The 32-bit rundll32.exe started with a WebDAV UNC path as its argument and export ordinal #1 as the function selector. The April 2026 telemetry event that opened the investigation showed that execution together with startup of the Windows WebClient service; for the pf.ch sample Talos reported the same WebDAV, disguised filename and ordinal launch but did not report the service start, which WebDAV UNC use implies rather than confirms. The two loaders use different code and protection methods, so the launch shape is the narrowest thing they share. Neither remote file ended in .dll: the names observed were pf.ch and verification.google, and the victim identifier was carried in the WebDAV path itself.

fields.note: the first export was moor in pf.ch and CfgInspectModuleData in verification.google, so the ordinal is what both share

markers.note: the pasted command reconstructed pushd, rundll32 and popd at run time using delayed expansion; pushd is a cmd.exe builtin and never appears on rundll32's own command line, so the alternation is what lets one event satisfy this marker alongside the process name
the WebDAV host was a randomised subdomain of this name

iocs.note: WebDAV host for the Windows branch; the host reached was a randomised subdomain of it

how.caveat: Document collaboration suites use WebDAV legitimately and some enterprise software loads libraries by ordinal, so neither half alone is worth an alert. Blocking outbound WebDAV, or disabling the WebClient service by policy, removes this branch entirely and is the cheaper control. The loader names are disposable; the launch shape is not.

how.logic: A compromised site overlaid a fake Google CAPTCHA-style checkbox, put a command on the clipboard and told the visitor to open the Windows Run dialog, paste and press Enter. The command was a batch command using delayed expansion to reconstruct pushd, rundll32 and popd at execution time, not an encoded PowerShell command, so a detection keyed on an encoded PowerShell argument does not fire on it. The macOS arm of the same framework instead instructed the visitor to paste a curl command with a macOS user-agent string into Terminal.

markers.note: the Run dialog history is the standard Windows record that a paste into that dialog happened; Talos describes the Run dialog paste but names no registry artefact, so this key is the known artefact of the described behaviour rather than a value read from the report

Talos states delayed expansion reconstructed pushd, rundll32 and popd at execution time but published the command only as an image; the enabling switch, the alternative enabler and the variable syntax here are the standard forms of that technique, not text read from the report
the Windows paste target was a randomised subdomain of this name

iocs.note: macOS branch; the pasted command reached a subdomain of this name and Talos did not pursue that branch further

how.caveat: The corpus pattern this cites carries PowerShell-shaped markers, and this campaign is the counter-example: the pasted command was a batch command with no encoded argument at all. Treat the interpreter identity as open. Administrators do paste into the Run dialog, so the discriminator is the remote path in the argument rather than the paste itself. The macOS arm is described in the logic but carries no markers here: Talos said only that the pasted curl command supplied a macOS user-agent string and published neither that string nor the subdomain, and the Windows registry and command-line markers in this block cannot co-occur with a macOS session anyway. Talos assessed with low to medium confidence that the two delivery chains were identical, and the front half of the government-organisation chain was never directly recovered.

how.logic: The chain queried a public blockchain twice at two different layers. The injected browser script read its next stage from a BNB Smart Chain testnet contract through a public node gateway, choosing a different contract for Windows and for macOS, then base64-decoded the response and evaluated it as JavaScript. Separately, the final cryptocurrency stealer resolved its own C2 domain by making a JSON-RPC eth_call through a second gateway, disguised as a routine ERC-20 token balance query whose supplied address the contract ignores. The observable is the gateway request from a host with no blockchain role, not the destination it yields.

fields.note: first stage, Windows stage, macOS stage and the stealer configuration contract in that order. The addresses are published in checksummed mixed case; on the wire the to field is lower-case hex and the address inside eth_call calldata is lower-case and zero-padded with no 0x prefix, so the test is a case-insensitive match on the 40 hex characters within the body rather than an equality against the whole body

iocs.note: gateway used by the injected browser script
gateway used by the final cryptocurrency stealer

how.caveat: The operator rotates the C2 by writing to the contract rather than by rebuilding the payload, so domain blocklists age immediately: the same wallet made 39 successful writes between 16 March and 26 July 2026, and six distinct domains were current during July alone. Blocking the two named gateways does not close it, because any public node for that chain will serve the same read. An estate doing genuine blockchain work needs an allow list first; for everyone else the legitimate population is near zero. The contract field test needs request-body capture, which is a much rarer collection than the declared proxy logging and, for HTTPS to a public gateway, needs TLS interception; without it only the gateway destination and the sequence are available.

how.logic: One of the two stealer builds carried no C2 address. It fetched a single article on a public publishing platform, which was dressed up as a short Rust programming tutorial with a base64 string hidden inside a code example, decoded that to an IPv4 address and then opened a socket directly to it on TCP 443. The signal is a host fetching one article from a publishing platform once and never again, immediately followed by a direct-to-address session.

markers.note: url_path resolves to the full URL field, so the test is a containment on the path rather than an equality

iocs.note: C2 decoded from that page; reached on TCP 443

how.caveat: The publishing platform is legitimate and widely read, so alerting on the domain is not defensible; the sequence is what carries it. The resolver page is disposable and its content was written to look like ordinary programming documentation, so content inspection will not help. Talos notes that this malware family is known to use gaming community profiles as dead drop resolvers: the analysed sample carried the string GETWELLV2, and the report gives GETWELL2, without the V, as the profile name seen in some previous samples. The two spellings are reproduced as the report gives them and are not reconciled here. The resolver actually used in this chain was the publishing platform page, not a gaming profile.

how.logic: The other stealer build decrypted a fixed address from an encrypted string and connected to it directly on TCP 443 while presenting github.com as both the TLS server name and the HTTP Host value. Talos reported the hard-coded address and that this build, unlike the other, does not use a public dead-drop resolver; that a name lookup never precedes the session follows from the address being fixed rather than being something the report states it observed. A rule comparing the presented name against what that host actually resolved catches it; a rule comparing the presented name against an allow list does not.

iocs.note: bootstrap C2 of the verification.google build

how.caveat: The borrowed brand here happened to be a code-hosting service, but nothing in the technique depends on that, so do not key the rule on the name. The presented name is carried by the logic and by the computed markers rather than by a header marker, because the session is TLS and the Host header is inside the tunnel: reading it needs interception this block does not assume. Content delivery networks legitimately serve many names from shared addresses, which is why the comparison has to be against this host's own resolution history rather than against a published address list. Where TLS metadata is not captured, the server name field does not exist and only the weaker no-lookup half of the rule can be built.

how.logic: The first tasked payload arrived as a ZIP archive. The loader extracted it to a temporary directory, enumerated the executables in it and launched one: platform_experience_helper.exe, a legitimate Google Chrome component, which imports GetUserNameExW from Secur32.dll and therefore side-loads the malicious Secur32.dll shipped beside it in the archive. That library is a NativeAOT loader which then starts C:\Windows\explorer.exe suspended, maps its own payload headers and sections into the child, rewrites the initial thread context and resumes it.

markers.note: the signed Chrome component that is launched; typed as the process so that it does not collide with the library name on the same field
the side-loaded library: the file written beside the executable on extraction, and the module loaded when it runs

iocs.note: ZIP archive carrying the Chrome component and the malicious Secur32.dll

how.caveat: The executable is genuine and its signature validates, which is the point, so reputation and signing checks pass the whole stage. The load path is the anomaly. Portable and per-user applications do legitimately ship libraries beside their executables, so restrict to system library names resolving outside the system directory. A ZIP whose contents are extracted and executed from a temporary directory is the earlier and cheaper place to intervene.

how.logic: The NativeAOT loader decrypted two PE files: a user-mode payload and a signed Windows driver whose original filename was DCRCVDrv.sys, which exposes the device \Device\DCRCVDRV_U. The loader enumerated running processes, hashed their names, compared them against an internal list of endpoint detection and other security products, and passed the process identifier of each match to the driver using IOCTL 0x2205c0. The driver's handler takes the four-byte identifier, opens a handle and calls ZwTerminateProcess, with no check on who is calling.
how.caveat: Talos described the kernel termination primitive and the missing authorisation check; it did not report agent telemetry actually going silent, so the absence half of this detection is a design consequence rather than something the report observed, and it is why the confidence here is medium rather than high. That half is also why network and authentication telemetry are declared alongside the endpoint ones: without them there is nothing to show the host is still alive while the agent is quiet. The driver is legitimately signed and its version strings name MOCOMSYS and DCRC, but that identifies this driver rather than the technique, and the operator can substitute another. A platform-enforced vulnerable-driver blocklist is the control; detection covers the window before the blocklist has the entry.

iocs.note: the driver's PE original filename, which is what Talos published; the name it was written under on disk was not reported, so this is not a file-name test

how.logic: The second tasked payload ran fileless from shellcode and was a 32-bit Go executable whose main package was github.com/acr/proxy-panel/cmd/bot. It reads the Windows MachineGuid and the hostname, sends them over a WebSocket Secure connection to a hard-coded address, then opens a Yamux multiplexing session over that same connection. Each logical stream carries a source and destination address, the client connects to the destination it is given and relays bytes both ways, which makes the victim host an exit point for traffic aimed at somebody else.

iocs.note: hard-coded wss C2 for the Go proxy
shellcode blob delivered by the tasking configuration
the Go proxy unpacked from that shellcode

how.caveat: The multiplexing means one outbound connection carries an arbitrary number of logical sessions, so session counting at the perimeter sees a single long connection and nothing else. The WebSocket upgrade itself is an HTTP exchange inside the TLS session, so none of the telemetry declared here observes it; the pattern carries it as a computed marker, and what these markers can carry is the hard-coded destination and the shape of the flow. The payload was never written to disk, so file-based hunting misses it and only memory or network evidence remains. Scoping an incident to what was taken from this host would miss the role it was playing: the proxy exists so that traffic aimed at a third party leaves from the victim's address.

how.logic: Before installing the remote access tool, the PowerShell stage ran seven environment gates: the C: volume serial against the hard-coded value 4E014A2F, system uptime from Win32_OperatingSystem.LastBootUpTime with anything under ten minutes exiting, a timed 500 ms NtDelayExecution measured with GetTickCount64 with under 400 ms elapsed exiting, processor count, total physical memory under 3.2 GiB exiting, the largest Win32_VideoController AdapterRAM value under 384 MiB exiting, and display-device friendly names and manufacturers against 36 strings for virtual graphics, remote displays, cloud platforms and generic virtual adapters. A single script reading all of these in sequence is the detectable shape.
how.caveat: Two of the seven gates are inverted and let execution continue early rather than rejecting the host: a matching volume serial short-circuits the remaining checks, and fewer than three processors also continues. Talos reported both without explaining either, so do not read the gate set as a coherent anti-analysis policy. The gate tokens Talos names -- Win32_VideoController, AdapterRAM, Win32_OperatingSystem.LastBootUpTime, NtDelayExecution and GetTickCount64 -- are stated here rather than carried as a command-line marker, because this stage is retrieved with DownloadString and run through Invoke-Expression and so never reaches a process command line; matching them needs script-block or interface-scan content, which neither declared telemetry type carries on its own. With that content available both surviving markers are conditions on a single script execution, which is why the shape is a filter rather than a join. The practical consequence is the one that matters for triage: a sandbox verdict of benign on this stage may only mean the sample recognised the sandbox, and the display-adapter checks specifically defeat virtual desktop and cloud analysis estates.

how.logic: The same PowerShell stage started two background runspaces that requested many legitimate URLs, of which Talos named six services: GitHub API, npm, Docker Hub, PyPI, NuGet and PowerShell Gallery. The requests bury the single malicious retrieval inside plausible developer activity. Count distinct well-known developer destinations per host in a short window, keep only hosts with no developer or build role, and treat the destinations in that window that are not in the well-known set as the candidates.

markers.note: Talos named six services -- GitHub API, npm, Docker Hub, PyPI, NuGet and PowerShell Gallery -- among many legitimate URLs requested, and published none of the request URLs, so the marker counts distinct destinations rather than listing hostnames. The bound of four is derived from that named set of six and is not a measured rate; measure it against the local estate before using it
the runspaces are in-process threads and no declared telemetry distinguishes a request issued from one; the interpreter identity is what is observable

how.caveat: Talos named six services among many legitimate URLs and did not publish the request URLs, so the marker set is deliberately a count of distinct well-known developer destinations rather than a domain list; filling in specific hostnames would be inventing values the report does not carry, and the named set is explicitly not exhaustive. The count bound is anchored on that set of six rather than measured, so measure it locally before the rule is used. Developer workstations and build agents match this constantly and must be excluded by role first. The decoys cost the operator nothing to drop, so this is a hunting lead with a short shelf life rather than a durable control.

how.logic: The PowerShell stage fetched a ZIP, validated its entry paths, extracted it under %APPDATA%, started hypersnap.exe with no visible window and created a scheduled task triggered at user logon. hypersnap.exe is a renamed, signed NetSupport Manager 12.44 client32.exe, and the stub calls the export _NSMClient32@8 in the signed PCICL32.DLL, which is where the remote access functionality actually lives. The actor-supplied client32.ini enables silent operation, hides the system tray interface, disables the visible chat, message, disconnect, replay and help controls, and sets an external HTTP gateway with a 60 second poll.

fields.note: licence issued as KAKAN; Talos treats it as shared deployment lineage across packages, not as an actor fingerprint

markers.note: the runtime library and the configuration file; neither can be renamed without breaking the product, and both bind to the same field so they are one test
Talos states the archive was extracted in the %APPDATA% directory; the path form here is that variable expanded
the configuration named the gateway as paternal-angrily.com:443; the port is what that configuration set, not a general property of the product

iocs.note: PowerShell stage retrieved with DownloadString and run through Invoke-Expression
ZIP carrying the remote access client
NetSupport HTTP gateway configured in client32.ini as paternal-angrily.com:443
address the gateway domain resolved to at analysis time, located in Russia

how.caveat: A detection keyed on the process name finds nothing here, because the executable was renamed; the runtime library, the configuration file and the configured gateway are what identify the product. An estate that legitimately licenses NetSupport Manager will match the library marker constantly, so the discriminator is the mismatch between the loading process name and the vendor executable, plus the install path. Talos could find no evidence in the victim's own logs that this URL was ever retrieved there, and recovered the archive independently, so this stage is the intended follow-on rather than a confirmed installation at that organisation.

how.logic: The payload delivered through the side-loading chain is a cryptocurrency stealer written in Zig. It polls the clipboard, recognises several cryptocurrency address formats and can replace a matching value with an address embedded in the payload. The substitution itself collects nothing and sends nothing, so detections built around collection or exfiltration do not see that behaviour; the same payload does hold a C2 channel, resolved through the ledger request described earlier in this record. The observable here is a process polling and rewriting the clipboard with no window the user is interacting with.
how.caveat: Most endpoint sensors do not record clipboard operations and fewer record content, so establish what is collected before designing around this; the confidence here reflects that the detection is derived from a described capability rather than from telemetry Talos published. No polling rate was reported, so this block carries no count and no bound: the ordering, a read followed by a replacement within the same session, is what it can state. The substitution addresses are embedded in the payload, so verifying a pasted address against a saved address book before confirming a transfer defeats the whole technique without any detection at all.

where.title: ClearFake WebDAV infection chain delivers Amatera stealer, ZigCryptoStealer, and NetSupport Manager

notes: Talos's own confidence statements, kept because they bound what this record can be used for. Moderate confidence that the activity is not targeted at a particular organisation and is a cryptocurrency and credential stealing operation; low to medium confidence that the two delivery chains are identical; moderate confidence that the verification.google branch was run by a Russian threat actor, resting on the remote access gateway resolving to an address in Russia. Talos tracks the actor behind the verification.google activity as UAT-10820. No record-level actor is asserted, because this record also carries the pf.ch chain and the two chains are linked only at low to medium confidence; a consumer wanting the attribution should take it as covering the verification.google branch alone. The only named victim is a Ukrainian government organisation, which is why government appears alongside cross_sector in the sectors; Talos assessed the campaign itself as untargeted, and Cisco Umbrella saw lookups for the stealer's current C2 domain from 98 countries, most often the United States, Indonesia, Brazil, India and Egypt. Two other accounts of Amatera delivery, by Malwarebytes in July 2026 and by Blackpoint Cyber, are referenced in the article and are deliberately absent from the corroborations: Talos states it found no common infrastructure or other evidence linking those activities to these chains, so they are separate campaigns sharing a payload family, not corroboration of this one. Infrastructure dates worth keeping: the stealer's configuration contract was deployed on 16 March 2026 and the deploying wallet made 39 successful setData writes through 26 July, giving a public history of the C2 values. The indicator list linked from the article was read on 12 September 2026 and holds 46 domains, 22 file hashes, four addresses and seven URLs; the article text ties only four of those hashes, three of the addresses and four of the URLs to a stage of either chain. The rest are not reproduced here, because assigning them to a stage would be a guess. That includes two URLs on one host in the list whose filename matches the tasking entry the article names: a filename correspondence, not a statement Talos made.
