who.versions_affected: Builds vulnerable to CVE-2023-42793

what.summary: A foreign intelligence service exploited a build automation server flaw at large scale from September 2023. Compromising a build server yields the source code it compiles, the signing certificates it holds, and the ability to alter what gets built and shipped, which turns one intrusion into a route to every downstream customer.

how.logic: The consequence that matters is not the intrusion but what a build server can be made to do afterwards. Three things need watching that ordinary server monitoring does not cover: changes to build definitions and pipeline configuration outside the normal review process, use of signing keys outside a build triggered by a reviewed commit, and build outputs whose hash does not match a rebuild from the same source. The last is the only check that survives an attacker with full control of the pipeline.

fields.note: compare against the accounts authorised to change pipeline definitions, and against a code review record
every use should map to a build triggered by a reviewed commit

how.caveat: Very few organisations can currently answer the reproducible-build question, which is the honest state of this control. Where they cannot, signing key usage records are the practical fallback.

how.logic: The exploited flaw is an authentication bypass on the web interface leading to code execution, so it surfaces as the build server's web process creating a shell. Build servers legitimately execute a great deal of arbitrary code, which is exactly what makes this harder here than on an ordinary web server: the distinguishing feature is a shell parented by the web process rather than by a build agent.
how.caveat: A build server runs untrusted code as its job, so process-based detection is weak here by nature. Parentage narrows it; the build definition change record is the stronger signal.

how.logic: Exploitation was described as large scale and began the month the flaw was published. Build and development infrastructure is frequently outside the main asset inventory because it belongs to engineering rather than IT, which is how an internet-facing build server stays unpatched.
how.caveat: The ownership gap is the real finding. Ask whether development infrastructure appears in the same inventory and patch process as everything else; usually it does not.

who.versions_affected: For CVE-2020-1631, Junos OS 12.3 through 20.1 across many branches, per the vendor advisory. For the 2023 flaws, EX Series and SRX Series web management

what.summary: Junos appears across three government advisories: web management flaws in the EX and SRX series listed among the most routinely exploited vulnerabilities of 2023, an earlier path traversal flaw chained by state actors against government and critical infrastructure targets, and separately a campaign that used stolen credentials with automated scripts to log into Cisco and Juniper routers over secure shell, run commands and exfiltrate each router's running configuration.

how.logic: The campaign authenticated with valid credentials over secure shell, ran commands, captured the output including the running configuration, and sent it off network. Because the credentials were valid, no authentication failure appears anywhere. What does appear is the shape: many devices accessed from one source in a short window, each session short and non-interactive, each running a similar command sequence, followed by an outbound transfer. On Junos this means watching the interactive command log and the login class in use, not just successful logins.

fields.note: configuration retrieval commands; the Junos and Cisco forms differ so cover both
count distinct devices reached per source in a short window; a script does many, a human does one or two

how.caveat: Configuration backup systems do exactly this on a schedule and will dominate the results. Enumerate them once by source address and account, and the remainder is small. Requires devices to forward command accounting centrally, which many do not.

markers.note: raw field device_command

how.logic: Both 2023 flaws are in the web management interface, which should not be reachable from anything except the management network. Restricting it removes those two vulnerabilities and every future one in the same interface, which on this platform has been a recurring source. Alert on any administrative access, web or secure shell, from outside management space.

fields.note: web management, secure shell and the network configuration protocol
compare against management network ranges

how.caveat: Out-of-band and emergency access paths are the legitimate exceptions and must be enumerated first, or the next outage produces a false positive at the worst moment.

how.logic: Configuration commits reconciled against approved changes. Junos keeps a commit history with the committing user and a comment field, which makes this more tractable here than on platforms without it, provided the history is exported somewhere the device cannot reach.
how.caveat: The commit history lives on the device, so a sufficiently privileged intruder can alter it. Export commits off-box for the record to be trustworthy.

how.logic: The 2023 flaws appear on the annual list of most routinely exploited vulnerabilities, and the earlier one was named alongside contemporaneous flaws in four other appliance vendors as part of a chaining campaign. Joining the published known-exploited catalogue to the device inventory catches all of them and is the only approach that scales across a mixed-vendor estate.
how.caveat: Network devices are frequently absent from the vulnerability inventory because scanners are pointed at servers. That absence is the more common problem than the patching itself.

where.publisher: CISA, NSA, FBI and international partners
where.title: Combined from PRC state-sponsored network device exploitation, 2023 Top Routinely Exploited Vulnerabilities, and APT vulnerability chaining advisories

notes: Distilled from three advisories to close a gap identified while consulting the corpus: Junos is a common enterprise and service provider platform and had no record at all. The configuration exfiltration campaign named Cisco and Juniper routers together, which is worth noting because it used valid credentials rather than any vulnerability, so patching would not have prevented it. A third advisory listed the 2020 path traversal flaw alongside contemporaneous flaws in Pulse Secure, Citrix and PAN-OS as vulnerabilities being chained against state, local, tribal and territorial government and critical infrastructure targets.

who.versions_affected: Reported against end-of-life MX series hardware and software; the injection flaw is addressed by the vendor advisory accompanying the report

what.summary: A China-nexus espionage group placed six distinct backdoors on carrier and enterprise routers, having first taken a terminal server used to manage them and reused its valid credentials. The notable part is not the implants but the handling: the platform verifies binaries before executing them, so rather than defeating that check the actor injected code into a process that had already passed it, and rather than leaving logging off, disabled it only for the duration of each hands-on session and put it back afterwards.

how.logic: Logging was not turned off and left off. The configuration was copied aside, rewritten to send entries to the null device, the logging daemon signalled to reload, the session's work carried out, and the original put back. On the collector this is not an error, it is a gap: a device that reports continuously stops for a bounded period and then resumes as if nothing happened. Detect the gap at the collector, because the device's own record of the gap is the thing being suppressed. Session-scoped suppression also means the login and logout that bracket the gap are themselves missing, so the account will look less active than it was.

fields.note: reload of the logging daemon after its configuration was rewritten

markers.expr: device_resumed_reporting after gap without intervening reboot_event

markers.note: the aside copy carries a suffixed name while suppression is active

how.caveat: A reboot produces the same gap and is far more common, so the rule needs the reboot record to subtract it, and the reboot record has to come from somewhere other than the device. Devices that report only on change rather than continuously cannot support this at all, which has to be established per platform before the rule is worth writing.

how.logic: Every implant was named to sit one or two characters away from a real platform daemon, so that a process listing reads as normal to somebody who does not know the exact daemon set by heart. The defence is the inventory, not the eye: the running daemon set on a network device is small, fixed per platform and version, and anything outside it is worth an alert on its own.
how.caveat: Needs a per-platform, per-version daemon inventory, which the vendor does not generally publish in a usable form and which therefore has to be built from known-good devices. Building it from a device that is already compromised bakes the implant into the baseline, so take it from a freshly imaged unit.

how.logic: Most of the implants never called out. They sat listening and woke on a crafted packet, which means every detection built on beaconing regularity, on domain reputation or on outbound volume sees nothing at all. What is left is the listener itself: a device offering a port that its platform baseline does not include, and traffic to that port from somewhere that is not the management network.
how.caveat: The absence of beaconing is the whole difficulty and the reason this is hunt rather than alert. A port scan of your own estate answers it far better than log analysis does, and it is the one detection here that needs an active measure rather than a query.

where.title: Ghost in the Router: China-Nexus Espionage Actor UNC3886 Targets Juniper Routers

who.versions_affected: Multiple releases across the J-Web management interface and the Evolved platform

what.summary: Three pieces of research on the same vendor: code execution reached through the web management interface on firewalls, code execution on the newer platform variant, and an observation about the release process itself. This vendor publishes security fixes on a fixed quarterly schedule, which means the interval between a flaw becoming known and a fix existing is not merely long but predictable in advance, by anyone. That changes what compensating control is needed, because the gap can be planned for rather than discovered.

how.logic: Where a vendor fixes on a fixed calendar rather than on discovery, the exposure window is known ahead of time and is the same for every customer. Measure your own deployment interval, then add the vendor's release cadence to it, because the true window is both. For a quarterly cadence the compensating control has to be restriction of the management surface rather than faster patching, since faster patching cannot help before a fix exists.
how.caveat: A scheduling constraint rather than a query, and the uncomfortable part is that the customer controls only one of the two intervals. Where the vendor cadence dominates, arguing about internal patch speed is arguing about the smaller number, and the honest conclusion is that the management interface should not be reachable rather than that patching should be faster.

how.logic: The recurring reachable component here is the device's web management interface, which is the same conclusion the class-level material reaches independently: on network infrastructure the management surface is the attack surface. Alert on administrative protocol sessions to infrastructure reaching from outside the management ranges, and treat the web interface specifically as the highest value of those because it carries the most code.
how.caveat: Disabling the web interface entirely is available on most of these platforms and removes the largest part of this surface in one change, which makes it worth raising before any detection is written. Out-of-band access paths legitimately originate elsewhere and must be enumerated first.

what.summary: An offensive research team demonstrated that a workload identity holding only a read verb on the node proxy resource can execute arbitrary commands in any pod on any reachable node, including control plane and privileged system pods. The cause is that a WebSocket handshake must begin as an HTTP GET, the node agent maps that GET to the read verb, authorises it, upgrades the connection and passes it to the execution handler without checking again for the create verb the operation actually requires. The grant is shipped by default in a large number of widely used monitoring and observability deployment templates, so the identities that hold it are typically third-party agents running in privileged namespaces on every node. Reaching the node agent directly rather than through the orchestrator API also produces no execution audit entry, only an authorisation check, making the route materially quieter than the equivalent through the API server.

how.logic: The privilege is ordinary and the path is not. Detect the combination: a connection to the node agent port carrying WebSocket upgrade headers and the Kubernetes exec subprotocol, against an execution path, from an identity whose grants contain only read verbs.
how.caveat: Not fixable by patching, by design. The identities that hold the grant are the monitoring stack, so suppressing on identity removes the detection entirely; suppress on nothing and distinguish on the path.

how.logic: Execution through the orchestrator API is recorded by name; the direct route to the node agent leaves only an authorisation check. An authorisation check for the proxy resource with no matching execution entry indicates the audited path was not the one used.
how.caveat: Check first whether node agent traffic is collected at all. Where it is not, the correct output is a coverage gap rather than a rule, because the rule would match nothing and read as an absence of the activity.

how.logic: Intersect the identities holding the read verb on the proxy resource with those having network reach to the node agent port. The intersection is the set that can execute code in any pod on those nodes.
how.caveat: Expect the answer to be non-zero and inherited from a third-party chart rather than chosen locally. Restricting network reach to the agent port is usually more tractable than renegotiating the grant with the monitoring stack's owner.

what.summary: An internet-facing instance of an LLM application framework was entered through a missing-authentication flaw in its code-validation endpoint, which executes submitted Python without authentication. Every payload arrived base64-encoded through that endpoint. Within the first minutes the operator enumerated the host and swept the environment for secrets by category in parallel -- model provider API keys, cloud credentials including Chinese providers, wallet seed phrases and database configuration -- then dumped the framework's own backing Postgres store for the credentials and user records held there, staged the output to local files, read them and deleted the staging files. Persistence was a single cron entry beaconing every thirty minutes. The framework is an attractive entry point precisely because it is AI-adjacent: these servers routinely hold provider keys and cloud credentials in their environment and are stood up quickly without network controls.

how.logic: Python interpreted under the web application's own process owner, with the payload arriving base64-encoded through the validation endpoint. The endpoint path is the anchor: nothing legitimate submits code to it from the internet.
how.caveat: The framework's normal function is to run user-authored flows, so interpreter spawning is not by itself anomalous on this host; the endpoint and the absence of an authenticated session are what carry it. Payload decoding happens inside the exec sink in later campaigns, so a shell-level search for base64 usage will not see it.

how.logic: Persistence was one crontab line invoking the language interpreter to open a URL, on a half-hourly schedule. A scheduled task whose command is an outbound network call is the shape, independent of the address it calls.
how.caveat: The address and port are campaign infrastructure and will not survive; the scheduled-task-makes-a-network-call shape is the durable half. Monitoring agents legitimately beacon on a schedule, so exclude them by identity rather than by the behaviour.

what.summary: A serial-to-IP converter used to put industrial equipment on a network could be commanded as root by anyone who could reach its management interface, because the web configuration layer built a log line from the submitted username after a failed login and then executed that line rather than writing it. The flaw was exploited in a research honeypot after the vendor patched it and before any technical detail was public.

how.logic: The configuration interface's remote procedure call module logs failed authentication attempts, concatenating the submitted username into the log string without sanitisation, then executes that string through the operating system. Commands injected into the username parameter of an authentication request therefore run as root, and no valid credential is needed because the path is on the failure branch.
how.caveat: Devices of this class carry no process telemetry, so nothing on the device will confirm execution and the request is the only evidence available. Where the management interface is not reachable by anything that inspects it, this cannot be detected at all and the answer is patching and segmentation.

markers.expr: authentication failure whose submitted username contains shell metacharacters

how.logic: The vendor patched on 20 February, the identifier reached the national database on 11 March, the researchers published on 21 April, and exploitation was observed on 5 April. The operator therefore did not use the published research; the publisher's assessment is that they reverse-engineered the patch.
how.caveat: The window between patch and detail is invisible from outside: no advisory detail to read, no public proof of concept to weigh, no indicator to match. On this class of device that inverts the usual prioritisation, because the patch is the proof of concept. Start any retrospective hunt at the patch date rather than the disclosure date.

where.publisher: CISA, ACSC, CCCS, NZ NCSC, NCSC-UK, FBI and NSA
where.title: 2021 Top Routinely Exploited Vulnerabilities

notes: The companion chain to the other Exchange entry in this corpus. Two separate four and three flaw chains in one product on consecutive annual lists, both requiring every element patched, is the strongest single argument here against severity-ranked patching.

what.summary: A three-flaw chain in on-premises mail servers combining server-side request forgery, a path traversal security feature bypass and an elevation of privilege, among the most routinely exploited vulnerabilities of 2022 and used by both state and ransomware actors.

where.title: 2022 Top Routinely Exploited Vulnerabilities

notes: The clearest chain in the corpus for the argument against severity-ranked patching: the security feature bypass scores lower than what it enables, and all three are required to close the path.

what.summary: A remote code execution flaw reachable from a document without macros being enabled, among the most routinely exploited vulnerabilities of 2022. It defeats the standard control for document-borne threats, which is macro restriction.

where.publisher: CISA, NSA, FBI and international partners
where.title: 2022 Top Routinely Exploited Vulnerabilities

notes: Worth recording because organisations that had disabled macros reasonably believed document-borne execution was addressed. This is why the office-application-spawns-script-engine detection matters more than the macro setting.

what.summary: A certificate validation flaw allowing an attacker to present a forged signature that the operating system accepts as valid, named in Chinese state-sponsored targeting. It undermines signature verification as a control, including for code the platform trusts.

where.title: Potential for China Cyber Response to Heightened US-China Tensions

notes: Belongs with the supply chain and code signing records: three separate mechanisms in this corpus produce a valid-looking signature over attacker-chosen content, which is the case for not treating signature validity as evidence of provenance.

what.summary: A wormable remote code execution flaw in the Windows DNS server role, named in Chinese state-sponsored targeting. The role usually runs on domain controllers, so the exposure sits on the highest-privilege hosts in the estate.

where.title: Potential for China Cyber Response to Heightened US-China Tensions

notes: The strategic point is placement rather than severity: a flaw in a supporting role that happens to be co-located with the directory service inherits the directory's blast radius.

who.versions_affected: Any domain

what.summary: Red teams compromised a domain controller and then moved freely using forged credentials, delegation abuse and directory replication, and the assessed organisations detected none of it. The advisory lists these explicitly as missed detection opportunities rather than as clever tradecraft.

how.logic: Directory replication requested by anything that is not a domain controller. Replication is how domain controllers synchronise with each other, so the legitimate set of requesting accounts and hosts is small, fixed and knowable. A request from a workstation or a non-controller service account is unambiguous.

fields.note: directory service access; look for the replication extended rights GUIDs
replication extended rights
exclude the domain controllers themselves and the accounts they replicate as

how.caveat: Needs directory service access auditing enabled, which is off by default and is why this is so often missed. Backup and identity synchronisation products legitimately hold replication rights; enumerate them once.

markers.note: raw field event_id

how.logic: Forged tickets and protocol abuse that lets a service impersonate any user leave inconsistencies rather than failures, because the ticket is cryptographically valid. Practical signals: a service ticket request with no preceding authentication ticket request for that account, tickets whose lifetime exceeds domain policy, and impersonation events where the impersonating service has no business acting for that user.

fields.note: authentication ticket, service ticket, ticket renewal
compare against the domain's configured maximum; a longer lifetime cannot be legitimate

how.caveat: A correctly forged ticket is valid by construction, so this detects carelessness rather than the technique. Once a domain controller is compromised the honest position is that authentication logs can no longer be trusted, and the remedy is rebuilding trust rather than better detection.

markers.note: raw field event_id

how.logic: Compromise of a server configured for unconstrained delegation yields the credentials of everything that authenticates to it, so the configuration is the exposure. Enumerate which accounts and computers hold unconstrained delegation and reduce the set; each one is a domain controller compromise waiting for a single server to fall.
how.caveat: Legacy applications sometimes require it, which is why the setting survives. Where it cannot be removed, treat those servers with domain-controller-tier protection rather than as ordinary servers.

how.logic: Directory enumeration was listed as a missed opportunity in its own right. Bulk directory queries from a host that has no administrative role, or query volumes far above that host's own history, indicate reconnaissance. The same applies to network file system enumeration, which was listed alongside it.

fields.note: count queries per source against that host's own baseline; workstations should be near zero

how.caveat: Identity management, inventory and monitoring products query the directory constantly and will dominate any volume ranking. Exclude by asset role first.

where.title: CISA red team assessment findings, combined from three published assessments

notes: The full published list of activities that were opportunities for detection and were missed: phishing, Kerberoasting, golden ticket generation and use, S4U2self abuse, anomalous directory traffic, anomalous network file system enumeration, unconstrained delegation server compromise, directory replication, anomalous account usage during lateral movement, anomalous outbound traffic, anomalous outbound secure shell connections to cloud servers from workstations, and proxy server use from hosts meant to have no internet access. Every one of those has a pattern in this corpus, which is the useful part: the gap was not knowledge but deployment.

what.summary: A state government organisation was told that documents containing host and user information with metadata had been posted for sale on a dark web brokerage site. Investigation found that an unidentified actor had obtained network administrator credentials through the account of a former employee that had not been removed from the directory, authenticated to an internal remote access point with it, moved through the on-premises environment and run directory queries against a domain controller. Responders established that the actor had not moved laterally into the organisation's cloud environment, which held its sensitive systems.

how.logic: The route in was the account of a former employee still present in the directory, and the advisory states directly that actors commonly rely on accounts of former employees that have not been properly removed. Two administrative accounts were involved, one of them the departed user's. The control is a scheduled reconciliation of enabled accounts against the current personnel roster, prioritising privileged groups, plus alerting on authentication by accounts long dormant.

markers.expr: authentication_success by account with last_activity older_than 90d

how.caveat: The failure sits between human resources and identity administration rather than in any technology, which is why it survives in organisations with otherwise mature programmes. It is also fully measurable: either the reconciliation runs on a schedule or it does not.

how.logic: The actor ran directory queries against a domain controller after gaining access. Directory enumeration from an account and host that do not normally perform it is one of the few reliable signals available when the credentials themselves are valid, because the authentication is correct and only the behaviour is wrong.
how.caveat: Administrative tooling and directory-integrated products generate large query volumes legitimately, so this needs a per-source baseline rather than a global threshold.

how.logic: Discovery came from notification that the data was for sale, not from any internal detection. What was listed, host and user information including metadata, is also unusually valuable to a buyer because it is the reconnaissance a second actor would otherwise have to perform. So the listing both revealed the breach and defined its scope.

markers.expr: external_exposure_monitoring covers own_identifiers, host_naming_conventions and supplier_names

how.caveat: Worth stating plainly: the detection that worked belonged to somebody else. Where that is the discovery route, the listing contents are usually the only available basis for scoping.

how.logic: Responders were able to state positively that the actor had not reached the cloud environment, which required sign-in logs, audit logs, unified audit logs, activity logs and endpoint telemetry to be present and exportable. A negative finding of that strength is only possible where the collection already existed, and the agency published a free tool specifically to gather those artefacts.
how.caveat: The most useful part of this record for a defender. Being able to prove where the actor did not go is what bounded the incident and avoided treating the cloud estate as compromised. That capability is a collection decision taken long before the incident.

where.publisher: CISA and Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center
where.title: Threat Actor Leverages Compromised Account of Former Employee to Access State Government Organization

notes: Useful precisely because nothing advanced happened. An account that should not have existed, used to reach a remote access point, followed by directory enumeration, and the data sold on. It is the corpus's clearest example of a purely procedural failure producing a reportable breach, and of the value of collection: the responders could prove the cloud estate was untouched, which bounded the incident rather than expanding it. Pairs with the service desk and account recovery material, since both concern identity lifecycle rather than technology.

who.versions_affected: Any domain controller

what.summary: A state-sponsored group pre-positioning on critical infrastructure networks obtained domain credentials by taking a volume shadow copy of a domain controller and extracting the directory database from it, rather than by touching the live file.

how.logic: The database engine underneath the directory writes application event log entries whenever the directory database is moved, created, mounted or detached, and those entries survive far longer on an endpoint than security events do. Four event IDs together describe the whole extraction: a location change pointing at a shadow copy path, creation of a new copy of the database in a temporary directory, the mounting of that copy, and its detachment on completion. Because dwell time on this kind of intrusion is measured in months, review these retrospectively rather than only watching them live.

fields.note: Windows ESENT Application Log; 216 location change, 325 new database created, 326 database attached, 327 detached, 637 new flush map
the shadow copy path is what separates extraction from ordinary directory maintenance

how.caveat: Backup software legitimately shadow-copies a domain controller and will generate the same event family. Allow-list the backup product's activity by schedule and account. The advisory notes that event detail strings vary between environments, so match on the event ID and the presence of the database name rather than on exact wording.

markers.note: raw field event_id

how.logic: A copy of the directory database appearing anywhere other than its proper location, particularly under a temporary directory, is staging for exfiltration. The file name is fixed by the product, so this is a cheap and precise file-path check that needs no log configuration at all.

fields.note: anywhere that is not the system NTDS directory

how.caveat: Directory restore and migration work produces copies in unusual places legitimately, but those are planned and rare. Reconcile against change records.

where.publisher: CISA, NSA and FBI with international partners
where.title: PRC State-Sponsored Actors Compromise and Maintain Persistent Access to U.S. Critical Infrastructure

corroborations.publisher: NSA, CISA, FBI and international partners

notes: Co-sealed by seven agencies across five countries, which is why attribution confidence is high rather than medium. The retrospective angle matters: the advisory tells defenders to assume significant dwell time and to review these application log IDs specifically because they persist longer on the endpoint than security event logs and other ephemeral artefacts. An earlier seven-agency advisory on the same actor, published nine months before this one, is linked in where.corroborating_url. It named two further initial access vulnerabilities in a network appliance and an identity self-service product, and established the living-off-the-land framing that the later advisory develops.

what.summary: Seven national authorities described a Russian foreign intelligence espionage group adapting to organisations moving to cloud infrastructure, noting that with cloud hosting the actor must first authenticate to the provider, so denying initial access can prevent compromise, whereas on premises far more of the network is exposed. Observed methods include brute force and password spraying against service accounts, which have no human behind them and so cannot easily carry a second factor while often being highly privileged; targeting dormant accounts of departed staff; using system-issued tokens to access accounts without a password; and bypassing a second factor by repeated push requests before registering the actor's own device onto the tenant where device validation rules are absent. Following an enforced password reset for all users during an incident, the actors logged into inactive accounts and completed the reset instructions themselves, regaining access after eviction. Targeting has expanded from government, think tanks, healthcare and energy to aviation, education, law enforcement, local government, government financial departments and military organisations.

how.logic: After an enforced password reset for all users during an incident, the actors logged into inactive accounts and followed the reset instructions, regaining access after eviction activities. A dormant account completing a password reset is anomalous by definition, because nobody is there to complete it. The correct procedure is to disable dormant accounts first and reset the remainder afterwards.
how.caveat: The most valuable single finding in this record, because it attacks the remediation rather than the estate. A mass reset issued to every account including dormant ones hands the actor a supported, logged and entirely legitimate way back in. Treat any dormant account completing a reset as confirmation the actor is still present.

how.logic: Service accounts run applications and services, have no human behind them so cannot easily be protected with a second factor, and are often highly privileged depending on what they manage. That makes them the natural target for brute force and spraying. Because the usual control is unavailable, the compensating ones are restricting where the account may authenticate from, knowing the credential age, scoping privilege to actual need, and alerting on authentication from anywhere the service does not run.
how.caveat: This is the population where standard authentication advice does not apply, which is exactly why it persists. These accounts also tend to be over-privileged because access was granted once at deployment to make something work and never revisited.

how.logic: Password authentication on personal accounts was bypassed by spraying and credential reuse, then the second factor was bypassed by repeatedly pushing requests until one was accepted, after which the actors registered their own device onto the tenant. The advisory states this succeeds where device validation rules are not configured, which makes the absence of those rules the finding rather than the registration event alone.

markers.expr: count(mfa_prompt) by account, bin(_time, 15m) preceding registration

how.caveat: Registration is the moment a stolen session becomes durable, policy-compliant access, so it matters more than the initial bypass. Note also that the personal accounts targeted here are outside the organisation's control, which is where the credential reuse becomes exploitable.

how.logic: The actors used system-issued tokens to access accounts without needing a password at all. The advisory notes default token validity varies by platform and that administrators can usually shorten it, which makes token lifetime a configuration control rather than only a detection problem. Detection is access with a token but no corresponding sign-in.
how.caveat: The fourth mechanism in this corpus for holding valid credentials without ever authenticating, alongside forged federated tokens, a stolen session cookie and forged Kerberos tickets. Shortening token validity is the one mitigation that applies to all of them.

how.logic: Campaigns targeted dormant accounts belonging to users who no longer work at the organisation but whose accounts remain on the system. That is the same gap recorded elsewhere in this corpus at a state government organisation, here being used deliberately and repeatedly by an intelligence service rather than opportunistically.

markers.expr: authentication_success by account with last_activity older_than 90d

how.caveat: Combined with the reset finding above, dormant accounts are both the way in and the way back in. That makes their removal a higher priority than its usual place as routine hygiene.

where.publisher: NCSC-UK, NSA, CISA, CNMF, FBI, ACSC, Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and GCSB
where.title: SVR Cyber Actors Adapt Tactics for Initial Cloud Access

notes: Contains the corpus's most instructive failure of remediation: after a mass password reset during an incident, the actors simply completed the reset on dormant accounts and were back in. Disable dormant accounts before resetting the rest, or the eviction becomes the re-entry. The advisory's framing is also worth keeping, that in cloud environments the actor must authenticate to the provider first, so initial access is a narrower and more defensible chokepoint than on premises, where far more is exposed. Service accounts are the structural weak point in that chokepoint because a second factor is not available to them.

what.summary: A companion advisory to the supply chain compromise, describing activity attributed to a Russian foreign intelligence service irrespective of how initial access was obtained. Three components are named: compromising or bypassing federated identity solutions, using forged authentication tokens to move laterally into cloud environments, and using privileged cloud access to establish persistence for interface-based access that is difficult to detect. The actor used compromised applications in the victim's cloud tenant and additional credentials and interface access to cloud resources. The agency published a tool to help defenders analyse their own tenant for this activity.

how.logic: Two of the three named components are forged tokens and compromised or bypassed federation. The advisory's framing matters as much as the technique: this activity is described irrespective of the initial access vector, which means the cloud identity abuse is the durable half and the compromised update was only one way in. Detection is the token anomalies rather than any authentication failure.
how.caveat: The most important structural point in this record: separating the cloud identity tradecraft from the initial access vector means an organisation that never ran the compromised product could still be affected, and several were.

how.logic: The third component is privileged cloud access used to establish persistence for interface-based access described as difficult to detect, alongside use of compromised applications already present in the tenant. Credential addition to an existing application identity is the observable moment; subsequent interface use is designed to resemble ordinary application activity.
how.caveat: The advisory's own description of this persistence as difficult to detect should be read literally. It is why the agency published tooling rather than a signature: the answer is exporting and reviewing tenant artefacts, not matching an indicator.

how.logic: The agency developed and published a tool to export and review sign-in and audit logs, unified audit logs, cloud activity logs and endpoint telemetry, narrowing a large set of available data to what matters for identity and authentication attacks. That the tool was necessary indicates the artefacts exist but are not routinely collected or reviewed.
how.caveat: Worth noting that the same tool appears in the former-employee record here, where it allowed responders to prove the cloud estate was untouched. The capability bounds incidents in both directions.

where.title: Detecting Post-Compromise Threat Activity in Microsoft Cloud Environments

notes: Recorded separately from the supply chain compromise because its central point is that the cloud identity tradecraft is independent of the initial access vector. An organisation that never installed the compromised update could still be affected, and the three named components, bypassing federation, forging tokens and establishing interface-based persistence, form a complete chain on their own. The agency publishing a tool rather than a signature is the practical measure of how detectable this is: the answer is exporting and reviewing tenant artefacts, not matching indicators.

what.summary: A federal agency identified suspicious activity in its hosted mail environment by observing mail item access events carrying a client and application identifier that did not normally access mailbox items in that environment. It reported the activity, and the provider determined that advanced actors had accessed and exfiltrated unclassified mail data from a small number of accounts, having used an acquired consumer account signing key to forge tokens impersonating both consumer and enterprise users. The provider remediated by blocking tokens issued with the acquired key and replacing the key, and determined the activity was part of a campaign against multiple organisations. The agency detected it by using enhanced logging of mail access events together with an established baseline of normal activity.

how.logic: The agency deemed the activity suspicious because the observed application identifier did not normally access mailbox items in its environment. That works against forged tokens precisely because the token is cryptographically valid while the application presenting it is not one the tenant uses. Baseline the application identifiers that legitimately access mailboxes, which is a small and stable set, and alert on anything outside it.
how.caveat: The most encouraging result in the corpus: a customer detected a nation-state token forgery before the provider did, using logging and a baseline rather than any indicator or threat feed. It depends entirely on the mail access event being generated and retained, which is not the default on every licensing tier.

how.logic: The actors used an acquired signing key to forge tokens impersonating both consumer and enterprise users, so authentication was cryptographically correct and no sign-in anomaly existed. Remediation was possible only by the provider, first blocking tokens issued with that key and then replacing it, which is the same shape as the on-premises token forgery record here but with the key held by a third party.
how.caveat: The customer could not remediate this and could only detect and report it, because the signing key belonged to the provider. That is a materially different position from the on-premises case, where rotating the certificate is at least available to the victim.

how.logic: The detection existed because the agency had enabled enhanced logging of the mail access event and had established a baseline of normal activity beforehand. Both are prerequisites rather than responses: the event has to be generated and retained, and somebody has to have recorded what normal looks like while nothing was wrong.
how.caveat: The entire advisory exists to recommend this logging to other organisations, which indicates it was not widely enabled. A baseline established during normal operation is the part that cannot be created retrospectively.

where.title: Enhanced Monitoring to Detect APT Activity Targeting Outlook Online

notes: The most encouraging record in the corpus and the best argument for baselining. A customer detected a nation-state token forgery before the provider did, with no indicator and no threat feed, simply by having enabled mail access logging and knowing which application identifiers normally read mail in its tenant. It is also a sharp illustration of the limits of shared responsibility: the forged tokens were signed with the provider's own key, so the customer could detect and report but could not remediate, and the fix required the provider to block and then replace the key.

what.summary: An agency observed actors chaining multiple legacy remote access and network vulnerabilities with a recent critical privilege escalation flaw in the directory authentication protocol, exploiting several flaws in a single intrusion to compromise a network. Activity was often directed at federal and state, local, tribal and territorial government networks. After initial access, exploitation of the escalation flaw compromised all directory identity services, after which the actors used legitimate remote access tooling. The agency records some instances of unauthorised access to elections support systems while stating it had no evidence that the integrity of elections data was compromised, and notes the analysis was ongoing and not comprehensive.

how.logic: The named tactic is vulnerability chaining: exploiting multiple flaws in one intrusion. Here that means legacy perimeter and remote access flaws for entry combined with a current critical escalation flaw that compromises every directory identity service at once. Exposure has to be assessed by path rather than by individual severity, because the perimeter element alone rarely scores high enough to be scheduled.
how.caveat: Severity-ranked patching addresses each element on its own merits and can leave the chain open indefinitely. Because the escalation flaw compromises all directory identity services, the outcome of any successful chain is the whole domain regardless of which perimeter product started it.

how.logic: Exploitation of the escalation flaw compromises the directory authentication protocol and therefore all identity services, so the detectable artefacts are on the directory: anomalous authentication using the domain controller's own account, and privileged authentication from hosts that should never originate it.
how.caveat: Once this flaw succeeds, every subsequent action uses valid credentials and correct authentication, so the escalation moment is effectively the last opportunity to detect anything anomalous rather than merely unauthorised.

how.logic: After compromising identity services the actors used legitimate remote access tooling, which is signed, reputable and often already present. The tractable form remains an allow-list of the remote access products the organisation actually licensed, with everything else alerting regardless of reputation.
how.caveat: The same conclusion as several other records here, and the reason maintaining that inventory is a detection control rather than an administrative task.

how.logic: Eight identifiers across six vendors covering remote access appliances, load balancers, device management and a firewall operating system, all published with fixes available. The mix is the point: no single-vendor programme answers it, and the agency notes its own analysis was ongoing and should not be considered comprehensive.
how.caveat: Worth noting the caution the agency attaches: the analysis was ongoing and the list not comprehensive, so treating a published set as the full extent of a campaign is unsafe.

where.title: APT Actors Chaining Vulnerabilities Against SLTT, Critical Infrastructure, and Elections Organizations

notes: The corpus's clearest argument against severity-ranked patching. A legacy perimeter flaw that never scores high enough to be scheduled, combined with a current critical escalation flaw, produces complete compromise of every directory identity service in one intrusion. Exposure therefore has to be assessed by reachable path rather than by individual score. The agency's own caution is worth carrying too: the analysis was ongoing and explicitly not comprehensive, so a published identifier list is a floor rather than a boundary.

who.versions_affected: Domain controllers vulnerable to CVE-2020-1472

what.summary: A ransomware group used a domain controller authentication protocol flaw to escalate directly to domain administrator, alongside exploitation of mail server and print subsystem vulnerabilities, as its route from initial access to full control.

how.logic: The flaw works by resetting a domain controller's own machine account password through a flood of authentication attempts using an all-zero challenge. That leaves two observables: a burst of authentication attempts against the controller from one source in seconds, and a machine account password change for a domain controller, which is a rare and consequential event that should never happen unexpectedly.

fields.note: computer account change, and netlogon authentication failure
restrict to domain controller machine accounts, where any password change warrants investigation

how.caveat: Patched long ago and enforcement mode is now default, so this is chiefly relevant to unpatched or legacy domain controllers. It stays in the corpus because those exist, and because a domain controller machine account password change is worth alerting on regardless of the mechanism.

markers.note: raw field event_id

how.logic: Once domain administrator is obtained the subsequent activity is authentication that is valid in every technical respect. The tiering check is what surfaces it: a privileged account authenticating to hosts outside the administrative tier.
how.caveat: Only meaningful where tiering is implemented. In a flat domain this fires constantly and is a finding about the design.

what.summary: An agency observed organisations migrating to cloud collaboration services at speed to support a fully remote workforce, and not fully considering the security configuration of those platforms, with hasty deployment leading to oversights that undermine the platform's own security model. Across multiple engagements since 2018 it continued to see organisations not implementing recommended practices, leaving them more exposed. The recommendations lead with enabling a second authentication factor for administrator accounts, noting that tenant global administrators hold the highest level of administrative privilege and are equivalent to a domain administrator in an on-premises directory.

how.logic: The named cause is speed of deployment rather than any weakness in the platform: organisations migrating quickly did not fully consider the security configuration, and the agency continued to see the same gaps across engagements over two years. The review therefore has to be scheduled after deployment rather than triggered by an incident, because nothing fails in the meantime.
how.caveat: The debt is invisible because the platform works exactly as intended while its protections sit unconfigured. That makes it discoverable only by deliberate review or by an incident, and the agency's observation that the same gaps persisted across years of engagements suggests reviews rarely happen.

how.logic: Tenant global administrators hold the highest administrative privilege available and are equivalent to a domain administrator on premises, which makes them the smallest and most consequential population to protect. A second factor on those accounts is the first recommendation, and the count of accounts holding that role is worth knowing and keeping small.
how.caveat: Several records in this corpus reach the tenant through exactly this population, by forging tokens, adding credentials to application identities or registering a device. Protecting it is the precondition for all of them.

how.logic: The recommendations are framed as configuring the environment to protect, detect and respond, which places logging alongside authentication rather than after it. Cloud audit sources are frequently disabled or short-retained by default, and several records here depend on them existing before the incident.
how.caveat: The mail access logging that allowed a customer to detect a nation-state token forgery, recorded elsewhere in this corpus, is exactly this kind of setting: available, not enabled by default, and decisive when it matters.

notes: Names a cause that recurs throughout this corpus without usually being stated: the security configuration was never completed because the deployment was urgent, and nothing subsequently failed to reveal it. The agency observed the same gaps across engagements spanning two years, which suggests the review is rarely scheduled. The specific population it leads with, tenant global administrators equivalent to on-premises domain administrators, is the one several cloud records here reach through, whether by forged tokens, added application credentials or device registration.

who.versions_affected: Builds vulnerable to CVE-2023-23397

what.summary: A Russian military intelligence unit targeting Western logistics and technology companies used a mail client flaw that leaks authentication material when a crafted message is processed, requiring no action by the recipient at all.

how.logic: The flaw causes the client to authenticate to a remote path specified in the message, so the observable is outbound file sharing authentication leaving the network. That should never happen, which makes blocking it at the perimeter both the detection and the fix. Because the exploit needs no user interaction, awareness training is irrelevant here and the network control is the only thing that helps.

fields.note: any external destination

how.caveat: Blocking outbound file sharing at the perimeter removes this entirely and breaks almost nothing. Where it is not blocked, every hit warrants investigation.

how.logic: The crafted content sits in a message property rather than in the body or an attachment, so gateway scanning of bodies and attachments does not see it. Detection requires examining the item properties themselves, and the vendor published a script for finding affected items retrospectively across a mailbox estate. Retrospective sweeping matters more than live detection here because the messages may have arrived long before the flaw was known.

fields.note: reminder and sound-file properties referencing a remote path

how.caveat: Needs a mailbox-level sweep rather than gateway inspection, which is a different operation and one most organisations do not have tooling for outside the vendor's own script.

what.summary: A ransomware group escalated to domain administrator through the print subsystem and through a pair of directory account flaws that together let a low-privileged account impersonate a domain controller.

how.logic: The directory pair works by creating or renaming a computer account so its name collides with a domain controller's, then requesting tickets as that controller. So the observables are computer account creation by a non-administrative account, and any computer account whose name matches or closely resembles a domain controller. Ordinary users can create computer accounts by default in most domains, which is the underlying exposure and is worth reducing to zero.

fields.note: computer account created and changed
flag names matching or resembling domain controller names, and any creation by a non-administrative account

how.caveat: The default machine account quota permitting ordinary users to create computer accounts is the root cause. Setting it to zero removes the technique and is a single directory attribute change, so detection here is the fallback rather than the fix.

markers.note: raw field event_id

how.logic: The print subsystem flaw allows loading a driver from a remote location with system privilege. The observables are the spooler service process writing or loading a library outside its own directories, and the spooler spawning a child process, which it has no ordinary reason to do.

fields.note: libraries written or loaded outside the spooler's own driver directories

how.caveat: Legitimate printer driver installation touches these paths. The stronger control is disabling the print service where it is not needed, which on servers is usually everywhere.

notes: The advisory was updated six months after publication with new techniques and refreshed indicators, and explicitly removed outdated ones. That practice is worth noting for anyone consuming these: an indicator list from the original publication would now contain entries the authors themselves consider stale.

who.versions_affected: All Windows builds

what.summary: Remote desktop session activity was one of the few places the group's movement left a durable record, because it operated with valid credentials and built-in tooling that produced almost nothing else to find.

how.logic: The session manager operational log records logon, shell start, logoff and disconnect as separate events, each carrying the source network address. Reviewing the whole sequence rather than just successful logons matters: the shell start event confirms an interactive session actually began, and the source address is what makes an unexpected session identifiable when the account itself is legitimate.

fields.note: Windows Terminal Services Local Session Manager Operational Log; 21 logon, 22 shell start, 23 logoff, 24 disconnected, 25 reconnected
compare against the addresses that account has used before

how.caveat: This log is not collected by default in many estates, which is the practical obstacle rather than the analysis. Where remote desktop is used routinely for administration the volume is high, so the value comes from joining the source address to the account's own history.

who.versions_affected: Builds vulnerable to CVE-2023-28252

what.summary: A ransomware operation escalated privilege through a log file system flaw, then established persistence by creating new domain accounts, and harvested service account credentials by requesting and cracking Kerberos service tickets.

how.logic: New domain accounts were created to abuse domain controller functions, in at least one case an administrative account under a name chosen to resemble IT staff naming. Domain account creation is infrequent and already governed by a process in most organisations, so every creation can be reconciled against a joiner record. Names resembling administrative or IT function are worth weighting up, since the choice is deliberate camouflage.

fields.note: names chosen to blend with administrative naming; itadm was the observed example

how.caveat: Automated provisioning creates accounts legitimately and at volume in larger estates. Reconcile against the joiner feed rather than against a name pattern alone; the name is a weighting, not the test.

markers.note: raw field new_account_name

how.logic: Requesting service tickets for many service accounts in a short window, particularly with weaker encryption negotiated, indicates harvesting for offline cracking. The volume and the encryption type together are the signal, since a single request is ordinary.

fields.note: Kerberos service ticket request
weaker types requested deliberately to make offline cracking feasible

how.caveat: This event is extremely high volume in any domain, so it needs aggregation per requesting account rather than per event. Service accounts with long random passwords make the cracking step fail even when the harvesting succeeds, which is the real mitigation.

who.versions_affected: Interoperable implants observed for Windows, macOS and Linux; the host artefacts described are the Windows variant

what.summary: A Russian intelligence service espionage implant in development and continuous redevelopment since 2003, assessed as the most sophisticated tool in that service's arsenal. It hides its components with a kernel module, keeps its configuration in an encrypted store on disk with per-implant keys, persists as a service named to resemble a genuine Windows service, and carries command traffic inside arbitrary HTTP headers. Infrastructure was identified in over fifty countries, with many infected hosts serving only as relay nodes for operations against other targets.

how.logic: The implant's user mode component decrypts a blob in the registry holding the key, initialisation vector and path needed to find its kernel driver. The advisory gives a location-independent method: search the whole registry for a value of at least 0x1000 bytes with entropy of at least 7.9. That keys on properties the data cannot shed, so it survives the operator moving the value, which the advisory says is easy.
how.caveat: Enumerate legitimate large registry values once, chiefly certificate and licensing blobs, and allow-list them. Without that the sweep returns a manageable but non-zero set on every host.

how.logic: Two encrypted files sit in predictable system locations: the driver and its loader in a single file in the component services directory, and the configuration store in the registration directory under a double-GUID name with hidden, system and archive attributes. The advisory supplies an entropy rule at or above 7.0 plus both a find and a PowerShell invocation, and notes the separate covert store has a size that is an even multiple of 220.
how.caveat: The advisory is explicit that names and paths shift easily between deployments. The entropy and the attributes are the durable part; the paths are where to look first. Content signatures are useless because the files are fully encrypted.

markers.note: raw field file_path

how.logic: Persistence is a registered service whose name differs from a real Windows service by three characters, executing a binary that reuses a genuine Windows executable name and hides among the many legitimate copies of that name in the side-by-side component store. Both lies are aimed at review by eye, so the check has to be a set comparison against a known-good service list and known-good binary paths.
how.caveat: Choosing a filename that legitimately exists many times over in a system directory is the more interesting half, because it defeats a path allow-list as well as a name review.

markers.note: raw field service_name

how.logic: Client-to-server traffic is carried in an arbitrary HTTP header field with a fixed structural shape, and the advisory publishes both regular expressions and the corresponding intrusion detection rules for two protocol variants. It names this the highest-confidence network-wide detection available for the implant while also warning it can be changed easily by the operator.
how.caveat: The advisory itself flags false positive potential. Deploy it anyway, because the alternative is no network visibility of this implant, but treat hits as leads rather than findings. Requires header inspection, not just flow records.

markers.note: raw field http_header_value

how.logic: The service built a covert peer-to-peer network in which many infected hosts exist only to route disguised traffic to and from implants on the actual targets. The advisory records infrastructure in over fifty countries including Russia itself, spanning all industries, while stating that targeting is purposeful and tactical. The signal is a host that both receives and originates sessions of the same shape with no local user activity to explain either.
how.caveat: This changes what a finding means, not just how to find it. An organisation of no intelligence value can still be carrying traffic for an operation against a government elsewhere, which the advisory illustrates with diplomatic documents taken from a victim in an alliance member state. Scoping the incident to your own data loss would miss the role the host was actually playing.

how.logic: The kernel module removes the implant's components from any listing the operating system returns and mediates all access to the encrypted store, which is keyed uniquely per implant. So a clean result from anything running under that kernel carries no information, and the advisory notes the unique keying also defeats signatures used by tools that are independent of the operating system. The detection is divergence between the live view and an offline or memory-derived one.
how.caveat: The advisory warns that some of its own recommended techniques can affect system availability or stability, so hunting for this needs to be planned against operational policy rather than run casually across an estate.

where.publisher: CISA, FBI, NSA and international partners
where.title: Hunting Russian Intelligence Snake Malware

target_regions: over 50 countries across North America, South America, Europe, Africa, Asia and Australia

notes: The longest-running single toolset in this corpus, in development since 2003 and repeatedly rebuilt rather than abandoned after public reporting, with the advisory noting the service changed techniques specifically in response to vendor disclosure. Two points make it worth its length here. First, the relay-node architecture means infection does not imply being targeted, which inverts the usual scoping assumption. Second, it is the clearest case in the corpus of an implant that defeats host-based detection categorically rather than incrementally, and the honest conclusion the advisory itself reaches is that no single method finds it: the detections are complementary and each has stated disadvantages.
