who.versions_affected: Current; this is documented behaviour rather than a defect

what.summary: Researchers documented two supported features of scoped administrative containers being turned against the tenant: restricted-management containers, which prevent tenant-level administrators from modifying members, can lock an attacker-held account against remediation, and hidden-membership containers can conceal the scope of an attacker's role assignment from anyone reviewing permissions.

how.logic: Alert on creation of an administrative unit, on one being switched to restricted management or hidden membership, and on a role assignment scoped to one. All three are rare and deliberate in most tenants. Separately, enumerate scoped role assignments through the directory API rather than the portal, because the portal honours the concealment the feature provides.
how.caveat: The publisher is explicit that this is not a vulnerability or a misconfiguration but the feature working as designed, and it fires on legitimate hardening -- protecting break-glass and executive accounts is the intended use. It is worth alerting anyway because the event rate is low and because the failure it prevents is an eviction that appears to succeed and does not.

markers.expr: administrative unit visibility is HiddenMembership or isMemberManagementRestricted is true

how.logic: Directory roles scoped to an administrative unit are a different plane from tenant-level directory roles and from resource-manager assignments. A permission review that reads one plane, or that reads the portal rather than the API, returns an answer that is true and incomplete.
how.caveat: A Global Administrator can reverse every one of these conditions, so the remediation is straightforward once the assignment is found. Finding it is the whole difficulty.

where.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Abusing Entra ID Administrative Units for Sticky Persistence

notes: Researcher-documented technique rather than observed intrusion, presented at a cloud security conference and implemented in the publisher's open-source attack emulation tool. The publisher updated the permissions detail in February 2025 after further research.

who.versions_affected: Any tenant holding non-human identities with long-lived secrets and directory-role-granting API permissions

what.summary: A leaked service principal secret, exposed for about a fortnight and replayed from rotating anonymisation infrastructure by several independent parties, was used by one of them to grant itself the directory's highest role about two and a half minutes after first sign-in, then to take root-level access over every resource, plant persistence across dozens of identities and take control of the telemetry pipeline meant to be watching.

how.logic: A permanent directory role assignment made outside the privileged identity management workflow, especially where the target is the tenant's highest role and the actor is a non-human identity. The interval here was under three minutes from first sign-in to directory ownership, so a detection that batches or runs on a schedule will report the outcome rather than prevent it.
how.caveat: The service principal was able to do this because it already held an API permission that allows exactly this, so nothing in the sequence was an exploit and every operation returned success. Reviewing which non-human identities hold role-granting API permissions is the preventive control; the alert only tells you it has happened.

value: Add member to role outside of PIM (permanent)

markers.expr: role_assignment target is a tenant-wide administrative role at directory scope
actor is a service principal rather than a user
assignment made permanent rather than through the privileged identity management workflow

how.logic: A non-human identity signing in from commercial virtual private network ranges, anonymity network exit nodes and small hosting providers across several countries, where its workload has a fixed and knowable origin. The variety of origins was itself the finding: it indicated the credential sitting in a shared pool being picked up by multiple opportunistic consumers rather than one tracked operator.
how.caveat: Most of the sessions did nothing but reconnaissance -- enumerate resources, query the directory, list storage and the secret store -- so an alert tuned to escalation would have missed the fortnight of warning that preceded it. A service principal signing in from anywhere other than its workload's own egress is the whole signal, and it needs no notion of what the session then did.

markers.expr: service principal sign-in from a source outside its workload's registered egress addresses
count(distinct source countries for one non-human identity) > 1 within 7d
source address belongs to a commercial VPN, anonymity network exit or hosting range

how.logic: Authority in this platform is held in at least five systems that share neither identifiers, data models nor logs. The operator moved between them, and the publisher's difficulty was not stopping the intrusion but answering afterwards what could still reach the tenant. Enumerate every plane and reconcile principals by identifier rather than display name.
how.caveat: The publisher's own summary is that stopping the attack was easy and analysing it was not. An eviction that clears the directory plane and reports success can leave root-level resource access and control of the telemetry pipeline untouched.

where.title: No single pane of glass: Anatomy of an Azure permission takeover

notes: The publisher reports from their own 2026 usage measurement that just over 38 per cent of service principals in this platform are risky, carrying a long-lived secret or certificate, holding excessive permission, or having no alerting on anomalous sign-in.

who.versions_affected: Hybrid deployments using password hash synchronisation, and any deployment with seamless single sign-on enabled

what.summary: An authorised internal test moved from name-resolution poisoning and relayed credentials to a reused local administrator password, to two separate domain administrator credentials, and from there to the directory synchronisation server, whose privileged access to both directories carried an on-premises domain compromise into the cloud tenant and every service that trusts it.

how.logic: The synchronisation server holds highly privileged access to both directories because that is what synchronisation requires, so it is the single host that converts a domain compromise into a tenant compromise. Treat it as tier-zero: alert on interactive logon by anyone outside its administration set, on credential-access tooling running on it, and in the tenant on its service principal performing any operation other than synchronisation.
how.caveat: The synchronisation account authenticates constantly and in volume by design, so any rule on its activity alone is unusable. The source host and the operation type are the discriminators, and both are narrow and stable. Where seamless single sign-on is enabled there is a further standing exposure: a shared computer account exists in the on-premises directory whose key can be used to mint tickets for cloud authentication, and its password is frequently never rotated.

markers.expr: interactive logon to the synchronisation host by an account outside its administration set
synchronisation service principal performs an operation other than directory synchronisation in the tenant
seamless single sign-on computer account password age exceeds policy

how.logic: The path to the synchronisation host ran through ordinary on-premises weaknesses: a relayed network credential against a server not requiring signing, a local administrator password reused across hosts, and memory dumps yielding two domain administrator credentials, one of them a machine account holding domain administrator rights.
how.caveat: Nothing in this half is cloud-specific and all of it is long-standing on-premises hygiene. It is recorded with the cloud outcome attached because the consequence has changed: the same reused local administrator password now reaches a cloud tenant and every third-party service federated to it, not merely a file server.

markers.expr: process reads memory of the local security authority subsystem
same local administrator credential authenticates successfully across multiple unrelated hosts
machine account holds membership of a domain administrative group

where.title: On-Prem Misconfigurations Lead to Entra Tenant Compromise

notes: Assumed-breach internal penetration test with no prior knowledge of the client's cloud tenant or hybrid configuration. The finding worth carrying is directional: hybrid identity means an on-premises directory compromise is a cloud tenant compromise, so on-premises tiering decisions now bound cloud blast radius.

who.versions_affected: Current; both products used as designed, with external chat permitted by default tenant policy

what.summary: An access broker working for ransomware operators has, since January 2026, mailbombed targets and then called them over the vendor's collaboration platform posing as internal support, persuading each victim to open a remote assistance session. From that session the operators ran scripted host reconnaissance and installed a Go backdoor whose command channel runs over a service-to-service remote procedure call framework, alongside reverse proxy tooling.

how.logic: A burst of unsolicited mail to one mailbox followed within the hour by an external chat or call to the same person is the opening move, and both halves are visible. The mailbombing exists to manufacture the problem the caller then offers to solve, so the pairing is the signal rather than either event.
how.caveat: External chat is permitted by default on this platform, so the control that closes the technique is a tenant policy decision rather than a detection: restrict who outside the organisation may initiate a chat, and separately establish that support never calls first. The mailbombing half is inferred by the publisher from similar campaigns rather than directly observed in every case.

markers.expr: inbound message volume to a single mailbox exceeds its own baseline by an order of magnitude within one hour
external federated chat or call initiated to that user within the same window
external chat initiation is restricted by tenant policy

how.logic: The remote access step uses the assistance utility that ships with the operating system, so nothing is dropped, nothing is unsigned and no software allow list is violated. Alert on it running at all where the service desk does not use it; where it does, alert on the sequence of an assistance session followed within minutes by scripted host and domain discovery.
how.caveat: Detection built on unapproved remote-access software does not see this, because the software is approved and already present. That is the point of choosing it.

markers.expr: scripting engine performing host or domain discovery within 15 minutes of the assistance session
built-in remote assistance is a sanctioned support channel on this estate

how.logic: The backdoor speaks to its controller over a remote procedure call framework normally used between services inside a datacentre, and the accompanying reverse proxy tooling uses the same framework or WebSockets. A long-lived stream of that shape leaving a user workstation for an external host is out of place in a way the protocol never looks.
how.caveat: The later variants obfuscate the framework's own protocol definition, so method names are not available to anchor on and only the transport shape and its placement remain. Four variants were observed in six months with differing capabilities, so anything anchored on a specific sample ages quickly.

markers.expr: long-lived HTTP/2 or WebSocket stream from a user-population endpoint to an external host
initiating process is a browser or an approved RPC client

where.title: Helpdesk Hijackers: Teams Vishing, Quick Assist, and GoGRPC Backdoor

notes: The publisher assesses the actor as an initial access broker for ransomware operations and names four backdoor variants observed between January and June 2026, plus a separate backdoor, two reverse proxy tools and two further utilities. Only the tradecraft that generalises is recorded here; the sample-specific detail ages within months and is in the source.

what.summary: 1 identifier affecting Microsoft Internet Key Exchange (IKE) Service Extensions is in the authoritative catalogue of vulnerabilities known to have been exploited, added to it in 2026. The catalogue describes it as: Microsoft Internet Key Exchange (IKE) Service Extensions contains a double free vulnerability that could enable remote code execution.

notes: Generated from the catalogue rather than written from an incident report, so it asserts only that these identifiers were exploited and carries no detection logic. Product class is derived from the vendor and product names and is not a catalogue field. Required actions, due dates and the forensicTriage flag CISA added in September 2026 are operational instructions to the agencies the catalogue binds, so they are held in the source rather than copied here. Common weakness types recorded: CWE-415.

who.versions_affected: The source names no vulnerability and no affected version. It also names one macOS sample of the same family, MD5 de10c6b3dc4619f59bc9c80a0aa15e6a.

what.summary: JSCeal, a stealer delivered as compiled V8 bytecode and executed by a bundled Node.js runtime, targets cryptocurrency applications and installs a locally generated, attacker-controlled root certificate on the victim machine so that it can read and rewrite HTTPS there. It generates an RSA key pair with a 2048-bit modulus and a certificate, drops the certificate as a temporary file, spawns certutil with the arguments -addstore, -f, root and that file path, and then removes the file. It creates a local proxy server with its own certificate and builds the proxy target from the literal 127.0.0.1 and a port value the source does not give, and it rewrites requests and responses for named services: the QR login value returned by Binance is replaced with a configured one, verification components in a Bybit response are forwarded through the malware's own network client and removed from the response, a passed Bybit risk result is converted into a new challenge with a randomly generated risk token, and the analytics script served from resources.live.ledger.app is substituted with a generated script that hides the existing React root and displays configured HTML in its place. Collected material leaves over an RPC endpoint built as https://api.<domain>/rpc, posted as application/octet-stream, with a WebSocket transport to the same path.

how.logic: The payload generates an RSA key pair with a 2048-bit modulus and a certificate on the host, writes the certificate to a temporary file, and spawns the platform certificate utility with the argument array -addstore, -f, root and that file path, then removes the file. The collectable event is the store-add itself. Nothing here tests the parent: the source shows the spawn call and its arguments and never names the process that issues it, and the same bundle ships winpty-agent.exe, an agent for a hidden Windows console, so a parent condition written from this source alone would be a guess. File telemetry sees only a short-lived artefact, because the certificate is written immediately before the store-add and deleted immediately after, and the source does not give the path.

fields.note: the source spawns the utility by this name
the argument array is built in this order: -addstore, -f, root, then the temporary certificate path

how.caveat: Inspection proxies, endpoint management and some development tooling install root authorities legitimately, so an approved list of authorities has to exist before this is a rule rather than a queue. Anything able to call the platform certificate API can add a store entry without this command line at all, so the inventory block below is the more durable half. The certificate file is removed within the same sequence, so a hunt run later has only the store contents and the process record to work with.

how.logic: The store entry outlives the process record and the deleted certificate file, so it is the half of this mechanism that a hunt run days later can still answer. Enumerate the root store on every host and compare the authorities in it against the ones the estate actually issued or approved; what this malware leaves behind is an authority generated on the machine that now trusts it. The source does not state whether the store-add runs elevated, so enumerate at machine and at user scope rather than assuming one.
how.caveat: Worthless without an approved-authority list, and building that list is the real work: inspection proxies, endpoint management and developer tooling all put authorities in the store legitimately. Until the list exists this is a queue to be triaged, not a rule.

markers.expr: root_store holds a certificate authority absent from the estate's approved trust list

how.logic: With its own authority in the root store, the payload creates a local proxy server with its own certificate; the strings recovered for that component include createServer, listen, address and the literal 127.0.0.1, and the proxy target is built as the literal string 127.0.0.1 followed by a colon and a value taken from the payload's own scope, which the source never resolves to a number. Two things the source does not give, and neither is assumed here: the port, and how traffic is steered into the listener. The rewriting is invisible to the network in any case, because it happens between the browser and a process on the same machine, which is why the store entry and the loopback listener are what is worth collecting.

fields.note: bind side of a listen event, matching the pattern's own sketch, which keys the listening host off xdm.source.host.hostname and xdm.source.port
the source does not give the port, so it has to be baselined per host role rather than matched

how.caveat: Development tooling, VPN clients and inspection products bind loopback listeners for good reasons, and with no port from the source the listener alone cannot carry an alert. It is worth running against a baseline of listening ports per host role, and it is much stronger joined to the trust-store finding on the same host. No flow record will help: loopback traffic never leaves the machine.

markers.note: the address the proxy target is built from; the port is not stated in the source

markers.expr: listening port on this host is present in the baseline of listening ports for its role

how.logic: The interception proxy carries a Ledger-specific handler registered against the host resources.live.ledger.app and the path /public_resources/analytics.min.js, which substitutes a generated script that hides the existing React root and displays configured HTML in its place. An egress proxy sees the request for that script but never the substitution, which happens locally, so this is a destination worth pivoting on for a host already flagged by the store-add or the listener and is not evidence by itself.
how.caveat: An ordinary destination for anybody who uses the service. On its own it says only that somebody visited Ledger. It earns its place as a pivot after an endpoint finding, never before one.

markers.note: bound to the web destination field rather than the DNS question name, so it can be true on the same proxy record as the path marker
the script whose response the handler replaces

how.logic: A router in the same proxy registers a response handler for the host iapi.kraken.com on the path /api/internal/account/balance/history. The handler takes the last entry of each series in historical_balances_per_asset_category and calls saveBalance with source EXCHANGE and name KRAKEN, so the balance is recorded by the malware; the source does not say the response itself is forwarded onward. Kraken is one of 25 platform identifiers the paper extracted from the saveBalance calls, so this destination is one worked example of a much wider target list rather than the target list itself.
how.caveat: An ordinary destination for anybody who uses the service, and only one of 25 named platforms, of which the source publishes host and path for this one. Treat it as a pivot for an already-suspect host, not as coverage of the capability.

markers.note: bound to the web destination field rather than the DNS question name, so it can be true on the same proxy record as the path marker
balance response the handler reads and records via saveBalance with source EXCHANGE and name KRAKEN

how.logic: The last PowerShell script in the chain triggers the payload with the command line .\node.exe -r .\preflight.js .\app.jsc. The -r option forces Node to run a JS file before loading the main module, the preloaded script decompresses the payload, and the main module is a Brotli-compressed V8 code cache rather than JavaScript source. Later campaigns renamed the launcher to preload.js and the payload to app.js, and the source states plainly that this rendered hunting based on the .jsc extension ineffective, so the durable anchor is the preload command shape rather than the extension.
how.caveat: node.exe is a legitimate signed runtime and -r is an ordinary option, so this is a hunt scoped to the user population rather than a rule for the estate; on a developer population it is noise. The file names in the regex are the ones the source names, and the source itself records them being changed once already, so expect them to age.

markers.expr: node runtime ancestry includes the PowerShell stage

how.logic: The last stage is two ZIP archives downloaded by PowerShell: node.zip holding a packaged Node.js runtime, and build.zip holding the payload and its supporting components, which the source lists as winpty-agent.exe, an agent for a hidden Windows console, winpty.dll, a module that allows interaction with that console, app.jsc, the payload itself, preflight.js, a decompression script, and native .node modules in PE format. The source marks both winpty components as open source, and node.zip is a packaged Node.js runtime, which is what defeats a file-by-file judgement of the bundle: the unit to assess is the set of names arriving together, not any one of them.

iocs.note: the payload used for the capability case study
last payload observed on the V8 10.2.154.26-node.25 generation, campaigns starting at the end of October 2025
first payload observed with the added AES-256-CBC layer, generated 2025-11-11
the one macOS example the source names
sample used for the control-flow flattening example
older payload using the simpler string-obfuscation variant; the appendix gives this hash for the unpacked file and no hash for the original

how.caveat: winpty-agent.exe and winpty.dll are open-source components with legitimate users, and node.zip and build.zip are unremarkable names, so no single hit here means anything; several of them landing in one directory within a short window is the signal. app.js is deliberately absent from the list because on its own that name is ordinary. The sample hashes age faster than the names, and the source records the names being changed once already.

markers.note: bundle contents named by the source, plus the renamed launcher from the later campaigns

how.logic: Among the strings recovered from the payload are fragments for deploying hidden PowerShell and for running content out of a Base64-encoded blob, of which the distinctive one is the reference to an unattend Extensions property inside a FromBase64String call. That fragment is specific enough to search command lines for on its own. The companion fragment, the hidden-window PowerShell invocation, is deliberately not tested alongside it: the source lists the strings separately and does not state that they form one command line, and that fragment is far too common to add as a condition.
how.caveat: These are strings inside the payload, not observed command lines, so this searches for what the payload is built to emit rather than for something the source watched it emit. The companion string, powershell -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden -Command, is recovered from the same payload and is worth having in a hunt library, but it is common enough in legitimate tooling that ANDing it here would only break the query.

markers.note: recovered payload string, used to run content from a Base64-encoded blob

how.logic: Collected secrets are submitted through an RPC router with two transports wired to the same URL builder; this block is the HTTP one, and the socket transport is the block after it, because no single request is both. The URL is constructed in the form https://api.<domain>/rpc, with machineId and token added as query parameters. The transport posts a binary body declared as application/octet-stream and expects an arraybuffer response. The source publishes no campaign domain, so the path, the api label, the parameter pair and the content type are what carry across samples.
how.caveat: A /rpc path under an api hostname is an ordinary shape for legitimate applications, and no campaign domain is published, so this is usable joined to the endpoint findings, or on a proxy log where the initiating process is not a browser, and not as a standalone rule.

markers.expr: request to a /rpc path carries both a machineId and a token query parameter
hostname serving the /rpc path has api as its first label

how.logic: The second transport on the same router opens a WebSocket, built by the same URL builder as wss://api.<domain>/rpc and carrying the same machineId and token query parameters. It is a separate block from the HTTP transport because a request cannot be both a binary POST and a socket upgrade, so the content type test from that block must not be carried into this one. What is testable here is the upgrade itself against the same path and hostname shape.
how.caveat: WebSocket sessions to an api hostname are ordinary for modern applications, and with no campaign domain published this needs the initiating process, or an endpoint finding on the same host, to be worth anything. Where the upgrade is not visible to the proxy, only the long-lived session remains, which is weaker still.

markers.expr: session is a WebSocket upgrade rather than a request-response exchange
request to a /rpc path carries both a machineId and a token query parameter
hostname serving the /rpc path has api as its first label

how.logic: The recovered entry point calls the Node.js dns module's setServers with the two addresses 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8, in the start function and ahead of the branch that initialises the malware modules. That is the whole of what the source shows. It does not say which of the runtime's resolution paths the call governs, and it describes no change to the host resolver configuration, so no resolver hijack is claimed here. What remains collectable is resolution traffic from the endpoint to either address, and the source gives no port for it.
how.caveat: Both addresses are hard-coded by a great deal of legitimate software and set by hand on plenty of endpoints, so this cannot carry a hunt of its own; it is a discriminator for a host already flagged by the store-add or the listener. An estate that blocks or redirects outbound resolution at the perimeter will not see it at all.

markers.note: the two addresses passed to setServers in the recovered start function

markers.expr: endpoint resolves names against an address outside the estate's own resolver set

where.title: Breaking the Seal: Static Deobfuscation of JSCeal's Compiled V8 Bytecode

notes: The source is primarily a deobfuscation methodology paper: it publishes a static pipeline for recovering compiled V8 bytecode, reports applying it to 23 JSCeal payloads, and the capabilities recorded here come from its case study of one of them, MD5 e27ae65977287bdfb7b0e15fd3603f85. Its optional LLM renaming stage is treated by the authors as a navigation aid whose proposed names are hypotheses rather than evidence, and they give a worked example of a wrong one, so nothing above rests on a proposed function name: every value is taken from a recovered string, a command line, an argument array or a code fragment printed in the article. Three things the source shows but this record deliberately does not turn into a detection. It never says how traffic is steered into the local proxy, so no host proxy configuration artefact is claimed. It never names the process that spawns the certificate utility, so no parent condition is written, even though the payload runs inside the bundled Node.js runtime and the bundle also ships a hidden-console agent that could sit between. And its dns.setServers call is printed as code with no statement about which resolution paths it governs, so no resolver hijack is claimed. Two evolution points matter for collection: later campaigns renamed the launcher to preload.js and the payload to app.js, and the source says this rendered hunting on the .jsc extension ineffective; and campaigns from early November 2025 moved to V8 13.6.233.10-node.28 and wrapped the Brotli-compressed payload in an AES-256-CBC layer whose key is supplied by an earlier stage of the deployment chain through an environment variable, which the source says puts recovery out of reach when only an isolated bundle or payload is held. The same source describes further behaviour that belongs in separate records rather than this one: credential, cookie and token theft across eight named Chromium-based browsers, including retrieval of the newer App-Bound encrypted key, and a Puppeteer-driven replay of recovered cookies against Google's Android authentication endpoint to obtain a fresh OAuth token marked with scope ANDROID; keyboard capture, screenshot capture and window control; and Telegram session collection. The payload also carries the attackers' public key and 25 platform identifiers extracted from its saveBalance calls, among them BINANCE, BYBIT, KRAKEN, OKX and KUCOIN. Other vendors tag the same malware WEEVILPROXY and MeadowLocust. The article cites accounts of the same campaigns by Microsoft Security and by Cato CTRL, but the copy read here carries their titles without URLs, so no corroboration is filed. when.published is the sitemap last-modified date recorded when the article was harvested, not a date printed in the article body. Blocks 3 and 4 deliberately carry no pattern_id: both are destination pivots on a single named host and path rather than a behaviour, and no shipped pattern describes that. Forcing one of the interception or injection patterns would file them by subject rather than by mechanism.

who.versions_affected: The publisher found twelve versions of the 64-bit MpEngine.dll across the Windows 10 and Windows 11 releases available to it, extracted five unique BTR.sys builds from them by SHA-256, and after adding distinct samples from VirusTotal and de-duplicating arrived at eighteen unique 64-bit Microsoft-signed BTR.sys versions by authentihash. It states that every one of those versions shares the same hard-coded 256-byte RC4 key, that the transaction structure is the same across all of them and supports every identified action id, and that its tool ran on Windows 7 Build 7601, Windows 8.1, Windows 10 22H2 and Windows 11 25H2, the last as of July 2026.

what.summary: Windows Defender completes a remediation that needs a reboot by dropping a signed kernel driver, BTR.sys, out of MpEngine.dll under a randomised eight-letter name and pointing that driver's service key at an RC4-encrypted instruction blob held in an alternate data stream on the driver file, and a researcher who reverse engineered the blob format showed that an administrator can stage the same Microsoft-signed driver with instructions of their own to delete files, move files, delete registry keys and values and set registry values from kernel mode, including deleting Defender's own binaries and service keys in the early boot window before the Defender user-mode service starts.

how.logic: The driver exposes no IOCTL interface and takes its whole configuration from an alternate data stream whose path is named by the Args value on its service key, so a stream creation whose target name ends in .sys:changelist appears in every use of the driver, legitimate Defender remediation included. Alert on that stream name. The publisher states the same event carries the encrypted configuration itself in its Contents field, so the transaction blob is recoverable from telemetry rather than only from disk.

fields.note: Sysmon FileCreateStreamHash, event id 15; this is the publisher's stated detection logic
the publisher states this event captures the RC4-encrypted configuration directly

how.caveat: Both legitimate remediation and abuse create the :changelist stream, so this fires whenever Defender schedules a removal across a reboot and its volume is whatever the estate's remediation rate is. The publisher's differentiator is where the driver's execution report is written, and it describes the legitimate destination only as a standalone file, typically in a protected path such as C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Scans\RebootActions\, so that is an example rather than an enumerated set and building an exclusion on it can blind the rule. The pattern's standing exclusion for the zone identifier stream does not help here, because the stream name is different. The research began as an incident response false positive on exactly this artefact, so expect the same on any estate that starts alerting on it.

markers.note: the configuration stream, named by the Args value on the driver's service key
Sysmon FileCreateStreamHash

how.logic: Separate legitimate remediation from abuse on where the driver's execution report goes. The published tool points the feedback path at a second alternate data stream on the driver file itself, a .dat stream on a .sys file, while MpEngine.dll points it at a standalone file. The publisher offers this as a secondary alert on .dat streams created on .sys files.

fields.note: Sysmon FileCreateStreamHash, event id 15

how.caveat: The publisher marks this half as specific to its current proof-of-concept tool rather than to the driver, so a weaponisation tool that writes its report anywhere else defeats it, and it says nothing about a driver used legitimately. Worth building only alongside the :changelist block, which is the half that is universal.

markers.note: the feedback report written to a second stream on the driver file
Sysmon FileCreateStreamHash

how.logic: Alert on the creation of a kernel driver service key whose Args value names a :changelist alternate data stream and whose Group value is Boot Bus Extender. The publisher shows the driver cannot run as a boot start driver, because it does file input and output inside DriverEntry before the object manager has established the SystemRoot link and before the storage stack is up, so it has to be configured as system start with Start set to 1; Boot Bus Extender then places it at one of the earliest practical execution slots in phase 1, immediately after the filesystem initialises. The Start=0 Defender drivers WdBoot.sys and WdFilter.sys are already loaded by that point, so what the driver gets ahead of is the security drivers in lower-priority groups and everything in user mode: the publisher's boot capture has UCPD.sys loading after it, the Defender user-mode service about 34 seconds after it finished, and the network inspection driver nearly four minutes later. The published tool writes these keys directly and loads the driver through NtLoadDriver rather than through the service control manager, so no service installation record, System event 7045, is written at all.

fields.note: Sysmon RegistryEvent, event id 12 or 13, on a key under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\
system start; the publisher states the driver cannot run as a boot start driver
kernel driver, as recorded on the service key the publisher observed
the publisher states the dropped driver filename matches [a-z]{8}.sys and gives mzqnjtaq.sys as the observed example; the eight-letter test is deliberately case-sensitive

how.caveat: Legitimate remediation stages the same keys, in the same group, with the same Args shape, so the discriminator the publisher gives is the route rather than the content: MpEngine.dll goes through the service control manager and leaves a service installation record in the Windows System log, event 7045, while the tool writes the keys directly and calls NtLoadDriver, so no 7045 is written. That comparison is a join between registry telemetry and the Windows System log and is left to the consumer; an estate that does not collect event 7045 cannot make it and is left with the bare key creation. The service name is randomised on both routes, so it carries nothing. Note also that the publisher states the [a-z]{8}.sys filename shape for the driver Defender itself drops and says only that its own tool generates a randomised name; the driver it renamed for the boot capture, mlrmqchs.sys, fits the same shape, but the shape is not stated as a property of the tool.

markers.note: the values the publisher lists on the service key; one event carries one of them, which is why the pairing below is a computed join
Sysmon RegistryEvent

markers.expr: registry value Args on a kernel driver service key contains ':changelist' and registry value Group on the same key equals 'Boot Bus Extender'
registry value ImagePath on the same service key names a driver under System32\drivers whose file name matches ^[a-z]{8}\.sys$
a service installation record, Windows System log event 7045, exists for the same service name

how.logic: The driver is a legitimate Microsoft-signed component that the published tool carves out of the local MpEngine.dll, so nothing external is brought in and no signature or blocklist test fails. The publisher's test is lineage: a driver load whose signature is Microsoft Windows and whose hashes match a known BTR.sys version, joined to the process that wrote the driver file or created its service key. In legitimate use the publisher names Defender's own MsMpEng.exe as what drops and registers the driver; the tool runs as an ordinary user-mode program, so a command shell, a script interpreter or an unrecognised binary appears in that role instead, the publisher's examples being cmd.exe and powershell.exe. Anchor on the write of the driver file, which is the event carrying the acting process, and join forward to the driver load.

fields.note: Sysmon DriverLoad, event id 6

the publisher counted eighteen unique Microsoft-signed BTR.sys versions by authentihash and published none of the values, so this set has to be built on the estate by extracting BTR.sys from the local MpEngine.dll copies; left unresolved deliberately
the process that wrote the driver file, Sysmon FileCreate event id 11; anchored to a path separator or the start of the string because this field carries a full path
process creation telemetry, not the driver load event; the publisher offers ParentImage or Image as the lineage side of the join, and Sysmon event 6 carries neither

how.caveat: Nothing here is unsigned and nothing is on a blocklist: the publisher's point is that the Microsoft vulnerable driver blocklist does not cover a driver being used for exactly what it was built to do, so signature and reputation tests pass it. Two things hold this at hunt rather than alert. The publisher counted eighteen unique Microsoft-signed BTR.sys versions by authentihash and published none of the values, so the hash half of the join is inert until the estate builds its own set from the MpEngine.dll copies it has; without it, signature equals Microsoft Windows matches every Microsoft driver load on every host at every boot. And the whole test rests on lineage, so the Defender process set has to be enumerated locally first -- the publisher names MsMpEng.exe only as an example of a legitimate stager -- and a tool that stages the driver from a process inside that set defeats it. cmd.exe and powershell.exe are the publisher's examples, not the boundary; the boundary is being outside the Defender ecosystem.

markers.note: Sysmon FileCreate: the write of the driver file, which is the event that records the acting process
the randomised driver filename shape the publisher states; case-sensitive on purpose
the acting process on the file write; the publisher's examples of a stager outside the Defender ecosystem, alongside unrecognised binaries

markers.expr: the process that wrote the driver file is not MsMpEng.exe, the Defender process the publisher names as the legitimate dropper and registrar
a driver load of the same file follows on the same host, Sysmon event 6, with Signature 'Microsoft Windows' and Hashes in a BTR.sys hash set built locally from the estate's own MpEngine.dll copies

how.logic: Once the driver runs, the file work happens in ring 0 and the endpoint record names the deleting image as System, process id 4, rather than the user-mode tool that asked for it, so any rule keyed on a process image or a command line has nothing to match. The publisher's test is to correlate System deleting files, especially security binaries, immediately after a driver load. Its own tests deleted WdFilter.sys, MsMpEng.exe and WdNisDrv.sys during the boot window, and removing the service binary before the service control manager tries to launch it stops the product starting at all, which is what takes self-healing and cloud reporting away with it.

fields.note: Sysmon FileDelete, event id 23; the publisher states the deleting image is recorded as System, process id 4, not the user-mode tool that triggered it

the example protected binaries the publisher confirmed deleting during the boot window; the MsMpEng.exe path it gives sits under a Defender platform version directory that changes with each platform update, so match on the file name rather than the version

how.caveat: The publisher gives WdFilter.sys, MsMpEng.exe and WdNisDrv.sys as examples of protected binaries it deleted, not as a target list, so the list has to be written for whatever security product the estate runs. Legitimate Defender remediation also deletes files through this driver, in kernel mode, attributed the same way, so the target is doing all the work. The harder limit is that the telemetry has to exist at all: the boot variant runs before user-mode security services start, and an agent that begins recording when its own service starts holds no record of any of it. The publisher's boot capture puts the Defender user-mode service about 34 seconds after the driver finished and the network inspection driver nearly four minutes later, but no window is given here because it has to be measured against the estate's own boot timeline.

markers.note: process id 4; the kernel is recorded as the actor rather than the tool that triggered it
the example protected binaries the publisher confirmed deleting during the boot window
Sysmon FileDelete

markers.expr: a driver load precedes the deletion on the same host inside a window measured against the estate's own boot timeline

how.logic: The driver creates a text log at \SystemRoot\Temp\BootClean.log in DriverEntry, and the publisher states that happens regardless of the caller. What the published tool adds is the deletion: it injects a delete-file action for that log as the first item in the transaction list, so the driver creates the log, performs the requested actions and then deletes its own log before unloading. Watch for the creation and the prompt deletion of that one path by System.

fields.note: Sysmon FileCreate event id 11 and FileDelete event id 23
the publisher names System, process id 4, as doing both

how.caveat: The creation is hardcoded in the driver and happens on every use, legitimate remediation included, so the creation on its own is a use-of-the-driver signal and not an abuse signal. Only the deletion is added by the tool, which makes the pair the discriminator and makes it as specific to that tool as the .dat feedback stream is; a weaponisation tool that leaves the log alone produces only the creation. As with the other boot-window signals, an agent that starts with its own user-mode service will not have recorded either event.

markers.note: process id 4
Sysmon FileCreate and FileDelete

markers.expr: a file create of BootClean.log is followed by a file delete of the same path on the same host inside a window measured locally

how.logic: Tamper protection is enforced primarily against user-mode processes, so a delete-key request arriving from a signed kernel driver goes through. The publisher deleted Defender's own service registry keys this way at runtime, naming HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\WdFilter in the text and issuing delete-key actions against both that key and HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\WinDefend in the demonstration, which blinds the operating system and stops WdFilter.sys loading on the next reboot. Alert on the deletion of either key.

fields.note: the publisher names event id 12 or 13 as the registry telemetry and names no field for the deletion itself, so this is bound to XDM rather than to an invented raw field name

how.caveat: The publisher demonstrates this against Defender's own service keys, so the alert list is those two keys plus whatever the estate's own security product uses, which has to be written locally. It states kernel attribution only for file deletion, where the image is recorded as System with process id 4, and says nothing about how a registry deletion driven from kernel mode is attributed, so do not assume the actor field on this event names the kernel. A Defender platform upgrade or an uninstall removes service keys legitimately and the publisher gives no way to separate those here, so the exclusion has to come from change records rather than from the event.

markers.note: deleted at runtime in the demonstration, past tamper protection, because the caller is a kernel driver
Sysmon RegistryEvent; the publisher names these two ids as the registry telemetry

where.title: BTR Reforged: Weaponizing Defender's Remediation Driver as a Kernel Operation Primitive

notes: The publisher states that across all collected samples and telemetry sources it saw no evidence of real-world abuse of this driver in the manner demonstrated, so this is a technique published before it is used rather than an intrusion report, and it argues that is the case for building the detection now. Following responsible disclosure, MSRC's position was that the findings do not meet the criteria for immediate servicing because the technique relies on pre-existing administrative privilege, specifically SeLoadDriverPrivilege, which the publisher names as the primary control: restrict and monitor the assignment and use of that right. A working proof-of-concept tool, BTR_CLI, was published alongside the research under the MIT licence with ready-to-run x64 and x86 executables, so the barrier to use is low. Two details help an analyst. The publisher prints the 256-byte RC4 key in full and states every analysed version shares it, and separately states that Sysmon event 15 captures the encrypted configuration in its Contents field. And the driver returns STATUS_DELETE_PENDING, 0xC0000056, on success rather than STATUS_SUCCESS, which is what makes the kernel unload it immediately, so it is not resident to be found afterwards. Finally, the research began as an incident response false positive: the randomly named driver, the transient service, the RC4 routines, the alternate data stream and the self-cleanup were all read as attacker tradecraft and turned out to be Defender remediation working as designed. Expect that same false positive on any estate that starts alerting on the :changelist stream.

who.versions_affected: Not version bound. The chain uses shipped Windows components as installed: the Finger client, the curl client, rundll32, the registry, Windows Management Instrumentation and the .NET common language runtime. The source reports no vulnerability being exploited anywhere in the chain and names no CVE.

what.summary: A security vendor analysed a new remote access tool it tracks as SloppyRAT and assesses is likely used by a ransomware-related actor to establish a foothold for lateral movement. Delivery was a ClickFix style lure whose command line used the shipped Finger client to fetch and run a batch script, which copied the shipped curl client under a numeric name to fetch a portable Python runtime from its official release page; further stages led to CastleLoader and then CastleRAT, and alongside CastleRAT a second Python interpreter was written to disk and used to run a script that reflectively loaded the implant DLL in memory. The implant carries 47 built-in commands written in native code that reproduce common PowerShell cmdlets by calling Windows APIs and Windows Management Instrumentation directly, so the discovery commands among them create no child process, no command line and no script block, and it reads and changes Microsoft Defender settings through the Defender management instrumentation provider rather than through the cmdlets its commands are named after.

how.logic: Delivery is a single command shell one-liner that a person runs themselves rather than anything being exploited, so the interpreter has no parent chain back to whatever presented the lure. The observable is the shape of the line. Two tokens are split with caret escapes so they do not appear whole: the start verb and the name of the Finger utility the line invokes. The rest of the line is written plainly, including the interpreter path, the minimise switch and the for-loop keywords that feed the utility's output back to the shell. A run of dashes and reassurance text is appended after the real command.

markers.note: a caret-split token; the interpreter ignores the carets, so the word never appears whole. Tolerates both the single and double caret forms the sample uses
the start verb is caret-split in the sample while the minimise switch that follows it is not
the caret-split utility name and the user-at-host argument form, as they appear on the shell's own command line; the Finger process's own command line is not published by the source
written plainly in the sample, not caret-split
the appended instruction text, padded with dashes

how.caveat: All five markers are conjunctive, and together they match the one command line the publisher printed, so this set is a rule for this lure rather than for the technique. The caret markers are the durable half, because administrators do not write command lines this way; the instruction text and the minimise switch are trivially changed. The publisher describes the delivery only as a ClickFix style lure and does not say what carried it, so the serving side of the shared pattern is not evidenced by this source.

how.logic: The shipped Finger client is used to retrieve a batch script from an attacker-run Finger service and hand its output straight back to the shell for execution, so the download and the execution are one statement. The publisher states that most corporate environments need neither the utility nor the protocol, which makes the process cheap to deny outright.
how.caveat: Blocking is the stronger control here and the publisher says so outright. The source does not publish the Finger process's own command line, only the shell line that invoked it, so no argument marker is carried and the image name stands alone. Where Finger is genuinely in use somewhere in an estate, the utility running on a workstation is still the anomaly.

how.logic: The Finger protocol usually talks to servers over TCP port 79, and the publisher's own recommendation is to block egress on that port. Outbound sessions to it are the flow-side half of the same control, independent of whether the utility executing was seen on the endpoint.

markers.note: the Finger protocol's usual TCP port, as the source states it

iocs.note: ClickFix script domain, as the publisher's indicator table labels it

how.caveat: Carried as a separate block from the process one because markers in a set are conjunctive and these two controls are alternatives, each worth an alert on its own. The domain is an atomic indicator rather than a marker for the same reason: a DNS query and a flow record are different events and cannot both be satisfied by one of them.

how.logic: The retrieved batch script copies the shipped curl client into the user's local application data directory under a name made only of digits with a .com extension, and uses it to fetch an archive from a software project's official release page, writing it to disk with a document extension. Two masquerades in one step: the running image name no longer matches the original filename recorded in the binary, and the written file's extension no longer matches its content.

markers.note: the numeric name is generated per run, so only the shape is sourced; no digit count is asserted
archive fetched, saved under a document extension

how.caveat: All three markers sit on one process-execution event, which is why the extension-versus-content test is not among them: it is a download-telemetry test on a different event, and the shared pattern does not carry it either, so an estate wanting it has to build it separately. The durable test is the original-filename comparison the shared pattern describes, which needs process telemetry carrying binary metadata. The --ssl-no-revoke switch has genuine uses behind an interception proxy and is not actionable on its own.

how.logic: The chain never uses the platform's own script engines. The archive fetched in the previous step is a portable language runtime taken from the project's official release page; the interpreter is renamed to a numeric name in the user's application data directory and passed an inline script that Base64-decodes and decompresses a payload, decodes the result with an unusual codec and launches it in a further interpreter process.

markers.note: the source shows one framework directory only; that segment is left open rather than pinned, and no digit count is asserted for the renamed interpreter
an unusual codec choice and a stable string in the stage-one argument

how.caveat: Developer and data science estates run portable interpreters legitimately, so the path shape alone is not the detection; the inline decode argument is what carries it. Retrieval from the project's own release infrastructure is what makes the download unremarkable, so the download is not the place to look.

how.logic: The inline script downloads and runs further stages, leading to CastleLoader and then CastleRAT. Those components were retrieved from a separate host with a short opaque user agent. They are a different payload from the implant this record is about, deployed by the same actor in the same intrusion, and the indicators in this block belong to them rather than to SloppyRAT.

markers.note: the publisher states this is the User-Agent string used for the CastleLoader and CastleRAT retrievals

iocs.note: CastleLoader and CastleRAT retrieval user agent

how.caveat: A ten-character opaque user agent is a build-time choice and rotates. Kept in its own block so a reader cannot take these values for SloppyRAT indicators. Note that the path segment in the CastleLoader URL is a different ten-character string from the user agent value and the two are easily conflated; both are reproduced here exactly as the publisher gives them.

how.logic: Alongside CastleRAT the actor downloaded and wrote a second, separate Python interpreter to disk rather than reusing the first one, and used its windowed executable to download and run a Python script from cloud object storage. A second interpreter arriving on a host that already has one is the shape here.

markers.expr: python interpreter executable written to disk and then executed with no corresponding installation record

how.caveat: The windowed Python interpreter is ordinary on developer and data science hosts, so the image name alone is not a detection and is carried only to scope the computed test. The source does not publish where the second interpreter was written, so no path marker is carried.

how.logic: The Python script the second interpreter runs exists to download the implant DLL over HTTPS from cloud object storage and load it reflectively in memory by a named export, so the implant never runs from disk under its own identity. The retrieval carries a distinctive non-browser user agent. The test is the retrieval joined to the loading process on host and time; the publisher names the export invoked as f3b980dea.

markers.note: the publisher calls this the loader script's distinctive user agent

markers.expr: script host retrieves a dll over https and loads it in memory by a named export with no new executable written to disk

how.caveat: The storage account name and the user agent are per-campaign and will change; the hashes are the twenty-one DLL samples and the one loader script the publisher listed and will not survive a rebuild. The in-memory half needs a sensor that records reflective loading; where it does not, the user agent on the retrieval is all that is left. The staged DLL file name is not carried as a marker; the publisher gives it only inside the retrieval URLs, and the path and the in-memory load are the discriminators.

how.logic: The implant communicates over HTTPS with JSON formatted messages to the destinations the publisher names. Where TLS is not inspected, and it cannot usefully be inspected here, the destination and the session shape are the only things left.

markers.note: the publisher gives the address and the port as one pair

how.caveat: Atomic indicators with a short life. The two C2 domains are carried as indicators rather than as markers alongside the address, because a DNS query and a flow record are different events and one event cannot satisfy both; a rule wanting the domains should filter DNS separately.

how.logic: The implant speaks a small fixed HTTP API. It authenticates by presenting a key compiled into its configuration in a custom header, receives a session token it then carries as a bearer credential, and polls a short list of stable paths for tasks, sending the token in a different custom header on proxy acknowledgements only. Host inventory, installed security product lists and command output are RC4 encrypted with a hardcoded key and Base64 encoded before posting.

markers.note: written as a regex, not as a list of bare paths, because this marker type binds to a field holding the whole URL

alternatives, not both on one request: the key header is on the authentication request and the token header on proxy acknowledgements. The source prints the key header as X-API-Key in prose and X-API-KEY in the raw request, so match the name case-insensitively. This marker type has no default field binding and a consumer must resolve it

how.caveat: Fidelity is hunt rather than alert because in practice no estate sees any of this. The implant pins the server certificate and drops the session when interception is present, so an estate that decrypts gets nothing and an estate that does not decrypt cannot read the header, the path or the user agent. The one-key-many-hosts count that would make a compiled-in credential findable is the shared pattern's generic scenario and is deliberately not repeated here, because it cannot be evaluated against this source's traffic at all. The header names, the paths and the user agent are build-time choices and will change.

how.logic: A reverse SOCKS connection is negotiated through the polling endpoint, which lets the operator use the infected host as a proxy to reach other systems on the internal network. The test joins the host's external polling sessions to the internal sessions it then originates, within a window.

markers.expr: host polling one external destination on a fixed path then originating internal sessions to destinations it has no history of

how.caveat: Jump hosts, management servers, vulnerability scanners and backup agents legitimately originate broad internal sessions, so a per-host baseline of normal internal destinations is the whole cost of this and is a prerequisite rather than a refinement.

how.logic: During the handshake the implant compares the SHA256 of the whole DER encoded server certificate against a value held in its configuration and closes the connection when it does not match, so an estate that intercepts TLS sees a session end after the server certificate is presented and never sees a request. Older builds do this over raw SChannel sockets, newer ones over WinHTTP, retrieving the leaf certificate through the query-option call.

markers.expr: tls session terminated by the client immediately after the server certificate is presented, with no request sent
interception proxy records a decrypt or pin failure for a destination absent from the pinned-application inventory
count of inspection failures by client process and destination
markers.note: more than one is the definitional minimum for a repeat, not a tuned bound; the count that separates this from ordinary pinned clients has to be measured in the estate and is left unresolved
the C2 the publisher names is reached on 443; the pinning behaviour itself is not tied to a port

how.caveat: Legitimate pinned clients, including update agents, security agents and some line of business applications, produce exactly this, which is why an inventory of them has to exist before the rule does. The publisher does not report what an inspecting estate actually saw; the expectation that the failure recurs is a consequence of the polling loop the source describes rather than an observation. This is a coverage statement as much as a detection: an estate that relies on TLS inspection to see malware command traffic has no visibility of this implant at all, and detection has to move onto the endpoint.

how.logic: Forty-seven operator commands are named after common PowerShell cmdlets and shell builtins, but are implemented in C++ and interact directly with Windows APIs and Windows Management Instrumentation rather than going through PowerShell. The discovery commands among them, covering local users, local group members, processes, services, registry values, file search by name through a management instrumentation query, network reachability and installed security product status, are serviced inside the implant process and create no child process, no command line and no script block, so process-creation rules, command-line rules and script block logging all see nothing. One command in the set is the exception and does create a process: the Start-Process family, which the publisher records as calling the process creation API. What is left observable is one process performing the discovery through direct API and management instrumentation calls, joined against process-creation telemetry that carries no event accounting for it.

markers.expr: single process performing user, local group, process, service, registry and security product discovery through direct Windows API and WMI calls with no child process created
wmi query of CIM_DataFile selecting Name and FileSize issued by a process outside the inventory and management agent set
process-creation telemetry contains no event accounting for the discovery activity recorded on the API and WMI paths

how.caveat: This is a coverage statement first. A detection library keyed on process creation and script block content has no coverage of any of it, and establishing whether the sensor records native API calls and management instrumentation activity at all is the first task rather than a refinement. Variants exist without the built-in command set, roughly 400KB smaller, which fall back to the PowerShell hosting paths and are correspondingly easier to see. Do not read the block as saying the implant never creates a process: the process-spawning command in the set does, and the separate management instrumentation execution path does too.

how.logic: The implant exposes commands named after the Defender preference cmdlets and implements them as a management instrumentation call: instantiate the locator through COM, connect to the Defender namespace, and execute a method on the preference class, with disabling real-time monitoring given as the worked example. Status is read the same way, by querying the status class in the same namespace. A rule watching for the cmdlet name, for a PowerShell process or for a command line will not fire. The test joins the configuration change the product itself records to management instrumentation activity against that namespace from a process with no management role.

markers.expr: wmi connection to namespace ROOT\Microsoft\Windows\Defender by a process outside the management agent inventory
method executed on MSFT_MpPreference or query issued against MSFT_MpComputerStatus by a process that is not a defender management component
defender real-time monitoring preference changed with no matching change record

how.caveat: Management tooling reconfigures the product through the same provider, so the inventory of what legitimately does it is a prerequisite rather than a refinement. Do not narrow this by excluding hosts that have a PowerShell process running: PowerShell runs routinely on managed Windows estates, for management agents, scheduled tasks and logon scripts, so such a clause silently suppresses the finding on almost every host. The discriminators are the caller's identity and a change with no matching change record. The point that outlives this malware is that the setting was changed with PowerShell never involved at all, so the cmdlet name is not the control surface and should not be what a rule watches.

how.logic: Some variants establish no persistence. Those that do write one of two registry entries, and the publisher's analysis is that both are written wrongly. This block is the first of the two: a value named rundll32 under the Run key in the current user hive, set to execute rundll32.exe without specifying the path to the implant DLL or the export to invoke, so the startup command resolves to nothing. No installer writes a startup command that cannot resolve, which makes the broken attempt better evidence than a working one would be.

markers.note: anchored at the end so that RunOnce and the other Run-prefixed keys do not match; the source names the current user hive

markers.expr: run value data invokes rundll32.exe with no module or export argument, so the startup command cannot resolve to a payload

how.caveat: The existing startup-entry patterns key on value data pointing into a user-writable directory, and this data names rundll32.exe with no arguments, so they do not match it; that is the reason to carry it separately. The source states only what the value data omits and does not publish the data itself, so nothing is claimed here about where it points. Some variants establish no persistence at all, so the absence of the entry says nothing about whether a host is affected.

how.logic: The second of the two persistence branches. If the Run value cannot be set, the code creates a CLSID key in the machine hive class store and sets its in-process server entry, but generates a brand new class identifier from a hash of the computer name instead of replacing an existing registered one, so nothing references the class and nothing loads it. As with the Run value, the correct DLL path and export are not supplied. No application registers a class nothing references.

markers.note: the source shows the plain class store path; the optional segment is a tolerance so that a 32-bit registration is not missed, and is not a value taken from the source

markers.expr: in-process server entry created under a class identifier that no installed component registers

how.caveat: Kept apart from the Run branch because the two are alternatives in the malware and markers in one set are conjunctive, so a single set spanning both keys could never match an event. The class-identifier test needs a view of which identifiers installed products actually claim, which is the cost of this half.

how.logic: Where a command does not match a built-in, the implant loads the managed runtime through COM inside its own process, loads the PowerShell automation assembly and invokes the script through the object model. There is no separate PowerShell process, so process-creation and command-line rules see nothing. The same handler caches the most recent command output in the temporary directory under a .png extension, writing a PNG header in front of a body encrypted with the configuration's hardcoded key, so the file passes both an extension check and a header check and is not an image. The test joins the module-load pair to the file write by the same process.

markers.expr: process loads clr.dll and System.Management.Automation.dll and is not powershell.exe or pwsh.exe
file written with a png extension whose bytes after the png signature do not decode as an image

markers.note: non-anchoring on its own; every process that writes a png into a temporary directory matches it, so it is carried to scope the computed tests and not as a signal

markers.expr: png file in the temporary directory written by the same process that loaded the powershell automation assembly

how.caveat: Legitimate software hosts the runtime this way, including management agents and some administrative tooling, so the inventory of those comes first. The module-load pair needs a sensor that records image loads; where it does not, this block cannot be built and the cached output file is the only residue left, and the content test rather than the path is what makes that residue usable. The publisher does not say whether script block logging still fires from a hosted engine, so do not assume either way.

how.logic: Where the hosted runtime cannot be instantiated, because the managed runtime is absent or the COM interface does not match the installation, the implant spawns a real PowerShell process but sets the desktop shell as its parent, by constructing an extended startup information structure with the explicit parent process attribute pointing at a handle for the shell process and then calling the process creation API. The resulting pair is the most ordinary parent and child on a Windows desktop, so a rule treating the shell as an exculpatory parent is defeated by it, and a rule keyed on the implant as the parent will never see it.

markers.expr: reported parent of the powershell process is explorer.exe while the creating process recorded by the sensor is a different process

how.caveat: Users launch PowerShell from the desktop shell constantly, so the first two markers are not a detection at any threshold and are carried only to scope the third. That third test, comparing the parent the process reports against the creating process the sensor recorded, is the whole of the detection and depends on the sensor capturing both separately.

how.logic: A third execution path. Where the task specifies the command shell rather than PowerShell, the implant launches the command line through Windows Management Instrumentation using the process creation method, so the new process is created by the management instrumentation service rather than by the implant and the implant does not appear in its ancestry at all.

markers.expr: process created through the wmi win32_process create method by a caller outside the management agent inventory

how.caveat: Remote administration and management tooling create processes this way routinely, so the inventory of legitimate callers is the whole cost. The publisher gives one sentence on this path and names no command that was run through it, so no command-line marker is carried.

how.logic: A build can take its command and control address from a smart contract on a public blockchain over JSON-RPC instead of carrying one, so taking down the named domains does not disconnect it. The contract address can be supplied either in the configuration at build time or, at run time, through a named environment variable, and that variable is the endpoint-side artefact.

markers.expr: process environment contains the variable LOADER_POLYGON_RESOLVER

how.caveat: Needs a sensor that captures process environment blocks, which many do not, and this block declares that telemetry rather than relying on flow or proxy records which cannot supply it. The publisher has found no sample with a contract address filled in, so this is reported as a capability rather than as observed activity.

how.logic: The only blockchain artefact the publisher has observed is the contract selector. A JSON-RPC request body carrying that selector is the network-side test, and it is a different telemetry requirement from the environment variable, which is why the two are not in one marker set.

markers.expr: json-rpc request body containing the contract selector 0xd6bd8727

how.caveat: This needs full request-body capture or an intrusion detection rule; proxy logs do not normally retain bodies and flow records cannot supply one at all. The publisher describes the capability as possibly still in development and reports no sample carrying a contract address, so treat it as a reason not to rely on domain blocking as containment rather than as a detection with a known hit rate. The shared pattern's gateway provider markers are the broader net, and this source names no gateway provider.

where.title: SloppyRAT: A New Tool For Ransomware Attacks

notes: Read in full on 2026-09-12. Four things the record deliberately does not claim. No actor, group or alias is named anywhere in the source and the ransomware link is the publisher's own hedged assessment of a ransomware-related actor, so actor_type is unattributed and attribution confidence is low; the source never uses the word affiliate and describes no ransomware-as-a-service structure. No ransomware deployment is reported, so that impact is absent, and no information-gathering-only impact is claimed either, because further action is described. No victimology of any kind appears in the source: no sector, industry, country, region or named victim, so target_sectors and target_regions are absent rather than set to a catch-all. And no attack surface is set, because the source describes the delivery only as a ClickFix style lure and never says what hosted or served it. Two reading notes on the how blocks. CastleLoader and CastleRAT are a separate payload deployed by the same actor in the same intrusion and are confined to their own block, so the domain, URL and user agent belonging to them are not read as SloppyRAT indicators. And the native command set does not mean the implant never creates a process: the process-spawning command in that set calls the process creation API, and a separate execution path launches a command line through the management instrumentation process creation method, each of which has its own block. Variant differences matter when reading the how blocks: some builds establish no persistence, some omit the built-in command set entirely and are about 400KB smaller, older builds use raw SChannel sockets where newer ones use WinHTTP, and the auto shell type is replaced by inline in some builds. The publisher also notes that both persistence methods are implemented incorrectly and neither functions, so a host can be affected with no working autorun present. Two further notes. The role is inline_tool because every named Microsoft component is used as attacker tooling rather than exploited; Defender appears in this record as the control reconfigured, and the corpus takes one role per record. The rce impact records that the implant gives an operator remote command execution on a host it is already running on, not that any Windows vulnerability was exploited. One vocabulary note: several blocks record Windows API and management instrumentation activity, for which evidence_type has no value; edr_process is used, because the vocabulary's process_telemetry means process values and operator actions from an industrial control system and would route a consumer to the wrong telemetry.

who.versions_affected: Not version-bound; the exposure is unchanged default credentials

what.summary: A self-hosted S3-compatible object store, reachable from a compromised application host on its canonical addresses, answered its unchanged default credentials. The operator listed every bucket, prioritised the ones whose names suggested infrastructure state and internal configuration, then fetched named files -- an environment file and a service credentials document -- and saved them to disk. The escalation was progressive: an anonymous health check, then the admin information API, then an authenticated bucket listing, then targeted retrieval of objects whose names implied secrets. The publisher notes this store is rarely seen in attacks despite being widely used to hold application data, backups, model artefacts and infrastructure state.

how.logic: An authenticated object-store session opened with the vendor's shipped credential pair, from a host whose role is not storage administration, followed by a bucket listing and then retrieval of individually named objects rather than a bulk sync. The name-directed retrieval is the discriminator against backup software, which walks everything.
how.caveat: The default credential pair is the strongest marker and the easiest to remove: once it is changed this logic needs the behavioural half to stand alone. Loopback and internal service names mean the traffic may never cross a monitored boundary, so the object store's own access log is the reliable source rather than the network.
