what.summary: Following two catalogued vulnerabilities in a widely deployed remote monitoring and management platform, researchers examining the patched release found further issues in a superseded API surface that had been left reachable without authentication. Chained, they allowed an unauthenticated attacker to read files from the server, including files leaking credentials, which in nearly all deployments examined led to the platform's own database. That database holds the integration secrets for everything the platform manages: domain credentials, user and device API keys, service keys and private keys. Roughly three thousand instances were visible on an internet-wide scanning service. The pattern of interest is not the individual flaws but that the modern interface being properly authenticated said nothing about the legacy one behind it.

how.logic: Traffic to superseded endpoints is close to zero in normal operation, so a baseline is cheap and a single request is meaningful. Look for legacy protocol paths and headers answered successfully with no preceding authentication event.
how.caveat: Confirm no live integration uses the old interface before treating a match as malicious; where one does, the output is an inventory question about which system and why, not an alert.

how.logic: Detect the fan-out rather than the read. After the credential store is taken, one origin authenticates to an unusual breadth of managed systems using accounts that legitimately exist, and integration accounts appear at hosts they have no history with.
how.caveat: Every credential used is valid, so nothing fails and failure-volume detection stays silent. Plan the response on the basis that remediation means rotating the managed estate, not the platform.

what.summary: Threat actors exploited an audit and monitoring product to deliver botnet malware against organisations in the United States and Canada, using a security tool with broad estate visibility as the delivery mechanism.

how.logic: A monitoring or audit product is granted broad read access across the estate and often broad network reach with it, so exploiting one yields visibility and position that would otherwise take considerable lateral movement. Treat security and monitoring products as high-value assets in their own right: check their exposure, their patch level, and whether their service process ever creates child processes or reaches destinations outside its documented set.

fields.note: the monitoring product's own service process, as a parent of anything unexpected
monitoring consoles are frequently exposed for remote administration

how.caveat: Monitoring products legitimately run scripts and reach widely across the estate, which makes behavioural detection on them harder than on an ordinary application. Exposure and patch currency are the more reliable controls.

what.summary: With the administrative account of an internet-exposed database server, the operator ran the extortion entirely in SQL and never delivered a binary. Configuration rows were copied into a new table through the database engine's own encryption function, the original table and its history table were dropped, and a ransom table was created carrying the demand, a payment address and a contact. The note claimed a stronger algorithm than the function's default mode provides. The key was generated from two random values, printed once, and never stored or transmitted, so the data cannot be recovered even if the demand is paid. Destruction then escalated from row deletion to dropping whole schemas, and when one drop failed on a cross-database foreign key the next statement disabled the constraint check, dropped the schema and restored the setting. Before this, the database's file primitives were used to survey a container escape: writing and reading a file through the engine, probing the container runtime socket and the process control group, and checking for a user-defined-function route to command execution.

how.logic: Extortion carried out in the database's own query language, so nothing executes on the host and file-based ransomware detection sees nothing. The observable sequence is in the query log: a create-table-as-select wrapping column data in the engine's encryption function, drops of the source and history tables, and creation of a table whose name reads as a message to a person rather than as a schema object.
how.caveat: This needs the database's own general or audit log, which is off by default on most deployments and is the single reason this class goes unseen; establish whether it is collected before building any of this. Disabling foreign key checks around a drop is also ordinary migration behaviour, so it earns its place only next to the encryption or the ransom table.

how.logic: Treat the recoverability question as separate from the encryption event, because it decides the response. Here the key existed only in the output of one statement and was never written down or sent anywhere, which makes this destruction wearing the costume of extortion. Where the history table has also been dropped there is no in-database route back.
how.caveat: Establishing that a key was never transmitted needs egress records for the session and is a negative, so it is weaker evidence than it reads. The practical use is to stop a payment decision being made on the assumption that a key exists somewhere.

what.summary: A geospatial data server flaw permitting unauthenticated remote code execution was the initial access route in an intrusion at a federal agency, paired with an eight-year-old Linux privilege escalation flaw to gain root.

how.logic: The application runs as a Java service, so exploitation surfaces as that process creating a shell. A geospatial data server exists to serve map data and has no reason to spawn a shell, which makes this high fidelity on that host.
how.caveat: Confirm no plugin or data ingestion process legitimately shells out before enabling.

how.logic: The escalation used a Linux kernel flaw disclosed in 2016 on a system reached through a 2024 application flaw, which is the pattern this corpus records repeatedly: a current vulnerability for entry, a long-unpatched one for privilege. Patch currency on the underlying operating system matters as much as on the application, and is more often neglected on single-purpose appliance-like servers.
how.caveat: Single-purpose servers built years ago for one application are the usual holders of ancient kernel flaws, because nobody wants to risk the application by patching underneath it.

how.logic: Both flaws here appear in the published known-exploited catalogue, so the catalogue join would have surfaced this asset before the intrusion. The advisory's own first recommendation is prioritising patching of public-facing systems and known exploited vulnerabilities.
how.caveat: Only works where the asset is in the inventory. A geospatial server owned by a mapping or planning team is exactly the kind of asset that is not.

where.title: CISA Shares Lessons Learned from an Incident Response Engagement

notes: A useful reminder that the exposed estate includes specialist applications nobody in security has heard of. A geospatial data server is not on any standard asset checklist, and neither are the equivalents in other organisations.

what.summary: A command injection flaw in the remote access portal of a firewall platform was among the appliance vulnerabilities state-sponsored actors used to compromise networks feeding an espionage programme.

how.logic: Exploitation of this class of flaw leaves files or scheduled activity on the appliance that no release installed. The device's own logs and any vendor integrity facility are the evidence, and both need deliberate collection because the appliance does not volunteer it.
how.caveat: Where compromise is suspected, out-of-band examination beats interrogating a device that may be lying about itself.

how.logic: Restarts or configuration writes on the appliance with no matching change record. Individually routine, and the pairing within a short window is what carries information.
how.caveat: Planned maintenance produces the same pair. Needs a change feed to suppress against.

how.logic: Another entry in the pattern this corpus records repeatedly: an internet-facing remote access appliance vulnerability turned into operational use quickly. The remediation tolerance for this asset class is hours to days, not a monthly cycle.
how.caveat: Patching these usually means an outage, which is why the window stays open. That is a scheduling problem rather than a detection one.

what.summary: A ransomware gang exploited a SQL injection flaw in a managed file transfer product at scale, stealing data from a very large number of organisations at once, having previously done the same through a flaw in a competing file transfer product.

how.logic: A managed file transfer product is internet-facing by design, holds the data being transferred, and is frequently owned by a business function rather than by IT. That combination is why this class has been exploited at scale twice by the same actor through two different vendors' products. The questions are which such products you run, whether they are in the patch cycle, and critically what data is retained on them rather than merely passing through, because retained data is what gets taken.

fields.note: the volume held at rest decides the impact, independent of the vulnerability

how.caveat: Retention on transfer appliances is usually configured for convenience and never revisited, so the impact of a compromise is far larger than the transfer volume suggests. Reducing retention limits the damage from the next flaw in this class, which is a more durable control than patching any one of them.

how.logic: Exploitation of the injection flaw led to code execution and web shell placement on the transfer server, so the application process creating a shell, and new servable files appearing, are the on-host observables.
how.caveat: Product updates write to the same directories; suppress against the patching window.

how.logic: The objective was theft rather than encryption, so the observable is bulk retrieval rather than damage. Volume of data read out of the application per session or per account, against that application's own baseline, is the signal. Because the product exists to move files, only the rate and the requesting identity distinguish theft from use.

fields.note: per session and per account, against the application's own baseline

notes: The defining feature is leverage: one vulnerability in one widely deployed product yielded data from a very large number of unrelated organisations simultaneously, including onward victims whose data was held by a third party using the product. what.summary: Multiple separate threat actors, including a state-sponsored one, exploited a deserialisation flaw in a user interface component library embedded in a web application on a federal agency's web server, giving remote code execution.

how.logic: The vulnerable code is a third-party interface component compiled into a web application, so nothing in the asset inventory names it and a scanner looking at the web server sees the server rather than the component. Finding it means enumerating the component libraries inside deployed applications, which usually requires asking the application owner or examining the deployed assemblies directly. This is the same structural problem as an embedded logging library or an embedded network stack, and it recurs often enough in this corpus to treat as a standing question rather than a one-off.

fields.note: populated from deployed assemblies and application documentation, not from active discovery

how.caveat: Application teams frequently do not know which component versions they ship, particularly for applications built years earlier by contractors who have since left. That uncertainty is the finding.

how.logic: Deserialisation exploitation runs code inside the web server worker process, so the observable is that process creating a shell or interpreter child. On a web server hosting a business application the legitimate set of children is small and enumerable.
how.caveat: Some applications shell out for reporting or file conversion. Baseline and allow-list by command line.

how.logic: Multiple actors exploited the same flaw at the same victim, which is the second instance of this in the corpus. A publicly known flaw on an exposed service is a shared opportunity, not one actor's discovery, so incident scoping should assume more than one entrant until the evidence rules it out.
how.caveat: An investigative discipline rather than a query. It matters because attributing all observed activity to the first actor identified produces a scoping error rather than merely an attribution one.

what.summary: A crafted archive that appears to contain a harmless document but executes code when the user opens that document was among the routes a Russian military intelligence unit used against logistics and technology targets.

how.logic: The exploit relies on the archive tool launching something other than the file the user selected, so the detection is the archiver process creating an executable or script child. An archive utility exists to extract files, not to run them, which makes the parent-child pairing close to unambiguous.
how.caveat: Self-extracting installers legitimately spawn processes from an archiver context. Those are identifiable by signer, and the exception list is short.

how.logic: The technique depends on a mismatch between what the archive appears to contain and what it actually runs, so inspecting archive contents at the gateway rather than only the archive itself is what catches it before delivery.
how.caveat: Requires a gateway that unpacks archives and inspects contents, including nested and password-protected ones, which is where most inspection stops.

who.versions_affected: Fixed in Switchvox 8.4.0.2, released 14 July 2026. The article names no affected version range below that build.

what.summary: An unauthenticated SQL injection in the /pa phone notification endpoint of Sangoma Switchvox, reached by posting XML whose PhoneIP element is concatenated into a query executed as PostgreSQL superuser, was exploited against internet-facing honeypots after the fixed build was released, the attacker submitting a netcat command piped into a shell and then a process listing whose output was carried out in the path of a cleartext HTTP request.

how.logic: Switchvox exposes an unauthenticated HTTP endpoint, /pa, which parses an XML message when it receives a request to notify another phone system. The handler validates only that the posted body starts with a PolycomIPPhone element, parses the rest as XML, and concatenates the PhoneIP element into an unparameterised SQL string executed as PostgreSQL superuser. Where request bodies are retained, the detection is a PhoneIP value that is not an address: one carrying a single quote, a semicolon, a comment sequence or SQL keywords.

markers.note: matched rather than compared because a proxy log records the absolute URL and a web server log records the path; anchored on the end so it does not also take /path and /patch

markers.expr: PhoneIP element in the posted XML contains a quote, a semicolon, a comment sequence or a SQL keyword

how.caveat: The payload travels in the body and most web logs keep the request line and not the body, so this block is answerable only where bodies are retained; the request-line fallback is a separate block because the two are alternatives selected by available telemetry and one marker list cannot carry an alternative. The article prints no example request as text -- the exploit appears only in figure images -- so the body test is written from the line-by-line data flow the article sets out rather than from a captured request. Matching the opening PolycomIPPhone element on its own identifies the endpoint and never the attack, because a legitimate notification carries it too, which is why it is not a marker here.

how.logic: Where request bodies are not retained, all that is left of the /pa endpoint is the request line. The publisher does not say which hosts legitimately post to /pa, so this half needs the observed caller set baselined on the estate before it can be used at all; once it is, a POST to /pa from outside that set is worth reading on the path and source address alone.

markers.expr: POST to the /pa endpoint from a source address outside the set baselined on the estate as legitimate callers

how.caveat: The publisher supplies nothing towards the baseline this rests on: the article describes the feature as letting supported phones receive notifications, describes the endpoint as receiving a request to notify another phone system, and names no legitimate source of POSTs to /pa. Until the caller set is measured locally this is a hunt and not a rule. It cannot separate an exploit from a malformed notification, on an internet-exposed device it will carry ordinary scanning with it, and an estate with teleworker handsets registering from the internet has no clean inside-outside line to draw.

how.logic: Switchvox records executed SQL in /var/log/switchvox/db-quirks.log, so an injection that ran leaves the statement that ran. In the example the publisher prints, the appended statement is a COPY of an empty select TO PROGRAM, which is how the injection reaches operating system command execution. A TO PROGRAM clause appearing in that log at all is the test, and it is short and literal enough to stand on its own.

markers.expr: logged SQL statement contains a TO PROGRAM clause

how.caveat: The log sits on the appliance and the article frames reading it as something done over SSH, so an estate that does not forward appliance logs holds this evidence and cannot query it. No marker names the log file, because the file is the source of the events rather than a field within them; the path is given here so a collector can be pointed at it. On the excerpt itself: the publisher presents it as being from the exploitation attempt, but both addresses in it are private -- 10.0.0.1 in the predicate and 10.0.18.42 as the callback destination -- so it is read here as a reproduction rather than the captured attempt. That reading is this record's inference and not the publisher's wording. Either way the port, the temporary file name and both addresses in that excerpt are not treated as indicators, and only the statement shape carries over.

how.logic: The second shape in the same log is the application's own auto_phone_config lookup on ip_address terminated early with a quote and a semicolon, with the remainder of the original query commented out. It catches an injection whether or not that injection went on to reach command execution.

markers.expr: logged SQL statement carries a statement separator or a comment sequence inside the predicate on auto_phone_config.ip_address

how.caveat: Held as a block of its own rather than conjoined with the TO PROGRAM test, because the publisher does not say whether db-quirks.log writes a submitted string as one line or one line per statement; if it logs per statement the two shapes land on different events and a conjunction of them could never match. The selected column list is deliberately not part of the test: the printed excerpt selects proposed_extension, but nothing in the article says that column list is fixed, and gating on it would break the rule if the query changed. Applications that build SQL by concatenation produce odd-looking statements legitimately, so characterise the appliance's normal log output once before alerting on this.

how.logic: The injected statement runs with PostgreSQL superuser rights and reaches the operating system through a TO PROGRAM clause, so the command is started by the database backend rather than by the web tier, and a rule keyed to the web server as the parent sees nothing. The confirming observation is an operating system process started by the database backend at all.

markers.expr: operating system process whose parent is the PostgreSQL backend serving the application
markers.note: the two commands the publisher quotes from the honeypot are a netcat connection piped into a shell and a single top process listing; they are held as context rather than as a second clause, because a rule that required them would match only this operator's two payloads and nothing else through the same mechanism

how.caveat: The article describes the execution mechanism and quotes the commands, but says nothing about what process telemetry a Switchvox appliance produces, and embedded appliances commonly produce none. Where that is so this block cannot be answered at all and the query log is the only evidence on the device. The publisher also does not say what the immediate child of the backend is named, so the test is written on the parentage alone and not on a process name list. Confidence is medium because the parentage is read off the mechanism the article describes rather than off a process event the publisher reports observing.

how.logic: The publisher names one source address that exploited several honeypots in quick succession and instructs readers to check whether it appears in any network requests related to their Switchvox device. This block is the inbound direction: that address as the source of traffic reaching the appliance, which is the half a device with no egress visibility can still answer.

iocs.note: source of the observed exploitation across several honeypots

how.caveat: One operator's infrastructure on one date, so it decays quickly and its absence proves nothing. The sweep reaches only as far back as flow and web log retention allows. Bound to the source side deliberately: the outbound callback to the same address is a separate block, because a marker list is conjunctive and cannot ask both directions at once. Fidelity follows the cited pattern, which is a retrospective sweep of retained data rather than a rule to wake someone with.

how.logic: The same address is the destination in the netcat command the publisher records as the attacker's initial payload, on port 39323. This block is the outbound direction: a session from the appliance to that address and that port.

iocs.note: destination in the netcat command the publisher records as the initial payload

markers.note: destination port in the submitted netcat command

how.caveat: Narrow by construction: it asks for one address on one port and a rotation of either defeats it. The publisher says the command was submitted, not that the callback connected, so finding nothing here is not evidence that the exploitation failed. On an appliance with no proxy in front of it the flow record is all there is. The publisher gives no further infrastructure, no hashes and no domains.

how.logic: After the netcat payload the attacker ran a process listing on the appliance and carried the output back inside the path of a cleartext HTTP request, base64 encoded and appended to an identifier for that exploit attempt, so the answer never appears in any request or response body. Look for cleartext HTTP originated by the telephony appliance, addressed to an address literal rather than a hostname, whose path carries a long base64 run.

markers.note: bound explicitly because the default binding for this marker type is the IP protocol, which holds tcp or udp and never http; the request being cleartext is why the path is readable at a proxy at all

markers.expr: HTTP request host is an address literal rather than a hostname
request path carries a base64 run longer than a length bound measured on the estate
markers.note: stated as a run rather than as the whole path, because in the observed request the encoded output is appended to a fixed exploit-attempt identifier after an underscore, so a test requiring the entire path to decode would not match it

how.caveat: The length bound must be measured against the estate and is deliberately left unresolved: applications legitimately carry base64 in paths, cache keys and tracking parameters, and a bound imported from elsewhere either fires constantly or never fires. Scoping to traffic the appliance originated is left to the rule author as a dataset and asset choice rather than expressed as a marker. The publisher prints the request with the destination and the attempt identifier redacted, so only the shape is available and not a literal path, and the article does not say the destination is the same address as the netcat callback. The destination being an address rather than a hostname is read off the publisher's own redaction placeholder and is not stated anywhere else in the article, so treat that clause as the weakest of the three. netflow is not declared here: a flow record keeps the destination and loses the path, so where no proxy terminates the appliance's egress this reduces to the destination checks in the two preceding blocks.

where.title: Off the Hook: Discovering and Observing Active Exploitation of Sangoma Switchvox CVE-2026-9586

notes: Exploitation followed the patch rather than preceding it: the fixed build shipped on 14 July 2026 and the honeypots tripped on 30 August 2026, so this is n-day activity even though the honeypot estate, run with Defused Cyber and deployed on 8 May 2026, was put there to catch zero-day use. The publisher reported 12 distinct vulnerabilities in Switchvox and covers only this one here, because only this one has been seen exploited; the other 11 are not described and are not part of this record. The FreePBX identifiers CVE-2025-57819 and CVE-2025-64328 are named in the article solely as the reason the researchers looked at the Sangoma ecosystem -- they concern a different product and no activity against them is reported here, so they are deliberately absent from what.vulnerabilities. Shodan is cited as showing roughly 4,000 internet-exposed instances, most in the United States; that is exposure, not a victim count, and the article gives no victim count, sector or region. who2.target_sectors is therefore absent rather than set to cross_sector: the observed targets were the publisher's own honeypots, so there is no victim sector to record, and the publisher's assessment that most internet-exposed instances will be or have already been targeted is about exposure rather than about any sector. That assessment rests on the same source address hitting several honeypots in quick succession. Provenance note: the URL circulated for this article, ending cve-2026-9586-sangoma-switchvox-active-exploitation, returns 404; the canonical link in the page itself is the one recorded here and it carries the same title, author and 1 September 2026 date.

who.versions_affected: Named MODICON and MODICON Nano families, with the advisory noting the list may not be exhaustive

what.summary: Four agencies warned that advanced actors had developed custom modular tooling giving full system access to named controller families from two vendors and to a widely used industrial data server standard. The tooling scans for, compromises and controls devices once the actors are inside the operational network, and presents a virtual console whose command interface mirrors that of the targeted device, which the advisory states enables lower-skilled actors to emulate higher-skilled capabilities. Modules can scan for devices, gather device detail, upload malicious configuration or code, back up or restore device contents, and modify device parameters. A companion tool installs a known-vulnerable signed motherboard driver to execute code in the operating system kernel on engineering workstations in either the information or operational technology environment.

how.logic: The modules interact over normal management protocols and the standard industrial protocol on its usual port, so the traffic is well formed and unremarkable. What is anomalous is the source and the authorisation: engineering protocol traffic from a host that is not a designated engineering workstation, and program or configuration operations with no authorising change record. Module capability includes uploading code and modifying device parameters, so a configuration write is the damage rather than a precursor to it.
how.caveat: The lasting significance is not the device list but the console. Purpose-built tooling that mirrors the target's own interface lowers the skill floor for attacking control systems, which breaks the assumption that these attacks require rare expertise and therefore come from rare adversaries. The set of actors able to execute now grows independently of the set able to build.

how.logic: One module runs a rapid scan identifying every controller of that vendor on the local network using the vendor's own multicast discovery on a fixed port, which the advisory notes is the same mechanism engineering workstations use legitimately. The protocol and the traffic are therefore entirely normal and the only discriminator is which host is doing it.
how.caveat: Cheap to build and stable to maintain, because the list of hosts entitled to run vendor discovery on a control network is short and rarely changes. It also fires at reconnaissance, which is unusually early relative to the damage in this class of intrusion.

how.logic: A companion tool installs and exploits a known-vulnerable signed motherboard driver to execute code in the kernel, which works on engineering workstations in either environment and enables lateral movement and disruption. The driver is legitimately signed, so signature checking passes; the detection is the presence of that driver where no corresponding hardware or vendor utility exists.
how.caveat: A vendor-signed driver with a known flaw is a legitimate file, so blocking by reputation fails. The tractable control is a driver allow-list on engineering workstations, which is more achievable there than on a general estate because the hardware population is small and fixed.

how.logic: The advisory's own prioritised actions are a second factor on all remote access to control networks and devices, and changing every password including all defaults to device-unique strong values on a consistent schedule, explicitly so that brute force is mitigated and so that monitoring has something to detect. That second clause is the interesting one: unique credentials are recommended partly to create detectable failures.
how.caveat: Worth noting the reasoning: shared or default credentials do not merely permit access, they remove the failed-authentication signal that would otherwise reveal an attempt. The third recommended action, continuous operational technology monitoring, presumes the first two have created something to observe.

where.publisher: Department of Energy, CISA, NSA and FBI
where.title: APT Cyber Tools Targeting ICS/SCADA Devices

notes: The most consequential operational technology record in the corpus, not because of what was done with the tooling but because of what the tooling is. A modular framework with a console mirroring the target device's own interface, explicitly assessed as letting lower-skilled actors emulate higher-skilled capabilities, breaks the assumption that control system attacks are rare because the expertise is rare. It also spans two controller vendors and an open industrial standard, so it is not a single-vendor problem. The vulnerable signed driver component is a reminder that the engineering workstation is the softest part of the chain and sits in whichever environment happens to be convenient.

what.summary: Five agencies described an active campaign building controller tooling out of the same open-source industrial library that legitimate monitoring software uses, with AI assistance to write the scripts around it. Because the library speaks S7comm correctly, nothing malformed reaches the wire and the resulting tool presents as an OT monitoring product. The activity observed is read and write access to data blocks, which the agencies assess as reconnaissance and pre-positioning rather than an attempt at immediate effect.

how.logic: The snap7 library -- snap7.dll on Windows, python-snap7 as its binding -- present, loaded or imported on a host that is not an approved engineering workstation. This is the one stage of the campaign that leaves a distinctive artefact, because the wire traffic it goes on to produce is protocol-correct by construction and the tool is dressed as monitoring software. The legitimate population of hosts carrying this library is small, enumerable and changes only when the engineering estate changes.

fields.note: catches the python-snap7 import; pair with the module-load event where the sensor emits one
compare against the approved engineering workstation list; the allow list is the detection, and without it this fires on every legitimate engineering host

how.caveat: snap7 is legitimate software and is exactly what an integrator's own tooling may be built on. The finding is the host, not the library, so this is only a detection where the approved engineering workstation list is maintained. Where endpoint agents are not permitted on engineering hosts for vendor support reasons, this block cannot be implemented at all and the network blocks below are the only route.

how.logic: S7comm to a controller on TCP 102 from a source that is not the engineering station that owns it. The tooling described here speaks the protocol correctly, so the source address is the discriminator rather than anything in the payload.

fields.note: compare against the engineering stations that own these controllers, and against any integrator remote-access range

how.caveat: Commissioning, firmware upgrades and vendor support all produce legitimate S7comm from unusual sources, and a third-party integrator with remote access is the case the advisory calls out specifically: the asset owner often does not know that path exists. Enumerate integrator access before treating an unknown source as hostile.

how.logic: Sequential addresses contacted on TCP 102 from one source, or repeated connections to one controller with varying parameters while CPU properties are enumerated. The actors reach the target list through internet scanning services rather than by scanning themselves, so the sweep that reaches your estate may be short and already targeted.

fields.note: count distinct xdm.target.ipv4 per source over a short window

how.caveat: Because the target list is bought from a scanning service rather than built by scanning, a low distinct-target count is not evidence of benign activity. Set the threshold low and expect the sweep against any one site to be small.

how.logic: Data block reads, and any write to a data block or configuration area, outside an authorised change window or with no corresponding work order. The agencies place the observed activity at read and write on data blocks, so this is the block that would have caught the campaign at the stage it is currently at.

fields.note: where the ICS sensor decodes S7comm function codes; otherwise fall back to session timing alone
compare against the maintenance calendar, not against a fixed hour range

how.caveat: Off-hours is a weak signal on its own in a continuous-process plant that runs three shifts, and the advisory's own framing is connections outside change windows rather than outside office hours. A site without a machine-readable change calendar cannot implement this block as written.

how.logic: Controllers reachable with unconfigured or default authentication, and protection levels left unset. The advisory names this as the access route rather than a vulnerability chain, so an inventory of protection-level configuration is the assessment that matters.

fields.note: join against the configured protection level per controller

how.caveat: This is a configuration audit rather than a detection, and it is the finding most likely to be actionable today: the agencies describe access to devices with unconfigured or minimally configured authentication, not exploitation of a specific flaw.

how.logic: Not a detection. The agencies state that AI assistance is being used to turn public vulnerability information into working ICS exploitation scripts, which shortens the interval between a disclosure being public and a usable exploit existing for equipment that is patched on an annual outage cycle. Treat the disclosure date of an S7 advisory, rather than the date exploitation is first reported, as the point at which exposure begins.

fields.note: the output is a revised patch-priority list, not an alert

how.caveat: The agencies assert the capability and describe its effect; they do not publish evidence of the generation step itself, and nothing here is observable in a defender's telemetry. Its value is in changing how an OT patch window is planned, and it should not be passed on as though it were a detectable event.

what.summary: A ransomware group operating since 2022 added a remote support platform vulnerability to its initial access set, alongside long-standing flaws in a remote access appliance and a mail server, and the advisory was refreshed eighteen months after publication with new techniques.

how.logic: The fourth distinct remote support or management product used as an entry route in this corpus. That establishes the class rather than any one product: internet-facing by design so technicians can reach it, holding privileged access to every endpoint it manages, and typically outside the patch cadence applied to servers. Inventory every such platform including ones inherited through acquisition or run by a supplier on your behalf, and treat their patch currency at domain controller priority.
how.caveat: Exposure is deliberate in this class, so reduction means changing how remote support is delivered rather than adjusting a firewall. That is a support-model decision and usually resisted.

how.logic: Once held, the platform does what it was built to do on the attacker's behalf and endpoint agents will not object, because it is trusted. The platform's own audit trail is the only place the activity is distinguishable, and it must be collected off the platform.
how.caveat: Legitimate mass support looks identical. Authorisation and timing are the only separators.

how.logic: The set spans a 2018 appliance flaw, a 2020 authentication bypass and 2022 mail server flaws alongside the 2024 one, so this group has been reusing the same reliable old vulnerabilities for years. Sorting exposed assets by the age of their oldest unpatched flaw surfaces exactly this.
how.caveat: The old flaws are the ones most likely to sit on assets nobody currently owns.

notes: A nearly three-year campaign whose advisory was updated once with new techniques and refreshed indicators, and which explicitly removed outdated ones. The mix of a 2018 flaw and a 2024 flaw in the same initial access set is the clearest single illustration of why patch programmes need both a fast lane for new disclosures and a sweep for old ones.

who.versions_affected: Servers with any federated authentication provider configured and a technician group associated with it

what.summary: A remote monitoring and management product validated federated authentication assertions insufficiently, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to have a privileged technician account created and authenticated for them. The resulting account could remote into managed endpoints and execute scripts by default. Where the server was configured to require a second factor for technicians, the requirement did not prevent this: technicians self-register their own factor at first login, so the attacker supplied it and the policy was satisfied rather than bypassed. The vendor had prior entries in the catalogue of vulnerabilities known to have been exploited, and the finding was produced by an automated vulnerability research pipeline against code that had previously been audited by hand.

how.logic: The account is created by the login itself, so there is no provisioning event and no administrator in the chain. Detect on a privileged account whose creation and first authentication fall in the same session, with no corresponding membership change on the identity provider side.
how.caveat: The application's own log records a successful login and, on its own reasoning, is correct. The discrepancy is only visible against provider-side records, so a detection built from application logs alone cannot show it.

how.logic: Nothing fails, so failure-based detection is silent. The observable is a factor enrolled during the account's first successful authentication, from the same session that the enrolment then authorises.
how.caveat: Real joiners generate the same sequence, so this needs a joiner source to be alertable. Here it is strengthened by the account being one that should not exist at all.

what.summary: A Russian foreign intelligence service inserted a backdoored library into a network management vendor's build process, where it was signed with the vendor's own code signing certificate and shipped as a normal update. Once inside, the actor stole the token signing certificate and minted its own valid federated identity tokens, added credentials to cloud application identities, and added federation trusts so that authentication could occur outside the victim's visibility. Other initial access routes were confirmed, including password spraying and a forged multi-factor cookie built from a stolen secret. The actor targeted the mailboxes of information technology and incident response staff.

how.logic: The malicious library was added to the vendor's software lifecycle and then signed by the legitimate vendor certificate, so signature verification, publisher allow-listing and reputation all returned correct and useless answers. What remained detectable was behaviour: the backdoor called out to a victim-specific subdomain using a protocol designed to imitate the product's own legitimate traffic. Detection has to be a comparison of what the product does after the update against what it did before, plus egress restriction for a platform that has no reason to reach arbitrary destinations.
how.caveat: The affected units are specific builds, not the product, so an inventory that records only product and major version cannot answer the exposure question at all. Note also that the platform is commonly configured with pervasive privilege in order to do its job, which the advisory states directly, so compromising it grants further access anywhere those accounts are trusted.

markers.note: raw field software_version

how.logic: The advisory is explicit that not all organisations that received the backdoor were targeted with follow-on actions, and that observing traffic to the initial beacon domain does not by itself mean the backdoor was leveraged. The discriminator it gives is additional canonical name resolutions associated with that domain, which indicate the operator selected the victim and acted. Retained resolver logs, including the answers rather than only the queries, are what separate a mass-delivery event from a mass-compromise event.
how.caveat: By the time the domain was sinkholed to a blocked address, the advisory notes that anyone whose command channel had already moved past the initial beacon would continue to be compromised regardless. So absence of beacon traffic after that date is not evidence of anything, and the triage only works against retained data from before it.

how.logic: Using escalated directory privilege the actor compromised the token signing certificate, then created unauthorised but cryptographically valid tokens and presented them to every service trusting that identity provider, reaching hosted mail, file storage, business intelligence, travel and timecard systems and exfiltrating through authorised interfaces. The advisory supplies four token anomalies: validity far longer than the usual hour, durations expressed in exact whole seconds, issue time identical to first use time, and a token in use with no sign-in for that account within the preceding hour. A fifth is missing or unusual multi-factor claims where multi-factor is enforced.
how.caveat: Authentication with no authentication event, valid across every federated service simultaneously. Requires identity provider logs correlated with cloud access logs, which are usually owned by different teams and retained for different periods, and remediation means rotating the signing certificate, which is disruptive enough to get deferred.

how.logic: The actor added new federation trusts to existing on-premises identity infrastructure. The advisory states that where this technique is used, authentication can occur outside the organisation's known infrastructure and may not be visible to the legitimate system owner at all. The only moment it is detectable is the configuration change itself, and the legitimate rate of such changes is close to zero.
how.caveat: The most complete persistence outcome in this corpus. Nothing downstream will ever flag it, because downstream services are correctly trusting the identity provider they were told to trust.

how.logic: The actor added tokens and certificates to existing cloud application service principals, giving both persistence and a programmatic route to hosted resources through the tenant's own interfaces. The advisory notes this generates little evidence or telemetry, and that the resulting activity appears to be the individual's own access, which is normal and on some licensing tiers is not logged at all. Alert on the credential addition, since subsequent use is designed to be unremarkable.
how.caveat: The licensing dependency matters: the same attack is detectable in one tenant and invisible in another with identical configuration. Establish which of those you are before relying on this.

how.logic: At one victim the actor used a previously stolen secret key to generate a cookie satisfying the multi-factor system protecting web mail. The factor was computed rather than evaded, so the sign-in is fully policy-compliant. Detection needs the multi-factor product's own logs alongside the application's: a successful second factor with no corresponding challenge recorded at the service that should have issued it.
how.caveat: This is where multi-factor stops being a terminal control. The shared secret underwriting it is a credential like any other, and its rotation is rarely on an incident checklist. The advisory notes this case also proves initial access routes existed beyond the compromised update.

how.logic: The actor targeted mailboxes of key personnel including information technology and incident response staff, and the advisory separately warns that organisations with suspected compromise must be conscious of operational security while responding and while planning remediation. During a response, treat responders as a monitored population: access to their mail and files, rules created on their accounts, and access to the incident documentation itself.
how.caveat: If eviction is planned in email the actor can read, the actor leaves before eviction and returns by a route the plan did not cover. Out-of-band coordination has to be arranged before it is needed, which makes this a preparedness item rather than a detection.

how.logic: The backdoor checked hard-coded address ranges including reserved space to recognise analysis environments and halted if found, and used threshold checks to keep the delay between command attempts unpredictable, which the advisory notes frustrates traditional network-based analysis. Reported steganography further obscured the channel. Where jitter defeats periodicity, fall back on the destination set over a long window, the send-to-receive byte ratio, and sessions with no name lookup and no browser string.
how.caveat: A benign dynamic-analysis verdict may only mean the sample recognised the sandbox. CISA notes it had not independently confirmed the steganography reporting, so that element is second-hand.

how.logic: Because the tokens and accounts used were valid, the advisory states detection requires the maturity to identify actions outside a user's normal duties, and gives a worked example: an account belonging to human resources would not need to reach a threat intelligence database. That is role-appropriate access as a detection rather than credential validity, and it needs an owner-approved statement of which populations should reach which systems.
how.caveat: The prerequisite is knowing what each population legitimately touches, which most organisations have never written down. Worth noting this is the fallback when every other signal is correct by construction.

how.logic: The actor used virtual private servers with addresses in the victim's own country for most communications, to sit among legitimate user traffic, and rotated last-mile addresses frequently. The advisory pairs this with impossible travel as the detection opportunity that survives it, while noting legitimate remote access products produce false positives against that check.
how.caveat: Geographic and reputational blocking is useless by design here, since the infrastructure is domestic to the victim. Frequent last-mile rotation also means an address blocklist decays immediately.

where.title: Advanced Persistent Threat Compromise of Government Agencies, Critical Infrastructure, and Private Sector Organizations

notes: The most consequential single record in this corpus for the number of controls it defeats at once: code signing, publisher allow-listing, reputation, multi-factor authentication, and the identity provider's own audit trail. The durable lesson is not the compromised update, which is well known, but that once directory administrator privilege is reached the identity layer itself becomes the persistence mechanism, and every downstream service then behaves correctly while being wrong. Note also that the government attribution arrived four months after the initial advisory, which is the normal order and a reason not to wait for attribution before acting. who.versions_affected: Console access to message history for accounts delivering authentication codes

what.summary: An operator running a persistent credential-phishing campaign against technology companies reached the internal console of a messaging provider used to deliver one-time codes, searched it for the mobile numbers of accounts whose passwords they already held, and read the codes issued in response to challenges they triggered themselves. The second factor was defeated at a supplier the account holders had no relationship with.

how.logic: Codes were requested by the operator using previously stolen passwords, then read in the supplier's console. At the identity provider the visible shape is a challenge triggered for an account whose credential is known to be exposed, satisfied without any interaction on the enrolled device.
how.caveat: The interception happens in a system you do not log, so the identity provider alone cannot see it and neither marker is available there in full. The publisher's own remedial action is the instructive one and it was architectural rather than detective: they moved this traffic to an alternative provider and, separately, promote an authenticator bound to the origin so that no code exists to intercept.

markers.expr: message-delivered passcode challenge triggered for an account whose credential appears in a known exposure set
passcode consumed successfully with no corresponding interaction on the enrolled device
third parties able to read authentication material are enumerated and access-reviewed

how.logic: The credentials used to trigger the challenges came from a long-running phishing campaign that stood up multiple sites against the same organisation within hours of each other. Repetition against one target inside a short window is itself the pattern, and it means a single takedown is not a response.
how.caveat: The publisher records observing this operator repeatedly targeting the same organisations with several phishing sites within hours. Treat the first sighting as the start of a campaign against you rather than as an isolated site, and hunt for the others.

markers.expr: more than one distinct lookalike sign-in domain for the same organisation observed within 24h

where.title: Detecting Scatter Swine: Insights into a Relentless Phishing Campaign

notes: Published by the identity provider whose customers were affected rather than by the breached supplier, and the numbers are theirs: 38 mobile numbers searched directly by the operator, nearly all belonging to one targeted organisation, with a code valid for five minutes. Carried for the dependency rather than the incident -- a code delivered by message is legible wherever it passes.

who.versions_affected: Vision Series programmable logic controllers with integrated human machine interface, including older models; devices may be rebranded and appear to originate from other manufacturers

what.summary: Actors affiliated with an Iranian military force, operating under a hacktivist persona, compromised at least 75 internet-facing controllers across four waves, including at least 34 in United States water and wastewater facilities. They authenticated to devices on the default port that had a default password or no password at all, left a political defacement message, then erased the original control program and downloaded one containing no inputs or outputs. They also renamed devices, reset the software version backwards, disabled upload and download functions and changed default port numbers, each of which obstructed the owner's ability to recover. Targeting was based on the equipment being Israeli-made rather than on the victim's sector.

how.logic: Every compromise in this campaign followed the same three conditions: the controller was reachable from the internet, it listened on the vendor default port, and it had the vendor default password or none. No vulnerability was exploited and no malware was used. Each of the three is answerable from an inventory scan, and removing any one of them defeats the campaign entirely.
how.caveat: The advisory notes these controllers may be rebranded and appear to come from other manufacturers, so an inventory search by vendor name will under-count. Search by the default port and by device fingerprint as well as by brand.

how.logic: The original ladder logic file was erased and replaced with one containing no inputs and no outputs, so the device kept running while directing nothing. Custom logic files were built for each device type, including older models. The confirming signal is not on the network: process values and outputs going static while the controller still answers as healthy.
how.caveat: A reachability or heartbeat check will report the device fine. This is the corpus's clearest case for monitoring the process rather than the equipment, because the equipment was never broken, only emptied.

how.logic: Devices were renamed, which delayed operators reconnecting because the device name is a required field when establishing a remote connection to these controllers. The rename is the denial mechanism rather than a cosmetic act.
how.caveat: If the recovery procedure requires connecting by device name, and the attacker controls the name, the procedure fails at step one. Keep an out-of-band record of device identity and addressing.

how.logic: The software version of the logic file was set to an older release, which stopped operators communicating with the controller from their engineering workstation unless the workstation's software was also downgraded to match. Version numbers only increase in legitimate operation, so a decrease is close to a pure signal and is cheap to poll for.
how.caveat: Together with disabling the upload and download functions and changing the default port, this is a deliberate anti-remediation set. The effect is that the owner's own tooling no longer works against their own equipment, so recovery becomes a tooling exercise before it is a configuration one.

how.logic: The defacement message states that any equipment made in Israel is a legitimate target, and the advisory records targeting in the United States, the United Kingdom and elsewhere as part of a wider campaign against Israeli-made technology. So the selection criterion is the manufacturer of the equipment, not the sector, size or location of the operator.
how.caveat: A targeting model no operator can influence and few risk assessments capture: the question is not what the device does or how critical it is, but where it was made. Worth holding an inventory dimension for equipment origin for exactly this reason.

how.logic: The persona claimed responsibility on a messaging channel for numerous attacks over several weeks, and the advisory records that several of those claimed compromises of critical infrastructure were false. So a public claim is an effect in its own right and has to be verified against telemetry before it is responded to.
how.caveat: The asymmetry favours the claimant: fabricating a claim costs nothing, refuting it requires retained evidence. Treat the claim and the compromise as two separate questions with two separate answers.

where.title: IRGC-Affiliated Cyber Actors Exploit PLCs in Multiple Sectors, Including US Water and Wastewater Systems Facilities

notes: The most instructive operational technology record in the corpus, because nothing sophisticated happened. No vulnerability, no malware, no exploit: internet-facing controllers with default or absent passwords on the default port. Seventy-five devices, thirty-four of them in water utilities. The genuinely novel material is the anti-remediation set, which is not represented anywhere else here: renaming the device so the owner cannot address it, rolling the software version backwards so the owner's engineering workstation cannot talk to it, disabling upload and download, and changing the port. Those four actions attack the recovery procedure rather than the equipment, which is a category of harm most response plans do not contemplate.

what.summary: A national authority reported active exploitation in its own jurisdiction of a critical authentication bypass in a widely deployed web hosting control panel, which lets an unauthenticated remote attacker reach the control panel and go on to execute code. The affected range is everything after a release from 2013, so the practical reading is that any unpatched instance is affected. No sector was being singled out, but the authority made a specific observation about how the damage propagated: instances managed by several managed service providers were compromised, and the providers' customers were compromised as a consequence. That makes the exposure question one an organisation may not be able to answer from its own estate, because the vulnerable panel belongs to the provider. The vendor published indicator detection scripts, and the identifier is also flagged in the known-exploited catalogue as having been used in ransomware campaigns.

how.logic: The authority's first two mitigations are both inventory questions rather than monitoring ones: which hosts run the control panel and at what version, and whether that interface needs to face the internet at all. Because the affected range starts at a 2013 release, a version comparison is nearly redundant -- presence plus internet exposure plus unpatched is the finding, and the second condition is the one an owner can actually change quickly.
how.caveat: A control panel is meant to be reachable by the customers who administer their own hosting, so exposure here is the product working as intended and cannot simply be removed. Restricting the source range and putting the panel behind an authenticated proxy is the achievable version of this mitigation for most owners.

how.logic: The propagation path named in the advisory is provider to customer, and the advisory's own instruction to affected organisations is to contact the provider and confirm patching and monitoring. Detection therefore starts as a register: which providers operate a hosting control panel on the organisation's behalf, what that panel can reach, and whether the organisation would see an intrusion that arrived through it. Where the provider holds administrative access into the estate, treat that access as a monitored population in its own right rather than as trusted.
how.caveat: The answer to this often sits in a contract rather than in telemetry, and the organisations most exposed are the ones least able to compel an answer. Record what the provider will not tell you as a gap rather than leaving the question open.

how.logic: The bypass reaches the panel; the consequence the advisory names is code execution. On the host that means the web or panel service process creating a shell or an interpreter, and content appearing in served directories that no deployment produced. This is the stage where the compromise becomes visible on a box whose authentication logs will show nothing wrong, because the authentication was bypassed rather than defeated.
how.caveat: Hosting control panels legitimately spawn shells and interpreters as part of their normal function, which makes this noisier here than on an ordinary web server. Baseline the panel's own behaviour first, and prefer the served-directory half on this product class. The vendor also published indicator detection scripts, which are the more direct check where the appliance can be reached.
