who.versions_affected: Releases carrying the authentication-bypass family, and any deployment still shipping the documented default token signing key

what.summary: An internet-exposed service-discovery and dynamic-configuration platform was attacked along three routes at once: the known authentication-bypass family, a forged token signed with the platform's default signing key -- documented publicly since 2020 and shipped unchanged in many deployments -- and, because the operator already held database access, an administrator account inserted directly into the platform's backing store, bypassing the application entirely. The database route is the one that worked. The first insertion produced an unusable password hash because the hashing helper was invoked as a subprocess that was not on the path; the account was deleted and recreated correctly thirty-one seconds later. The token-forgery route was abandoned as soon as the platform reported a custom secret in use.

how.logic: A privileged account that appears in the application's user and role tables with no corresponding account-creation event in the application's own audit log, because it was written to the database rather than created through the product. The mismatch between the two records is the detection; either alone looks legitimate. A failed authentication for that same new name, followed within a minute by its deletion, recreation and a successful authentication, is the agentic signature on top.
how.caveat: The account name is this campaign's and will change; the audit mismatch is the durable half, and it only works if the application's audit log is collected separately from the database it writes to. Legitimate migrations and seeding scripts also write users directly, so exclude the deployment tooling by identity before relying on it.

where.title: JADEPUFFER: Agentic ransomware for automated database extortion

who.versions_affected: Self-managed Kubernetes clusters and EC2 instances left on Instance Metadata Service v1

what.summary: An operator exploited an internet-exposed service in a Kubernetes cluster, read the worker node's temporary AWS credentials from the instance metadata service, and used the node role's excessive read permissions to enumerate the whole cloud account rather than the one bucket the role was meant to reach.

how.logic: A process inside a container requests the instance metadata endpoint for the node's IAM role and then for that role's temporary credentials, and the same role identifier appears shortly afterwards in cloud audit records making API calls that the workload has no reason to make. The metadata request on its own is ordinary; the pairing with a first-ever API call by that role is not.
how.caveat: Legitimate SDKs in the workload retrieve credentials from the same endpoint on every cold start, so the metadata request alone is worthless as a signal. What separates this is the second half -- an API call the role has never made before -- and estates still on metadata service v1 cannot distinguish a pod's request from the node's, which is the reason the fix is v2 and per-pod roles rather than a detection.

markers.note: instance metadata service credential paths
link-local metadata address

markers.expr: metadata_credential_request originates from a container network namespace rather than the node

how.logic: Enumerate every role attached to a compute node or workload and resolve what its policy actually permits against what it was intended to permit. The role in this case was written to allow reading one storage bucket and in fact allowed reading everything in the account, which is what turned a container compromise into an account compromise.
how.caveat: Read-only is routinely treated as a low-severity finding. Read access to serverless function code, function environment variables and object storage is credential access and source code theft, so the severity of a read grant depends entirely on what can be read.

where.title: SCARLETEEL: Operation leveraging Terraform, Kubernetes, and AWS for data theft

notes: Named SCARLETEEL by the publisher. The campaign is split across four records, one per technology and behaviour: this one, the state-file pivot, the audit-log disable and the serverless code theft.

who.versions_affected: Any account storing Terraform state in object storage without object-level audit logging

what.summary: Having obtained read access to object storage, the operator recovered more than a terabyte of data and found a Terraform state file holding a clear-text access key and secret key for an IAM user in a second, connected cloud account, which they then used to restart the intrusion there.

how.logic: A principal outside the pipeline identity that maintains a state file reads that object. The set of legitimate readers of any given state file is small and stable, so a read from outside it is worth an alert on its own.
how.caveat: Object-level reads in this storage service are not logged unless that logging is explicitly turned on, and it was not turned on here -- the publisher stated they could not confirm which objects were read and inferred it from the rest of the intrusion. Where object-level logging is off this detection cannot fire at all, and the honest substitute is to inventory the state files and rotate what is inside them.

how.logic: Credentials belonging to one account authenticate from a source that has just been active in a different account under your control. The identity call that survives every permission restriction is the one that returns the caller's own identity, so a lone such call from a new source is often the first and only trace of a pivot that then failed on permissions.
how.caveat: In this case the second account's user was tightly scoped and every enumeration attempt failed, leaving only the default identity call in the record. A failed pivot looks like almost nothing, which is precisely why the almost-nothing is worth hunting.

markers.expr: source_ip seen in another account under management within 24h

markers.note: the enumeration that follows is denied

where.title: SCARLETEEL: Operation leveraging Terraform, Kubernetes, and AWS for data theft

notes: The publisher recovered the keys during investigation with the same secret-scanning tooling an intruder would use, which is the practical point: a state file is a credential store whether or not anyone intended it to be.

who.versions_affected: Any account where the trail can be stopped or deleted by a principal other than a small controlled set

what.summary: Holding credentials for a user with more permissions than it needed, the operator stopped audit logging inside the compromised account, and the publisher recorded that this succeeded and cost them the remainder of the evidence.

how.logic: A call that stops, deletes or reconfigures the account's audit trail, or that removes the trail's storage destination. The stopping call is itself recorded before logging ends, so the last event in the trail is frequently the event that ended it.
how.caveat: Trail reconfiguration happens legitimately during account restructuring and logging migrations, so this fires on real change. It is still worth alerting because the population of principals that should ever be able to do it is small enough to enumerate, and because an absence of the alert is not evidence -- a trail deleted rather than stopped can take its own record with it.

how.logic: Treat a gap in the audit stream as an event in its own right. Where the trail is delivered to a destination outside the account being logged, stopping it in the compromised account does not remove what has already arrived, and the delivery gap is visible from the receiving side.
how.caveat: Quiet accounts produce genuine gaps and low-activity accounts produce many, so this needs a per-account baseline before it means anything.

markers.expr: audit_event_delivery_gap exceeds the account's own observed maximum quiet period

where.title: SCARLETEEL: Operation leveraging Terraform, Kubernetes, and AWS for data theft

notes: The publisher's own recommendation is the useful one and is a permissions question rather than a detection: keep the ability to stop or delete a trail with as few principals as possible, and make deletion impossible without a separate backup.

who.versions_affected: Any account where a role can list and read function code and configuration across the account

what.summary: The operator listed the account's serverless functions, retrieved the download location for their code and exfiltrated it, taking proprietary software and the keys needed to run it, then read the functions' environment variables and recovered further credentials for other users in the account.

how.logic: A principal calls the list-functions operation and then, within a short window, calls the get-function operation across many distinct functions. Reading one function's configuration is routine for its own maintainers; walking the account's functions in sequence is an enumeration, and the get-function response carries both the code download location and the environment variables.
how.caveat: Deployment pipelines and inventory tooling perform the same walk on a schedule, so the principal identity is what separates them and the allow list has to be maintained. Note that the code download itself happens against a presigned storage URL rather than the function API, so the exfiltration leaves no serverless-service record; the read is the last event you will see.

markers.expr: count(distinct function_names read by principal) > count expected for that principal's own workload

where.title: SCARLETEEL: Operation leveraging Terraform, Kubernetes, and AWS for data theft

notes: The publisher's framing is worth carrying: the motive was not cryptomining. A miner ran throughout and was either the original goal or a deliberate distraction from the theft of proprietary code.

who.versions_affected: Accounts with long-lived IAM access keys and no service control policy restricting model access

what.summary: An operator using compromised long-lived access keys attempted to invoke hosted language models, and on failing created fresh IAM users, access keys and a permissions policy granting model access, then a console profile in order to complete the model agreement flow, repeating the whole sequence with further users as each attempt was refused.

how.logic: Repeated model invocation attempts by a principal with no history of them, particularly a run of failures returning access-check errors, followed by identity changes that grant exactly the permission that was refused. The failure run is the better signal than the invocation itself, because an operator probing for model access generates far more denials than a workload does.
how.caveat: A developer newly enabling model access produces the same denial-then-grant shape. The naming scheme and the policy name below are what make this campaign identifiable, and they are campaign artefacts rather than technique artefacts -- an operator who renames is invisible to them, so the behavioural markers have to carry the detection.

markers.note: IAM user naming scheme used consistently across observed environments
asynchronous HTTP client rather than an AWS SDK

markers.expr: run of denied model invocation attempts by principal followed by identity or policy creation granting model permissions

how.logic: Creation of a user, an access key and a console login profile for that user in one session, by a principal that is not part of identity administration. The console profile is the tell here: an operator who already holds programmatic keys only needs a console login to complete a flow the API will not do for them.
how.caveat: Legitimate onboarding creates the same three objects. The distinguishing features are that the creating principal is not an identity administrator and that the created user is granted a single narrow permission unrelated to any role description.

markers.expr: policy_document grants only model invocation actions on Resource *

where.title: Inside a New Wave of LLM Hijacking on AWS

notes: Every attempt failed, blocked by service control policies at the organisation tier. The record is kept because a control that worked is as instructive as one that did not: the organisation-level policy stopped an operator who already held administrator permissions in the account.

who.versions_affected: Any account where a compromised principal can create roles and start workloads in services the account does not otherwise use

what.summary: An operation ran mining workloads across several second-tier cloud services rather than the ordinary compute service, creating its own roles as it went, which avoided the approval that a burst of ordinary instances would have required and meant eradication needed a separate hunt in every service. The publisher put the cost to a victim at more than ten thousand dollars a day.

how.logic: Role creation followed within the same session by workload creation in a service the account has never used, repeated across several services. The reliable half is the cost signal: spend rising in several services at once with no matching rise in resource counts and no change record.
how.caveat: First use of a service is normal in an account under active development, and platform teams legitimately create roles ahead of workloads. The multi-service simultaneity is what separates abuse from adoption. The spend bound is deliberately unresolved because it has to be measured against the account's own baseline.

markers.expr: role_created and workload_started_with_that_role within same session
count(distinct services with first-ever workload creation) >= 3 within 24h

how.logic: A workload started from a public registry image that the estate has no build provenance for. The images behind this operation passed static scanning cleanly and only revealed their behaviour at run time, so the check that works is on the image's origin rather than on its contents.
how.caveat: The publisher's measurement is the point worth carrying: analysing 1.7 million public images, they found roughly ten per cent of malicious images are missed by static scanning alone. Treating a clean scan as evidence of a clean image is the error this record exists to correct.

markers.expr: image_digest present in internal build provenance records

how.logic: Sustained outbound connections from a cloud workload to mining pool infrastructure, or resolution of pool hostnames from a service that has no reason to resolve anything.
how.caveat: Network telemetry does not reach every one of these services in the way it reaches ordinary compute, which is part of why they were chosen. Where it does not, the cost signal is the only one left.

markers.expr: sustained outbound session from managed service workload to mining pool infrastructure

where.title: AWS's Hidden Threat: AMBERSQUID Cloud-Native Cryptojacking Operation

notes: Named AMBERSQUID by the publisher, who attributed it with medium confidence to Indonesian operators on language evidence in scripts and account names. Delivery was by public container images, some with over a hundred thousand downloads.

who.versions_affected: Behaviour present until the provider's fix of 24 October 2022

what.summary: Researchers found an undocumented identity service backing the management console which answered the same questions as the documented one and produced no audit records, allowing reconnaissance of identity configuration inside an account without leaving any trace in the account's audit trail.

how.logic: Compare the audit log against an independent record of the same principal's activity. A principal whose network layer shows sustained conversation with the provider's API endpoints while the audit trail shows little or nothing is transacting on a surface the trail does not cover. The service target is carried in a request header, so a proxy that sees the header can enumerate which services an estate actually calls and that list can be checked against audit coverage.
how.caveat: This specific surface was fixed in October 2022 and searching for its name now finds nothing. The class is the durable part: console-backing and legacy API surfaces exist on every provider, are not enumerable from documentation, and their audit coverage is a provider decision that can change without notice.

markers.note: X-Amz-Target for the unlogged surface; the audited service used AWSIdentityManagementV20100508
console path, against /iamv2/api/iam for the documented service
a batched wrapper around the audited single-user operation

markers.expr: provider_api_conversation_in_network_telemetry without matching audit events for principal

where.title: AWS CloudTrail vulnerability: Undocumented API allows CloudTrail bypass

notes: Reported to the provider in March 2022 and fixed in October 2022, with public disclosure in January 2023. No exploitation in the wild was reported; this is researcher discovery, and it is carried for the class rather than the instance.

who.versions_affected: Any tenant whose console sign-in permits a second factor that is not bound to the origin

what.summary: A wave of sites cloning the cloud console sign-in page harvested credentials and relayed the second factor in real time, branching server-side to whichever factor the victim's account used. The domains were registered in a forty-eight hour window through one registrar, fronted by a content delivery network, and the phishing mail was sent through legitimate bulk mail platforms to pass authentication checks.

how.logic: Resolution of, or a browser request to, a hostname that reproduces the provider's sign-in branding on a domain the provider does not own. Registration age is the strongest single filter here -- every domain in this wave was days old when used.
how.caveat: Fronting by a content delivery network means the destination address tells you nothing about the operator, and it puts the phishing site behind the same infrastructure as a great deal of legitimate traffic, so address-based blocking is not available. Hunt on the hostname and its age.

markers.note: observed June 2026 wave; treat as expired indicators and hunt the shape

markers.expr: domain_registration_age < 30d at time of first resolution

how.logic: A console sign-in event for a principal from a source address, client or geography that does not match that principal's history, arriving shortly after the same principal interacted with a newly registered lookalike domain. The provider records console sign-in as a distinct event type, which makes the second half of this cheap to query.
how.caveat: A relayed session looks exactly like a legitimate one to the identity provider, because it is one. Nothing in the sign-in record distinguishes it; the correlation with the lookalike domain is what does, so this fails if browser or resolver telemetry is absent.

markers.expr: console_sign_in from source not previously seen for that principal
same principal resolved a lookalike sign-in domain within the preceding hour

how.logic: Phishing delivered through a reputable bulk mail platform so that sender authentication passes and reputation filtering does not engage. The lure impersonated the provider's support function and cited a fabricated ticket about bandwidth throttling.
how.caveat: The sending platform is legitimate and carries an enormous volume of wanted mail, so neither the sending domain nor its addresses can be blocked. The signal has to come from the link destination rather than the sender.

markers.expr: message passes sender authentication via a bulk mail platform and links to a domain registered within 30d

where.title: Behind the console: An AiTM phishing kit harvesting AWS console credentials and beyond

notes: The publisher's own guidance is to hunt DNS for the listed domains and check the audit trail for console sign-in events. The domains are recorded here as expired indicators; the registration-age and branding shape is what carries forward.

who.versions_affected: Any account holding a role whose trust policy names a wildcard principal

what.summary: In an external test with no credentials supplied, an operator enumerated role names in the target's accounts by brute force against a wordlist of common names, found one whose trust policy admitted any principal in any account of the provider, assumed it from an account of their own, and obtained read, write and delete access to the target's object storage.

how.logic: Enumerate every role in every account you own and read its trust policy, flagging any naming a wildcard principal. Only the account identifier and the role name are needed to use one, and neither is secret: account identifiers appear in ordinary integration documentation and role names are guessable.
how.caveat: The provider warns about this configuration and still permits it to be set, so it exists in real estates rather than being theoretical. Cross-account trust itself is ordinary and heavily used; the finding is the wildcard and the unrecognised counterparty, not the cross-account grant.

markers.expr: role trust policy Principal contains a wildcard rather than an enumerated account
assuming account identifier outside organisation accounts and approved third-party integrations

how.logic: The enumeration phase is a run of assumption attempts against role names that do not exist, and it precedes any successful access. Where those attempts reach your logs they are the earliest available warning.
how.caveat: Whether the failures are visible at all depends on where the attempt was made, and an attempt against a role that does not exist in your account may not produce a record you can see. Absence of the enumeration is therefore not evidence it did not happen, and the configuration check does not depend on it.

markers.expr: burst of failed role assumption attempts against role names that do not exist

where.title: AWS Misconfiguration Leads to Buckets of Data

notes: Observed during an authorised external penetration test, with the client supplying only its account identifiers. Publicly documented tooling exists to find and exploit this configuration, so the barrier is knowledge of the account identifier and nothing else.

who.versions_affected: Any account releasing public addresses while DNS records still resolve to them

what.summary: Researchers documented and tooled a takeover class in which a public cloud address is released back to the provider's shared pool while a DNS record still resolves to it, so that whoever next receives that address from the pool receives the hostname's traffic and whatever the hostname is trusted for.

how.logic: Reconcile two lists rather than watch a stream: every public address currently allocated to accounts you own, and every address your DNS records resolve to. A record resolving to a provider address absent from the first list is dangling and takeable.
how.caveat: The researchers' own warning is the one that matters and the tool enforces it: the check requires complete coverage of every cloud account you own, and it degrades silently rather than failing. An account you did not enumerate makes its own addresses look unowned and produces confident false findings.

markers.expr: dns A record resolves to a provider address not allocated to any account under your control
cloud account enumeration for the reconciliation is complete

how.logic: Once the address is held, the name validates for certificate issuance, so a certificate transparency entry for one of your hostnames that you did not request is both a confirmation and, often, the first external evidence available.
how.caveat: Certificate transparency monitoring finds this after the fact rather than preventing it, and it will not fire where the operator does not request a certificate. The inventory reconciliation is the control; this is the backstop.

markers.expr: certificate issued for an owned hostname without a matching internal issuance record

where.title: Eliminating Dangling Elastic IP Takeovers with Ghostbuster

notes: Published with open-source tooling that performs the reconciliation. The class generalises past this one provider and past addresses to any released cloud resource a DNS name still points at.

who.versions_affected: Projects whose webhook filters used unanchored expressions to authorise the triggering account, prior to the vendor's mitigation.

what.summary: A build service authorised the account that triggered a build by matching an identifier against a filter expression that was not anchored at either end, so the check passed on any identifier that merely contained an approved one. Account identifiers on the forge are assigned in sequence and have grown in length over time, so a short legacy maintainer identifier is necessarily a substring of some longer modern identifier, and the point at which new registrations reach that range is predictable. Researchers sampled the current range, timed the window, registered applications in bulk through the manifest flow to capture a qualifying identifier, and used it to trigger a build on a pull request. The build environment held a long-lived personal access token, which a malicious build dependency recovered from memory; its scopes permitted adding a repository administrator and pushing to protected branches. Reported against four vendor-owned repositories including a widely distributed cloud SDK. The vendor stated it found no evidence any other party had used the flaw, so this is a disclosed weakness rather than an observed intrusion.

how.logic: An inventory question with a decisive answer: any filter expression used for an authorisation decision that lacks start and end anchors is a substring match pretending to be an equality check. Enumerate every webhook and integration filter and test the expression, rather than waiting to observe abuse. The run-time half is a build triggered by an account created recently and with no history against the repository, followed by an administrator addition or a protected-branch push.
how.caveat: The anchoring marker closes the class and costs one pass over configuration; everything else here is consolation for not having done it. Note the second half of the chain is independent of the first and worth its own attention: a long-lived token sitting in a build environment was what turned a filter bypass into repository control, and short-lived credentials would have blunted it regardless of the regex.

where.title: CodeBreach: Infiltrating the AWS Console Supply Chain and Hijacking AWS GitHub Repositories via CodeBuild

who.versions_affected: Not applicable

what.summary: A password spraying campaign made failed console authentication attempts against the AWS account root user at more than 150 organisations over a month, with no successful authentication observed.

how.logic: A console sign-in event recorded for the account root identity, treated as notable on its own rather than counted. In CloudTrail the event is eventName ConsoleLogin with userIdentity.type Root, and the outcome in responseElements.ConsoleLogin is either Failure or Success. The publisher's own affected-check query tests those three over its CloudTrail log source and then narrows by user agent; its sample event also carries eventSource signin.amazonaws.com, which is available as a further narrowing but is not part of that query. No outcome filter belongs in this block, because both outcomes are in scope.

fields.note: taken from the publisher's sample event rather than from its affected-check query. Carried as a field and not as a marker because the XDM path a CloudTrail modelling rule writes the event source into is not known from this source, and binding it here would be a guess
the publisher's query accepts both outcomes, which is why the markers carry no outcome clause

markers.note: in CloudTrail this is userIdentity.type equal to Root, which is a login class rather than a group membership. Resolve it against the raw userIdentity.type field as the modelling rule maps it; it is left computed here because no XDM field is known to hold it, and a group field would be the wrong one

how.caveat: An organisation's own root sign-ins produce the same event, which is why the publisher frames this as alerting on all root activity rather than on this campaign. Nothing here separates the campaign from legitimate use without the user agent test in the next block. On volume, the publisher reports only a per-organisation figure, a median of two attempts and at most eight across the month, so a rule counting attempts per organisation would not have fired; it publishes no per-source-address or per-account volume, so whether a rule counting per source address would have fired cannot be told from this source.

how.logic: Root console sign-in events carrying either of the two client strings the publisher gives as a campaign fingerprint. The publisher's affected-check query is its root ConsoleLogin filter restricted to these two user agent values.

fields.note: from the publisher's sample event, as in the preceding block, and carried as a field for the same reason

value: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/85.0.4183.83 Safari/537.36 Edg/85.0.564.41
Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:120.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/120.0

markers.note: CloudTrail userIdentity.type equal to Root, resolved against the raw field as in the preceding block. Keep this marker and its twin in step: the user agent test cannot carry alert fidelity without the identity test

value: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/85.0.4183.83 Safari/537.36 Edg/85.0.564.41
Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:120.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/120.0

iocs.value: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/85.0.4183.83 Safari/537.36 Edg/85.0.564.41
iocs.note: one of two client strings given as a campaign fingerprint

iocs.value: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:120.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/120.0

how.caveat: Both values are ordinary browser strings rather than bespoke tooling, so matching the user agent outside the root sign-in context will collide with real browsers. A client string is changed at no cost, so this fingerprint has a short shelf life; the identity test in the preceding block is the durable half. Where the user agent marker resolves to must be confirmed against the modelling rule that maps CloudTrail, since the client string is a field of the audit record rather than of an observed web session.

how.logic: A failed root console sign-in is itself evidence that the email address bound to the account root user is known outside the organisation, because the sign-in flow requires that address before a ConsoleLogin event can be generated at all. The publisher draws the inference that the actor either held a list of root user email addresses or brute forced through a list of account email addresses until one resolved. Read each such event as an exposure fact about the account rather than only as a failed login.

fields.note: value shown in the publisher's sample event

markers.note: CloudTrail userIdentity.type equal to Root, resolved against the raw field
the failure case only, unlike the two blocks above. In the publisher's sample this is responseElements.ConsoleLogin of Failure with errorMessage 'Failed authentication'

how.caveat: The publisher does not resolve which of the two acquisition routes was used, so this establishes that the address was known, not how. It says nothing about the password source. The errorMessage string has no marker type in the vocabulary and is carried as a field only, so a consumer working from markers alone gets the failure outcome but not that string.

where.title: Password spraying campaign targets AWS root user accounts across 150+ organizations

notes: what.impact is deliberately absent. No authentication succeeded in anything the publisher observed and it states plainly that it cannot determine the actor's intent, so any impact value here would be an intent claim the source declines to make. Campaign scale, which is reported but which no single-tenant rule can see and which is therefore not built into a how block: one effort attempting the root identity at more than 150 organisations between 24 July and 23 August 2026, a median of two attempts per organisation and at most eight across the whole window, with the authentication requests tunnelled through proxies. The publisher states that the source addresses span a wide range of countries and autonomous systems and that threat intelligence sources flag all of them as hosting infrastructure, residential proxies or similar, but it publishes no addresses and no autonomous system numbers, so no reputation list can be seeded from this source. It publishes no per-source-address and no per-account volume at all, so no threshold form of this detection can be sized or ruled out from it; the per-organisation figure rules out only a rule that counts attempts per organisation. Targeted organisations showed no clear victimology, varying widely by country and industry. Two pieces of the primer are context rather than campaign observation and are likewise not built into the how blocks: AWS has enforced multi-factor authentication for root users across all account types since June 2025, with a 35-day grace period between the first console sign-in attempt and factor registration, and AWS recommends monitoring all root user activity. The publisher presents its CloudTrail event as shortened for readability, and its source address (192.0.2.0) and account number (123456789012) are the standard documentation and placeholder values, so the sample yields field names and the Failed authentication error string but no usable network indicators.

who.versions_affected: Any tenant permitting a second factor that is not bound to the origin

what.summary: An active campaign against organisations using one identity provider for single sign-on hijacked the sign-on flow itself: the first-stage page took the target tenant as a URL parameter and proxied the organisation's real sign-in page so that its own branding rendered, then injected script that rewrote outbound requests to the attacker host and stole the session cookies needed to impersonate the session.

how.logic: Requests to a hostname that impersonates the identity provider's naming, carrying a URL parameter that names your own tenant. That parameter is the distinguishing artefact: a legitimate sign-in page has no reason to take the tenant it is imitating as an argument, and it makes the kit's targeting explicit in the request line.
how.caveat: Because the page proxies the genuine tenant, every visual check a user is taught to make succeeds -- the organisation's own logo, its password recovery text and its customisations are all present, because they are being served from the real site.

markers.note: observed December 2025; treat as expired indicators
the target tenant carried as a parameter to the phishing host

how.logic: The kit enumerates the identity provider's session cookies by name and exfiltrates them as they are set, before and after authentication, so the operator resumes an authenticated session without reauthenticating. Detection falls to session reuse: the same session identifier presenting from a second address, client or geography.
how.caveat: Multi-factor authentication is completed by the genuine user against the genuine tenant, so the authentication record is clean and shows a successful, factor-satisfied sign-in. Only phishing-resistant factors bound to the origin break this; a code or a push does not.

markers.expr: session identifier presented from more than one source address or user agent within its lifetime
authentication succeeded with a factor not bound to the origin

how.logic: The injected script replaces the browser's own fetch implementation so that requests the genuine identity provider's front-end code makes are rewritten to the attacker host with credentials attached. Where content inspection is available, a page serving the identity provider's front-end alongside a script that reassigns window.fetch is the artefact.
how.caveat: This is only visible where the proxy inspects response bodies, which many estates do not do for encrypted traffic to an apparently legitimate sign-in host. Where it is not available, the domain and session-reuse halves carry the detection.

markers.expr: response body reassigns window.fetch and rewrites the identity provider hostname to the serving host

where.title: Investigating an adversary-in-the-middle phishing campaign targeting Microsoft 365 and Okta users

notes: The publisher observed the lure sent to hundreds of users across dozens of organisations and reported the campaign as still active at publication. First record in this corpus filed under vendor Okta.

who.versions_affected: Any tenant permitting a second factor that is not bound to the origin

what.summary: A phishing-as-a-service platform sold real-time interception of sign-in flows against two large identity providers, and redirected accounts protected by a third-party single sign-on provider to a second-stage page. It captured credentials, one-time codes and the session token issued during the sign-in, and lowered the skill needed to run this attack to that of a subscriber.

how.logic: Lures arrived from compromised accounts at legitimate mail service providers so that sender reputation passed, then through link shorteners with several redirects, then to landing sites on low-cost disposable top-level domains behind a shared reverse proxy, and only then to an interactive challenge and a serverless function that chose which lure to load. Each layer defeats a different automated check.
how.caveat: Because the chain is built to defeat automated analysis, a link scanner returning clean on this shape of URL should be read as no verdict rather than a good one. No single marker here is actionable alone and the correlation is what carries it.

markers.note: serverless gatekeeper and lure loader

markers.expr: mail-borne link traverses more than two redirects before its final host
interactive challenge served before content on a first visit from a mail-borne link

how.logic: The platform proxies the genuine sign-in, so the identity provider records a successful authentication with the second factor satisfied. The token issued to that session is captured and reused, and the only trace at the identity provider is the same session presenting from a second source.
how.caveat: The publisher's own observation is the most useful line of defence recorded here: accounts enrolled in an authenticator bound to the origin could not complete the flow through this infrastructure and were warned their account was under attack. Codes from a message or an authenticator application do not have that property and were captured.

markers.expr: session identifier presented from more than one source address or user agent within its lifetime
authentication satisfied by a factor not bound to the origin

how.logic: Delivery came from compromised accounts at named legitimate mail service providers, so sender authentication passed and reputation filtering did not engage. The sending infrastructure cannot be blocked; the signal has to come from the link.
how.caveat: These are marketing and transactional mail platforms carrying enormous volumes of wanted mail. Blocking by sending domain is not available as a response.

markers.expr: message passes sender authentication from a bulk mail platform and links to a shortener that redirects off-platform

where.title: Uncloaking VoidProxy: a Novel and Evasive Phishing-as-a-Service Framework

notes: The publisher withholds the full infrastructure analysis and indicators behind customer authentication, so what is recorded here is the tradecraft stated in the public write-up and nothing that depends on the restricted advisory.

who.versions_affected: Legitimate current versions of the cloudflared client, used as designed

what.summary: Operators install the vendor's tunnel client on a compromised host and run it with a token that ties it to a tunnel they already configured in their own account, producing an outbound-only encrypted channel that reaches internal services without any inbound firewall change, and that can be reconfigured or silenced from the operator's dashboard between sessions.

how.logic: Execution of the tunnel client with a subcommand that runs a tunnel, either bound to a token or exposing a local address. The token form is the one that matters, because it needs no configuration file on the host and carries the operator's tunnel identity in a single argument.
how.caveat: The client is signed, legitimate and in wide sanctioned use, so the binary cannot be the signal. The workable question is whether tunnelling is approved on this estate at all: if it is not, any execution is unauthorised by definition, and if it is, the allow list is of hosts rather than of the tool. Note the client writes its output to standard output only, so a service installation leaves no log file to find.

how.logic: The client resolves and connects to the vendor's tunnel control and update endpoints before it carries any traffic, and the data channel runs over QUIC to a fixed port at the vendor's nearest edge. Both halves are visible without decrypting anything, and the network signal survives a renamed or unsigned binary that process-name detection misses.
how.caveat: Legitimate tunnels produce identical network behaviour, which the rule authors of both public detection corpora say plainly. Where the estate has no sanctioned use, blocking the namespace at the resolver and the port at the firewall is a better control than detecting it.

markers.note: QUIC data channel to the vendor edge

markers.expr: outbound session to provider edge with no corresponding inbound firewall rule for the service being reached

how.logic: The same client executed under a different filename. The tunnel subcommand grammar is unusual enough to be identifiable on its own, so a process whose command line takes tunnel arguments while its image name is anything else is worth an alert regardless of what it is called.
how.caveat: This is the detection that survives an operator who reads the same public rules you do, and it is the reason a process-name allow list alone is not enough. It needs full command-line capture, which many estates do not have on every host.

markers.expr: command line matches the tunnel client argument grammar while process name is not cloudflared
original_file_name in binary metadata differs from process name on disk

where.title: Tunnel Vision: cloudflared abused in the wild

notes: This is the vendor-named counterpart to obs-generic-remote-access-tools-as-persistence-and-c2, which lists the same client among a market of tools under vendor any and deliberately carries no product-specific markers. That record makes the allow-list argument; this one makes the tool findable and carries the argument grammar, the tunnel namespace and the port. Corroborated by seven rules in the public detection corpora already held in sections 5 and 6, one of which is rated high specifically for the renamed-binary case.

who.versions_affected: The vendor's free trial tunnel service, used as designed

what.summary: A sustained campaign used the vendor's trial tunnel feature, which issues a working hostname under the vendor's own domain without an account, to stage shortcut files and scripts behind mail lures on tax, invoice and delivery themes, ending in commodity remote access trojans. Message volumes ran from hundreds to tens of thousands, reaching thousands of organisations.

how.logic: A link or a resolution to a hostname under the provider's trial tunnel namespace. The provider generates a random multi-word label per tunnel, so the hostname is unrepeatable and unguessable, and the parent domain is old and reputable, which means it defeats domain-age and registrar reputation entirely.
how.caveat: Developers use this namespace legitimately to expose work in progress, so on an engineering estate this alerts on real work. On the mail path it does not: a link into a throwaway tunnel hostname arriving in email has no legitimate business explanation, and that is where to place the rule.

markers.note: observed labels take the form ride-fatal-italic-information and spectrum-exactly-knitting-rural

markers.expr: hostname appears as a link in inbound mail rather than in developer-initiated traffic

how.logic: The chain is consistent across the campaign and each hop is separately detectable: an internet shortcut or an HTML attachment carrying a search protocol query, then a shortcut or script fetched over a remote file-sharing protocol, then a batch helper, then a scripting engine that downloads a language runtime and its script, then the payload. The remote-share hop is the strongest single place to break it, because a shortcut resolving to a remote share reached from a mail-borne file is not ordinary user behaviour.
how.caveat: The final stage installs a full language runtime, so detection anchored on a named malware binary sees nothing. The publisher's own guidance is blunt and structural rather than signature-based: restrict that runtime where it is not needed, and allow-list the external file-sharing servers your estate may reach.

markers.note: search protocol query in an HTML attachment, used to render a remote share as though it were a local folder

markers.expr: shortcut or script retrieved over WebDAV from a host outside the approved file-sharing set
scripting engine spawned from a mail-delivered file downloads and installs a language runtime

where.title: Threat Actor Abuses Cloudflare Tunnels to Deliver RATs

notes: Delivered Xworm principally, with AsyncRAT, VenomRAT, GuLoader and Remcos also observed. Lures ran in English, French, Spanish and German against law, finance, manufacturing and technology. The tunnel is the delivery host here rather than the command channel, which is the distinction from the cloudflared record: same vendor feature, different role in the intrusion.

who.versions_affected: The vendor's ordinary reverse-proxy service, used as designed

what.summary: Domains cloning a cloud provider's console sign-in page and relaying second factors in real time were placed behind the vendor's reverse proxy, so that the addresses a defender sees belong to the proxy rather than the operator and are shared with a large volume of legitimate traffic.

how.logic: Because the destination address belongs to a widely used reverse proxy, address-based blocking and address-based reputation are both unavailable, and the resolved address tells you nothing about who runs the site. Detection has to move to the hostname and its age: every domain in the observed wave was days old, registered through one registrar inside a forty-eight hour window, and carried sign-in branding for a provider that did not own it.
how.caveat: This is the general case that makes destination-address controls unreliable for a large and growing share of hostile web infrastructure, and it is not a defect in the proxy: the same properties serve the legitimate majority of its customers. Blocking the proxy's ranges is not available as a response.

markers.expr: resolved address belongs to a shared reverse proxy provider rather than to the site operator
page presents sign-in branding for an organisation that does not control the domain

where.title: Behind the console: An AiTM phishing kit harvesting AWS console credentials and beyond

notes: Filed under Cloudflare because the question a consultation is asked is what this vendor's products are caught up in, and fronting is the most common way this one appears in an intrusion. The victim technology in the same campaign is recorded separately at obs-amazon-console-sign-in-cloned-with-live-second-factor-capture.

who.versions_affected: The build platform as architected until the vendor's rebuild; a later rebuilt platform was also found reachable

what.summary: Researchers evaluating the vendor's static-hosting service obtained command execution inside its build steps, escalated within the build container and escaped it, and recovered source-control tokens belonging to themselves and to the vendor, platform API keys for the vendor's own organisation, and the vendor's credentials for the third-party cloud the build platform ran on. After the vendor rebuilt the platform on a different cloud with a sandboxed runtime, source-control secrets were reachable again through the orchestrator's node agent.

how.logic: The service executes customer-supplied build commands, and the environment those commands ran in also held the provider's operational credentials. Command injection in the steps that clone the repository and publish assets gave execution outside the intended build command, and from there the environment was simply readable.
how.caveat: For a consumer of this service the actionable half is not the injection but the authorisation: connecting a repository grants the platform read access, and that grant is commonly organisation-wide when it needs to be repository-scoped. Narrowing it is the control that bounds what a compromise of any such platform takes from you.

how.logic: Having reached the build user and then a privileged user inside the container, the researchers moved to code execution on the build host itself. The container was treated as the boundary by the platform's design and did not hold as one.
how.caveat: The lesson the vendor drew is the useful one and it was structural rather than a patch: after several rounds of fixing individual injection points, they rebuilt the platform on different infrastructure with a sandboxed container runtime and non-root execution. Patching injection sites one at a time did not close the class.

how.logic: On the rebuilt platform the build ran as a non-root user in a sandboxed runtime with no access to instance metadata, and the orchestrator's node agent API was still reachable from inside the build network and still returned source-control secrets. Restricting the workload did not restrict what the workload could talk to.
how.caveat: Sandbox hardening and metadata blocking are both real improvements and neither addresses reachability of the orchestration control plane from a workload network. Network policy is the control that does.

markers.expr: workload network can reach the orchestrator node agent API port
network policy restricts workload egress to the control plane

where.title: Cloudflare Pages, parts 1 to 3: the fellowship of the secret, the two privescs, the return of the secrets

notes: Coordinated disclosure through a bug bounty programme, with the vendor publishing its own account of receiving the reports. Researcher-found rather than observed in an intrusion, and carried because the class -- a build service executing tenant code in the same context as provider credentials -- applies to every managed build and static-hosting platform, not to this one.

who.versions_affected: The vendor's serverless compute and challenge services, used as designed

what.summary: A phishing-as-a-service platform used the vendor's serverless compute namespace to filter incoming traffic and load the right lure for each target, its interactive challenge to prove a real browser before serving anything, and its reverse proxy to conceal the origin server, alongside dynamic DNS. Four separate services of one provider, each doing legitimate work for an illegitimate site.

how.logic: The gatekeeper is a serverless function on the provider's own namespace, loaded by the landing page rather than linked in mail, so it appears as a subresource fetch from a reputable domain. Decide whether your estate has any legitimate use of that namespace; where it has none, a request to it is worth an alert regardless of context.
how.caveat: Engineering estates use this namespace for real work, and there the discriminator is that the request is a subresource of a page reached from mail rather than developer-initiated. This is the second independent report in this corpus placing hostile infrastructure on this namespace, and an external measurement on the same day found it the most abused of the provider's developer namespaces.

markers.expr: serverless namespace host loaded as a subresource of a page reached from a mail-borne link

how.logic: The origin sits behind the provider's reverse proxy, so the resolved address belongs to the proxy and is shared with a very large volume of legitimate traffic. Address-based blocking and address reputation are both unavailable and the hostname and its age carry the detection.
how.caveat: This is the provider working correctly for a customer who happens to be hostile, and blocking its ranges is not available as a response. The landing domains here were on low-cost disposable namespaces and treated as consumable, so hostname blocklists age within days.

markers.expr: resolved address belongs to a shared reverse proxy rather than the site operator
interactive challenge from that provider served before any content on a first visit
hostname resolves through a dynamic DNS service

where.title: Uncloaking VoidProxy: a Novel and Evasive Phishing-as-a-Service Framework

notes: Filed under the infrastructure provider rather than the identity provider; the same source produces obs-okta-phishing-as-a-service-intercepts-the-sign-in-in-real-time for the victim technology. Independently corroborated by section 21's measurement of the public malicious-URL corpus, where this namespace was the most abused of the provider's developer namespaces.

who.versions_affected: The platform's shareable conversation feature, used as designed

what.summary: Operators distributing a macOS credential stealer bought search advertising against the platform's own name, sent the traffic to a shared conversation hosted on the platform's genuine domain, and used that page to carry paste-and-run installation instructions. The conversation was labelled with the operator's chosen display name so it presented as coming from a hardware vendor's support function.

how.logic: The hosting domain is the platform's own and carries its reputation, so domain age, registrar analysis and category-based filtering all pass. The distinguishing artefacts are the path shape of a shared conversation and the fact that the visit arrived from a paid search placement rather than from the application itself.
how.caveat: This cannot be blocked at the domain, and blocking the share feature blocks a legitimate function. The author label is attacker-chosen -- set by changing a display name before generating the link -- so the apparent identity of a shared conversation is worth exactly nothing, which is the part worth telling users.

markers.expr: navigation to an AI platform share path arriving from a paid search placement rather than from the platform application
share page author label names an organisation unrelated to the platform

how.logic: The victim is instructed to paste a command into a terminal. The command decodes a Base64 string to a URL, retrieves a shell script and pipes it straight to an interpreter, so the first stage never lands on disk. The pipe from a network retrieval tool into a shell is the durable artefact and it is visible in command lines.
how.caveat: No exploit is involved and the user performs every step, so nothing upstream of the terminal will stop it. The later stages pipe into the platform's scripting host directly, leaving no file trace at all, which is why the command line at the moment of paste is the best and sometimes only place to catch this.

markers.expr: network retrieval tool output piped directly into an interpreter with no intermediate file

how.logic: Collected material is archived to a temporary path and then sent out in fixed-size parts by HTTP upload, with the part index and total carried in the query string. Chunked upload to a single external host, from a workstation, in a short window, is the network shape.
how.caveat: The chunking exists to survive size limits rather than to evade, but it has the side effect that no single request looks large. A volume threshold on individual requests will miss it; the aggregate to one destination is the measure.

markers.expr: repeated fixed-size uploads to one external host within a short window

where.title: ClaudeFix: Shared Claude Chats Meet ClickFix

notes: The publisher notified the platform owner and the shared conversations were unreachable by publication. Recorded for the class rather than the campaign: a share feature that mints a page on a reputable domain with an attacker-chosen author label is a hosting surface, and every large platform now has one.

who.versions_affected: Current; the agents are signed, sanctioned and used as designed

what.summary: On a macOS developer workstation, a coding agent session was the execution parent for a chain that authenticated over HTTP to an ephemeral tunnel hostname, published a local service to the internet through a free tunnel broker without any inbound firewall change, and wrote user-scope persistence to keep the path alive across logout. Related cases on other hosts showed a keychain dump filtered toward integration and protocol credentials, and quarantine stripping with ad-hoc re-signing of an unsigned binary fetched over plaintext HTTP.

how.logic: The agent is the ancestor rather than the immediate parent: its direct children were ordinary shells, and those shells did the work. Every step is a normal developer action and the ancestry terminates in an approved, signed application, so parent reputation resolves to approved. Alert on the subtree combination within one session -- tunnel hostname, credentialed request to it, persistence write -- rather than on any component.
how.caveat: The publisher is explicit that validation is the hard part rather than detection, because trusted parents, dual-use destinations and a high-severity outcome all land in one alert pile. Their guidance is to treat it as high severity even where it looks like informal operations rather than confirmed malware, since a local administrative application ends up on the internet either way.

markers.expr: process ancestry includes a coding agent and the immediate parent is a shell
one agent session contains an ephemeral tunnel hostname, credentialed HTTP to it, and a persistence write

markers.note: requests observed against the published tunnel URL

how.logic: Three free tunnel brokers appear side by side in the same window, each issuing a working public hostname under its own reputable domain with no account and no registration record. The tunnel publishes a local service outbound-only, so no inbound firewall rule is created and none is missing.
how.caveat: Reputation flags on the broker apex domains stay useful as hunt signals precisely because these services are widely abused, but they cannot be blocked outright on a developer estate that uses them legitimately. This is the corpus's third independent report of this provider's ephemeral namespace being used this way, and the first from the endpoint rather than the network side.

markers.expr: local service published outbound through a tunnel broker with no corresponding inbound firewall rule

how.logic: User-scope startup material written in the same session keeps the reverse tunnel alive across logout and reboot, with the session polling that the public link is still up. On this platform the artefact is a property list in the user's own agent directory, which needs no administrative rights.
how.caveat: Legitimate developer tooling writes to the same directory. What distinguishes this instance is that the write happens in the same session as the tunnel and the credentialed request, which is the correlation the first block carries.

markers.expr: persistence written by a process whose ancestry includes a coding agent

where.title: Living off the coding agent: Two tales of tunnels and LaunchAgents

notes: Three related cases on other hosts are recorded in the source and not split out here because they are variants of one class: signed interpreters staging scripts from a temporary path, a keychain dump filtered toward integration and protocol credentials which endpoint controls blocked, and quarantine stripping with ad-hoc re-signing. Worth noting the publisher observed the agent's own durable memory file being read by a process that was not the agent's usual writer, which is a novel artefact class.

who.versions_affected: Any device exposing the LuCI web configuration interface to the internet

what.summary: The web configuration interface of a Linux distribution that underlies a great many consumer, industrial and embedded network devices received more than four thousand brute force login attempts across four months in one research environment, against a population the publisher measured at roughly thirty-two thousand internet-exposed instances, with public tooling available to automate it.

how.logic: Repeated authentication failures against the configuration interface from one source, followed by a success. On this class of device the success is frequently the only event that will ever be recorded, so the failures matter chiefly as the thing that makes the success interpretable.
how.caveat: Default and weak credentials are what make the brute force worth attempting, and replacing them removes the outcome without removing the traffic. Note that the same interface carries the injection path recorded on the sibling Lantronix record, so a run of failed logins against it is worth reading for what is in the username as well as for how many there are.

markers.expr: repeated authentication failures against a device configuration interface from one source followed by a success
device configuration interface reachable from outside the management network

how.logic: The underlying distribution and its configuration interface are shared across many vendors' products, so the exposure is not enumerable by vendor name. Inventory by what the device runs rather than by who sold it, and treat any device exposing this interface to the internet as in scope regardless of badge.
how.caveat: This is the reason a vendor-keyed vulnerability programme misses this class entirely. The publisher lists further identifiers on the same interface in unrelated vendors' products within months of each other, and a well-known consumer router flaw on the same interface has been in the authoritative exploited-vulnerability catalogue since 2023 and is used by several botnet families.

where.title: Analyzing active exploitation of Lantronix and OpenWRT LuCI

notes: Filed under the distribution rather than under any device vendor, because that is what the exposure is a property of. The publisher's own earlier research found many industrial routers built on the same base.

who.versions_affected: Any consumer installing affected package versions, and any maintainer whose publish credentials were reachable

what.summary: Attackers compromised the maintainer of a widely used storage library, trojanised the whole repository, and embedded a self-propagating worm that used stolen registry credentials to backdoor every other package that maintainer could publish. Over four hundred packages were affected, the directly compromised library alone accounting for six hundred million monthly downloads. The payload harvested credentials against more than three hundred patterns and retrieved its exfiltration endpoint from a public ledger rather than carrying one. Two further publishers analysed the same campaign within the following week, independently describing the maintainer-credential propagation and the ledger-resolved exfiltration endpoint. Three unrelated vendors reaching the same mechanism inside seven days is the strongest corroboration available short of an incident of one's own, and it is the reason this is one record rather than three.

how.logic: Execution is triggered by a pre-install hook, so installing the package is enough and no further interaction is needed. The dropper checks for an alternative JavaScript runtime, downloads it from the vendor's own release page if absent, uses it to run the payload, then deletes its temporary directory. Two payload filenames share one hash, which makes the filename an indicator of whether a package was compromised directly or by propagation.
how.caveat: Fetching the runtime from the official release page means the download itself is to a reputable host over a legitimate path, and will not fail a reputation check. The republish half is what makes this a worm rather than an incident: stolen publish credentials backdoor everything else the maintainer owns, so the blast radius is a credential's reach and not a package's dependents.

markers.note: dropper, and payload named by infection generation

markers.expr: package manager pre-install hook spawns a process that downloads and executes an alternative runtime
commit author name and message match the worm's fixed pair rather than the maintainer's usual pattern

how.logic: Beyond the install path, the worm plants configuration in the repository that runs on events a developer does not think of as execution: a session-start key for a coding agent and a folder-open task for an editor. Where a code-hosting application token was among the stolen credentials it committed those files to as many as fifty branches per accessible repository, so opening the project is enough to be infected.
how.caveat: This is the half that survives every dependency control. A locked lockfile, a private registry mirror and a policy of never installing untrusted packages all fail against a hook that fires when somebody opens the folder. Sweep your own repositories for these paths rather than relying on install-time controls.

markers.expr: repository configuration executing a script from the project's own hidden directory on session start or folder open
same configuration file committed across many branches of one repository by a single author

how.logic: The payload carries no command-and-control domain. It queries a smart contract on a public ledger at run time for the current exfiltration endpoint, using several gateway providers as fallbacks, so the operator rotates infrastructure by updating the contract without touching any deployed copy. Where that lookup fails it searches a public code-hosting service's commit history for the endpoint instead.
how.caveat: Domain blocklists and payload hashes both age immediately against this, and the lookup traffic goes to reputable gateway providers rather than to anything that looks hostile. The observed dead-drop domains are recorded as expired indicators; the lookup behaviour is the durable signal, and the code-history fallback means blocking the gateways alone does not close it.

markers.expr: package manager or build tool makes requests to distributed ledger gateway providers

markers.note: dead-drop endpoints observed during detonation; treat as expired

markers.expr: ledger gateway request followed within minutes by a first-seen outbound destination

how.logic: The collector component scans more than three hundred patterns across the credential stores found on a developer machine, and its targeting is worth reading as a statement of what is now valuable: assistant and model-provider keys alongside cloud provider credentials, code-hosting tokens of three kinds, secret-manager tokens, private keys, orchestrator service-account tokens and registry tokens. Collected material is compressed, encrypted with a fresh symmetric key, and that key encrypted to the operator's public key.
how.caveat: The encryption is the reason interception does not help: only the holder of the private key can read what left. The response is credential rotation scoped to everything a developer workstation held, which is a far wider set than the incident appears to touch, and the AI tooling credentials are the class most likely to be missing from an existing rotation runbook.

markers.expr: one process reads many distinct credential store paths across providers within a short window
credential material compressed and encrypted before egress, with no plaintext secret on the wire

Detection came from their own supply-chain monitoring project rather than from a customer incident, which is why the timeline is hours rather than weeks. Zscaler reported earlier waves of the same family and that reporting is registered in section 23 but was not distilled.
