products: Progress Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX
who.versions_affected: Internet-facing Windows and Linux web servers carrying publicly disclosed remote code execution flaws. The ASP.NET half is gated on MachineKey material being known to the attacker rather than on a version.

what.summary: A financially motivated Chinese-speaking group compromising internet-exposed web servers at scale for search-engine fraud and data theft, notable less for its exploits -- all one-day, all public -- than for the degree to which the operation around them is machine-generated. The reporting vendor observed AI-produced exploitation playbooks, companion automation scripts and exploit quality-assurance workflows on the actor's own infrastructure, and assesses the operation as a move from AI-assisted scripting toward semi-autonomous offensive orchestration.

how.logic: Two different HTTP 500 responses on a ViewState endpoint mean opposite things, and the one that means success is the one a defender is least likely to escalate. A MAC validation failure means the MachineKey used was wrong; an InvalidCastException means the key was right and the payload deserialised. The actor's own documented procedure is to send a deliberately malformed payload and read which of the two comes back, so key validity is confirmed before any command runs. Alert on the exception type in the application error log, and treat repeated MAC validation failures from one source as key trial rather than as application noise.

fields.note: the parameter appears in the POST body; where only the access log is available, match on the endpoint and method instead
from the application error log, not the access log; the access log records only the 500

how.caveat: This inverts the usual reading of a 5xx and it inverts the caveat on pat-deserialisation-failure-in-application-log, which says a successful attack may raise no exception at all. For ViewState specifically, success does raise one, and it is distinguishable from the failure case by exception type. The cost is that status code alone is useless here -- a monitor alerting on 5xx volume drowns, while the successful exploit passes as one more error. Needs the application error log, which is a separate source from the access log and often is not forwarded.

how.logic: An antivirus exclusion path added for a directory the web server loads native modules from, written immediately before a module is dropped there. Observed here as PowerShell Add-MpPreference and direct registry writes naming System32\inetsrv and SysWOW64\inetsrv. Nothing legitimate excludes a server's own module directory from scanning, and because the exclusion has to precede the drop this is the earliest point in the chain at which the intrusion is catchable.
how.caveat: Some vendor installers and backup agents do write exclusions, so the marker that carries the fidelity is the path rather than the act: an exclusion for a web server module directory has no legitimate reading. Where an operations team genuinely maintains such an exclusion, this fires every time policy is reapplied, and the answer is to remove the exclusion rather than to tune the rule.

how.logic: Enumeration of site configuration with the server's own management tool, followed by a native module appearing in the module directory. Observed as appcmd list site /config /xml to find injection targets, then the BadIIS module dropped into the directory the previous block had just excluded from scanning.
how.caveat: appcmd is the supported administration tool and runs legitimately during deployment. Pair it with the module write rather than alerting on it alone, and expect legitimate bursts of both during a scheduled application release.

how.logic: A scheduled task named to resemble a browser updater, running at highest privilege on every logon, plus a new local account added to both Administrators and Remote Desktop Users. The pair is the persistence: the task restores the implant and the account restores the operator's own interactive access if the implant is removed.

fields.note: the observed name; treat the shape -- a task named for a product whose real updater is a service -- as the durable part

how.caveat: The literal task name is the weakest marker here and will be changed; the durable finding is a scheduled task impersonating an updater for software that does not update by scheduled task. Membership of both Administrators and Remote Desktop Users at creation is the stronger half, because legitimate provisioning rarely grants both in one action.

how.logic: Exploitation output POSTed to an attacker-controlled instance of a legitimate cloud configuration-management service, which the actor then polls to see which victims answered. There is no inbound connection and no persistent reverse shell to find: the sink absorbs the result and the operator collects it later, so the victim side shows only a short outbound POST to a service class that administrators genuinely use.

fields.note: the observed service; the shape is any configuration or secrets service the estate does not itself use
restrict to internet-facing web servers, which have no reason to POST to an external configuration service

how.caveat: Asynchronous by design, so there is no session to catch in progress and no beacon interval to find. The discriminator is the direction and the source: a web server posting its own hostname and user identity to an external configuration service is the finding, and an estate that legitimately uses such a service externally cannot separate the two on destination alone.

how.logic: Not a detection, and for a reason worth stating precisely: every AI artefact in this campaign was found on the actor's own management and command infrastructure, not in victim telemetry. Source-audit and pentest frameworks installed on the C2, generated exploitation guides, companion scripts and validation workflows. What reaches the victim is an ordinary one-day exploit. The consequence for a defender is about tempo rather than signature -- the interval between a disclosure being public and a competent, validated, documented exploitation workflow existing is now short enough that patch scheduling, not detection engineering, is the control this changes.

fields.note: the output is a revised patch-priority list for internet-facing services, not an alert

how.caveat: Nothing in this block is observable in a defender's own telemetry, and it must not be passed on as though it were. The reporting vendor's own confidence in the agentic-orchestration assessment is moderate to high, and the evidence is possession and installation of the tooling rather than observation of it driving a specific intrusion end to end.

where.title: UAT-10147: Chinese-speaking adversary integrates agentic AI into post-compromise operations

notes: Financially motivated rather than state-directed: search-engine fraud and data theft. The exploits are all public one-days -- CVE-2022-27925 in Zimbra, CVE-2021-23758 in AjaxPro, CVE-2021-29441 and CVE-2021-29442 in Nacos, CVE-2019-18935 in Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX, and a Linux privilege-escalation set including CVE-2022-0847, CVE-2022-0995 and CVE-2021-3156 -- so nothing here requires a novel vulnerability. A companion post on the same actor's SPECTRE implant was read this pass and was deferred rather than refused. One reverse-shell artefact carries a distinctive naming convention, DLLs named as ten digits, a dot, seven digits, dot dll.

who.versions_affected: arrayref 0.3.10, internment 0.8.7 and append-only-vec 0.1.9, all published from one compromised maintainer account within 23 minutes on 2026-08-20 and since deleted; the last safe versions are 0.3.9, 0.8.6 and 0.1.8. Two dropper crates carry the malicious build script, proc-macro1 and proc-macro-en, all versions of both. Exposure is decided by whether a build ran in the window, not by what is installed now.

what.summary: Three Rust crates republished from a compromised maintainer account with a typosquatted dependency whose build script downloads and runs a remote payload. The distinguishing property is when it fires: Cargo executes build scripts during compilation, so building any project whose lockfile resolved the bad version was sufficient, without the crate's code ever being called. arrayref carries roughly 245 million all-time downloads and sits under tiny-skia, winit, blake3 and much of the Solana and Ethereum tooling; one account puts it in over a third of all environments and three quarters of those where Rust is present. The upstream security team assesses the maintainer's machine or credentials as compromised.

how.logic: The build tool spawning a network client or interpreter during compilation, and that child writing an executable into a temporary directory and running it. Observed as a build script reconstructing a C2 address from Base64 fragments, fetching a payload chosen by operating system and architecture, writing it to /tmp/rust-setup on Unix or %TEMP%\rust-setup.ps1 on Windows, and executing it with the beacon address as an argument. The build then completes and the crate works normally, so nothing downstream fails.

fields.note: the parent is the build tool, which is what makes this compile-time rather than run-time

how.caveat: Build scripts are a supported feature used legitimately by every crate that compiles native code, so the script running is not the signal; the network fetch and the write-then-execute are. The named paths will change and are the weakest markers here. Note that this pattern's own caveat recommends disabling install scripts estate-wide as the cheaper control -- that advice is npm-specific and does not carry to Cargo, which has no stable equivalent, so for Rust the detection is not optional in the way it is for npm.

how.logic: A dependency added to a package whose dependency set has been stable for years. proc-macro1 was the first dependency arrayref had taken on in its ten-year history, which is a far stronger signal than the name itself: typosquat detection needs a candidate list and a string-distance threshold, whereas a package that has added no dependency since publication and suddenly adds one is anomalous on its own history with nothing to tune. Compare each upgrade's manifest against the version being replaced and gate on the delta rather than on the version number.
how.caveat: This is a check on the dependency graph rather than on a host, so it belongs in the build pipeline and not in the SIEM, and it needs the previous manifest to compare against -- an estate that resolves dependencies fresh on every build holds no baseline. It produces findings on legitimate releases too, because mature packages do occasionally take a first dependency; the value is that the population is small enough to read by hand, which is not true of any version-number-based rule.

how.logic: One implant carrying a persistence mechanism per platform, installed on command rather than at first execution: a Registry Run key on Windows, a LaunchAgent on macOS, a systemd user service on Linux. The user-scoped choice on all three is deliberate, since none of them requires administrative rights and all three survive logout.

fields.note: macOS half; the Linux equivalent is ~/.config/systemd/user
the parent being a build or developer tool is what separates this from ordinary software installing itself

how.caveat: All three locations are used constantly by legitimate software, so persistence alone is not the finding. What makes it one here is the ancestry -- persistence written by something descended from a build -- and persistence installed on command means a host can be compromised and beaconing while showing none of this.

how.logic: A fallback name generator producing ten .com domains every five days when the hardcoded C2 is unreachable. None of the generated names was registered at the time of reporting, which makes the detectable residue a burst of failed lookups on a fixed cadence rather than any successful connection. Group NXDOMAIN responses by host and look for a count that repeats on a period.

fields.note: count distinct failed names per host per day and look for a repeating cadence rather than a threshold

how.caveat: Unregistered domains mean there is nothing to block and nothing to sinkhole, and the generator only runs when the primary C2 fails -- so a host in normal contact with its operator produces none of this. It is a hunt over retained DNS rather than an alert, and it only pays where NXDOMAIN responses are retained at all, which many estates discard.

how.logic: Because the trigger is compilation, the population at risk is every machine that built an affected project inside the exposure window -- reported as 07:11 to 09:25 UTC on 2026-08-20 -- which includes ephemeral CI runners that no longer exist. The question is which builds ran in that window, not which lockfiles are dirty now. Search lockfiles across repositories for the withdrawn versions, and search the local package cache for the downloaded archives, since a lockfile updated since leaves the cache as the only remaining evidence.
how.caveat: The withdrawn versions are gone from the registry and the maliciously yanked releases have been restored, so a project resolving fresh today is clean and tells you nothing about what it built on the day. Ephemeral build agents are the gap this cannot close: they executed the payload and were destroyed, and for those the only remaining evidence is egress records inside the window. Note that removing one typosquat did not disarm the campaign -- proc-macro-en shipped the same build script -- so a search keyed to a single crate name under-reports.

where.title: Rust Supply Chain Attack on arrayref: Significant Overlap with DPRK Campaigns

notes: Attribution is overlap rather than assertion: a shared C2 endpoint path with the Mastra campaign that Microsoft attributes to DPRK, a shared TLS issuer string between the beacon address and a Mastra address, a victim-reported address appearing in Mandiant's analysis of the UNC1069 axios npm attack, and both campaigns preferring the same Hostwinds range. Recorded as medium confidence for that reason. The implant configuration is AES-128-GCM under a hardcoded key and its commands are authenticated with an embedded RSA-2048 private key, so possession of the sample yields the command channel. The campaign was staged rather than opportunistic: two further attacker-owned crates, arone and aronenao, were published on 2026-08-18 -- two days before the arrayref push -- and also executed code through a build script, and the typosquat proc-macro1 was published four minutes before arrayref took it as a dependency, by an account impersonating a well-known Rust maintainer. A fifth crate, tinymember, was deleted by association and carried no malicious code. NOTE ON ACCURACY: the source carries its own published correction stating that the browser routines only enumerate saved logins and do NOT retrieve encrypted credential material; this record follows the correction, and the impact list therefore does not claim credential_theft.

who.versions_affected: Not stated. The article names no affected version range and no fix, and frames the behaviour as a property of the trust assumption that the node is trusted rather than as a defect in a release.

what.summary: Researchers demonstrated that an attacker holding root on a Kubernetes node can move a process of their own into the control group of another pod so that the SPIRE agent, which identifies a caller by reading the cgroup path of the calling process, attributes the caller to the co-located workload and issues that workload's SVID to it over the local Workload API socket. The same fetch was refused with a permission denied response before the cgroup was forged and succeeded afterwards, returning a JWT SVID carrying the victim workload's SPIFFE ID. The researchers also released a tool, Spooffe, that repeats the step across every workload on a node in order to collect all of the identities present there, and state that they have not observed the technique used in the wild.

how.logic: Workload attestation reads the cgroup path of the calling process out of the proc filesystem and derives the pod identifier and container identifier from it, so the identity decision is only as good as the mapping from a process to a control group. The observable is one event: a process identifier written into the cgroup.procs file of a Kubernetes pod container scope by something that is not the container runtime, the kubelet or the init system, where the identifier written belongs to a process outside that container. Two acts precede it and are deliberately not part of this filter, because each is a separate event: the container runtime command line interface is used to map a workload name to its host process identifier, and the proc filesystem entry for that identifier is read to recover the workload's control group path. An author building a sequence rule has both from this sentence; a single event filter cannot carry them.

markers.note: the cgroup membership file of a pod container scope; the article writes a host process identifier into one of these. The article shows one node's layout, with slice and scope segments between kubepods and the leaf file, and the segments in between depend on how the node is configured, so confirm the shape on your own nodes before narrowing this.

how.caveat: The container runtime, the kubelet and the init system write to cgroup.procs continually as a matter of course, so the exclusion by process identity carried in the second marker is the whole fidelity of this block and has to be built for the estate before it is run. Node debugging and profiling tools that deliberately enter a container's control group produce the identical event and are not excluded by anything here, which is why this is a hunt and not an alert. The prerequisite is telemetry that records writes to cgroup pseudo-files at all, which is not universal; where it is absent the honest output is a collection gap rather than a rule. The separate mock directory in the article is a laboratory courtesy to avoid disturbing the victim workload, not tradecraft: the article states that writing the process identifier straight into the original cgroup path works just as well, so nothing here keys on a suspicious-looking directory name and a rule that does would miss the simpler case.

how.logic: The agent issues identity material to whatever connects to its Workload API Unix socket and passes attestation, and on success returns an X.509 SVID with its private key and the trust bundle, or a signed JWT SVID. The caller is therefore worth watching independently of whether attestation succeeded. The observable is the agent's Workload API socket being opened by a process that is not running inside a pod. In the demonstration the same caller was refused before the cgroup was forged and served afterwards, so where the agent records its own decisions a refusal followed by a success for one caller is the sharper form of the same signal; the article shows no such log line, so that form is described here and is not written as a marker.

markers.note: the article names /run/spire/sockets/agent.sock as the socket and hedges it as the typical path; it is configurable, so resolve the real path from the agent configuration rather than treating that literal as a field test

how.caveat: No value in the evidence vocabulary describes a Unix socket connection, so the first question is whether the sensor records one at all, and where it does not this block is a collection gap rather than a rule. Platform engineers troubleshoot workload identity from a node shell, which opens the same socket from outside a pod, so expect legitimate hits from named administrators and separate them by account rather than by binary; that allow list is not written here because the article supplies none. The refusal-then-success sequence needs the agent's own logs, which the article does not show.

how.logic: The researchers fetched the identity with the agent's own command line client, run from a node shell rather than from inside a pod. The observable is a single process execution whose command line asks the Workload API for a JWT SVID. The article shows exactly one such invocation and it is the JWT fetch; it describes the X.509 form as what the Workload API returns rather than as a subcommand it ran, so only the JWT form is written here.

markers.note: the researchers used the agent's own CLI as a convenient Workload API client; any client speaking the API is equivalent, so this marker catches the demonstration rather than the technique

how.caveat: Platform engineers troubleshoot workload identity from a node shell with exactly this command, so expect it from named administrators. This is a literal hunt for the tooling the article used and not a rule for the technique: the client is interchangeable, and an attacker writing a few lines against the same API leaves nothing here to match. The durable half of the same idea is the socket block above.

how.logic: Spooffe, the tool published with the research, automates the single-workload step: it scans the node for running workloads, discovers their cgroup paths, replicates each as a mock cgroup for its own process, and queries the local agent for the resulting identity, so that every identity present on the host is collected. The distinguishing shape is repetition by one caller rather than any single action, so count the distinct container control groups joined by one process inside a window. More than one is already abnormal for a genuine workload, which needs only its own; the working bound and the window have to be measured against how many workloads the node actually runs.
how.caveat: The bound of more than one is the arithmetic minimum of repetition, not a tuned threshold, and it is stated here only because a legitimate workload needs exactly one identity; measure the real bound and the window locally before shipping this. Node-level agents that inspect containers read many cgroup paths as part of their job, so the test has to be joining a control group rather than reading one, or the monitoring stack becomes the top result. This block counts the cgroup joins, which the same telemetry that records the first block also records; counting the identities handed back needs a different source and is the next block.

how.logic: The same repetition is visible from the issuer's side wherever the agent records what it hands out: count the distinct SPIFFE identifiers returned to one caller inside a window. A genuine workload asks for its own identity and no other, so more than one identifier returned to one caller is the signal. This is the same thesis as the previous block against a different telemetry source, and it is kept separate because an estate may hold one and not the other.
how.caveat: This block rests on telemetry the article never shows. It records no agent-side log line for an issued or a refused SVID, so whether the agent logs its issuance decisions, and in what form, has to be established before any of this is written; where it does not, this is a collection gap and not a rule. The confidence is medium for that reason: the harvesting is what the article demonstrates, the issuance record is an assumption about logging. The bound of more than one is the arithmetic minimum of repetition rather than a measured threshold, and the window has to be measured locally.

how.logic: Not an event detection. For each node, list the registration entries whose selector set is satisfied by any workload scheduled on it; that list is what a single root compromise of that node yields, because the agent holds the cached SVIDs for all of them and the attestation that separates them is decided by attributes the node controls. Rank nodes by the number of distinct identities obtainable on them and treat the top of that list as the blast radius of one host compromise. Entries selecting only on namespace and service account are satisfied by every pod sharing those two attributes, so one entry can cover many workloads; that sharpens the ranking and is not a condition, because every node is exposed to the extent that any selector it supplies is decided by it.

markers.expr: count_distinct(spiffe_id whose registration entry selector set is satisfied by a pod scheduled on the node) by node

how.caveat: This is a scheduling and registration fact rather than an attack, so it can be answered before there is an incident. The count is bounded at more than one because that is what co-location means; a node running a single identity is not interesting here, and the answer for every other node will not be zero. The two lists come from different places: which pods run on which node is asset state, while the registration entries are the SPIRE server's own configuration and are read from the server API, so the declared evidence type covers one side of the join and not the other. The article's own mitigations are node hardening, restricting root access, prohibiting privileged containers and host access, and minimising reliance on weak selectors; none of them is a detection and no detection substitutes for them. Nothing here says which selectors are strong, only that a selector set the node itself supplies is decided by the node.

where.title: The Machine With Many Faces: Post-Exploitation Identity Misuse in SPIFFE/SPIRE

notes: No in-the-wild activity. The publisher states plainly that it has not observed this technique exploited, so there is no campaign, no actor and no observed_start; the record exists for the detection logic and the inventory question, not for a timeline. Scope boundaries worth keeping: the demonstration ran in the researchers' own cluster with the k8s and unix workload attestor plugins enabled, and nothing here establishes how the docker, systemd or windows attestors behave. The tool released with the research is named Spooffe. The article names agent impersonation as a further capability of it and describes it only as examining whether an attacker could impersonate the agent to the server; no detection in this record covers that, and none should be written until something describes it. Node attestation, which establishes trust in the agent itself, is defined but not examined; the article states it is focusing on workload attestation. The mock cgroup directory in the worked example carries an obviously artificial name, which is a laboratory convenience rather than attacker tradecraft, and no marker in this record depends on it.
